And.name: Andromeda
And.description: Andromeda is bordered by Cassiopeia, Lacerta, Pegasus, Perseus, Pisces and Triangulum. It covers 722 square degrees, ranking 19th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alpheratz (α And) (2.07m).

babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, stars in Andromeda's region formed a constellation representing a fertility goddess called Anunitum or the Lady of the Heavens.
greek: Andromeda was the daughter of Queen Cassiopeia and King Cepheus of Aethiopia. When Cassiopeia boasted that Andromeda was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs were offended and petitioned Poseidon for revenge.

Poseidon sent the sea monster Cetus to destroy Aethiopia. The Oracle of Ammon told Cepheus that the only way to save his kingdom was to sacrifice Andromeda to the monster. She was chained to a rock by the sea.

The hero Perseus rescued Andromeda, either by turning Cetus to stone with Medusa's head or by slaying it with his sword. Perseus and Andromeda married and had nine children, founding the dynasty of Mycenae.

After her death, the goddess Athena placed Andromeda in the sky as a constellation to honor her. The neighboring constellations Perseus, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Cetus all represent characters from this myth.
history: Andromeda was one of Ptolemy's 48 original constellations in his 2nd-century Almagest. She is typically depicted with α Andromedae as her head, ο and λ as her chains, and δ, π, μ, β, and γ as her body and legs.

In 1787, German astronomer Johann Bode combined stars from Andromeda and Lacerta to form 'Honores Friderici' (Frederick's Glory) to honor King Frederick II of Prussia, but it quickly fell into disuse.
arab: Arab astronomers included a second constellation called 'al-Hut' (the fish) overlapping Andromeda's body, with the Andromeda Galaxy M31 marking the fish's nose.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, nine stars from Andromeda formed part of Kui (奎宿, Legs), representing either a walking person's foot or a wild boar.
Gamma Andromedae was called Tian Dajiangjun (天大将军), Heaven's Great General.
hindu: In Hindu legends, the figure Antarmada was also depicted chained to a rock, suggesting connections between Hindu and Greek astronomical traditions.
polynesian: In the Marshall Islands, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Triangulum, and Aries together form a constellation representing a porpoise, with Andromeda forming the body.

stars_text: α And (Alpheratz, 2.1m) is the brightest star, an A0p binary located 97 light-years away with 96 solar luminosities. It represents Andromeda's head and forms the Great Square of Pegasus with three stars in Pegasus.
β And (Mirach, 2.06m) is a red giant star 198 light-years away with a planet orbiting it. Its name comes from the Arabic "al-Maraqq" meaning "the loins."

γ And (Almach, 2.14m) is an orange giant at the southern tip of the constellation. It's a beautiful multiple star system with a yellow primary and blue-green secondary. William Herschel described it as resembling "a sun and its planet."
The Frederick's Glory asterism includes ι And (Rasalnaqa), κ And (Kaffalmusalsala), λ And (Udkadua), ο And (Alfarasalkamil), and ψ And, ranging from 86 to 988 light-years away.
υ And (Titawin, 4.1m) is notable for its planetary system with 4 confirmed planets. The system is only 44 light-years from Earth.
Ross 248 (HH Andromedae) is the ninth-closest star to Earth at just 10.3 light-years. It's a red dwarf variable star.
R And is a Mira-type variable star that ranges from magnitude 5.8 to 14.8 over a 409-day period, located 1,250 light-years away.
14 And (Veritate) is a yellow giant 251 light-years away with one confirmed exoplanet discovered in 2008.
deep_sky_objects: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31, NGC 224) is the most famous deep-sky object in this constellation. At 2.2-2.5 million light-years away, it's one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye.

M31 is the largest member of the Local Group and approximately 200,000 light-years in diameter—twice the size of the Milky Way. It appears as a hazy patch under dark skies and was first recorded by Arab astronomer al-Sufi in AD 964.
In about five billion years, the Andromeda and Milky Way galaxies may collide, triggering extensive new star formation.
In 1923, Edwin Hubble used Cepheid variables in M31 to prove it was far beyond the Milky Way, demonstrating that "nebulae" were actually distant galaxies—"island universes" in their own right.
M32 (NGC 221) and M110 (NGC 205) are two small elliptical galaxies that orbit M31. M32 appears superimposed on the larger galaxy, while M110 lies about 1° northwest of M31's core.
The Andromeda Galaxy has 15 satellite galaxies total. Nine lie in a single plane, suggesting a common origin.
NGC 891 (Caldwell 23) is a barred spiral galaxy seen edge-on, located 30 million light-years away near Almach. A dark dust lane runs down its center.
NGC 752 (Caldwell 28) is Andromeda's most celebrated open cluster at magnitude 5.7. It's a loosely scattered cluster in the Milky Way measuring 49 arcminutes across with about 60 visible stars.
NGC 7662 (Caldwell 22), the "Blue Snowball Nebula," is a planetary nebula 4,000 light-years away. It appears as a faint blue-green disk with magnitude 9.2 and is popular among amateur astronomers.
meteor_showers_detail: The Andromedids meteor shower radiates from Andromeda each November, peaking in mid-to-late November with a typical rate of fewer than 2 meteors per hour.
The shower is associated with Biela's Comet, which was destroyed in the 19th century. Andromedid meteors are very slow and sometimes appear as red fireballs.

The Andromedids produced two of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. The 1872 and 1885 outbursts had peak rates of 2 meteors per second (10,000 per hour), compared to falling rain by a Chinese astronomer.

On December 3-5, 2011, the Andromedids had their most active shower since 1885, with rates reaching 50 meteors per hour. The outburst was linked to material ejected when Biela's Comet passed near the Sun in 1649.

Ant.name: Antlia
Ant.description: Antlia is bordered by Hydra, Pyxis, Vela and Centaurus. It covers 239 square degrees, ranking 62nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Ant (4.25m). This faint constellation was created by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille to honor the air pump invented by Denis Papin.

history: French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first described the constellation in 1751-52 as 'la Machine Pneumatique' (the Pneumatic Machine), commemorating the air pump invented by physicist Denis Papin.

De Lacaille observed and catalogued almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope, devising fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. He named all but one in honor of instruments that symbolized the Age of Enlightenment.

Lacaille depicted Antlia as a single-cylinder vacuum pump used in Papin's initial experiments, while German astronomer Johann Bode chose the more advanced double-cylinder version. Lacaille Latinised the name to Antlia pneumatica on his 1763 chart.

English astronomer John Herschel proposed shrinking the name to one word in 1844. This was universally adopted. The International Astronomical Union adopted it as one of the 88 modern constellations in 1922.

Although visible to the Ancient Greeks, Antlia's stars were too faint to have been commonly recognized as a figurative object. The stars that now comprise Antlia are in a zone associated with the ancient constellation Argo Navis, the ship of the Argonauts.
chinese: Chinese astronomers incorporated Antlia's stars into two different constellations. Several stars in the southern part were a portion of 'Dong'ou', which represented an area in southern China.
Epsilon, Eta, and Theta Antliae were incorporated into the celestial temple, which also contained stars from modern Pyxis.

stars_text: α Ant (4.25m) is an orange giant of spectral type K4III, a suspected variable ranging between magnitudes 4.22 and 4.29. Located 320 light-years away, it shines with around 480-555 times the Sun's luminosity. It is most likely an aging star on its way to becoming a Mira variable, having converted all its core fuel into carbon.

ε Ant (4.5m) is an evolved orange giant of spectral type K3 IIIa, located 590 light-years away. It has swollen to 69 times the Sun's diameter with a luminosity around 1279 Suns. It is slightly variable.
ι Ant (4.6m) is an orange giant of spectral type K1 III, located 202 light-years distant.

δ Ant (5.6m) is a binary star 450 light-years distant. The primary is a blue-white main sequence star of spectral type B9.5V and magnitude 5.6, while the secondary is a yellow-white F9Ve star of magnitude 9.6.

ζ Ant is a wide optical double star. ζ¹ Ant is a true binary system composed of two white main sequence stars of magnitudes 6.20 and 7.01 separated by 8 arcseconds, located 410 light-years away. ζ² Ant is 386 light-years distant with magnitude 5.9.

S Ant is an eclipsing binary W Ursae Majoris variable that varies from magnitude 6.27 to 6.83 over 15.6 hours. The two stars share a common envelope and will eventually merge to form a single fast-spinning star. The system is thought to be around 5-6 billion years old.
T Ant is a yellow-white supergiant of spectral type F6Iab and Classical Cepheid variable ranging between magnitude 8.88 and 9.82 over 5.9 days.
U Ant is a red C-type carbon star and irregular variable that ranges between magnitudes 5.27 and 6.04. At 910 light-years distant, it is around 5819 times as luminous as the Sun.

HR 4049 (AG Ant) is an unusual hot variable aging star of spectral type B9.5Ib-II undergoing intense mass loss. It ranges between magnitudes 5.29 and 5.83 with a period of 429 days, located around 6000 light-years away. It is a unique variable that does not belong to any known class.
HD 93083 is an orange dwarf star of spectral type K3V that is smaller and cooler than the Sun. It has a Saturn-mass planet discovered in 2005 that orbits every 143 days at 0.477 AU.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 2997 is the brightest galaxy in Antlia at magnitude 10.6. It is a loosely wound face-on spiral galaxy of type Sc. Though nondescript in amateur telescopes, it presents bright clusters of young stars and many dark dust lanes in photographs.
The Antlia Dwarf is a 14.8m dwarf spheroidal galaxy discovered in 1997 that belongs to the Local Group of galaxies.
Antlia 2 is a very low surface brightness satellite galaxy of the Milky Way near Epsilon Antliae, discovered in 2018.

The Antlia Cluster (Abell S0636) is a cluster of galaxies in the Hydra-Centaurus Supercluster. It is the third nearest cluster to the Local Group after Virgo and Fornax, located 132-133 million light-years away.
The cluster contains around 234 galaxies total, with giant elliptical galaxies NGC 3268 and NGC 3258 as the main members of southern and northern subgroups.
The Antlia Supernova Remnant is one of the largest supernova remnants in the sky.

Aps.name: Apus
Aps.description: Apus is bordered by Triangulum Australe, Circinus, Musca, Chamaeleon, Octans, Pavo and Ara. It covers 206 square degrees, ranking 67th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Aps (3.83m). The constellation represents the bird-of-paradise and was created from observations of Dutch navigators.

history: Apus was one of twelve constellations published by Petrus Plancius from observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman who sailed on the first Dutch trading expedition (Eerste Schipvaart) to the East Indies.

It first appeared on a 35-cm diameter celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius. De Houtman included it in his 1603 southern star catalogue under the Dutch name 'De Paradijs Voghel' (The Bird of Paradise).
Plancius called the constellation Paradysvogel Apis Indica; 'Apis' (Latin for 'bee') is assumed to have been a typographical error for 'avis' ('bird').

The constellation's first known appearance in a celestial atlas was in German cartographer Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. Bayer called it Apis Indica while Johannes Kepler and Jakob Bartsch called it Apus or Avis Indica.

The name Apus is derived from Greek 'apous', meaning 'without feet'. This referred to the Western misconception that the bird-of-paradise had no feet, which arose because specimens arriving in Europe had their feet and wings removed.

Such specimens began to arrive in Europe in 1522 when survivors of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition brought them home. The constellation later lost some of its tail when Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille used those stars to establish Octans in the 1750s.

stars_text: α Aps (3.8m) is an orange giant of spectral type K3III located 430 light-years away. It spent much of its life as a blue-white B-type main sequence star before expanding, cooling and brightening. It has swollen to 48 times the Sun's diameter and shines with approximately 928 times the Sun's luminosity, with a surface temperature of 4312 K.
β Aps (4.2m) is an orange giant 149 light-years away. It is around 1.84 times as massive as the Sun, with a surface temperature of 4677 K.
γ Aps (3.87m) is a yellow giant of spectral type G8III located 150 light-years away. It is approximately 63 times as luminous as the Sun, with a surface temperature of 5279 K.

δ Aps is a double star with components 103 arcseconds apart, visible through binoculars. δ¹ Aps is a red giant star of spectral type M4III located 630 light-years away. It is a semiregular variable ranging from magnitude 4.66 to 4.87, with pulsation periods of 68.0, 94.9 and 101.7 days. δ² Aps is an orange giant of spectral type K3III, located 550 light-years away with magnitude 5.3.
ζ Aps (4.8m) is an orange giant of spectral type K1III with a surface temperature of 4649 K and a luminosity 133 times that of the Sun. It is 300 light-years distant.

θ Aps is a cool red giant of spectral type M7 III located 350 light-years distant. It shines with approximately 3879 times the Sun's luminosity and has a surface temperature of 3151 K. A semiregular variable, it varies by 0.56 magnitudes with a period of 119 days. It is losing mass through its stellar wind and has formed a bow shock as it moves through the galaxy.
The five brightest stars in Apus are all red-tinged, which is unusual among constellations. Beta, Gamma and Delta Apodis form a narrow triangle, with Alpha Apodis lying to the east.

HD 134606 is a yellow sunlike star of spectral type G6IV that has begun expanding off the main sequence. Three planets orbit it with periods of 12, 59.5 and 459 days, successively larger as they are further from the star.

HD 137388 is a K2IV star cooler than the Sun. Around 47% as luminous and 88% as massive as the Sun, it is thought to be around 7.4 billion years old. It has a planet 79 times Earth's mass that orbits every 330 days at 0.89 AU.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6101 is a globular cluster of magnitude 9.2 located around 50,000 light-years distant, which is around 160 light-years across. Around 13 billion years old, it contains a high concentration of massive bright stars known as blue stragglers, thought to result from two stars merging.
IC 4499 is a loose globular cluster in the medium-far galactic halo with magnitude 10.6.
IC 4633 is a very faint spiral galaxy surrounded by a vast amount of Milky Way line-of-sight integrated flux nebulae—large faint clouds thought to be lit by large numbers of stars.
The Milky Way covers much of the constellation's area, and the galaxies in Apus are generally faint.

Aql.name: Aquila
Aql.description: Aquila is bordered by Sagitta, Hercules, Ophiuchus, Serpens Cauda, Scutum, Sagittarius, Capricornus, Aquarius and Delphinus. It covers 652 square degrees, ranking 22nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Altair (α Aql) (0.76m), one of the three stars of the Summer Triangle.

greek: In Greco-Roman mythology, Aquila represents the eagle which held Zeus's/Jupiter's thunderbolts. The constellation is also associated with the eagle that kidnapped Ganymede, a son of one of the kings of Troy (associated with Aquarius), to Mount Olympus to serve as cup-bearer to the gods.
history: Aquila was one of the 48 constellations described by the second-century astronomer Ptolemy. It had been earlier mentioned by Eudoxus in the fourth century BC and Aratus in the third century BC.

It is now one of the 88 constellations defined by the International Astronomical Union. The constellation was also known as Vultur volans (the flying vulture) to the Romans, not to be confused with Vultur cadens which was their name for Lyra.
Ptolemy catalogued 19 stars jointly in this constellation and in the now obsolete constellation of Antinous, which was named in the reign of emperor Hadrian (AD 117-138).
The Greek Aquila is probably based on the Babylonian constellation of the Eagle.

stars_text: α Aql (Altair, 0.76m) is the brightest star in this constellation and one of the closest naked-eye stars to Earth at 17 light-years. Its name comes from Arabic 'al-nasr al-tair', meaning 'the flying eagle'. It is one of the three stars of the Summer Triangle, along with Vega and Deneb.
Altair is an A-type main-sequence star with 1.8 times the mass of the Sun and 11 times its luminosity. The star rotates quickly, giving it an oblate shape where it is flattened towards the poles.

β Aql (Alshain, 3.7m) is a yellow-hued star 45 light-years from Earth. Its name comes from Arabic 'shahin-i tarazu', meaning 'the balance'. The primary is a G-type subgiant of spectral type G9.5 IV with three times the Sun's radius and six times its luminosity. The secondary is a red dwarf.

γ Aql (Tarazed, 2.7m) is an orange-hued giant star 460 light-years from Earth. Its name, like Alshain, comes from Arabic for 'the balance'. It is the second-brightest star in the constellation and is an unconfirmed variable star.
ζ Aql (Okab, 3.0m) is a binary star 83 light-years from Earth. The primary is an A-type main sequence star, and the secondary has half the mass of the Sun.

η Aql is a yellow-white-hued supergiant star 1200 light-years from Earth. Among the brightest Cepheid variable stars, it ranges from magnitude 3.5 to 4.4 with a period of 7.2 days. The variability was originally observed by Edward Pigott in 1784. There are also two companion stars orbiting the supergiant.

FF Aql is a yellow-white-hued supergiant Cepheid variable 2500 light-years from Earth, ranging from magnitude 5.2 to 5.7 with a period of 4.5 days. It is a spectroscopic binary of spectral type F6Ib with at least three companion stars in the system.

R Aql is a red-hued giant star 690 light-years from Earth. It is a Mira variable with a minimum magnitude of 12.0, a maximum magnitude of 6.0, and a period around 9 months. It has a diameter of 400 solar diameters.

Aquila, which lies in the Milky Way, contains many rich starfields and has been the location of many novae. Nova Aquilae 1918 briefly shone brighter than Altair, reaching peak magnitude -0.5—the brightest nova recorded since the invention of the telescope.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6804 is a planetary nebula showing a small but bright ring.
NGC 6781 is a planetary nebula discovered by William Herschel in 1788 that bears some resemblance to the Owl Nebula in Ursa Major.
NGC 6751, also known as the Glowing Eye, is a planetary nebula estimated to be roughly 0.8 light-years in diameter.

NGC 6709 is a loose open cluster containing roughly 40 stars ranging in magnitude from 9 to 11. It is about 3000 light-years from Earth with an overall magnitude of 6.7. There are 305 confirmed member stars and one candidate red giant.
NGC 6755 is an open cluster of magnitude 7.5, made up of about a dozen stars with magnitudes 12-13. It is located approximately 8,060 light-years away.
NGC 6760 is a globular cluster of magnitude 9.1 with at least two pulsars discovered within it. It has a Shapley-Sawyer Concentration Class of IX.

W51 (3C400) is one of the largest stellar nurseries in the Milky Way. Located about 17,000 light-years away, W51 is about 350 light-years across. It's located in an area so thick with interstellar dust that it's opaque to visible light.

The Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, discovered in November 2013, is what may be the largest single mass concentration of galaxies in the Universe. It has a size of 10 billion light years and is the biggest and most massive structure in the Universe known.
meteor_showers_detail: The June Aquilids meteor shower radiates from Aquila in June.
The Epsilon Aquilids meteor shower also originates from this constellation.

Aqr.name: Aquarius
bordering: Pisces, Pegasus, Equuleus, Delphinus, Aquila, Capricornus, Piscis Austrinus, Sculptor, Cetus
Aqr.meteor_showers: March Aquariids, Eta Aquariids, Delta Aquariids, Iota Aquariids
Aqr.description: Aquarius is bordered by Pisces, Pegasus, Equuleus, Delphinus, Aquila, Capricornus, Piscis Austrinus, Sculptor, Cetus. It covers 980 square degrees, ranking 10th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is β Aqr (Sadalsuud) (2.91m). This large zodiacal constellation represents the water-bearer.

babylonian: In the Babylonian star catalogues, Aquarius was identified with the god Ea, who is commonly depicted holding an overflowing vase. The Babylonian star-figure appears from the Middle Bronze Age on boundary stones and cylinder seals.
It contained the winter solstice in the Early Bronze Age, with the name Mul.Apin ('The Mul Apin') in Babylonian astronomy meaning 'the constellation of the water-jar' or 'pitcher'.
greek: In Greek mythology, Aquarius is identified with Ganymede, the beautiful youth whom Zeus abducted to become the cup-bearer to the Olympian gods. Zeus was so enamored of Ganymede that he sent an eagle (represented by Aquila) to carry the boy to Mount Olympus.

Ganymede's name is connected to the Greek words for 'gladdening' and 'genitals', or 'rejoicing in virility'. He became the only mortal lover of Zeus among the gods. In Olympus, Ganymede became the cup-bearer of the gods, serving them nectar and ambrosia.

Another myth associates Aquarius with Deucalion, the son of Prometheus, who became king of Phthia after his father. When Zeus decided to end the Bronze Age with a great deluge, Deucalion built an ark and took his wife Pyrrha. The flood covered all habitable land, and they floated for nine days before landing on Mount Parnassus.

After the deluge, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulated the earth by throwing stones that transformed into people. Because of the association with the great flood, Aquarius became known as the 'Water Bearer' or 'Water Pourer'.
history: Aquarius was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy in his Almagest, and it remains one of the 88 modern constellations.
It was sometimes called Hydrochous (Ὑδροχόος), the 'water-pourer', in ancient Greek. The Latin translation 'Aquarius' has the same meaning.

stars_text: β Aqr (Sadalsuud, 2.91m) is the brightest star in Aquarius, a yellow supergiant of spectral type G0 Ib located 540 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic 'sa'd al-su'ūd', meaning 'luck of lucks'. It is approximately 2200 times as luminous as the Sun.

α Aqr (Sadalmelik, 2.96m) is a yellow supergiant of spectral type G2 Ib located 520 light-years away. Its name means 'luck of the king' in Arabic. Despite being Alpha, it is slightly fainter than Beta Aquarii.
δ Aqr (Skat, 3.27m) is an A-type main-sequence star 113 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic 'as-saq', meaning 'the shin' or 'leg'.
γ Aqr (Sadachbia, 3.84m) is a blue-white A-type star 158 light-years away. Its name means 'lucky star of hidden things' or 'lucky star of the tents' in Arabic.
ζ Aqr is a binary star system 92 light-years away. Both components are F-type main-sequence stars. The system has an orbital period of 587 years.

R Aqr is a symbiotic star consisting of a white dwarf and Mira-type variable red giant. It is located approximately 600 light-years away and is a strong source of radio waves. Material from the red giant is being accreted onto the white dwarf, causing periodic eruptions.
ψ¹ Aqr is a K-type orange giant star 148 light-years away with magnitude 4.24.
The star 91 Aquarii (ψ³ Aqr) is an orange giant of spectral type K0 III located 148 light-years away.

Gliese 876 is a red dwarf star with a system of four planets, including one planet that was one of the first discovered with a mass close to that of Earth. It is located about 15 light-years from Earth.
TRAPPIST-1 is not in Aquarius, but Gliese 876 represents Aquarius's planetary systems with terrestrial-mass planets.
deep_sky_objects: M2 (NGC 7089) is a globular cluster of magnitude 6.3, one of the largest and brightest globular clusters. It is located about 37,000 light-years from Earth and contains about 150,000 stars. It was discovered by Jean-Dominique Maraldi in 1746.
M72 (NGC 6981) is a globular cluster of magnitude 9.4, located about 53,000 light-years from Earth. It was discovered by Pierre Méchain in 1780.
M73 (NGC 6994) was once thought to be an open cluster but is now known to be an asterism of four stars. It has magnitude 9.0 and was discovered by Charles Messier in 1780.

NGC 7009, the Saturn Nebula, is a planetary nebula of magnitude 8.0 discovered by William Herschel in 1782. It is one of the brightest planetary nebulae in the sky and lies about 2,400 light-years away. It earned its name because it resembles Saturn through a telescope.

NGC 7293, the Helix Nebula, is one of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth at about 700 light-years away. With a diameter of about 2.5 light-years, it is one of the largest planetary nebulae. Though it has magnitude 7.6, its large size makes it difficult to see without a telescope.
NGC 7727 is a peculiar galaxy in Aquarius formed by the merger of two galaxies about 1 billion years ago. It is located about 76 million light-years away.
NGC 7184 is a barred spiral galaxy located approximately 114 million light-years from Earth.
The Atoms for Peace Galaxy (NGC 7252) is a peculiar elliptical galaxy formed by a galaxy merger. Its tidal tails give it a distinctive appearance. It is located about 220 million light-years away.
meteor_showers_detail: The March Aquariids meteor shower radiates from Aquarius in March.
The Eta Aquariids meteor shower, associated with Halley's Comet, radiates from Aquarius in early May. Peak rates can reach 30-40 meteors per hour in the Southern Hemisphere.
The Delta Aquariids occur in late July and early August, with two branches (Southern and Northern). The Southern Delta Aquariids are more prominent with rates of 15-20 meteors per hour.
The Iota Aquariids occur in early August and have moderate rates of about 7-8 meteors per hour.

Ara.name: Ara
Ara.description: Ara is bordered by Corona Australis, Scorpius, Norma, Triangulum Australe, Apus, Pavo, Telescopium. It covers 237 square degrees, ranking 63rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is β Ara (2.84m). This ancient southern constellation represents an altar.

greek: In Greek mythology, Ara represents the altar where the gods first made offerings and formed an alliance before their battle with the Titans. The gods swore their loyalty to Zeus at this altar before the great war.
After the Olympians' victory over the Titans, the altar was placed in the heavens to honor the alliance. Smoke from the altar rises southward to the Milky Way.

Another myth associates Ara with the altar of King Lycaon, who was punished by Zeus for trying to serve him human flesh. Zeus destroyed Lycaon's palace with a thunderbolt and transformed him into a wolf.
Some versions identify Ara as the altar of Dionysus, or the altar that Chiron the Centaur created to honor the gods.
history: Ara was one of the 48 constellations described by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and remains one of the 88 modern constellations defined by the International Astronomical Union.

It is one of the southernmost constellations described by Ptolemy and was probably based on earlier Mesopotamian traditions. The ancient Greeks saw it as representing an altar with smoke rising from it.
Ancient Greek observers positioned Ara upside down, with the altar's base pointing toward the south celestial pole. In this traditional depiction, the smoke (the Milky Way) rises northward.

stars_text: β Ara (Cervantes, 2.84m) is the brightest star in Ara, an orange giant or supergiant of spectral type K3 Ib-IIa located approximately 600 light-years away. It is about 8500 times as luminous as the Sun.

α Ara (Choo, 2.93m) is a blue-white Be star of spectral type B3Ve located 270 light-years away. It is slightly variable in brightness. The star is rotating rapidly and is surrounded by a circumstellar disk of gas.

γ Ara (3.34m) is a blue supergiant of spectral type B1 Ib located approximately 1110 light-years away. It is one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye, with a luminosity around 120,000 times that of the Sun.
δ Ara (3.62m) is a blue-white B-type main-sequence star of spectral type B8V located 187 light-years away. It is about 840 times as luminous as the Sun.
ζ Ara (3.13m) is an orange giant of spectral type K3 III located about 490 light-years from Earth. It shines with a luminosity around 3000 times that of the Sun.
η Ara (3.77m) is an orange giant of spectral type K5 III, located approximately 299 light-years from Earth.
R Ara is an Algol-type eclipsing binary that varies from magnitude 6.0 to 6.9 over a period of 4.43 days. The system is located about 298 light-years away.

μ Ara (Cervantes, 5.15m) is a G-type main-sequence star 50 light-years away with four confirmed exoplanets. The star is similar to the Sun in mass and temperature. The planetary system has been extensively studied and one planet orbits in the habitable zone.

Westerlund 1-26 (W26) is one of the largest known stars, a red supergiant or hypergiant located in the super star cluster Westerlund 1, about 11,500 light-years away in Ara. It has a radius estimated to be over 1500 times that of the Sun.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6193 is an open cluster of magnitude 5.2, located about 4,000 light-years away. It contains about 30 stars visible in small telescopes and is associated with the emission nebula NGC 6188.

NGC 6188 is an emission nebula located about 4,000 light-years away. It is illuminated by the hot, young stars of NGC 6193 and appears as a faint glow in photographs. Dark dust lanes create dramatic shapes within the nebula.

NGC 6397 is one of the two nearest globular clusters to Earth (along with M4 in Scorpius), at a distance of about 7,800 light-years. It has magnitude 5.6 and contains about 400,000 stars. Discovered by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1752, it is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye under good conditions.
The Stingray Nebula (Hen 1357) is the youngest known planetary nebula, having formed around 1985. It is located about 18,000 light-years away and is still evolving rapidly.

Westerlund 1 is a super star cluster located about 11,500 light-years away in Ara. It is one of the most massive young star clusters in the Milky Way, containing some of the largest and most luminous stars known.
The Ara OB1 association is a large stellar association containing many bright, young stars and several open clusters.
IC 4651 is an open cluster of magnitude 6.9, located about 3,000 light-years away. It contains about 80 stars and is approximately 1.7 billion years old.

Ari.name: Aries
Ari.meteor_showers: May Arietids, Autumn Arietids, Delta Arietids, Epsilon Arietids, Daytime Arietids, Aries-Triangulids
Ari.description: Aries is bordered by Perseus, Triangulum, Pisces, Cetus, Taurus. It covers 441 square degrees, ranking 39th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Ari (Hamal) (2.01m). This zodiacal constellation represents the ram with the golden fleece from Greek mythology.

babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, Aries was known as MUL LU.HUN.GA, 'The Agrarian Worker' or 'The Hired Man'. It marked the beginning of spring in the northern hemisphere.
The constellation was associated with Dumuzi the Shepherd, who later became identified with the ram. The stars of Aries were important in determining the beginning of the new year.
greek: In Greek mythology, Aries represents the ram whose fleece became the Golden Fleece. The story begins with King Athamas of Boeotia, who had two children by his first wife Nephele: a son Phrixus and a daughter Helle.

Athamas later took a second wife, Ino, who was jealous of the children and plotted to kill them. She roasted all the crop seeds so they would fail to grow. When the desperate people consulted an oracle, Ino bribed the messengers to say that Phrixus must be sacrificed to save the harvest.

Before the sacrifice could take place, Nephele sent a golden ram with a flying fleece to rescue her children. The ram carried both children on its back eastward toward Colchis. During the flight, Helle fell off and drowned in the strait now called the Hellespont in her honor.

Phrixus safely reached Colchis, where he sacrificed the ram to Zeus and gave its golden fleece to King Aeëtes, who hung it in a sacred grove guarded by a dragon. Zeus placed the ram among the stars as the constellation Aries.
The Golden Fleece became the object of the quest by Jason and the Argonauts. The story is one of the most famous adventures in Greek mythology.
history: Aries was one of the 48 constellations described by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and remains one of the 88 modern constellations.

It is a mid-sized constellation that is one of the twelve zodiacal constellations. In ancient times, the vernal equinox (first day of spring) was located in Aries. This point has since moved into Pisces due to precession of the equinoxes.
The 'First Point of Aries' still refers to the position of the vernal equinox, even though it is no longer in the constellation Aries. This point is used as the zero point for celestial longitude.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Aries formed parts of several constellations. The brightest stars were part of Lou (娄宿), the Bond, the 16th lunar mansion.
Other stars in Aries were incorporated into several Chinese asterisms representing various administrative and agricultural concepts.

stars_text: α Ari (Hamal, 2.01m) is the brightest star in Aries, an orange giant of spectral type K2 III Ca-1 located 66 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic 'ras al-hamal', meaning 'head of the ram'. It is about 91 times as luminous as the Sun and has 15 times the Sun's radius.

β Ari (Sheratan, 2.64m) is the second-brightest star, a white A-type main-sequence star of spectral type A5 V located 60 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic 'ash-sharatain', meaning 'the two signs', referring to the vernal equinox formerly located near this star.

γ Ari (Mesarthim, 3.86m) is a binary star system 164 light-years away. The name comes from Arabic meaning 'the fat ram'. Both components are white A-type main-sequence stars. The system was one of the first binary stars discovered by Robert Hooke in 1664.
δ Ari (Botein, 4.35m) is an orange giant of spectral type K2 III located 168 light-years away. Its name means 'the belly' in Arabic, referring to its position in the figure of the ram.
41 Ari (Bharani) is a triple star system 160 light-years away. The primary is a blue-white B-type main-sequence star of magnitude 3.6. It has two faint companions.
ε Ari is a binary star 293 light-years away. The primary is a white A-type star with magnitude 5.2.

Teegarden's Star is one of the nearest stars to the Solar System at about 12 light-years away. It is a dim red dwarf of magnitude 15.1, far too faint to see without a telescope. It has two confirmed exoplanets, both potentially habitable.
HIP 14810 is a G-type star 171 light-years away with three known exoplanets in its system.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 772 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 11.3, located about 130 million light-years away. It is a large unbarred spiral galaxy with a prominent spiral arm. A smaller companion galaxy, NGC 770, is visible nearby.
NGC 697 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 12.7, located about 200 million light-years away.
NGC 972 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 12.1, located about 70 million light-years away. It is classified as an intermediate spiral galaxy.
NGC 1156 is an irregular dwarf galaxy of magnitude 12.3, located about 25 million light-years away. It is a member of the M81 Group of galaxies.
The constellation contains several other faint galaxies, but no Messier objects. Most deep-sky objects in Aries are distant galaxies requiring moderate to large telescopes to observe.
meteor_showers_detail: The May Arietids are a daytime meteor shower that peaks in mid-May. They are not visible to the naked eye because they occur during daylight hours, but can be detected by radar.
The Autumn Arietids, also called the Delta Arietids, occur in mid-September to early October with peak rates of about 5 meteors per hour.
The Epsilon Arietids occur in early October with low rates.
The Daytime Arietids peak in early June and are one of the strongest daytime meteor showers, with rates possibly exceeding 60 meteors per hour. They are associated with asteroid 1566 Icarus.
The Aries-Triangulids are a minor shower in May with very low rates.

Aur.name: Auriga
Aur.meteor_showers: Alpha Aurigids, Delta Aurigids, Aurigids, Zeta Aurigids
Aur.description: Auriga is bordered by Camelopardalis, Perseus, Taurus, Gemini, Lynx. It covers 657 square degrees, ranking 21st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Aur (Capella) (0.08m), the sixth-brightest star in the night sky. This prominent northern constellation represents a charioteer.

greek: In Greek mythology, Auriga is usually identified with Erichthonius, the mythical king of Athens. He was the son of Hephaestus (in some versions, his father was Daedalus). Erichthonius was lame in both legs, so he invented the four-horse chariot to get around.

The invention so impressed Zeus that he placed Erichthonius among the stars as the constellation Auriga. The charioteer is usually depicted holding the reins in his right hand and a goat (Capella) with her two kids on his left arm.

Another myth identifies Auriga with Myrtilus, the charioteer of King Oenomaus. Myrtilus was bribed by Pelops to sabotage the king's chariot, leading to Oenomaus's death. Pelops later killed Myrtilus by throwing him into the sea, and his father Hermes placed him in the sky.

Yet another version identifies the constellation with Hippolytus, the son of Theseus. He was a skilled charioteer who was killed when his horses bolted after seeing a sea monster sent by Poseidon. He was revived by Asclepius and placed among the stars.
history: Auriga was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and remains one of the 88 modern constellations.
The constellation is home to Capella, the sixth-brightest star in the night sky and third-brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere, after Arcturus and Vega.
The asterism known as 'The Kids' consists of Epsilon, Zeta, and Eta Aurigae, representing the young goats held by the Charioteer. These stars are near Capella, the 'she-goat' star.
arab: Arab astronomers knew the constellation as Al Ayyuk, 'the rein-holder'. The name Capella comes from Latin meaning 'little she-goat'.

stars_text: α Aur (Capella, 0.08m) is the brightest star in Auriga and the sixth-brightest star in the night sky. Located 43 light-years away, it is actually a spectroscopic quadruple star system. The two brightest components are yellow giants of spectral types G1 III and G8 III that orbit each other every 104 days.

β Aur (Menkalinan, 1.90m) is a white subgiant of spectral type A2 IV located 81 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic 'mankib dhi-l-'inan', meaning 'shoulder of the rein-holder'. It is an eclipsing binary system with a period of 3.96 days.
θ Aur (2.65m) is a blue-white giant star of spectral type A0p located 173 light-years away. It is the second-brightest member of the Ae Aurigae moving group.
ι Aur (Hasseleh, 2.69m) is an orange giant of spectral type K3 II located 512 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic meaning 'the two forelegs of the ram'.

ε Aur (Almaaz, 2.92-3.83m) is one of the most mysterious stars in the sky. It is an eclipsing binary system with one of the longest orbital periods known—27.1 years. The primary is a yellow-white supergiant. The nature of the companion is uncertain, but it may be surrounded by a huge opaque disk that causes the eclipses.

ζ Aur (Saclateni, 3.75m) is an orange giant of spectral type K4 II that is part of an eclipsing binary system. The eclipses occur every 972 days (2.7 years) and last about 38 days. The companion is a blue dwarf star.
η Aur (Hoedus II, 3.18m) is a blue-white giant of spectral type B3 V located 243 light-years away. It is the fainter of 'The Kids'.
δ Aur (3.72m) is an orange giant of spectral type K0 III located 140 light-years away.
AE Aurigae is a blue runaway star of magnitude 6.0 that is illuminating the Flaming Star Nebula (IC 405). It was likely ejected from the Orion Nebula region about 2.5 million years ago.
AB Aurigae is a young Herbig Ae star surrounded by a protoplanetary disk. Observations have revealed a spiral structure in the disk that may indicate planet formation in progress.
deep_sky_objects: M36 (NGC 1960) is a bright open cluster of magnitude 6.3, located about 4,100 light-years away. It contains about 60 stars and is approximately 25 million years old. The cluster is easily visible in binoculars.

M37 (NGC 2099) is the brightest and richest of the three Messier open clusters in Auriga, with magnitude 6.2. Located about 4,500 light-years away, it contains about 500 stars and is approximately 300 million years old. It is one of the finest open clusters in the sky.

M38 (NGC 1912) is an open cluster of magnitude 7.4, located about 4,200 light-years away. It contains about 100 stars arranged in a cross or oblique bar pattern. The cluster is approximately 220 million years old.

IC 405, the Flaming Star Nebula, is an emission and reflection nebula of magnitude 6.0 surrounding the runaway star AE Aurigae. It is located about 1,500 light-years away and glows red from ionized hydrogen.

IC 410 is an emission nebula surrounding the open cluster NGC 1893. It is located about 12,000 light-years away and features the 'tadpole' structures—columns of dense gas being sculpted by radiation from hot young stars.
IC 417, the Spider Nebula, is an emission nebula surrounding the open cluster Stock 8, located about 10,000 light-years away.
The Tadpole Nebula (Simeis 147) is a supernova remnant in Auriga, though it extends into Taurus. It is one of the largest apparent supernova remnants in the sky.
NGC 2281 is an open cluster of magnitude 5.4, located about 1,500 light-years away. It contains about 30 stars.
meteor_showers_detail: The Alpha Aurigids are a meteor shower that peaks in late August and early September. They typically produce 5-10 meteors per hour, but occasional outbursts have produced rates of 30-40 per hour.
The Delta Aurigids peak in mid-October with low rates of about 2 meteors per hour.
The Aurigids peak in early September with typical rates of 5-10 meteors per hour. They are associated with Comet Kiess.
The Zeta Aurigids peak in December with very low rates. These are minor showers with limited activity.

Boo.name: Boötes
Boo.meteor_showers: Quadrantids, January Bootids, June Bootids, Bootids
Boo.description: Boötes is bordered by Draco, Ursa Major, Canes Venatici, Coma Berenices, Virgo, Serpens Caput, Corona Borealis, Hercules. It covers 907 square degrees, ranking 13th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Boo (Arcturus) (-0.05m), the fourth-brightest star in the night sky. This prominent northern constellation represents a herdsman or plowman.

greek: In Greek mythology, Boötes represents a plowman or herdsman driving the oxen of the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) around the celestial pole. The name Boötes comes from Greek meaning 'ox-driver' or 'plowman'.

One myth identifies Boötes with Arcas, the son of Zeus and Callisto. Callisto was transformed into a bear (Ursa Major) by the jealous Hera. When Arcas nearly killed his mother while hunting, Zeus placed them both in the sky to prevent the tragedy—Callisto as Ursa Major and Arcas as Boötes, eternally following his mother across the heavens.

Another legend identifies Boötes with Icarius, an Athenian who was taught viticulture (grape-growing and winemaking) by the god Dionysus. Icarius shared wine with shepherds who, unaccustomed to its effects, thought they had been poisoned and killed him. His daughter Erigone and dog Maera searched for him. When she found his body, Erigone hanged herself in grief. Zeus placed all three in the sky: Icarius as Boötes, Erigone as Virgo, and Maera as Canis Minor or Procyon.
Yet another version identifies Boötes with Philomenus, son of Demeter, who invented the plow and ox-drawn cart. As a reward, Demeter placed him among the stars.
history: Boötes was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy and remains one of the 88 modern constellations.

The constellation contains Arcturus, the fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere. Ancient cultures worldwide recognized Arcturus as a significant star.
The obsolete constellation Quadrans Muralis (the Mural Quadrant) was located between Boötes and Draco. Though the constellation is no longer recognized, the Quadrantid meteor shower retains its name.
polynesian: In Hawaiian astronomy, Arcturus was known as Hokule'a, 'Star of Gladness'. It was used for navigation by Polynesian voyagers crossing the Pacific Ocean.
arab: Arab astronomers called Boötes 'Al Awwa', 'the Barker', from dogs barking at the bear (Ursa Major). They also knew Arcturus as 'Al Simak al Ramih', 'the leg of the lance-bearer'.

stars_text: α Boo (Arcturus, -0.05m) is the brightest star in Boötes and the fourth-brightest star in the night sky. Located 37 light-years away, it is an orange giant of spectral type K0 III with about 170 times the Sun's luminosity. Its name comes from Greek meaning 'guardian of the bear'.

Arcturus is notable for its high proper motion—it moves across the sky faster than almost any other bright star. It is about 7.1 billion years old, older than the Sun, and is a member of the thick disk population of the Milky Way.

ε Boo (Izar or Pulcherrima, 2.35m) is a binary star 203 light-years away. The primary is an orange giant of spectral type K0 II-III, and the companion is a blue-white main-sequence star of spectral type A2V. The name Pulcherrima means 'most beautiful' in Latin, given by Friedrich Struve who admired the color contrast.

η Boo (Muphrid, 2.68m) is a yellow subgiant of spectral type G0 IV located 37 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic meaning 'the solitary one of the lancer'. It is evolving off the main sequence and will eventually become a red giant.
γ Boo (Seginus, 3.03m) is a white giant star of spectral type A7 III located 85 light-years away. It is a Delta Scuti variable star with very small amplitude variations.
ρ Boo is an orange giant of spectral type K3 III located 150 light-years away. It is a semiregular variable star that varies from magnitude 3.6 to 4.0.
δ Boo is a yellow giant of spectral type G8 III located 117 light-years away with magnitude 3.5. It forms a wide optical double with Pi Boötis.
β Boo (Nekkar, 3.49m) is a yellow giant of spectral type G8 IIIa located 225 light-years away. Its name comes from Arabic meaning 'the cattle driver'.

τ Boo (Tevel) is a yellow-white F-type main-sequence star 51 light-years away. It has a confirmed 'hot Jupiter' exoplanet that was one of the first extrasolar planets detected. The planet orbits extremely close to the star with a period of just 3.3 days.
44 Boo (i Boo, Asellus Primus) is a yellow-white G-type subgiant 42 light-years away. It has two confirmed exoplanets discovered by the radial velocity method.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 5248 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 10.2, located about 50 million light-years away. It is a grand design spiral galaxy with prominent, well-defined spiral arms.

NGC 5466 is a globular cluster of magnitude 9.1, located about 52,000 light-years away. It is a relatively loose and diffuse globular cluster that is easy to resolve into individual stars with moderate telescopes.
NGC 5548 is a Seyfert galaxy of magnitude 13.3, located about 250 million light-years away. It is an active galaxy with a supermassive black hole at its center that is actively accreting matter.
NGC 5676 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 10.9, located about 90 million light-years away. It is nearly edge-on to our line of sight.

The Boötes Void is one of the largest known voids in the universe, discovered in 1981. It is a roughly spherical region of space about 330 million light-years in diameter that contains very few galaxies—only about 60 galaxies compared to the 2,000 that would normally be expected.
NGC 5557 and NGC 5529 are two galaxies visible in the same telescope field. NGC 5557 is an elliptical galaxy and NGC 5529 is a spiral galaxy, both about 150 million light-years away.
meteor_showers_detail: The Quadrantids are one of the strongest annual meteor showers, peaking in early January with rates that can exceed 100 meteors per hour. The radiant point was originally in the obsolete constellation Quadrans Muralis, now part of Boötes. The parent body is asteroid 2003 EH1, possibly an extinct comet.
The January Bootids are a minor meteor shower in mid-January with very low rates, typically fewer than 2 meteors per hour.

The June Bootids are a variable meteor shower that peaks in late June. Normally very weak with only 1-2 meteors per hour, it has produced outbursts with rates of 100+ meteors per hour (1916, 1921, 1927, 1998). The shower is associated with Comet 7P/Pons-Winnecke.
The Bootids (or Theta Bootids) are a minor shower in May with very low rates.

Cae.name: Caelum
Cae.description: Caelum is bordered by Dorado, Pictor, Horologium, Eridanus, Lepus, and Columba. It covers 125 square degrees, ranking 81st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cae (4.45m).

history: Caelum was created as one of fourteen southern constellations by French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in the 18th century. It was originally named Caelum Sculptoris (Engraver's Chisel) in his 1763 catalogue.

Francis Baily shortened the name to Caelum, following John Herschel's suggestion. In Lacaille's original chart, it depicted a pair of engraver's tools: a standard burin and an échoppe tied by a ribbon.
Johann Elert Bode proposed the plural name Caela Scalptoris (the Engraver's Chisels), but this did not stick. The constellation came to be represented by a simple chisel.

stars_text: α Cae (4.45m) is the brightest star, a double star containing an F-type main-sequence star and a magnitude 12.5 red dwarf companion, located 66 light-years from Earth.
β Cae (5.05m) is an F-type subgiant star located 94 light-years away, slightly evolved from the main sequence.
δ Cae (5.05m) is a B-type subgiant located much farther at 700 light-years from Earth.

γ1 Cae (4.58m) is a double star with a red giant primary and magnitude 8.1 secondary, located 181 light-years away. The components are difficult to resolve with small telescopes due to their brightness difference and close separation.
X Cae (previously γ2 Cae) is a Delta Scuti variable star located 321 light-years away. It forms an optical double with γ1 Cae, though they are physically unrelated.
RV Cae is a pulsating red giant of spectral type M1III that varies between magnitudes 6.44 and 6.56.

RR Cae is an eclipsing binary 66 light-years away, consisting of a red dwarf and white dwarf. The system will become a cataclysmic variable in 9-20 billion years. Two planets are believed to orbit this system.

LHS 1678 is an astrometric binary 65 light-years away with a red dwarf primary hosting three Earth-sized exoplanets and a likely brown dwarf companion. It is just 3.3 light-years from α Cae, where Alpha would shine at magnitude -2.01, brighter than Sirius in our sky.
deep_sky_objects: Caelum is devoid of bright deep-sky objects due to its small size and location away from the galactic plane. It contains no Messier objects.
HE0450-2958 is an unusual Seyfert galaxy where a jet appeared to emanate from nothing. The host galaxy is now known to be a small galaxy obscured by light from the jet and a nearby starburst galaxy.
PN G243-37.1 is a 13th magnitude planetary nebula in the galactic halo, located 20,000 light-years below the Milky Way's disk. It is one of only a few planetary nebulae found in the halo.
The Carafe Group consists of galaxies NGC 1595, NGC 1598, and the Carafe Galaxy. The Carafe Galaxy is a Seyfert galaxy with a ring structure.

Cam.name: Camelopardalis
Cam.description: Camelopardalis is bordered by Draco, Ursa Minor, Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Perseus, Auriga, Lynx, and Ursa Major. It covers 757 square degrees, ranking 18th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is β Cam (4.03m).

history: Camelopardalis was created by Petrus Plancius in 1613. It first appeared in a globe designed by him and produced by Pieter van den Keere.
One year later, Jakob Bartsch featured it in his atlas. Johannes Hevelius depicted this constellation in his works, and it was referred to as Camelopardali Hevelii or Camelopard. Hevel.
In 1810, William Croswell carved out part of the constellation to form Sciurus Volans, the Flying Squirrel, but this was not adopted by later cartographers.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Camelopardalis are located within the Purple Forbidden Enclosure (紫微垣 Zǐ Wēi Yuán), a group of circumpolar stars.

stars_text: β Cam (4.03m) is the brightest star, a double star with components of magnitudes 4.0 and 8.6. The primary is a yellow-hued supergiant 1,000 light-years from Earth.
α Cam (4.3m) is a blue-hued supergiant over 6,000 light-years from Earth, one of the most distant stars easily visible to the naked eye.
11 Cam (5.2m) is a star 650 light-years away that appears very close to magnitude 6.1 12 Cam, but they are not a true double star with considerable separation.
Σ 1694 (Struve 1694, 32H Cam) is a binary star 300 light-years away. Both components have a blue-white hue; the primary is magnitude 5.4 and the secondary is magnitude 5.9.
CS Cam (4.21m) is the second brightest star, though it lacks a Bayer or Flamsteed designation. It is slightly variable.
Z Cam is the prototype of Z Camelopardalis variable stars. It varies from amateur telescope visibility to extremely faint and is frequently observed by the AAVSO.
U Cam, VZ Cam, and Mira variables T Cam, X Cam, and R Cam are other variable stars in the constellation.
RU Cam is one of the brighter Type II Cepheids visible in the night sky.
deep_sky_objects: Camelopardalis faces away from the galactic plane, making many distant galaxies visible within its borders.

NGC 2403 is a galaxy in the M81 group, located 12 million light-years from Earth with a redshift of 0.00043. It is classified between an elliptical and spiral galaxy with faint arms and a large central bulge. Discovered by William Herschel, it has magnitude 8.0 and spans 0.25°.

NGC 1502 is a magnitude 6.9 open cluster about 3,000 light-years away with about 45 bright members. It features a magnitude 7.0 double star at its center and is associated with Kemble's Cascade, a 2.5° chain of stars parallel to the Milky Way pointing toward Cassiopeia.
NGC 1501 is a planetary nebula located 1.4° south of NGC 1502.
Stock 23 (Pazmino's Cluster) is an open star cluster at the southern border between Camelopardalis and Cassiopeia.
IC 342 is one of the brightest galaxies in the IC 342/Maffei Group.
NGC 1569 is a magnitude 11.9 starburst dwarf irregular galaxy about 11 million light-years away.
NGC 2655 is a large lenticular galaxy with visual magnitude 10.1.
UGC 3697 is known as the Integral Sign Galaxy.

MS0735.6+7421 is a galaxy cluster with redshift 0.216, located 2.6 billion light-years away. It features two 600,000 light-year cavities caused by its central supermassive black hole. It is one of the largest and most distant examples of this phenomenon.

Tombaugh 5 is a dim open cluster with overall magnitude 8.4, located 5,800 light-years away. It is a Shapley class c and Trumpler class III 1 r cluster with more than 100 stars of 15th and 16th magnitude.
NGC 2146 is an 11th magnitude barred spiral starburst galaxy warped by interaction with a neighbor.
MACS0647-JD, one of the possible candidates for the farthest known galaxies in the universe (z=10.7), is in Camelopardalis.
meteor_showers_detail: The May Camelopardalids meteor shower from comet 209P/LINEAR has a radiant in Camelopardalis.

Cnc.name: Cancer
Cnc.description: Cancer is bordered by Gemini, Lynx, Leo Minor, Leo, Hydra, and Canis Minor. It covers 506 square degrees, ranking 31st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is β Cnc (Tarf) (3.53m). Under city skies, Cancer is invisible to the naked eye.

greek: In Greek mythology, Cancer represents the crab that appeared while Heracles fought the many-headed Lernaean Hydra. The crab bit Heracles in the foot during the battle.
Hercules slew the crab after it attacked him. Afterwards, the goddess Hera, an enemy of Heracles, placed the crab among the stars as a reward for its service.
history: Cancer was first recorded by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE in The Mathematical Syntaxis (Almagest), under the Greek name Καρκίνος (Karkinos).

Cancer was often considered the 'Dark Sign' and described as 'black and without eyes' due to its faintness. Dante alluded to this in Paradiso, mentioning it being visible for the whole night when it culminated at midnight in Northern Hemisphere winter.

Cancer was the backdrop to the Sun's most northerly position (summer solstice) in ancient times. The Tropic of Cancer is named after this, though precession has shifted the solstice position to Taurus.

The close conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in 1563, observed by Tycho Brahe, occurred in Cancer not far from Praesepe. This observation led Brahe to note the inaccuracy of existing ephemerides and begin his own astronomical measurements.
babylonian: In Babylonia, the constellation was known as MUL.AL.LUL, a name that can refer to both a crab and a snapping turtle. Boundary stones show images of turtles or tortoises, believed to represent Cancer.
There appears to be a strong connection between the Babylonian constellation and ideas of death and passage to the underworld, which may be the origin of these ideas in later Greek myths.
egyptian: In Egyptian records from about 2000 BC, it was described as Scarabaeus (Scarab), the sacred emblem of immortality.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Cancer lie within the Vermilion Bird of the South (南方朱雀, Nán Fāng Zhū Què).

stars_text: β Cnc (Tarf or Altarf, 3.5m) is the brightest star, an orange giant binary 290 light-years away that varies slightly from magnitude 3.53. It has expanded to 50 times the Sun's diameter and shines with 660 times its luminosity. A faint magnitude 14 red dwarf companion orbits it every 76,000 years.

δ Cnc (Asellus Australis, 3.9m) is an orange giant 131 light-years away with radius 11 times and luminosity 53 times that of the Sun. Its name means 'southern donkey' and it holds the record for the longest star name: Arkushanangarushashutu, from ancient Babylonian meaning 'the southeast star in the Crab.'
γ Cnc (Asellus Borealis, 4.67m) is a white-hued A-type subgiant 181 light-years away. Its name means 'northern donkey.' It is 35 times as luminous as the Sun.

ι Cnc (4.0m) is a wide double star with a yellow G-type bright giant primary 330 light-years away, and a white magnitude 6.57 secondary. Despite different measured distances, they share common proper motion and appear to be a natural binary system.

α Cnc (Acubens, 4.26m) is a quadruple star system 181 light-years away. The name means 'the claw.' The primary is actually two white main sequence stars 5.3 AU apart, with a secondary pair of red dwarfs 600 AU from the main pair.

ζ Cnc (Tegmine, 5.4m) is a multiple star system 82 light-years away containing at least four stars. The name means 'the shell.' The two brightest form a binary with 1,100-year orbital period; the brighter component is itself a binary pair with 59.6-year period.

55 Cnc (Rho1 Cnc or Copernicus) is a binary star 41 light-years away consisting of a yellow dwarf and smaller red dwarf. Five planets orbit the primary star. It is a rare 'super metal-rich' star ranked 63rd on NASA's Terrestrial Planet Finder target list.
YBP 1194 is a sunlike star in open cluster M67 that has three planets.
deep_sky_objects: Praesepe (M44, the Beehive Cluster) is an open cluster 590 light-years away, one of the nearest to the Solar System. It contains about 50 stars, the brightest being magnitude 6.3 Epsilon Cancri. The cluster spans 1.5 square degrees, three times the size of the full Moon.

Ptolemy described the Beehive as 'the nebulous mass in the breast of Cancer.' Galileo observed 40 stars in the cluster in 1609 with his telescope. Today, about 1,010 high-probability members are known, most (68%) being red dwarfs.

The Greeks and Romans identified the Beehive as a manger from which two donkeys (Asellus Borealis and Asellus Australis) were eating. The stars represent donkeys that Dionysus and his tutor Silenus rode in the war against the Titans.
Ancient Chinese interpreted the Beehive as a ghost or demon riding in a carriage, calling it 'a cloud of pollen blown from under willow catkins.'
M67 is a smaller, denser open cluster 2,600 light-years away. It spans 0.5 square degrees (the size of the full Moon) and contains approximately 200 stars, the brightest being 10th magnitude.
QSO J0842+1835 is a quasar used to measure the speed of gravity in a VLBI experiment by Edward Fomalont and Sergei Kopeikin in September 2002.

OJ 287 is a BL Lacertae object 3.5 billion light-years away that has produced quasi-periodic optical outbursts for approximately 120 years, first apparent on photographic plates from 1891. Its central supermassive black hole is among the largest known, with a mass of 18 billion solar masses.
meteor_showers_detail: The Delta Cancrids meteor shower radiates from Cancer.

CVn.name: Canes Venatici
CVn.pronunciation: /ˈkeɪniːz vɪˈnætɪsaɪ/ KAY-neez vin-AT-iss-eye, genitive /ˈkeɪnəm vɪnætɪˈkɔːrəm/ KAY-nəm vin-AT-ih-KOR-əm
CVn.description: Canes Venatici is bordered by Ursa Major to the north and west, Coma Berenices to the south, and Boötes to the east. It covers 465 square degrees, ranking 38th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Cor Caroli (α CVn) (2.90m).

history: In classical times, the stars of Canes Venatici were listed by Ptolemy as unfigured stars below Ursa Major in his star catalogue.

In medieval times, the identification as dogs arose through a mistranslation. Boötes's stars were described as representing a club (Greek: κολλοροβος, kollorobos). When Ptolemy's Almagest was translated from Greek to Arabic, Hunayn ibn Ishaq rendered it as العصا ذات الكُلاب (al-'aşā dhāt al-kullāb), meaning 'the staff having a hook.'

When translated from Arabic to Latin, Gerard of Cremona mistook كُلاب kullāb ('hook') for كِلاب kilāb ('dogs'), writing Hastile habens canes ('spearshaft-having dogs'). In 1533, Peter Apian depicted Boötes with two dogs.

Johannes Hevelius made these dogs a separate constellation in 1687, naming them Asterion (northern dog, meaning 'little star') and Chara (southern dog, meaning 'joy' in Greek). Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář later assigned Asterion to β CVn and Chara to α CVn.
Although the IAU dropped several medieval and Renaissance constellations in 1930, Canes Venatici survived to become one of the 88 designated constellations.

stars_text: α CVn (Cor Caroli, 2.9m) is the brightest star, named by Sir Charles Scarborough in memory of King Charles I. It is a wide double star with magnitude 2.9 primary and magnitude 5.6 secondary, located 110 light-years away. The primary has an unusually strong variable magnetic field.

β CVn (Chara, 4.25m) is a yellow main sequence star 27 light-years from Earth. Its name comes from the word for 'joy.' It has been listed as an astrobiologically interesting star due to its proximity and similarity to the Sun, though no exoplanets have been discovered.
Y CVn (La Superba) is a semiregular variable carbon star that varies between magnitudes 5.0 and 6.5 over a period of about 158 days. It is deep red in color with spectral type C54J(N3).

AM CVn is a very blue magnitude 14 star that is the prototype of a special class of cataclysmic variables where the companion is a white dwarf rather than a main sequence star. It is 143 parsecs distant.
RS CVn is the prototype of a special class of binary stars with chromospherically active and optically variable components.
R CVn is a Mira variable that ranges between magnitudes 6.5 and 12.9 over a period of approximately 329 days.
deep_sky_objects: The Whirlpool Galaxy (M51, NGC 5194) and NGC 5195 are the most significant objects. M51 was the first galaxy recognized as having spiral structure, observed by Lord Rosse in 1845. It is a face-on spiral galaxy 37 million light-years away with many star-forming regions coloring its arms pink and blue.
NGC 5195 is M51's smaller companion, a barred spiral galaxy with few star-forming regions appearing yellow. It is passing behind M51 and may be causing the larger galaxy's prodigious star formation.
M63 (the Sunflower Galaxy, NGC 5055) is a spiral galaxy with integrated magnitude 9.0, named for its appearance in large amateur telescopes.

M94 (NGC 4736) is a small face-on spiral galaxy with magnitude 8.0, about 15 million light-years away. It has very tight spiral arms and a bright core, with a ring of new stars 7,000 light-years in diameter surrounding the core. The outskirts are incredibly luminous in ultraviolet.
M106 (NGC 4258) is another notable spiral galaxy.
NGC 4631 is a barred spiral galaxy and one of the largest and brightest edge-on galaxies in the sky.

M3 (NGC 5272) is a globular cluster 32,000 light-years away. At magnitude 6.3 and 18' in diameter, it is bright enough to be seen with binoculars and can even be seen with the naked eye under particularly dark skies.

The Giant Void, an extremely large void containing very few galaxies, is in the vicinity of this constellation. It is the second largest void ever discovered, 1,200 times the volume of expected typical voids. Its center is approximately 1.5 billion light-years away.

Ton 618 is a hyperluminous quasar and blazar near the border with Coma Berenices. It possesses a black hole with a mass 66 billion times that of the Sun, making it one of the most massive black holes ever measured.
meteor_showers_detail: The Canes Venaticids meteor shower radiates from Canes Venatici.

CMa.name: Canis Major
CMa.pronunciation: /ˌkeɪnɪs ˈmeɪdʒər/ KAY-niss MAY-jər, genitive /ˌkeɪnɪs məˈdʒɔːrəs/ KAY-niss mə-JOR-iss
CMa.description: Canis Major is bordered by Monoceros to the north, Puppis to the east and southeast, Columba to the southwest, and Lepus to the west. It covers 380 square degrees, ranking 43rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Sirius (α CMa) (−1.46m), the brightest star in the night sky.

babylonian: In ancient Mesopotamia, Sirius was named KAK.SI.SA2 by the Babylonians and seen as an arrow aiming towards Orion. The southern stars of Canis Major and part of Puppis were viewed as a bow named BAN.

In MUL.APIN, the arrow (Sirius) was linked with the warrior Ninurta, and the bow with Ishtar, daughter of Enlil. Ninurta was linked to Marduk, who was said to have slain the ocean goddess Tiamat with a great bow.
greek: In Greek mythology, Canis Major represented Laelaps, a gift from Zeus to Europa; or the hound of Procris, Diana's nymph; or the one given by Aurora to Cephalus, so famed for its speed that Zeus elevated it to the sky.
It was also considered one of Orion's hunting dogs, pursuing Lepus the Hare or helping Orion fight Taurus the Bull. Aratos, Homer, and Hesiod refer to it this way.
The ancient Greeks referred to only one dog, but by Roman times, Canis Minor appears as Orion's second dog.
roman: Roman myth refers to Canis Major as Custos Europae, the dog guarding Europa but failing to prevent her abduction by Jupiter in the form of a bull, and as Janitor Lethaeus, 'the watchdog.'
arab: In medieval Arab astronomy, the constellation became al-Kalb al-Akbar, 'the Greater Dog,' transcribed as Alcheleb Alachbar. Islamic scholar Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī referred to Orion as Kalb al-Jabbār, 'the Dog of the Giant.'
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, Canis Major is located in the Vermilion Bird (南方朱雀; Nán Fāng Zhū Què). The stars were classified in several asterisms.
The Military Market (軍市; Jūnshì) was a circular pattern containing Nu3, Beta, Xi1, Xi2, and some stars from Lepus. The Wild Cockerel (野雞; Yějī) was at its center.
Sirius was Tiānláng (天狼), the Celestial Wolf, denoting invasion and plunder.
Húshǐ (弧矢) was the celestial Bow and Arrow asterism, containing Delta, Epsilon, Eta, Kappa Canis Majoris and Delta Velorum.
polynesian: The Māori people recognized Te Huinga-o-Rehua (The Assembly of Rehua), a constellation that included both Canis Minor and Canis Major with surrounding stars. They called Sirius Rehua and Takarua.
The Tuamotu people called Canis Major Muihanga-hetika-o-Takurua, 'the abiding assemblage of Takarua.'
The Tharumba people of the Shoalhaven River saw three stars as Wunbula (Bat) and his two wives. All three were placed in the sky as the constellation Munowra.
To the Boorong people of Victoria, Sigma Canis Majoris was Unurgunite (now its official name), with Delta and Epsilon as his two wives.

stars_text: Sirius (α CMa, -1.46m) is the brightest star in the night sky and one of the closest at 8.6 light-years. Its name comes from the Greek word for 'scorching.' It is a binary star; its companion Sirius B is a magnitude 8.4 white dwarf, 10,000 times fainter. They orbit every 50 years.
β CMa (Mirzam or Murzim, 2.0m) is a blue-white Beta Cephei variable 500 light-years away. Its name means 'the announcer,' referring to its position rising before Sirius.
γ CMa (Muliphein, 4.12m) is a blue-white bright giant of spectral type B8IIe located 441 light-years away.

ε CMa (Adhara, 1.5m) is the second-brightest star in Canis Major and the 23rd-brightest in the sky. It is a blue-white supergiant about 404 light-years away and one of the brightest known extreme ultraviolet sources. It is a binary star; the secondary is magnitude 7.4. About 4.7 million years ago, it shone at magnitude -3.99.

δ CMa (Wezen, 1.84m) is a yellow-white supergiant 1,605 light-years away. Its name means 'the weight.' It is 17 times as massive and 50,000 times as luminous as the Sun. Its diameter is 200 times that of the Sun; if placed at the Solar System's center, it would extend to Earth's orbit.
σ CMa (Unurgunite, 3.43-3.51m) is a red supergiant that varies irregularly, nestled between Adhara and Wezen. Its name comes from the Boorong and Wotjobaluk people.
η CMa (Aludra, 2.38-2.48m) is a blue-white supergiant with luminosity 176,000 times the Sun and diameter 80 times solar. It is an Alpha Cygni variable 1,120 light-years away.

VY CMa is a remote red hypergiant about 3,800 light-years away. It is one of the largest stars known with a radius varying from 1,420 to 2,200 times the Sun's, and luminosity around 300,000 times greater. It is surrounded by a red reflection nebula made from material expelled by strong stellar winds.
deep_sky_objects: The Milky Way band goes through Canis Major with only patchy obscurement. It is bright in the northeastern corner and in a triangular area between Adhara, Wezen, and Aludra.

M41 (NGC 2287) is the only Messier object, an open cluster with combined magnitude 4.5, located 2,300 light-years away. It is 4 degrees south of Sirius and contains contrasting blue, yellow, and orange stars covering an area the size of the full Moon (25 light-years in diameter).

NGC 2360 (Caroline's Cluster) is an open cluster discovered by Caroline Herschel, located 3.5 degrees west of Muliphein with magnitude 7.2. About 15 light-years in diameter and 3,700 light-years away, it is about 2.2 billion years old.

NGC 2362 is a small, compact open cluster 5,200 light-years away containing about 60 stars. Tau Canis Majoris is its brightest member. Located 3 degrees northeast of Wezen, it covers about 12 light-years in diameter. Its member stars are only a few million years old.

NGC 2359 (Thor's Helmet or the Duck Nebula) is a relatively bright emission nebula with magnitude 10, located 10,000 light-years away. The nebula is shaped by HD 56925, an unstable Wolf-Rayet star embedded within it.
The Canis Major Dwarf, announced in 2003 as the closest satellite galaxy to Earth, remains debated. It may represent a disrupted dwarf galaxy or a variation in the Milky Way's disk populations.

NGC 2207 and IC 2163 are a pair of face-on interacting spiral galaxies 125 million light-years away. About 40 million years ago they had a close encounter. IC 2163 will eventually be incorporated into NGC 2207. Four supernovae have been observed in NGC 2207.

CMi.name: Canis Minor
CMi.pronunciation: /ˌkeɪnɪs ˈmaɪnər/ KAY-niss MY-nər, genitive /ˌkeɪnɪs mɪˈnɔːrɪs/ KAY-niss min-OR-iss
CMi.description: Canis Minor is bordered by Monoceros to the south, Gemini to the north, Cancer to the northeast, and Hydra to the east. It covers 183 square degrees, ranking 71st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Procyon (α CMi) (0.34m).

babylonian: Canis Minor originates from ancient Mesopotamia. Procyon and Gomeisa were called MASH.TAB.BA or 'twins' in the Three Stars Each tablets, dating to around 1100 BC.
In MUL.APIN, this name also applied to other star pairs. The meaning evolved to represent twin deities Lulal and Latarak, opposite from Papsukkal, the True Shepherd of Heaven.
Canis Minor was given the name DAR.LUGAL, representing a rooster. The constellation was then called tarlugallu in Akkadian astronomy.
greek: Canis Minor was one of Ptolemy's original 48 constellations in the 2nd-century Almagest. Ptolemy identified only two stars, making depiction impossible.
The Ancient Greeks called it προκυων/Procyon, 'coming before the dog,' transliterated to Latin as Antecanis or Praecanis.

In Greek mythology, Canis Minor was sometimes connected with the Teumessian Fox, turned into stone with its hunter Laelaps by Zeus, who placed them in heaven as Canis Major (Laelaps) and Canis Minor (Teumessian Fox).

Hyginus linked it with Maera, a dog owned by Icarius of Athens. Upon discovering Icarius's death, the dog and his daughter Erigone took their lives. All three were placed in the sky—Erigone as Virgo, Icarius as Boötes, and the dog along the 'banks' of the Milky Way where he would never suffer from thirst.
arab: Medieval Arabic astronomers maintained the depiction as a dog (al-Kalb al-Asghar). Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi included a diagram with a canine figure in his Book of the Fixed Stars.
Procyon was called ash-Shi'ra ash-Shamiya, the 'Syrian Sirius,' and Gomeisa was called ash-Shira al-Ghamisa, the Sirius with bleary eyes.
egyptian: The ancient Egyptians thought of this constellation as Anubis, the jackal god.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, Procyon, Gomeisa, and Eta Canis Minoris form Nánhé, the Southern River. With its counterpart Beihe (Castor and Pollux), Nánhé was associated with a gate or sentry.
With Zeta, 8 Cancri, 6 CMi, and 11 CMi, they formed Shuiwei ('water level'), representing an official who managed floodwaters.
polynesian: Polynesian peoples often did not recognize Canis Minor as a constellation but saw Procyon as significant. In the Tuamotu Archipelago it was Hiro ('twist as a thread of coconut fiber') and Kopu-nui-o-Hiro ('great paunch of Hiro').
In the Society Islands, Procyon was called Ana-tahua-vahine-o-toa-te-manava, 'the pillar for elocution.'

The Wardaman people of Australia gave Procyon and Gomeisa the names Magum and Gurumana, describing them as humans transformed into gum trees in the Dreaming who could speak with a human voice by rustling their leaves.

stars_text: Procyon (α CMi, 0.34m) is the eighth-brightest star in the night sky and one of the closest at 11.4 light-years. Its name means 'before the dog,' as it rises an hour before Sirius. It is a binary system with a yellow-white F5 IV-V main-sequence star (Procyon A) and magnitude 10.7 white dwarf companion (Procyon B) that orbits every 41 years.

Gomeisa (β CMi, 2.89m) is the second-brightest star, a blue-white main-sequence star 160 light-years away. It is 250 times as luminous and three times as massive as the Sun. It is classified as a shell star (Gamma Cassiopeiae variable) surrounded by a disk of gas that emits radiation.

γ CMi (4.34m) is an orange K-type giant 318 light-years away. It is a multiple system with spectroscopic binary Gamma A and three optical companions. The two components of Gamma A orbit every 389.2 days in an eccentric orbit.
ε CMi (4.99m) is a yellow bright giant 730-810 light-years away with 13 times the Sun's diameter and 750 times its luminosity.
η CMi (5.24m) is a giant of spectral class F0III with a yellowish hue and a faint magnitude 11.1 companion 4 arcseconds away that takes 5,000 years to orbit.

HD 66141 (4.39m) is an orange giant 222 light-years away, 6.8 billion years old with diameter 22 times the Sun's. It is orbited by planet HD 66141b, which has a mass 6 times Jupiter and a 480-day period. It was mistakenly catalogued as 13 Puppis.
YZ CMi is a red dwarf flare star of magnitude 11.2, about three times Jupiter's size and 20 light-years away. It emits unpredictable outbursts of energy.
Luyten's Star (GJ 273) is a red dwarf of spectral type M3.5V with magnitude 9.9, located just 12.39 light-years away.
deep_sky_objects: The Milky Way passes through much of Canis Minor, yet it has few deep-sky objects.
NGC 2459 is a group of five 13th-14th magnitude stars that appear close together but are unrelated.
NGC 2394 is a collection of fifteen unrelated stars of ninth magnitude and fainter.
NGC 2508 is a lenticular galaxy of 13th magnitude, estimated at 205 million light-years distant with a diameter of 80,000 light-years.

NGC 2402 is actually a pair of near-adjacent galaxies that appear to be interacting. The elliptical and spiral galaxy are 14th and 15th magnitudes, thought to be approximately 245 million light-years distant, each measuring 55,000 light-years in diameter.
meteor_showers_detail: The 11 Canis-Minorids (Beta Canis Minorids) are a meteor shower discovered in 1964 by Keith Hindley that arise near 11 Canis Minoris. They last from December 4-15, peaking over December 10-11.
A proposed link to comet D/1917 F1 Mellish has been refuted as the number of orbits analyzed was low and trajectories too disparate to confirm.

Cap.name: Capricornus
Cap.meteor_showers: Alpha Capricornids, Chi Capricornids, Sigma Capricornids, Tau Capricornids, Capricornids-Sagittariids
Cap.description: Capricornus is bordered by Aquarius, Aquila, Sagittarius, Microscopium, and Piscis Austrinus. It covers 414 square degrees, ranking 40th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is δ Cap (Deneb Algedi) (2.85m).
