babylonian: Despite its faintness, Capricornus has one of the oldest mythological associations. The constellation was first attested in depictions on a cylinder-seal from around the 21st century BCE and was explicitly recorded in Babylonian star catalogues before 1000 BCE.
The Babylonians used MULSUḪUR.MAŠ "The Goat-Fish" as a symbol of their god Ea. It has been consistently represented as a hybrid of a goat and a fish since the Middle Bronze Age.

In the Early Bronze Age the winter solstice occurred in the constellation. Due to the precession of the equinoxes, the December solstice now takes place in Sagittarius. The Sun is now in the constellation Capricorn from late January through mid-February.
greek: In Greek mythology, Capricornus is sometimes identified as Amalthea, the goat that suckled the infant Zeus after his mother Rhea saved him from being devoured by his father Cronos. Amalthea's broken horn was transformed into the cornucopia or "horn of plenty."
The constellation is also sometimes identified as Pan, the god with a goat's horns and legs, who saved himself from the monster Typhon by giving himself a fish's tail and diving into a river.
history: Although the solstice during the northern hemisphere's winter no longer takes place while the sun is in Capricornus, as it did until 130 BCE, the astrological sign called Capricorn is still used to denote the position of the solstice.

The latitude of the sun's most southerly position continues to be called the Tropic of Capricorn, a term which also applies to the line on the Earth at which the sun is directly overhead at local noon on the day of the December solstice.

The planet Neptune was discovered by German astronomer Johann Galle near Deneb Algedi (δ Capricorni) on 23 September 1846, though by modern constellation boundaries Neptune lay within Aquarius at the time of its discovery.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, constellation Capricornus lies in The Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武; Běi Fāng Xuán Wǔ).
other: The Nakh peoples called this constellation Roofing Towers (Chechen: Neģara Bjovnaš).
In the Society Islands, the figure of Capricornus was called Rua-o-Mere, "Cavern of parental yearnings."
In Indian astronomy and Indian astrology, it is called Makara, the crocodile.

stars_text: Capricornus is a faint constellation, with only one star above magnitude 3. Its alpha star has a magnitude of only 3.6.

δ Cap (Deneb Algedi, 2.9m) is the brightest star in Capricornus, located 39 light-years from Earth. Its name comes from the Arabic for "tail of the goat" (deneb al-gedi). It is a Beta Lyrae variable star (an eclipsing binary) that ranges by about 0.2 magnitudes with a period of 24.5 hours.

α Cap (Algedi or Giedi) is a multiple star with two components distinguishable by the naked eye. The primary (α2 Cap), 109 light-years away, is a yellow giant of magnitude 3.6. The secondary (α1 Cap), 690 light-years away, is a yellow supergiant of magnitude 4.3. Both are themselves multiple stars. The traditional name comes from the Arabic word for "the kid."

β Cap (Dabih, 3.1m) is a double star 340 light-years from Earth. The primary is a yellow giant and the secondary is a blue-white star of magnitude 6.1, distinguishable in binoculars. The traditional name comes from the Arabic phrase for "the lucky stars of the slaughterer," referencing ritual sacrifices performed by ancient Arabs at the heliacal rising of Capricornus.
γ Cap (Nashira, 3.7m) means "bringing good tidings." It is a white giant star 139 light-years from Earth.
π Cap is a double star 670 light-years away with a blue-white primary of magnitude 5.1 and a white secondary of magnitude 8.3. The components are distinguishable in a small telescope.
deep_sky_objects: Messier 30 (NGC 7099) is a centrally-condensed globular cluster of magnitude 7.5, located 30,000 light-years away. It has chains of stars extending to the north that are resolvable in small amateur telescopes.
The constellation harbors the wide spiral galaxy NGC 6907.

One galaxy group located in Capricornus is HCG 87, a group of at least three galaxies located 400 million light-years from Earth (redshift 0.0296). It contains a large elliptical galaxy, a face-on spiral galaxy, and an edge-on spiral galaxy.

The face-on spiral galaxy in HCG 87 is experiencing abnormally high rates of star formation, indicating interaction with one or both members of the group. The large elliptical galaxy and the edge-on spiral galaxy, both with active nuclei, are connected by a stream of stars and dust.
Astronomers predict that the three galaxies may merge millions of years in the future to form a giant elliptical galaxy.
visualization: Capricornus's brighter stars are found on a triangle whose vertices are α2 Capricorni (Giedi), δ Capricorni (Deneb Algiedi), and ω Capricorni. Ptolemy's method of connecting the stars has been influential. Capricornus is usually drawn as a goat with the tail of a fish.

H. A. Rey has suggested an alternative visualization that graphically shows a goat. The goat's head is formed by the triangle of stars ι Cap, θ Cap, and ζ Cap. The goat's horn sticks out with stars γ Cap and δ Cap. The goat's tail consists of stars β Cap and α2 Cap. The goat's hind foot consists of stars ψ Cap and ω Cap.

Car.name: Carina

source.discoverer: Ancient Greeks (as part of Argo Navis)
source.year: divided by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1763

Car.description: Carina is bordered by Vela, Puppis, Pictor, Volans, Chamaeleon, Musca, and Centaurus. It covers 494 square degrees, ranking 34th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Canopus (α Car) (−0.72m), the second-brightest star in the night sky.

greek: Carina was once a part of Argo Navis, the great ship of the mythical Jason and the Argonauts who searched for the Golden Fleece. The constellation of Argo was introduced in ancient Greece.

Due to the massive size of Argo Navis and the sheer number of stars that required separate designation, Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille divided Argo into three sections in 1763, including Carina (the hull or keel).

In the 19th century, these three became established as separate constellations and were formally included in the list of 88 modern IAU constellations in 1930. Lacaille kept a single set of Greek letters for the whole of Argo, and separate sets of Latin letter designations for each section. Therefore, Carina has α, β and ε, Vela has γ and δ, Puppis has ζ, and so on.
chinese: From China (especially northern China), the stars of Carina can barely be seen. The star Canopus (the south polar star in Chinese astronomy) was located by Chinese astronomers in the Vermilion Bird of the South (南方朱雀, Nán Fāng Zhū Què).

The rest of the stars were first classified by Xu Guangqi during the Ming dynasty, based on knowledge acquired from western star charts, and placed among The Southern Asterisms (近南極星區, Jìnnánjíxīngōu).
polynesian: Polynesian peoples had no name for the constellation in particular, though they had many names for Canopus. The Māori name Ariki ("High-born"), and the Hawaiian Ke Alii-o-kona-i-ka-lewa, "The Chief of the southern expanse" both attest to the star's prominence in the southern sky.
The Māori Atutahi, "First-light" or "Single-light," and the Tuamotu Te Tau-rari and Marere-te-tavahi, "He who stands alone," refer to the star's solitary nature.
Canopus was also called Kapae-poto ("Short horizon"), because it rarely sets from the vantage point of New Zealand, and Kauanga ("Solitary"), when it was the last star visible before sunrise.

stars_text: α Car (Canopus, −0.72m) is the second-brightest star in the night sky. It is a white bright giant 313 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name comes from the mythological Canopus, who was a navigator for Menelaus, king of Sparta.
β Car (Miaplacidus, 1.7m) is a blue-white star 111 light-years from Earth.
ε Car (Avior, 1.9m) is an orange giant star similarly bright to Miaplacidus, 630 light-years from Earth.
θ Car (2.7m) is a blue-white star 440 light-years from Earth. It is the most prominent member of the cluster IC 2602.
ι Car (2.2m) is a white supergiant star 690 light-years from Earth.

η Car (Eta Carinae) is the most prominent variable star in Carina, with a mass of approximately 100 solar masses and 4 million times as bright as the Sun. It was first discovered to be unusual in 1677, when Edmond Halley observed its magnitude suddenly rise to 4.

Eta Carinae is inside NGC 3372, the Carina Nebula. It had a long outburst in 1827, brightening to magnitude 1. Its most prominent outburst made it equal to Sirius in 1843 when it brightened to magnitude −1.5. In 1998, it brightened again to magnitude 5.0.
Eta Carinae is a binary star with a companion that has a period of 5.5 years. The two stars are surrounded by the Homunculus Nebula, composed of gas ejected in 1843.

l Car is a Cepheid variable noted for its brightness—the brightest Cepheid variable to the unaided eye. It is a yellow supergiant with a minimum magnitude of 4.2 and a maximum magnitude of 3.3, with a period of 35.5 days.

V382 Car is a yellow hypergiant, one of the rarest types of stars. It is a slow irregular variable with magnitudes ranging from 3.77 to 4.05. It has 212,000 times more luminosity than the Sun and over 480 times the Sun's size.
R Car is a Mira variable red giant with a minimum magnitude of 10.0 and maximum of 4.0, with a period of 309 days. It is 416 light-years from Earth.
S Car is similar to R Carinae, with a minimum magnitude of 10.0 and maximum of 5.0, but a shorter period of 150 days. It is 1,300 light-years from Earth.

υ Car is a binary star with two blue-white giant components 1,600 light-years from Earth. The primary is of magnitude 3.0 and the secondary is magnitude 6.0, distinguishable in a small amateur telescope.
asterisms: The Diamond Cross is composed of the stars Beta, Theta, Upsilon and Omega Carinae. It is visible south of 20ºN latitude and is larger but fainter than the Southern Cross in Crux.

The False Cross is composed of four stars, with two stars in Carina (Iota Carinae and Epsilon Carinae) and two stars in Vela (Kappa Velorum and Delta Velorum). It is often mistaken for the Southern Cross, causing errors in astronavigation.
deep_sky_objects: The Carina Nebula (NGC 3372) was discovered by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1751. It is an extended emission nebula approximately 8,000 light-years away and 300 light-years wide that includes vast star-forming regions. It has an overall magnitude of 8.0 and an apparent diameter of over 2 degrees.

The Keyhole Nebula is the central region of the Carina Nebula. It was described in 1847 by John Herschel and likened to a keyhole by Emma Converse in 1873. The Keyhole is about seven light-years wide and is composed mostly of ionized hydrogen with two major star-forming regions.

The Homunculus Nebula is a planetary nebula visible to the naked eye being ejected by Eta Carinae, the most massive visible star known. Eta Carinae is so massive it has reached the theoretical upper limit for the mass of a star and is therefore unstable.

Eta Carinae is known for its outbursts. In 1840 it briefly became one of the brightest stars in the sky due to a particularly massive outburst that largely created the Homunculus Nebula. Because of this instability, Eta Carinae is considered a prime supernova candidate for the next several hundred thousand years.

NGC 2516 is an open cluster visible to the unaided eye, approximately half a degree square. It is 1,100 light-years from Earth and has approximately 80 stars, the brightest of which is a red giant of magnitude 5.2.
NGC 3114 is an open cluster similar in size to NGC 2516 but more distant at 3,000 light-years. It is more loose and dim, with its brightest stars only 6th magnitude.

IC 2602, also called the "Southern Pleiades," is the most prominent open cluster in Carina. It contains Theta Carinae along with several other stars visible to the unaided eye—approximately 60 stars total. The cluster has a diameter of approximately one degree, making it particularly large for an open cluster.

NGC 3532 is visible to the unaided eye and comparable in size to IC 2602. It possesses approximately 150 stars arranged in an unusual shape approximating an ellipse with a dark central area. Several prominent orange giants are among the cluster's bright 7th magnitude stars.
NGC 2808 is a naked-eye globular cluster.

The Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56) is a noted galaxy cluster at a distance of 4 billion light-years (redshift 0.296). It is named for the shock wave seen in the intracluster medium, which resembles the shock wave of a supersonic bullet.

The bow shock in the Bullet Cluster is thought to be due to the smaller galaxy cluster moving through the intracluster medium at a relative speed of 3,000–4,000 kilometers per second. Because this gravitational interaction has been ongoing for hundreds of millions of years, the smaller cluster is being destroyed and will eventually merge with the larger cluster.
meteor_showers_detail: Carina contains the radiant of the Eta Carinids meteor shower, which peaks around January 21 each year.
future: Carina is in the southern sky quite near the south celestial pole, making it never set (circumpolar) for most of the southern hemisphere. Due to precession of Earth's axis, by the year 4700 the south celestial pole will be in Carina.

Three bright stars in Carina will come within 1 degree of the southern celestial pole and take turns as the southern pole star: Omega Carinae (mag 3.29) in 5600, Upsilon Carinae (mag 2.97) in 6700, and Iota Carinae (mag 2.21) in 7900.
About 13,860 CE, the bright Canopus (−0.7) will have a greater declination than −82°.

Cas.name: Cassiopeia
Cas.pronunciation: /ˌkæsiəˈpiːə, -sioʊ-/ Cássiopéia, esp. for the constellation also /ˌkæsiˈoʊpiə/ Cássiópeia;, genitive /ˌkæsiəˈpiːaɪ, -sioʊ-, -iː/
Cas.description: Cassiopeia is bordered by Camelopardalis, Cepheus, Lacerta, Andromeda, and Perseus. It covers 598.4 square degrees, ranking 25th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cas (Schedar) (2.24m). High in the northern sky, it is circumpolar to viewers in the British Isles, Canada and the northern United States.

greek: The constellation is named after Cassiopeia, the queen of Aethiopia. Cassiopeia was the wife of King Cepheus of Aethiopia and mother of Princess Andromeda. Cepheus and Cassiopeia were placed next to each other among the stars, along with Andromeda.

She was placed in the sky as punishment after enraging Poseidon with the boast that her daughter Andromeda was more beautiful than the Nereids or, alternatively, that she herself was more beautiful than the sea nymphs.

She was forced to wheel around the north celestial pole on her throne, spending half of her time clinging to it so she does not fall off. Poseidon decreed that Andromeda should be bound to a rock as prey for the monster Cetus. Andromeda was then rescued by the hero Perseus, whom she later married.
history: Cassiopeia has been variously portrayed throughout her history. In Persia, she was drawn by al-Sufi as a queen holding a staff with a crescent moon in her right hand, wearing a crown, as well as a two-humped camel.
In France, she was portrayed as having a marble throne and a palm leaf in her left hand, holding her robe in her right hand. This depiction is from Augustin Royer's 1679 atlas.

In the 17th century, various Biblical figures were depicted in the stars of Cassiopeia. These included Bathsheba, Solomon's mother; Deborah, an Old Testament prophet; and Mary Magdalene, a follower of Jesus.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars forming Cassiopeia are found among three areas: the Purple Forbidden enclosure (紫微垣, Zǐ Wēi Yuán), the Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武, Běi Fāng Xuán Wǔ), and the White Tiger of the West (西方白虎, Xī Fāng Bái Hǔ).

The Chinese astronomers saw several figures in what is modern-day Cassiopeia. Kappa, Eta, and Mu Cassiopeiae formed a constellation called the Bridge of the Kings; when seen along with Alpha and Beta Cassiopeiae, they formed the great chariot Wang-Liang.
The charioteer's whip was represented by Gamma Cassiopeiae, sometimes called "Tsih," the Chinese word for "whip."
hindu: In Hindu Mythology, Cassiopeia was associated with the mythological figure Sharmishtha—the daughter of the great Devil (Daitya) King Vrishparva and a friend to Devayani (Andromeda).
welsh: In Welsh Mythology Llys Dôn (literally "The Court of Dôn") is the traditional Welsh name for the constellation. At least three of Dôn's children also have astronomical associations: Caer Gwydion ("The fortress of Gwydion") is the traditional Welsh name for the Milky Way, and Caer Arianrhod ("The Fortress of Arianrhod") being the constellation of Corona Borealis.
arab: A figure called the "Tinted Hand" appeared in the stars of Cassiopeia in some Arabic atlases. This is variously said to represent a woman's hand dyed red with henna, as well as the bloodied hand of Muhammad's daughter Fatima. The hand is made up of α, β, γ, δ, ε, and η Cas. The arm is made up of stars in Perseus.

Another Arabic constellation that incorporated the stars of Cassiopeia was the Camel. Its head was composed of stars in Andromeda; its hump was Beta Cassiopeiae; its body was the rest of Cassiopeia, and the legs were composed of stars in Perseus and Andromeda.
other: Other cultures see a hand or moose antlers in the pattern. The Sámi saw the W of Cassiopeia as an elk antler. The Chukchi of Siberia similarly saw the five main stars as five reindeer stags.

The people of the Marshall Islands saw Cassiopeia as part of a great porpoise constellation. The main stars of Cassiopeia make its tail, Andromeda and Triangulum form its body, and Aries makes its head.
In Hawaii, Alpha, Beta, and Gamma Cassiopeiae were named. Alpha was called Poloahilani, Beta was called Polula, and Gamma was called Mulehu.
The people of Pukapuka saw the figure of Cassiopeia as a distinct constellation called Na Taki-tolu-a-Mataliki.

stars_text: The five brightest stars of Cassiopeia—Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon Cassiopeiae—form the characteristic W-shaped asterism. All five are prominent naked eye stars, three are noticeably variable, and a fourth is a suspected low amplitude variable. The asterism is oriented as a W when below Polaris during northern spring and summer nights. In northern winter, and when seen from southern latitudes, it appears inverted.

α Cas (Schedar, 2.2m) is an orange giant 228 light-years from Earth. With a luminosity of around 771 times that of the Sun, it has swollen and cooled after exhausting its core hydrogen over its 100 to 200 million-year lifespan, spending much of it as a blue-white B-type main-sequence star. The name comes from the Arabic Al Sadr, "the breast."

β Cas (Caph, 2.3m) means "hand." It is a white star 54.7 light-years from Earth. Around 1.2 billion years old, it has used up its core hydrogen and begun expanding and cooling off the main sequence. Rotating at about 92% of its critical speed, Caph completes a full rotation every 1.12 days, giving the star an oblate spheroid shape with an equatorial bulge 24% larger than the polar radius. It is a Delta Scuti variable with a small amplitude and period of 2.5 hours.

γ Cas (Tiansi, ~2.2m) is the prototype Gamma Cassiopeiae variable star, a type with a variable disc of material flung off by the star's high rotation rate. It has a minimum magnitude of 3.0 and a maximum of 1.6, but is generally near magnitude 2.2, with unpredictable fades and brightenings. It is a spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of 203.59 days. It is 550 light-years from Earth.

δ Cas (Ruchbah or Rukbat, 2.7m) means "knee." It is a possible Algol-type eclipsing binary that has been reported to show eclipses of less than 0.1 magnitudes with a period of 2 years and 1 month, but this has never been confirmed. It is 99.4 light-years from Earth. Delta Cassiopeiae was the star used by Jean Picard in 1669 to establish the length on Earth's surface corresponding to one degree, and hence the radius of the Earth.

ε Cas (Segin, 3.3m) is located 410 light-years from Earth. It is a hot blue-white star with a surface temperature of 15,680 K. It is 6.5 times as massive and 4.2 times as wide as the Sun, and belongs to a class known as Be stars—rapidly spinning stars that throw off a ring or shell of matter.
ζ Cas (Fulu) is a suspected slowly pulsating B-type star.

κ Cas (Cexing) is a blue supergiant that is 302,000 times as luminous as the Sun and has 33 times its diameter. It is a runaway star, moving at around 2.5 million mph relative to its neighbors (1,100 kilometers per second). Its magnetic field and wind of particles creates a visible bow shock 4 light-years ahead of it, colliding with interstellar gas and dust. The bow shock is around 12 light-years long and 1.8 light-years wide.

η Cas (Achird) is the nearest star in Cassiopeia, located 19.13 light-years away. It is a binary star made up of a G-dwarf star similar to the Sun (apparent magnitude 3.45) and a K-dwarf star (apparent magnitude 7.51). It is visually located between Alpha and Gamma Cassiopeiae and is one of the nearest G-type / K-type stars to Earth.

ρ Cas (Rho Cassiopeiae) is a semi-regular pulsating yellow hypergiant, among the most luminous stars in the galaxy at approximately 500,000 L☉. It has a minimum magnitude of 6.2 and a maximum of 4.1, with a period of approximately 320 days. It has around 450 times the Sun's diameter and 17 times its mass. It is about 10,000 light-years from Earth.
V509 Cas is a second example of the extremely rare yellow hypergiants, around 400,000 times as luminous as the Sun and 14 times as massive.

PZ Cas is a red supergiant and one of the largest known stars with an estimate of 1,190–1,940 R☉. It is a semiregular variable between 240,000 and 270,000 times as luminous as the Sun, around 9,160 light-years distant.
Tycho Brahe's supernova was visible within Cassiopeia in 1572. The star Tycho G is suspected of being the donor of the material that triggered that explosion.
deep_sky_objects: A rich section of the Milky Way runs through Cassiopeia, stretching from Perseus towards Cygnus, and it contains a number of open clusters, young luminous galactic disc stars, and nebulae.
The Heart Nebula and the Soul Nebula are two neighboring emission nebulae about 7,500 light-years away.

M52 (NGC 7654) is an open cluster once described as "kidney-shaped," containing approximately 100 stars and located 4,600 light-years from Earth. Its most prominent member is an orange-hued star of magnitude 8.0 near the cluster's edge.

M103 (NGC 581) is far poorer than M52, with only about 25 stars included. It is between 8,000 and 9,500 light-years from Earth. Its most prominent member is actually a closer, superimposed double star consisting of a 7th-magnitude primary and 10th-magnitude secondary.

NGC 457 is an open cluster with about 80 stars. It is looser than others, and its brightest member is Phi Cassiopeiae, a white supergiant of magnitude 5.0 (though it is uncertain whether Phi Cas is part of the cluster). The stars are arrayed in chains, approximately 10,000 light-years from Earth. Also called the E.T. Cluster, the Owl Cluster, and Caldwell 13.
NGC 663 is another open cluster with about 80 stars. It is both closer at 8,200 light-years and larger at 0.25 degrees in diameter.

Cassiopeia A (Cas A) is a supernova remnant within the W asterism. It is the remnant of a supernova that took place approximately 300 years ago (as observed now from Earth; it is 10,000 light-years away). It has the distinction of being the strongest radio source observable outside the Solar System. It was perhaps observed as a faint star in 1680 by John Flamsteed.

Cassiopeia A was the subject of the first image returned by the Chandra X-Ray Observatory in the late 1990s. The shell of matter expelled from the star is moving at 4,000 kilometres (2,500 mi) per second with a temperature of 30,000 K on average.
3C 10, or Tycho's Supernova Remnant, is the aftermath of the supernova called Tycho's Star. It was observed in 1572 by Tycho Brahe and now exists as a bright object in the radio spectrum.

NGC 185 is a magnitude 9.2 elliptical galaxy of type E0, 2 million light-years away. Though it does not appear in Andromeda, this dwarf galaxy is gravitationally bound to the far larger Andromeda Galaxy.
NGC 147 is a magnitude 9.3 elliptical galaxy of type E0, 2.3 million light-years from Earth. Like NGC 185, it is gravitationally bound to the Andromeda Galaxy.
IC 10 is an irregular galaxy that is the closest known starburst galaxy and the only one in the Local Group of galaxies.

Cassiopeia also contains part of the closest galaxy group to our Local Group, the IC 342/Maffei Group. The galaxies Maffei 1 and Maffei 2 are located just to the south of the Heart and Soul nebulae. As a result of this location in the Zone of Avoidance, both are surprisingly faint despite both being within 10 million light-years away.
meteor_showers_detail: The December Phi Cassiopeiids are a recently discovered early December meteor shower that radiates from Cassiopeia. Phi Cassiopeiids are very slow, with an entry velocity of approximately 16.7 kilometers per second.
The shower's parent body is Biela's Comet, although the identity of the parent body was unknown for a number of years.

Cen.name: Centaurus
Cen.meteor_showers: Alpha Centaurids, Omicron Centaurids, Theta Centaurids
Cen.description: Centaurus is bordered by Antlia, Carina, Circinus, Crux, Hydra, Libra, Lupus, Musca, and Vela. It covers 1,060 square degrees, ranking 9th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cen (−0.27m). Centaurus is a large constellation with many bright stars, two stars brighter than magnitude 1, and a number of the best-known deep-sky objects.

babylonian: The figure of Centaurus can be traced back to a Babylonian constellation known as the Bison-man (MUL.GUD.ALIM). This being was depicted in two major forms: firstly, as a 4-legged bison with a human head, and secondly, as a being with a man's head and torso attached to the rear legs and tail of a bull or bison.
It has been closely associated with the Sun god Utu-Shamash from very early times. By the late 3rd millennium the Bison-man had been replaced by a new constellation, the Wild Boar.
greek: The Greeks depicted the constellation as a centaur and gave it its current name. It was mentioned by Eudoxus in the 4th century BC and Aratus in the 3rd century BC. In the 2nd century AD, Claudius Ptolemy catalogued 37 stars in Centaurus, including Alpha Centauri.

Large as it is now, in earlier times it was even larger. The constellation Lupus was treated as an asterism within Centaurus, portrayed in illustrations as an unspecified animal either in the centaur's grasp or impaled on its spear.

The Southern Cross, which is now regarded as a separate constellation, was treated by the ancients as a mere asterism formed of the stars composing the centaur's legs. Additionally, what is now the minor constellation Circinus was treated as undefined stars under the centaur's front hooves.

According to the Roman poet Ovid (Fasti v.379), the constellation honors the centaur Chiron, who was tutor to many of the earlier Greek heroes including Heracles (Hercules), Theseus, and Jason, the leader of the Argonauts. It is not to be confused with the more warlike centaur represented by the zodiacal constellation Sagittarius.
The legend associated with Chiron says that he was accidentally poisoned with an arrow shot by Hercules, and was subsequently placed in the heavens.
history: While Centaurus now has a high southern latitude, at the dawn of civilization it was an equatorial constellation. Precession has been slowly shifting it southward for millennia, and it is now close to its maximal southern declination.
In a little over 7,000 years it will be at maximum visibility for those in the northern hemisphere, visible at times in the year up to quite a high northern latitude.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Centaurus are found in three areas: the Azure Dragon of the East (東方青龍, Dōng Fāng Qīng Lóng), the Vermillion Bird of the South (南方朱雀, Nán Fāng Zhū Què), and the Southern Asterisms (近南極星區, Jìnnánjíxīngōu).

Not all of the stars of Centaurus can be seen from China, and the unseen stars were classified among the Southern Asterisms by Xu Guangqi, based on his study of western star charts. However, most of the brightest stars of Centaurus, including α Centauri, θ Centauri (Menkent), ε Centauri and η Centauri, can be seen in the Chinese sky.
polynesian: Some Polynesian peoples considered the stars of Centaurus to be a constellation as well. On Pukapuka, Centaurus had two names: Na Mata-o-te-tokolua and Na Lua-mata-o-Wua-ma-Velo. In Tonga, the constellation was called by four names: O-nga-tangata, Tautanga-ufi, Mamangi-Halahu, and Mau-kuo-mau.

Alpha and Beta Centauri were not named specifically by the people of Pukapuka or Tonga, but they were named by the people of Hawaii and the Tuamotus. In Hawaii, the name for Alpha Centauri was either Melemele or Ka Maile-hope and the name for Beta Centauri was either Polapola or Ka Maile-mua. In the Tuamotu islands, Alpha was called Na Kuhi and Beta was called Tere.

The Pointer (α Centauri and β Centauri) is one of the asterisms used by Bugis sailors for navigation, called bintoéng balué, meaning "the widowed-before-marriage." It is also called bintoéng sallatang meaning "southern star."

stars_text: Centaurus contains several very bright stars. Its alpha and beta stars are used as "southern pointer stars" to help observers find the constellation Crux. Centaurus has 281 stars above magnitude 6.5, meaning that they are visible to the unaided eye—the most of any constellation.

α Cen (Alpha Centauri, −0.28m) is a triple star system and the closest star system to the Sun, located 4.4 light-years away. It has a high proper motion and will be a mere half-degree from Beta Centauri in approximately 4,000 years.

Traditionally called Rigil Kentaurus (from Arabic رجل قنطورس, meaning "foot of the centaur") or Toliman (from Arabic الظليمين meaning "two male ostriches"), the system has two yellow-hued stars: the primary is magnitude −0.01 and the secondary is 1.35.

Proxima Centauri, the tertiary star, is a red dwarf of magnitude 11.0, currently the nearest star to the Sun. It appears almost 2 degrees away from the close pairing of Alpha and has a period of approximately one million years. It is also a flare star, with minutes-long outbursts where it brightens by over a magnitude.

The Alpha couple revolve in 80-year periodicity and will next appear closest as seen from Earth's telescopes in 2037 and 2038. Together as they appear to the naked eye they present the third-brightest "star" in the night sky.

β Cen (Beta Centauri, 0.6m), also called Hadar and Agena, is a double star 525 light-years from Earth. The primary is a blue giant and the secondary is of magnitude 4.0 with a modest separation, appearing only under intense magnification due to its distance. It is positioned beyond Proxima and toward the narrow axis of Crux, thus with Alpha forming a far-south limb of the constellation.
θ Cen (Menkent, 2.06m) is an orange giant star and the only bright star of Centaurus that is easily visible from mid-northern latitudes.
γ Cen (Gamma Centauri, 2.2m) is a binary star which appears to the naked eye at magnitude 2.2. The primary and secondary are both blue-white hued stars of magnitude 2.9, with a period of 84 years.
R Cen is a Mira variable star with a minimum magnitude of 11.8 and a maximum magnitude of 5.3. It is about 1,250 light-years from Earth and has a period of 18 months.

BPM 37093 is a white dwarf star whose carbon atoms are thought to have formed a crystalline structure. Since diamond also consists of carbon arranged in a crystalline lattice (though of a different configuration), scientists have nicknamed this star "Lucy" after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds."
PDS 70 (V1032 Centauri) is a low mass T Tauri star. In July 2018 astronomers captured the first conclusive image of a protoplanetary disk containing a nascent exoplanet, named PDS 70b.
deep_sky_objects: ω Cen (Omega Centauri, NGC 5139) is a naked-eye globular cluster, 17,000 light-years away with a diameter of 150 light-years. Despite being listed as the constellation's "omega" star, it is in fact a globular cluster. It is the largest and brightest globular cluster in the Milky Way; at ten times the size of the next-largest cluster, it has a magnitude of 3.7.

Omega Centauri is also the most luminous globular cluster in the Milky Way, at over one million solar luminosities. It is classified as a Shapley class VIII cluster, which means that its center is loosely concentrated.
Omega Centauri is one of only two globular clusters to be given a stellar designation—in its case a Bayer letter. The other is 47 Tucanae (Xi Tucanae), which has a Flamsteed number.

Omega Centauri contains several million stars, most of which are yellow dwarf stars, but also possesses red giants and blue-white stars. The stars have an average age of 12 billion years. This has prompted suspicion that Omega Centauri was the core of a dwarf galaxy that had been absorbed by the Milky Way.

Omega Centauri was determined to be nonstellar in 1677 by Edmond Halley, though it was visible as a star to the ancients. Its status as a globular cluster was determined by James Dunlop in 1827. To the unaided eye, it appears fuzzy and is obviously non-circular. It is approximately half a degree in diameter, the same size as the full Moon.
NGC 3766 is an open cluster 6,300 light-years from Earth that is visible to the unaided eye. It contains approximately 100 stars, the brightest of which are 7th magnitude.
NGC 5460 is another naked-eye open cluster, 2,300 light-years from Earth, that has an overall magnitude of 6 and contains approximately 40 stars.

NGC 3918, also known as the Blue Planetary, is a bright planetary nebula. It has an overall magnitude of 8.0 and a central star of magnitude 11.0; it is 2,600 light-years from Earth. The Blue Planetary was discovered by John Herschel and named for its color's similarity to Uranus, though the nebula is apparently three times larger than the planet.

NGC 4622 is a face-on spiral galaxy located 200 million light-years from Earth (redshift 0.0146). Its spiral arms wind in both directions, which makes it nearly impossible for astronomers to determine the rotation of the galaxy. Astronomers theorize that a collision with a smaller companion galaxy near the core could have led to the unusual spiral structure.

NGC 5253 is a peculiar irregular galaxy located near the border with Hydra and M83, with which it likely had a close gravitational interaction 1–2 billion years ago. This may have sparked the galaxy's high rate of star formation, which continues today and contributes to its high surface brightness. NGC 5253 includes a large nebula and at least 12 large star clusters.

NGC 4945 is a spiral galaxy seen edge-on from Earth, 13 million light-years away. It is visible with any amateur telescope, as well as binoculars under good conditions. It has been described as "shaped like a candle flame," being long and thin (16' by 3').

Centaurus A (NGC 5128) is one of the closest active galaxies to Earth at 11 million light-years away (redshift 0.00183). It has a supermassive black hole at its core, which expels massive jets of matter that emit radio waves due to synchrotron radiation.

Astronomers posit that Centaurus A's dust lanes, not common in elliptical galaxies, are due to a previous merger with another galaxy, probably a spiral galaxy. In the optical spectrum it appears as a fairly large elliptical galaxy with a prominent dust lane. Its overall magnitude is 7.0 and it has been seen under perfect conditions with the naked eye, making it one of the most distant objects visible to the unaided observer.

NGC 4650A is a polar-ring galaxy 136 million light-years from Earth (redshift 0.01). It has a central core made of older stars that resembles an elliptical galaxy, and an outer ring of young stars that orbits around the core. The plane of the outer ring is distorted, which suggests that NGC 4650A is the result of a galaxy collision about a billion years ago.

This galaxy has also been cited in studies of dark matter, because the stars in the outer ring orbit too quickly for their collective mass. This suggests that the galaxy is surrounded by a dark matter halo, which provides the necessary mass.

The Centaurus Cluster is one of the closest galaxy clusters to Earth at c. 160 million light-years away, having redshift 0.0114. It has a cooler, denser central region of gas and a hotter, more diffuse outer region. The intracluster medium in the Centaurus Cluster has a high concentration of metals (elements heavier than helium) due to a large number of supernovae. This cluster also possesses a plume of gas whose origin is unknown.

Cep.name: Cepheus
Cep.description: Cepheus is bordered by Cygnus, Lacerta, Cassiopeia, Camelopardalis, Draco, and Ursa Minor. It covers 588 square degrees, ranking 27th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cep (Alderamin) (2.45m).

greek: Cepheus was the King of Aethiopia. He was married to Cassiopeia and was the father of Andromeda, both of whom are immortalized as modern day constellations along with Cepheus.
Cepheus is most commonly depicted as holding his arms aloft, praying for the deities to spare the life of Andromeda. He also is depicted as a more regal monarch sitting on his throne.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of the constellation Cepheus are found in two areas: the Purple Forbidden enclosure (紫微垣, Zǐ Wēi Yuán) and the Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武, Běi Fāng Xuán Wǔ).

stars_text: α Cep (Alderamin, 2.51m) is the brightest star in the constellation.

γ Cep (Errai, 3.21m) is the second-brightest star in the constellation. It is a binary star made up by an orange giant or subgiant and a red dwarf. The primary component hosts one exoplanet, Gamma Cephei Ab (Tadmor).

δ Cep (Delta Cephei) is a yellow supergiant star 980 light-years from Earth and the prototype of the class of the Cepheid variables. It was discovered to be variable by John Goodricke in 1784. It varies between 3.5m and 4.4m over a period of 5 days and 9 hours.

The Cepheids are a class of pulsating variable stars. Delta Cephei has a minimum size of 40 solar diameters and a maximum size of 46 solar diameters. It is also a double star; the primary star has a wide-set blue companion of magnitude 6.3.

μ Cep (Mu Cephei, the Garnet Star) is known for its deep red color. It is a semiregular variable star with a minimum magnitude of 5.1 and a maximum magnitude of 3.4. Its period is approximately 2 years. The star's radius has been estimated to be from 972 solar radii (4.52 AU) to 1,420 solar radii (6.6 AU). If it were placed at the center of the Solar System, it would likely extend past the orbit of Jupiter.

VV Cep A is a semiregular variable star located approximately 5,000 light-years from Earth. It has a minimum magnitude of 5.4 and a maximum magnitude of 4.8, and is paired with a blue main sequence star called VV Cephei B. The red supergiant primary is around 1,050 times larger than the Sun.
VV Cephei is an unusually long-period eclipsing binary, but the eclipses, which occur every 20.3 years, are too faint to be observed with the unaided eye.

ζ Cep (Zeta Cephei, 3.35m) is not as large as Mu Cephei and VV Cephei A with a diameter less than 200 times that of the Sun; however, its surface would lie between the orbits of Venus and Earth if placed at the center of the Solar System. It is the fourth-brightest star in the constellation.

V381 Cep Aa is a red supergiant with a maximum magnitude of 5.5. It is part of a triple star system similar to VV Cephei and has a diameter 980 times that of the Sun. All four red supergiants (Mu, VV, Zeta, and V381) have initial masses more than eight times that of the Sun and are accepted core-collapse supernova candidates.

ν Cep (Nu Cephei) is a blue supergiant similar to Deneb with an initial mass of over 20 solar masses. It belongs to the Cepheus OB2 stellar association along with Mu Cephei and VV Cephei, which have similar initial masses.
ο Cep (Omicron Cephei) is a binary star with a period of 800 years. The system, 211 light-years from Earth, consists of an orange giant primary of magnitude 4.9 and a secondary of magnitude 7.1.
ξ Cep (Xi Cephei) is another binary star, 102 light-years from Earth, with a period of 4,000 years. It has a blue-white primary of magnitude 4.4 and a yellow secondary of magnitude 6.5.

Krüger 60 is an 11th-magnitude binary star consisting of two red dwarfs. The star system is one of the nearest, being only 13 light-years away from Earth. It was once proposed as a possible home system for 2I/Borisov, the first accepted interstellar comet, but this was later rejected.
deep_sky_objects: The constellation Cepheus is rich in star-forming regions and emission nebulae of various kinds. Most of the structures visible lie in the Orion Arm of the Milky Way, roughly 2,800 to 3,600 light-years away.
NGC 188 is an open cluster that has the distinction of being the closest open cluster to the north celestial pole, as well as one of the oldest-known open clusters.
NGC 6946, sometimes called the Fireworks Galaxy, is a spiral galaxy in which ten supernovae have been observed—more than in any other galaxy.
IC 469 is a spiral galaxy characterized by a compact nucleus, of oval shape, with perceptible side arms.
The nebula NGC 7538 is home to the largest-yet-discovered protostar.

NGC 7023 is a reflection nebula with an associated star cluster (Collinder 429). It has an overall magnitude of 7.7 and is 1,400 light-years from Earth. The nebula and cluster are located near Beta Cephei and T Cephei.
Sh 2-155, also known as the Cave Nebula, is a dim and very diffuse bright nebula within a larger nebula complex containing emission, reflection, and dark nebulosity.
The quasar 6C B0014+8120 is one of the most powerful objects in the universe, powered by a supermassive black hole which is as massive as 40 billion Suns.
Sh 2-131 is ionized by the stars of the cluster IC 1396 (the two are often treated as essentially the same object). Embedded within it is a dark nebula known as the Elephant's Trunk.
NGC 7822 (also known as Sh 2-171) is an H II region with an apparent diameter of about 3°.

Cet.name: Cetus
Cet.symbolism: the Whale, Shark, or Sea Monster
Cet.meteor_showers: October Cetids, Eta Cetids, Omicron Cetids
Cet.description: Cetus is bordered by Aries, Pisces, Aquarius, Sculptor, Fornax, Eridanus, and Taurus. It covers 1231 square degrees, ranking 4th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Diphda (β Cet) at magnitude 2.02.

greek: Cetus is most strongly associated with the sea monster sent by Poseidon to destroy Aethiopia. When Queen Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter Andromeda was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs petitioned Poseidon for revenge.

The hero Perseus rescued Andromeda from Cetus by either turning it to stone with Medusa's head or slaying it with his sword. The neighboring constellations Perseus, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, and Andromeda all represent characters from this myth.

Cetus may have originally been associated with a whale in Mesopotamian cultures. It lies in the middle of 'The Sea,' a set of water-associated constellations including Eridanus, Pisces, Piscis Austrinus, and Aquarius.
history: Cetus was one of Ptolemy's 48 original constellations in his 2nd-century Almagest. It has been depicted in many ways throughout history.

In the 17th century, Johann Bayer depicted Cetus as a 'dragon fish,' while both Willem Blaeu and Andreas Cellarius showed it as a whale-like creature. Cetus has also been depicted with animal heads attached to a piscine body.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Cetus are found among two areas: the Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武) and the White Tiger of the West (西方白虎).
amazon: The Tukano and Kobeua people of the Amazon used stars of Cetus to create a jaguar, representing the god of hurricanes and violent storms. Lambda, Mu, Xi, Nu, Gamma, and Alpha Ceti represented its head; Omicron, Zeta, and Chi marked its body.
hawaiian: In Hawaii, the constellation was called Na Kuhi, and Mira (Omicron Ceti) may have been called Kane.

stars_text: Mira (ο Cet, 'wonderful') was the first variable star to be discovered and the prototype of its class. Over 332 days, it reaches magnitude 3 (visible to the naked eye) and dips to magnitude 10 (invisible). Discovered by David Fabricius in 1596, it lies 420 light-years away.
β Cet (Diphda, 2.0m) is the brightest star in Cetus. It's an orange giant 96 light-years from Earth. The traditional name 'Deneb Kaitos' means 'the whale's tail.'
α Cet (Menkar, 'the nose', 2.5m) is a red giant 220 light-years away. It forms a wide double star with 93 Ceti, a blue-white star of magnitude 5.6 at 440 light-years.
γ Cet (Kaffaljidhma, 'head of the whale', 3.5m) is a very close double star. The primary is blue-hued at 82 light-years from Earth, and the secondary is an F-type star of magnitude 6.6.
τ Cet (3.5m) is noted for being a near Sun-like star at just 11.9 light-years distance. It's a yellow main-sequence star.

UV Cet is an unusual binary variable star 8.7 light-years away, consisting of two red dwarfs (both magnitude 13). One is a flare star prone to sudden outbursts that increase brightness to magnitude 7.

AA Cet is a triple star system (magnitude 6.2). The primary and secondary are separated by 8.4 arcseconds. It's an eclipsing variable that decreases by 0.5 magnitudes when the tertiary passes in front of the primary.
deep_sky_objects: Cetus lies far from the galactic plane, so many distant galaxies are visible unobscured by Milky Way dust.

Messier 77 (NGC 1068) is a 9th magnitude spiral galaxy near Delta Ceti. It appears face-on with a clearly visible nucleus of magnitude 10. At 50 million light-years away, M77 is also a Seyfert galaxy and bright in the radio spectrum.

The Pisces-Cetus Supercluster Complex is a galaxy filament that is one of the largest known structures in the observable Universe. It contains the Virgo Supercluster, which contains the Local Group with the Milky Way.
The massive cD galaxy Holmberg 15A is found in Cetus, as are spiral galaxy NGC 1042, elliptical galaxy NGC 1052, and ultra-diffuse galaxy NGC 1052-DF2.
IC 1613 (Caldwell 51) is an irregular dwarf galaxy near star 26 Ceti and a member of the Local Group.

NGC 246 (Caldwell 56), the 'Cetus Ring,' is a planetary nebula of magnitude 8.0 at 1600 light-years. Some amateur astronomers call it the 'Pac-Man Nebula' because of its central stars and surrounding star field.
The Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte (WLM) galaxy is a barred irregular galaxy discovered in 1909 by Max Wolf, located on the outer edges of the Local Group.
ecliptic_note: Cetus is not among the 12 true zodiac constellations. The ecliptic passes less than 0.25° from one corner. The Moon and planets enter Cetus briefly in 50% of their orbits, and the Sun appears in Cetus for about 14 hours each year on March 27-28.

Cha.name: Chamaeleon
Cha.description: Chamaeleon is bordered by Musca, Carina, Volans, Mensa, Octans, and Apus. It covers 132 square degrees, ranking 79th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cha at magnitude 4.05.

history: Chamaeleon was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman.
It first appeared on a 35-cm diameter celestial globe published in 1597 (or 1598) in Amsterdam by Plancius and Jodocus Hondius.

Johann Bayer was the first uranographer to put Chamaeleon in a celestial atlas. It was one of many constellations created by European explorers in the 15th and 16th centuries from unfamiliar Southern Hemisphere stars.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars forming Chamaeleon were classified as the Little Dipper (小斗; Xiǎodǒu) among the Southern Asterisms (近南極星區) by Xu Guangqi.
australian: Chamaeleon is sometimes also called the Frying Pan in Australia.

stars_text: Lacaille gave 17 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Pi in 1756, but omitted Omicron and Xi, and labelled two stars as Delta, Mu and Pi.
Four bright stars in Chamaeleon form a compact diamond shape approximately 10 degrees from the south celestial pole and about 15 degrees south of Acrux.
α Cha (4.1m) is a white-hued star 63 light-years from Earth.
β Cha (4.2m) is a blue-white hued star 271 light-years from Earth.
γ Cha (4.1m) is a red giant 413 light-years from Earth.
δ Cha is a wide double star. The brighter δ² Cha is a blue star of magnitude 4.4, while δ¹ Cha is an orange giant of magnitude 5.5. They both lie about 350 light-years away.
Chamaeleon is also the location of Cha 110913, a unique dwarf star or proto solar system.
deep_sky_objects: In 1999, a nearby open cluster was discovered centered on η Chamaeleontis. The cluster, known as either the Eta Chamaeleontis cluster or Mamajek 1, is 8 million years old and lies 316 light-years from Earth.

The constellation contains a number of molecular clouds (the Chamaeleon dark clouds) forming low-mass T Tauri stars. The cloud complex lies 400 to 600 light-years from Earth and contains tens of thousands of solar masses of gas and dust.
The most prominent cluster of T Tauri stars and young B-type stars are in the Chamaeleon I cloud, associated with the reflection nebula IC 2631.
Chamaeleon contains one planetary nebula, NGC 3195, which is fairly faint. It appears in a telescope at about the same apparent size as Jupiter.

Cir.name: Circinus
Cir.description: Circinus is bordered by Centaurus, Musca, Apus, Triangulum Australe, Norma, and Lupus. It covers 93 square degrees, ranking 85th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Cir (Xami) at magnitude 3.19.

history: In 1756, French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille introduced the constellation of Circinus with the French name 'le Compas,' representing a pair of dividing compasses on a chart of the southern sky.
On that chart, Lacaille portrayed Norma, Circinus, and Triangulum Australe as a set square and ruler, a compass, and a surveyor's level in a set of draughtsman's instruments.
Circinus was given its current name in 1763, when Lacaille published an updated sky map with Latin names for the constellations he introduced.
The constellation lies adjacent to the Alpha and Beta Centauri stars. At declination −50° to −70°, it is only visible south of latitude 30° N.

stars_text: Lacaille charted and gave 8 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Theta in 1756.

α Cir (Xami, 3.19m) is a white main sequence star 54 light-years away and 4° south of Alpha Centauri. It's the brightest example of a rapidly oscillating Ap (RoAp) star in the night sky, with the unusual spectral type A7 Vp SrCrEu.
α Cir forms a binary system with an orange dwarf companion (K5, magnitude 8.5). The stars are separated by 260 AU and take 2600 years to orbit their common center of gravity.
β Cir (4.07m) is a white main sequence star (spectral type A3Va) about 100 light-years away, with around 1.8 times the Sun's diameter.

γ Cir is a binary star 450 light-years away whose components are only 0.8 arcseconds apart. The brighter component is a bluish Be star (B5IV+, magnitude 4.51), while the dimmer is a yellow star (magnitude 5.5). They orbit every 180 years.

δ Cir is a multiple star system over 3600 light-years away. The main components are hot blue O-type stars with 22 and 12 solar masses. If placed 32 light-years away, this system would outshine Venus at magnitude −4.8.
AX Cir is a Cepheid variable ranging between magnitudes 5.6 and 6.19 over 5.3 days. It's a yellow-white supergiant (F8II+) 1600 light-years away.
BX Cir is a faint helium star (over 99% helium) that fluctuates between magnitudes 12.57 and 12.62 over 2 hours 33 minutes. Its origin is unclear but thought to result from a white dwarf merger.
As this constellation intersects the Milky Way plane, it contains many massive stars including 9 Wolf-Rayet stars—a very high number for such a small constellation.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 5823 (Caldwell 88) is an 800-million-year-old open cluster 3500 light-years away, spanning 12 light-years. Despite having magnitude 7.9, it can be seen by star hopping from Beta Circini or Alpha Centauri. It contains 80-100 stars.
NGC 5715 is a fainter open cluster (magnitude 9.8) and smaller (7.0 arcminutes), comprising only 30 stars.
Pismis 20 contains 12 stars in 4.5 arcseconds with magnitude 7.8. At 8270 light-years, it requires an amateur telescope with aperture over 300 mm to be easily discerned.
NGC 5315 is a planetary nebula of magnitude 9.8 around a central star of magnitude 14.2, located 5.2 degrees west-southwest of Alpha Circini.

The Circinus Galaxy (ESO 97-G13), discovered in 1977, is a relatively unobscured spiral galaxy (magnitude 10.6). This oblong galaxy is 13 million light-years away and is the closest Seyfert galaxy to the Milky Way, hosting an active galactic nucleus.
Circinus X-1 is an X-ray binary star system that includes a neutron star. Observations in July 2007 revealed X-ray jets normally found in black hole systems.
The Circinus Pulsar (PSR B1509-58), located 19,000 light-years away, has expelled a 20-light-year-long jet of material from its southern pole, clearly visible in the X-ray spectrum.
RCW 86 is the remnant of SN 185, recorded by Chinese observers in 185 AD. It was visible in the night sky for around eight months and covers an area larger than the typical full moon.
meteor_showers_detail: Circinus is the radiant of an annual meteor shower, the Alpha Circinids (ACI). First observed in Queensland in 1977, the meteors have an average velocity of 27.1 km/s and are thought to be associated with a long-period comet.

In 2011, Peter Jenniskens proposed that the debris trail of comet C/1969 T1 could intersect with Earth's orbit and generate a meteor outburst. The ACI shower peaks on June 4, the day it was first observed.

Col.name: Columba
Col.description: Columba is bordered by Lepus, Caelum, Pictor, Puppis, and Canis Major. It covers 270 square degrees, ranking 54th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Phact (α Col) at magnitude 2.65.

history: Early 3rd century BC: Aratus's astronomical poem Phainomena mentioned faint stars where Columba is now but did not assign any name or figure to them.
In the 2nd century AD, Ptolemy listed 48 constellations in the Almagest. While Columba was not among them, several stars south of Canis Major that would eventually become part of Columba were listed.

In 1592, Petrus Plancius first depicted Columba on the small celestial planispheres of his large wall map to differentiate the 'unformed stars' of Canis Major. Plancius named it Columba Noachi ('Noah's Dove'), referring to the dove that gave Noah information that the Great Flood was receding.
In 1603, Frederick de Houtman listed Columba as 'De Duyve med den Olijftack' ('the dove with the olive branch'). In the same year, Bayer's sky atlas Uranometria included Columba as Columba Noachi.
In 1757 or 1763, Lacaille listed Columba as a constellation and catalogued its stars.
biblical: The name Columba Noachi refers to the dove that Noah sent from the ark to find dry land after the Great Flood. The dove returned with an olive branch, signaling that the waters were receding.

stars_text: Lacaille gave 17 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Sigma in 1756, but omitted Zeta, Iota, and Xi, and labelled two stars as Nu and Pi. In 1879, Benjamin Gould added Xi Columbae.
α Col (Phact, 2.7m) is the brightest star, a blue-white star 268 light-years from Earth. The traditional Arabic name Phact means 'ring dove.'
β Col (Wazn, 3.1m) is an orange giant 87 light-years away.
μ Col is a notable runaway star in the constellation.
The constellation contains the solar antapex—the opposite to the net direction of the Solar System's motion.
deep_sky_objects: The globular cluster NGC 1851 appears in Columba at 7th magnitude. Located 39,000 light-years away in a far part of our galaxy, it is resolvable in medium-sized amateur telescopes under good conditions south of latitude +40° N.
exoplanets: Exoplanet NGTS-1b and its star NGTS-1 are located in Columba.

Com.name: Coma Berenices
Com.description: Coma Berenices is bordered by Boötes to the east, Canes Venatici to the north, Leo to the west and Virgo to the south. Covering 386.5 square degrees, it ranks 42nd of the 88 constellations by area. Its brightest star is Beta Comae Berenices (4.26m).

greek: Coma Berenices is the only modern constellation named for an historic figure. It was introduced to Western astronomy during the third century BC by Conon of Samos, the court astronomer of Egyptian ruler Ptolemy III Euergetes.

Berenice II, consort of Ptolemy III, vowed to sacrifice her long hair as a votive offering if Ptolemy returned safely from battle during the Third Syrian War. The sacrifice likely happened around March-June 245 BC.

According to legend, Berenice dedicated her tresses in the temple of Arsinoe II at Zephyrium. By the next morning the tresses had disappeared. Conon proposed that the goddess had placed them in the sky as an acknowledgement of Berenice's sacrifice.

Callimachus called the asterism plokamos Berenikēs or bostrukhon Berenikēs in Greek, translated into Latin as "Coma Berenices" by Catullus. Ptolemy did not include it among his 48 constellations in the Almagest, considering it part of Leo.
history: Coma Berenices became popular during the 16th century. In 1536 it appeared on a celestial globe by Caspar Vopel, who is credited with the asterism's designation as a constellation.
Tycho Brahe included it in his 1602 star catalogue. Brahe recorded fourteen stars in the constellation; Johannes Hevelius increased its number to twenty-one, and John Flamsteed to forty-three.
Coma Berenices and the now-obsolete Antinous are considered the first post-Ptolemaic constellations depicted on a celestial globe.
babylonian: Coma Berenices was known to the Akkadians as Ḫegala. In Babylonian astronomy a star tentatively considered part of Coma Berenices was known as ḪÉ.GÁL-a-a ("which is before it").
arab: In Arabic astronomy Coma Berenices was known as Al-Dafira الضفيرة ("braid"), Al-Hulba الهلبة and Al-Thu'aba الذؤابة (both meaning "tuft"). These formed the tuft of the constellation Leo.
Al-Sufi included it in Leo. Ulugh Beg regarded Al-Dafira as consisting of two stars, 7 and 23 Comae Berenices.
chinese: The North American Pawnee people depicted Coma Berenices as ten faint stars on a tanned elk-skin star map dated to at least the 17th century.
polynesian: The people of Tonga had four names for Coma Berenices: Fatana-lua, Fata-olunga, Fata-lalo and Kapakau-o-Tafahi.
The Boorong people called the constellation Tourt-chinboiong-gherra, and saw it as a small flock of birds drinking rainwater from a puddle in the crotch of a tree.

stars_text: β Com (4.26m) is the brightest star, a yellow-hued F-type main-sequence star (F9.5V) located 29.95 light-years away. A solar analog, it is 36% brighter and 15% more massive than the Sun, with a radius 10% larger.

α Com (Diadem, 4.3m) is a double star in the southeastern part of the constellation. Despite its Alpha designation, it is dimmer than Beta. The system has spectral classes of F5V and F6V, located 58.1 light-years from Earth.

γ Com (4.4m) is an orange-hued giant star (K1III) located 169 light-years away. It is the brightest star in the Coma Star Cluster. With Alpha and Beta, it forms a 45-degree isosceles triangle from which Berenice's imaginary tresses hang.

FK Comae Berenices is the prototype for the FK Comae Berenices class of variable stars. It varies from magnitude 8.14 to 8.33 over 2.4 days, and is the star in which the "flip-flop phenomenon" was discovered.
R Comae Berenices is a Mira variable with a maximum magnitude of almost 7. Over 200 variable stars are known in Coma Berenices, including 123 RR Lyrae variables, many in the M53 cluster.
deep_sky_objects: The Coma Star Cluster (Melotte 111) represents Berenice's sacrificed tresses. A large, diffuse open cluster of about 50 stars ranging between magnitudes 5 and 10, it is spread over more than five degrees near Gamma Comae Berenices, only 280 light-years away.

M53 (NGC 5024) is a magnitude-7.7 globular cluster 56,000 light-years from Earth. Discovered independently by Johann Elert Bode in 1775 and Charles Messier in February 1777, William Herschel was the first to resolve it into stars.
NGC 5053 is a globular cluster only 1° away from M53, with a sparser nucleus. Its total luminosity equals about 16,000 suns, one of the lowest luminosities of any globular cluster.

The Coma Supercluster contains the Coma and Leo Cluster of galaxies. The Coma Cluster (Abell 1656) is 230 to 300 million light-years away and one of the largest-known clusters, with at least 10,000 galaxies (mainly elliptical).
NGC 4889 is a giant elliptical galaxy with one of the largest-known black holes (21 billion solar masses). NGC 4921 is the cluster's brightest spiral galaxy.

After observing the Coma Cluster, Fritz Zwicky first postulated the existence of dark matter during the 1930s. The massive galaxy Dragonfly 44 discovered in 2015 consists almost entirely of dark matter.
NGC 4676 (Mice Galaxies) is a pair of interacting galaxies 300 million light-years from Earth. The name originates from huge tidal tails formed due to the spiral galaxies' original rotation.
Coma Berenices contains the northern portion of the Virgo Cluster, about 60 million light-years away, including six Messier galaxies: M85, M88, M91, M98, M99, and M100.

M64 (Black Eye Galaxy) is known for the prominent dark dust lane in front of its bright nucleus, located about 17.3 million light-years away. Interstellar gas in its outer regions rotates in the opposite direction from the inner regions.

M100 (NGC 4321) is a magnitude-nine spiral galaxy seen face-on, one of the cluster's brightest. Photographs reveal a brilliant core, two prominent spiral arms, an array of secondary arms and several dust lanes.
NGC 4565 (Needle Galaxy) is an edge-on spiral galaxy which appears superimposed on the Virgo Cluster. It has a prominent dust lane and a central bulge, with at least two satellite galaxies.
Malin 1 discovered in 1986 is the first-known giant low-surface-brightness galaxy. With UGC 1382, it is also one of the largest low-surface-brightness galaxies.

A dwarf galaxy named Coma Berenices was discovered in 2006 from Sloan Digital Sky Survey data. It is one of the faintest satellites of the Milky Way, with integrated luminosity about 3700 times that of the Sun.
meteor_showers_detail: The Coma Berenicids meteor shower peaks around 18 January. Despite the shower's low intensity (averaging one or two meteors per hour), its meteors are some of the fastest, with speeds up to 65 kilometers per second.

CrA.name: Corona Australis
CrA.description: Corona Australis is a small constellation bordered by Sagittarius to the north, Scorpius to the west, Telescopium to the south, and Ara to the southwest. Covering 128 square degrees, it ranks 80th in area. Its brightest star is Alfecca Meridiana (α CrA) (4.10m).

greek: Corona Australis was described by Greek astronomer Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD. Ascribing 13 stars to the constellation, he named it Στεφάνος νοτιος (Stephanos notios), "Southern Wreath".

Other authors associated it with either Sagittarius (having fallen off his head) or Centaurus. With Sagittarius, it was called Corona Sagittarii. The Romans called it the "Golden Crown of Sagittarius".

Corona Australis has been associated with the myth of Bacchus and Stimula. Jupiter had impregnated Stimula, causing Juno to become jealous. After Stimula's death, Bacchus honored his mother by placing a wreath in the sky.
history: The 18th-century French astronomer Jérôme Lalande gave it the names Sertum Australe ("Southern Garland") and Orbiculus Capitis.
German poet Philippus Caesius called it Corolla ("Little Crown") or Spira Australis ("Southern Coil"), and linked it to the Crown of Eternal Life from the New Testament.
Seventeenth-century celestial cartographer Julius Schiller linked it to the Diadem of Solomon. Sometimes it was depicted as arrows held in Sagittarius's hand.
babylonian: Corona Australis may have been recorded by ancient Mesopotamians in the MUL.APIN as MA.GUR ("The Bark"). This constellation, adjacent to the Goat-Fish (Capricornus), was one of the fifteen "stars of Ea".
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Corona Australis are located within the Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武). The constellation itself was known as ti'en pieh ("Heavenly Turtle").
During the Western Zhou period, it marked the beginning of winter. However, precession over time meant the Milky Way became the more accurate marker and supplanted the turtle.
arab: Arabic names for Corona Australis include Al Ķubbah "the Tortoise", Al Ĥibā "the Tent" or Al Udḥā al Na'ām "the Ostrich Nest".
It was later given the name Al Iklīl al Janūbiyyah, transliterated by European authors as Alachil Elgenubi, Elkleil Elgenubi and Aladil Algenubi.
african: The ǀXam speaking San people of South Africa knew the constellation as ≠nabbe ta !nu "house of branches"—owned originally by the Dassie (rock hyrax). The star pattern depicted people sitting in a semicircle around a fire.
polynesian: The indigenous Boorong people of northwestern Victoria saw it as Won, a boomerang thrown by Totyarguil (Altair).

The Aranda people of Central Australia saw Corona Australis as a coolamon carrying a baby, accidentally dropped to earth by sky-women dancing in the Milky Way. The impact created Gosses Bluff crater, 175 km west of Alice Springs.

Torres Strait Islanders saw Corona Australis as part of Tagai's canoe. Eta Sagittarii and Theta Corona Australis mark the bottom of the canoe. On Futuna, it was called Tanuma; in the Tuamotus, Na Kaua-ki-Tonga.

stars_text: α CrA (Alfecca Meridiana or Meridiana, 4.10m) is the only named star in the constellation. The name combines the Arabic name of the constellation with Latin for "southern". It is a white main sequence star (A2Va) 125 light-years away.

Alfecca is a rapidly rotating star, spinning at almost 200 km per second at its equator, completing a revolution in around 14 hours. Like Vega, it has excess infrared radiation indicating a dust disk.

β CrA (4.11m) is an orange giant (K0II) 474 light-years from Earth. It has evolved from a B-type to a K-type star, with luminosity 730 times that of the Sun. Alpha and Beta are indistinguishable in brightness to the naked eye.

γ CrA is a pair of yellowish white stars 58 light-years away, orbiting each other every 122 years. The two F8V dwarf stars can be separated with a 100 mm telescope; they have a combined magnitude of 4.2.

ε CrA is an eclipsing binary and W Ursae Majoris variable (F4VFe-0.8+). A contact binary, the component stars are so close they touch. It varies by 0.25 magnitude around 4.83 every seven hours, lying 98 light-years away.
RX J1856.5-3754 is an isolated neutron star thought to lie 460 light-years away with a diameter of 14 km. It was once suspected to be a strange star, but this has been discounted.
deep_sky_objects: The Corona Australis Molecular Cloud is a dark molecular cloud just north of Beta Coronae Australis. It contains 7000 solar masses and is one of the closest star-forming regions at 430 light-years.
The Coronet cluster (R CrA Cluster) lies at the center of the active star-forming region and is used in studying star and protoplanetary disk formation.

R Coronae Australis (R CrA) is an irregular variable star ranging from magnitudes 9.7 to 13.9. A very young B5IIIpe star, it is still accumulating interstellar material. It illuminates NGC 6729, which brightens and darkens with it.

TY Coronae Australis illuminates reflection nebula NGC 6726/NGC 6727. It ranges irregularly between magnitudes 8.7 and 12.4. The largest young stars (R, S, T, TY and VV CrA) all eject jets causing Herbig-Haro objects to form.
NGC 6723 is a globular cluster that appears adjacent to the nebulosity but is actually in Sagittarius and much farther away.

IC 1297 is a planetary nebula of magnitude 10.7 surrounding the variable star RU Coronae Australis. Only 7 arcseconds in diameter, it appears as a green-hued roundish object or "square with rounded edges".

NGC 6541 is a dense globular cluster halfway between Theta Coronae Australis and Theta Scorpii. Magnitude 6.3-6.6, it is visible in binoculars, around 22,000 light-years away and 100 light-years in diameter, estimated to be 14 billion years old.
meteor_showers_detail: The Corona Australids meteor shower takes place between 14 and 18 March each year, peaking around 16 March. The shower does not have a high peak hourly rate, typically 4-6 meteors per hour.

In 1992, astronomers detected a peak rate of 45 meteors per hour. The shower's duration is particularly short at only six days, and its meteoroids are small. Meteors have an entry velocity of 45 kilometers per second.
The Beta Coronae Australids appear in May, originating near Beta Coronae Australis. They were designated as a separate shower in 2006.

CrB.name: Corona Borealis
CrB.description: Corona Borealis is bordered by Boötes to the north and west, Serpens Caput to the south, and Hercules to the east. Covering 179 square degrees, it ranks 73rd of the 88 constellations by area. Its brightest star is Alphecca (α CrB) (2.21m).

greek: In Greek mythology, Corona Borealis was linked to the legend of Theseus and the minotaur. It was generally considered to represent a crown given by Dionysus to Ariadne, daughter of Minos of Crete, after she had been abandoned by Theseus.
When Ariadne wore the crown at her marriage to Dionysus, he placed it in the heavens to commemorate their wedding.

An alternative version has Dionysus give the crown to Ariadne, who gives it to Theseus after he arrives in Crete to kill the minotaur. The hero uses the crown's light to escape the labyrinth after disposing of the creature.
Corona Borealis was one of the 48 constellations mentioned in the Almagest of classical astronomer Ptolemy.
babylonian: In Mesopotamia, Corona Borealis was associated with the goddess Nanaya.
welsh: In Welsh mythology, it was called Caer Arianrhod, "the Castle of the Silver Circle", and was the heavenly abode of the Lady Arianrhod.
baltic: To the ancient Balts, Corona Borealis was known as Darželis, the "flower garden".
arab: The Arabs called the constellation Alphecca (later given to Alpha Coronae Borealis), meaning "separated" or "broken up" (الفكة al-Fakkah), referring to the resemblance to a loose string of jewels or broken dish.
Among the Bedouins, it was known as qaṣʿat al-masākīn (قصعة المساكين), "the dish/bowl of the poor people".
native_american: The Skidi people saw the stars representing a council of stars whose chief was Polaris. The constellation also symbolized the smokehole over a fireplace, which conveyed messages to the gods.

The Shawnee people saw the stars as the Heavenly Sisters, who descended from the sky every night to dance on earth. Alphecca signifies the youngest and most comely sister, seized by a hunter who transformed into a field mouse.
The Mi'kmaq of eastern Canada saw Corona Borealis as Mskegwǒm, the den of the celestial bear (Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Delta Ursae Majoris).
polynesian: Polynesian peoples often recognized Corona Borealis. It was named Na Kaua-ki-tokerau in the Tuamotus, Kaua-mea in Hawaii, Rangawhenua in New Zealand, and Te Wale-o-Awitu in the Cook Islands atoll of Pukapuka.
In Tonga it was either called Ao-o-Uvea or Kau-kupenga.
aboriginal: In Australian Aboriginal astronomy, it is called womera ("the boomerang") due to the shape of the stars.
The Wailwun people of northwestern New South Wales saw it as mullion wollai "eagle's nest", with Altair and Vega as the pair of eagles accompanying it.
The Wardaman people of northern Australia held it to be a gathering point for Men's Law, Women's Law and Law of both sexes to consider matters of existence.

stars_text: α CrB (Alphecca or Gemma, 2.21m) is the brightest star, a blue-white Algol-type eclipsing binary that varies by 0.1 magnitude with a period of 17.4 days. Lying 75 light-years from Earth, it is believed to be a member of the Ursa Major Moving Group.

The primary is a white main-sequence star (A0V) that is 2.91 times the mass of the Sun and 57 times as luminous, surrounded by a debris disk out to around 60 AU. The secondary is a yellow main-sequence star (G5V) a little smaller than the Sun.

β CrB (Nusakan, 4.3m) is a spectroscopic binary 112 light-years away whose components orbit each other every 10.5 years. The brighter component is a rapidly oscillating Ap star, pulsating with a period of 16.2 minutes.

γ CrB is a binary star system whose components orbit each other every 92.94 years and are roughly as far apart as the Sun and Neptune. The brighter component has been classed as a Delta Scuti variable. The components are main sequence stars of spectral types B9V and A3V.

δ CrB (4.06m) is a yellow giant (G3.5III) 170 light-years away that is around 2.4 solar masses and has swollen to 7.4 solar radii. It has just crossed the Hertzsprung gap, having finished burning core hydrogen.

T Coronae Borealis (the Blaze Star) is a cataclysmic variable star. Normally magnitude 10, it brightens to magnitude 2 in hours due to nuclear reaction and explosion. Outbursts occurred in 1866 and February 1946.
T CrB dimmed in March 2023 and was expected to go nova between March and September 2024. It is a recurrent nova with a red giant primary and white dwarf secondary, orbiting every 8 months.

R Coronae Borealis is a yellow variable supergiant over 7000 light-years away, prototype of the R Coronae Borealis variables. Normally magnitude 6, it periodically drops to magnitude 15 as ejected dust obscures it.
S Coronae Borealis is a Mira-type variable ranging between magnitudes 5.8 and 14.1 over 360 days. Located around 1946 light-years distant, it shines with 16,643 times the Sun's luminosity at 3033 K.

V Coronae Borealis is one of the reddest stars in the sky with a surface temperature of 2877 K. It shines with 102,831 times the Sun's luminosity and is 8810 light-years distant, varying between magnitudes 6.9 and 12.6 over 357 days.
deep_sky_objects: Corona Borealis contains few galaxies observable with amateur telescopes. NGC 6085 and 6086 are a faint spiral and elliptical galaxy close enough to be seen in the same visual field.
Abell 2142 is a huge (six million light-year diameter), X-ray luminous galaxy cluster resulting from an ongoing merger. It has a redshift of 0.0909 and is about 1.2 billion light-years away.

RX J1532.9+3021 is a galaxy cluster approximately 3.9 billion light-years from Earth. At its center is a large elliptical galaxy containing one of the most massive and powerful supermassive black holes yet discovered.
Abell 2065 is a highly concentrated galaxy cluster containing more than 400 members, the brightest 16th magnitude, over one billion light-years from Earth.
Abell 2065, along with Abell 2061, 2067, 2079, 2089, and 2092, make up the Corona Borealis Supercluster.

Crv.name: Corvus
Crv.description: Corvus is bordered by Virgo to the north and east, Hydra to the south, and Crater to the west. Covering 184 square degrees, it ranks 70th of the 88 constellations in area. Its brightest star is Gienah (γ Crv) (2.59m).

babylonian: In Babylonian star catalogues dating from at least 1100 BCE, Corvus was called the Raven (MUL.UGA.MUSHEN). It was placed sitting on the tail of the Serpent (Greek Hydra).
The Babylonian constellation was sacred to Adad, the god of rain and storm. In the second Millennium BCE it would have risen just before the autumnal rainy season.
John H. Rogers proposed that Corvus and Crater (along with Hydra) were death symbols and marked the gate to the underworld. Corvus and Crater featured in the iconography of Mithraism.
greek: Corvus is associated with the myth of Apollo and his lover Coronis the Lapith. When Apollo learned from a pure white crow (or raven called Lycius) that Coronis had been unfaithful, he turned its feathers black in a fit of rage.

Another legend tells that a crow stopped on his way to fetch water for Apollo to eat figs. Instead of telling the truth, he lied that a snake (Hydra) kept him from the water, holding a snake in his talons as proof.

Apollo, realizing this was a lie, flung the crow (Corvus), cup (Crater), and snake (Hydra) into the sky. He punished the bird by ensuring it would forever be thirsty, with the Cup just out of reach in the heavens.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Corvus are located within the Vermilion Bird of the South (南方朱雀, Nán Fāng Zhū Què). The four main stars depict a chariot, Zhen, the 28th and final lunar mansion.
Alpha and Eta mark the linchpins for the wheels, and Zeta is Changsha, a coffin.
indian: In Indian astronomy, the five main stars of Corvus represent a hand or fist corresponding to the Hasta, the 13th nakshatra or lunar mansion.
polynesian: Corvus was recognized by several Polynesian cultures and used as a guide for ocean navigation. In the Marquesas Islands, it was called Mee; in Pukapuka, Te Manu; and in the Society Islands, Metua-ai-papa.
To Torres Strait Islanders, Corvus was the right hand (holding kupa fruit) of the huge constellation Tagai, a man fishing.
south_american: The Bororo people of Mato Grosso in central Brazil regarded the constellation as a land tortoise Geriguigui, while the Tucano people of the northwestern Amazon saw it as an egret.
To the Tupi people of São Luís Island in Brazil, Corvus might have been seen as a grill or barbecue—seychouioura, on which fish were grilled.

stars_text: γ Crv (Gienah, 2.59m) is the brightest star in Corvus. Its name means "wing", marking the left wing in Bayer's Uranometria. 154 light-years from Earth, it is a blue-white giant (B8III) that is 4.2 times as massive and 355 times as luminous as the Sun.

Gienah is around 160 million years old and has largely exhausted its core hydrogen. It is a binary star with a companion orange or red dwarf (K5V to M5V) about 0.8 solar masses, orbiting in 158 years at about 50 AU.

δ Crv (Algorab, 2.9m) is a double star divisible in small telescopes. The primary is a blue-white star (A0IV) around 87 light-years away, 2.7 times as massive as the Sun. Its common name means "the raven", marking the right wing.

Delta Corvi is an enigmatic star—either a 3.2 million year-old very young pre-main sequence star, or a 260-million-year-old star that has begun to exhaust its core hydrogen. Warm circumstellar dust has been detected around both components.

β Crv (Kraz, 2.7m) marks the raven's breast, a yellow bright giant (G5II) 146 light-years away. Roughly 206 million years old and 3.7 times as massive as the Sun, it spent most of its existence as a blue-white main sequence star.

ε Crv (Minkar, 3.0m) marks the raven's nostril, a red giant (K2III) 318 light-years away. It is around 54 times the Sun's radius and 930 times its luminosity. Around 4 times as massive as the Sun, it spent much of its life as a B5V main-sequence star.

α Crv (Alchiba, 4.0m) is a white-hued star (F1V) 48.7 light-years from Earth. It is likely a pulsating Gamma Doradus-type variable estimated to be 1.39 times as massive as the Sun. It lies above the bird's beak.
