η Crv (4.3m) marks the raven's right wing, a yellow-white main-sequence star (F2V) 59 light-years distant. Two debris disks have been detected orbiting it, one warm within 3.5 AU and another at ~150 AU.

31 Crateris (5.26m) is a remote binary star system that was once mistaken for a moon of Mercury. On 27 March 1974, Mariner 10 detected emissions that were found to emanate from this star. The primary is around 15.5 times as massive as the Sun and 52,262 times as luminous.
deep_sky_objects: Corvus contains no Messier objects. It has several galaxies and a planetary nebula observable with amateur telescopes.
NGC 4361 is a planetary nebula at the center of Corvus with magnitude 10.3. The nebula resembles a small elliptical galaxy, but the magnitude 13 star at its center gives away its true nature.

The Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038 and 4039) consist of two interacting galaxies that appear to have a heart shape from Earth. The name originates from huge tidal tails formed due to the spiral galaxies' original rotation.

Both galaxies are experiencing extensive star formation due to the interaction of gas clouds. Located 45 million light-years from Earth, each has multiple ultraluminous X-ray sources. They appear in a telescope at 10th magnitude.

SN 2004gt was a type Ic supernova that erupted on December 12, 2004 in the Antennae. The progenitor was either a type WC Wolf-Rayet star with a mass over 40 times that of the Sun, or a star 20-40 times as massive in a binary system.

NGC 4027 (Ringtail Galaxy) is a member of the NGC 4038 group, notable for its extended spiral arm. A barred spiral galaxy, its distorted shape is probably due to a past collision, possibly with nearby NGC 4027A.
NGC 4782 and NGC 4783 are a pair of merging elliptical galaxies in the northeastern part of the constellation, around 200 million light-years distant.
meteor_showers_detail: German astronomer Cuno Hoffmeister discovered and named the Corvids in 1937, after observing them between June 25 and July 2. They have not been seen since, nor was there evidence when previous records were examined.
The shower's trajectory was similar to comet 11P/Tempel-Swift-LINEAR, though not confirmed. The shower has been tentatively linked with 4015 Wilson-Harrington.
The Eta Corvids were discovered by the MO Video Meteor Network in January 2013, with some 300 meteors seen between January 20 and 26. Their existence was confirmed by data analysis later that year.

Crt.name: Crater
Crt.description: Crater is bordered by Leo, Sextans, Hydra, Corvus, and Virgo. It covers 282 square degrees, ranking 53rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is δ Crateris (3.57m). The constellation represents the cup of Apollo.

babylonian: In Babylonian star catalogues dating from at least 1100 BC, the stars of Crater were possibly incorporated with those of Corvus in the Babylonian Raven (MUL.UGA.MUSHEN).
John H. Rogers proposed that Corvus and Crater (along with Hydra) were death symbols and marked the gate to the underworld. Corvus and Crater also featured in the iconography of Mithraism.
greek: Crater is identified with a story from Greek mythology in which a crow or raven serves Apollo, and is sent to fetch water, but it delays its journey as it finds some figs and waits for them to ripen.
The crow retrieves the water in a cup and takes back a water snake, blaming it for drinking the water. Apollo saw through the fraud, and angrily cast the crow, cup, and snake into the sky.
The three constellations were arranged so that the crow was prevented from drinking from the cup, seen as a warning against sinning against the gods.
Phylarchus wrote of a different origin. The city of Eleusa near Troy was beset by plague. Its ruler Demophon consulted an oracle which decreed that a maiden should be sacrificed each year.

Nobleman Mastusius objected to Demophon's exclusion of his own daughters from the lottery. Later, Mastusius killed Demophon's daughters and tricked the ruler into drinking a cup containing a mixture of their blood and wine.
Upon discovering the deed, the king ordered Mastusius and the cup to be thrown into the sea. Crater signifies this cup.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Crater are located within the Vermillion Bird of the South. They depict, along with some stars from Hydra, Yi, the Red Bird's wings.
Yi also denotes the 27th lunar mansion. Alternatively, Yi depicts a heroic bowman with his bow composed of other stars in Hydra.
polynesian: In the Society Islands, Crater was recognized as a constellation called Moana-'ohu-noa-'ei-ha'a-moe-hara ("vortex-ocean-in-which-to-lose-crime").

stars_text: δ Crt (Alkes, 3.6m) is the brightest star in Crater, an orange giant K0III located 163 light-years away. It has expanded to 22.4 times the Sun's radius and radiates 171 times the Sun's luminosity at 4,408 K.
α Crt (Alkes, 4.1m) is an orange-hued star 141 light-years away. With 1.75 solar masses, it has expanded to 13.2 times the Sun's diameter, shining with 69 times its luminosity at 4,600 K.
β Crt (4.5m) is a binary star system 296 light-years away, consisting of a white giant A1III and a white dwarf DA1.4 that cannot be resolved even by the Hubble Space Telescope.

γ Crt (4.1m) is a double star resolvable in small amateur telescopes, 85.6 light-years away. The primary is a white A7V main sequence star 1.81 solar masses, while the secondary (9.6m) is likely an orange dwarf with 75% the Sun's mass.
ε Crt (3.6m) is a K5III giant marking the Cup's rim, 366 light-years away. It has the Sun's mass but has expanded to 44.7 solar radii, radiating 391 times the Sun's luminosity.
ζ Crt (4.95m) is a binary system 326 light-years away. The primary is a G8III red clump star that has expanded to 13 solar radii and shines with 157 times the Sun's luminosity.
R Crt is a semiregular variable star of type SRb ranging from magnitude 9.8 to 11.2 over 160 days, located 770 light-years away.
TT Crt is a cataclysmic variable composed of a white dwarf and an orange K5V dwarf orbiting every 6 hours 26 minutes. It ranges from magnitude 15.9 when quiescent to 12.7 in outburst.
deep_sky_objects: The Crater 2 dwarf is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, located approximately 380,000 light-years from the Sun.
NGC 3511 is a spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on at magnitude 11.0, located 2° west of Beta Crateris.
NGC 3513 is a barred spiral galaxy located 11' from NGC 3511.
NGC 3981 is a spiral galaxy with two wide and perturbed spiral arms. It is a member of the NGC 4038 Group, part of the Crater Cloud of 45 galaxies within the Virgo Supercluster.
RX J1131 is a quasar located 6 billion light-years away. The black hole in its center was the first black hole whose spin has ever been directly measured.
GRB 011211 was a gamma-ray burst detected on December 11, 2001. The burst lasted 270 seconds, making it the longest burst detected by BeppoSAX up to that point.
GRB 030323 lasted 26 seconds and was detected on March 23, 2003.
meteor_showers_detail: The Eta Craterids are a faint meteor shower that takes place between January 11 and 22, peaking around January 16 and 17, near Eta Crateris.

Cru.name: Crux
Cru.description: Crux is the smallest of the 88 constellations, covering just 68 square degrees. It is bordered by Centaurus (on three sides) and Musca to the south. Its brightest star is Acrux (α Crucis) at magnitude 0.87. Known as the Southern Cross, it is a prominent navigational asterism in the Southern Hemisphere.

greek: The bright stars in Crux were known to the Ancient Greeks, where Ptolemy regarded them as part of the constellation Centaurus. They were entirely visible as far north as Britain in the fourth millennium BC.
By 400 AD, precession of the equinoxes had lowered the stars below the European horizon, and they were forgotten by northern inhabitants.
Dante may have known about the constellation in the 14th century, as he describes an asterism of four bright stars in the southern sky in his Divine Comedy.
history: Venetian navigator Alvise Cadamosto in 1455 made note of what was probably the Southern Cross on exiting the Gambia River, calling it the carro dell'ostro ("southern chariot").

João Faras was the first European to depict it correctly. He sketched and described the constellation (calling it "las guardas") in a letter written on the beaches of Brazil on May 1, 1500 to the Portuguese monarch.
Explorer Amerigo Vespucci seems to have observed the Southern Cross and the neighboring Coalsack Nebula on his second voyage in 1501-1502.
Andrea Corsali, an Italian navigator, wrote a letter in 1516 describing his observations of the southern sky, including a crude map of the stars around the south celestial pole.

Petrus Plancius and Jodocus Hondius first showed Crux in its correct position on celestial globes in 1598 and 1600. Its stars were first catalogued separately from Centaurus by Frederick de Houtman in 1603.
indian: In India, a story relates the creation of Trishanku Swarga (त्रिशंकु), meaning Cross (Crux), created by Sage Vishwamitra.
chinese: In Chinese, 十字架 (Shí Zì Jià), meaning Cross, refers to an asterism consisting of γ Crucis, α Crucis, β Crucis, and δ Crucis.
aboriginal: In Australian Aboriginal astronomy, Crux and the Coalsack mark the head of the Emu in the Sky in several Aboriginal cultures.

Crux itself is said to be a possum sitting in a tree (Boorong people of Victoria), a representation of the sky deity Mirrabooka (Quandamooka people), a stingray (Yolngu people), or an eagle (Kaurna people).
Torres Strait Islanders saw Gamma Centauri as the handle and the four stars as the left hand of Tagai, with the stars of Musca as the trident of his fishing spear.
In Aranda traditions of central Australia, the four Cross stars are the talon of an eagle and Gamma Centauri as its leg.
polynesian: The Māori name for the Southern Cross is Māhutonga and it is thought of as the anchor (Te Punga) of Tama-rereti's waka (the Milky Way), while the Pointers are its rope.
In Tonga it is known as Toloa ("duck"); depicted as a duck flying south, with one wing (δ Crucis) wounded because Ongo tangata ("two men", α and β Centauri) threw a stone at it.
In Samoa the constellation is called Sumu ("triggerfish") because of its rhomboid shape, while α and β Centauri are called Luatagata (Two Men).
south_american: In Mapudungun, the language of Patagonian Mapuches, the Southern Cross is Melipal, which means "four stars".
In Quechua, the language of the Inca civilization, Crux is known as "Chakana", which means literally "stair" but carries deep symbolism within Quechua mysticism.
The Mocovi people of Argentina saw a rhea including the stars of Crux. Their rhea is attacked by two dogs, represented by bright stars in Centaurus and Circinus.
The Kalapalo people of Brazil saw the stars of Crux as Aganagi angry bees having emerged from the Coalsack, which they saw as the beehive.
african: Among Tuaregs, the four most visible stars of Crux are considered iggaren, four Maerua crassifolia trees.
The Tswana people of Botswana saw the constellation as Dithutlwa, two giraffes – Alpha and Beta Crucis forming a male, and Gamma and Delta forming the female.

stars_text: α Cru (Acrux, 0.8m) is the brightest star, a triple star 321 light-years from Earth. Blue in color, it has two close components of magnitudes 1.3 and 1.8, plus a much wider fifth magnitude component.
β Cru (Mimosa, 1.3m) is a blue giant star 353 light-years away. It is a Beta Cephei-type variable star with a variation of less than 0.1 magnitudes.
γ Cru (Gacrux, 1.6m) is an optical double star. The primary is a red giant 88 light-years away, one of the closest red giants to Earth. Its secondary component is magnitude 6.5, 264 light-years away.
δ Cru (Imai, 2.8m) is a blue-white star about 345 light-years from Earth. Like Mimosa, it is a Beta Cepheid variable.
ε Cru (Ginan, 3.6m) is an orange giant star 228 light-years from Earth, often included with the Southern Cross as a fifth star.
ι Cru (4.6m) is a visual double star 125 light-years away. The primary is an orange giant and the secondary is magnitude 9.5.
μ Cru (μ1,2 Cru, 4.0m and 5.1m) is a wide double star where the components are about 370 light-years from Earth. Both are blue-white and easily divisible in small telescopes or large binoculars.
BG Cru is a Cepheid variable ranging from magnitude 5.34 to 5.58 over 3.34 days.
BH Cru (Welch's Red Variable) is a Mira variable ranging from magnitude 6.6 to 9.8 over 530 days. It has become redder and brighter since its discovery in 1969.
deep_sky_objects: The Coalsack Nebula lies partially within Crux and partly in Musca and Centaurus. It is the most prominent dark nebula in the skies, easily visible to the naked eye as a prominent dark patch in the southern Milky Way.

The Jewel Box Cluster (NGC 4755, Caldwell 94) is an open cluster near β Crucis. At magnitude 4.2, it contains about 100 stars including several red supergiants and blue supergiants, creating a "casket of variously colored precious stones."
NGC 4349 is an open cluster located 2° east-southeast of γ Crucis, containing about 40 stars scattered over 16 arcminutes.
The Crux OB1 association is a stellar association in the southern Milky Way, containing many young hot blue stars.
HD 106906 is a binary star system 336 light-years away that hosts the planet HD 106906 b, which has one of the widest known planetary orbits at 650 AU.
The Southern Cross is backlit by the multitude of stars of the Scutum-Crux Arm of the Milky Way, the main inner arm in the local radial quarter of the galaxy.
meteor_showers_detail: The Crucids meteor shower is associated with comet 107P/Wilson-Harrington and can produce outbursts of activity.

Cyg.name: Cygnus
Cyg.description: Cygnus is bordered by Cepheus, Draco, Lyra, Vulpecula, Pegasus, and Lacerta. It covers 804 square degrees, ranking 16th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Deneb (α Cygni) at magnitude 1.25. The constellation represents a swan flying along the Milky Way.

greek: In Greek mythology, Cygnus has been associated with several different swan legends. The most common is that the constellation represents Orpheus, who was murdered by the Bacchantes of Thrace and transformed into a swan.
Another story identifies Cygnus with the son of Ares who was transformed into a swan. Zeus placed him among the stars after his death.
A third legend tells of Zeus disguising himself as a swan to seduce Leda, the Queen of Sparta. This union produced Helen of Troy and Polydeuces.
Yet another myth identifies Cygnus with Cycnus, a close friend of Phaethon. When Phaethon died, Cycnus mourned so deeply that he was transformed into a swan and placed in the sky.
The constellation was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the 2nd century and has remained one of the 88 modern constellations.
babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, Cygnus was known as the Forest Bird.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Cygnus are found in two different areas. Deneb is located in the Black Tortoise of the North.
The Chinese name for Deneb is Tiān Jīn (天津), meaning "Celestial Ford" or "Ford in the Milky Way."
Cygnus also plays a role in the Qixi Festival legend, where it represents part of the bridge formed by magpies allowing the separated lovers Niulang and Zhinu to meet once a year.
polynesian: In Polynesian astronomy, Cygnus was called Manu ("bird").
hindu: In Hindu astronomy, Cygnus corresponds to Brahma Muhurta, a sacred time period before dawn.

stars_text: α Cyg (Deneb, 1.25m) is the brightest star, a white supergiant A2Ia located approximately 2,600 light-years away. It is one of the most luminous stars known, with 196,000 times the Sun's luminosity.
Deneb forms the Summer Triangle asterism with Vega in Lyra and Altair in Aquila. It also marks the tail of the swan and the top of the Northern Cross asterism.

β Cyg (Albireo, 3.1m) is a beautiful double star 380 light-years away, appearing as a golden star and blue companion when viewed through a telescope. It is considered one of the finest double stars in the sky.
γ Cyg (Sadr, 2.2m) is a yellow-white supergiant F8Ib located 1,800 light-years away. It marks the center of the Northern Cross and the swan's breast.
δ Cyg (2.9m) is a blue-white giant star forming part of the Northern Cross pattern.
ε Cyg (Gienah, 2.5m) is an orange giant K0III star 72 light-years away, marking one of the wings of the swan.
61 Cyg is a binary star system just 11.4 light-years away. It was the first star to have its distance measured by parallax (by Friedrich Bessel in 1838).

Cygnus X-1 is one of the strongest X-ray sources in the sky and was the first widely accepted black hole candidate. The system contains a supergiant star orbiting a compact object with 14.8 solar masses.
χ Cyg is a Mira-type variable star ranging from magnitude 3.3 to 14.2 over a period of 409 days.
P Cyg is a luminous blue variable star surrounded by a nebula, giving rise to the "P Cygni profile" seen in many astronomical spectra.
deep_sky_objects: M39 (NGC 7092) is an open cluster of magnitude 4.6, located 825 light-years away. It contains about 30 stars spread over a degree of sky.
M29 (NGC 6913) is a small open cluster near γ Cygni, magnitude 6.6, containing about 50 stars.
The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) is a large emission nebula near Deneb, resembling the shape of North America. It is visible in binoculars under dark skies.
The Pelican Nebula (IC 5070) neighbors the North America Nebula and is part of the same large cloud of hydrogen gas.
The Veil Nebula (NGC 6960, 6979, 6992, 6995) is a large supernova remnant about 1,500 light-years away. It is the remains of a star that exploded 5,000 to 8,000 years ago.
The Crescent Nebula (NGC 6888, Caldwell 27) is an emission nebula about 5,000 light-years away, formed by the fast stellar wind from the Wolf-Rayet star WR 136.
The Blinking Planetary Nebula (NGC 6826) is a planetary nebula that appears to blink on and off when viewed through a telescope due to averted vision effects.
The Fireworks Galaxy (NGC 6946, Caldwell 12) is a spiral galaxy on the border with Cepheus. It has had 10 observed supernovae, more than any other galaxy.
Cygnus A is one of the strongest radio sources in the sky. It is a supermassive black hole at the center of a giant elliptical galaxy 600 million light-years away.
The Cygnus OB2 association is one of the largest regions of star formation within 2,000 light-years, containing over 2,600 massive stars.
meteor_showers_detail: The October Cygnids are an annual meteor shower active from late September to early October, with a peak around October 10.
The Kappa Cygnids are a minor meteor shower active in mid-to-late August.

Del.name: Delphinus
Del.description: Delphinus is bordered by Vulpecula, Sagitta, Aquila, Aquarius, Equuleus, and Pegasus. It covers 189 square degrees, ranking 69th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Rotanev (β Delphini) at magnitude 3.63. The constellation is small but distinctive, resembling a dolphin.

greek: In Greek mythology, Delphinus is associated with the story of Arion of Lesbos, a famous poet and musician. When Arion was thrown overboard by pirates, a dolphin that had been charmed by his music carried him safely to shore.
Another Greek legend tells that Poseidon wanted to marry the sea nymph Amphitrite, but she fled from him. Poseidon sent messengers to find her, including the dolphin Delphinus.
Delphinus found Amphitrite hiding in the Atlas Mountains and convinced her to marry Poseidon. As a reward, Poseidon placed the dolphin among the stars.
The constellation was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the 2nd century.
history: The constellation's two brightest stars, α and β Delphini, have the unusual names Sualocin and Rotanev. When reversed, they spell "Nicolaus Venator," the Latinized name of Nicolaus Cacciatore.
Cacciatore was the assistant to astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi at the Palermo Observatory. He named the stars after himself in a star catalog published in 1814, and the names stuck.
arab: In Arabic astronomy, Delphinus was known as al-Dulfim ("the dolphin").
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Delphinus are located within the Black Tortoise of the North.
The main stars form the asterism called Féi (螣), meaning "Flying Serpent" or "Soaring Serpent."

stars_text: β Del (Rotanev, 3.63m) is the brightest star, a binary star system 97 light-years away. The primary is an F5III giant and the secondary is an F5IV subgiant orbiting every 26.7 years.
α Del (Sualocin, 3.8m) is a multiple star system 241 light-years away. The primary is a blue-white B9IV subgiant.
γ Del (4.3m) is a binary star system 101 light-years away. The primary is a K1IV orange subgiant and the secondary is an F7V yellow-white dwarf.
δ Del (4.4m) is a white A7IIIp star 230 light-years away.
ε Del (4.0m) is a blue-white B6III giant star 359 light-years away.
The asterism known as "Job's Coffin" is formed by the four main stars α, β, γ, and δ Delphini, creating a distinctive diamond shape.
R Del is a Mira-type variable star ranging from magnitude 7.6 to 13.8 over a period of 285 days.
U Del is a semiregular variable star ranging from magnitude 5.6 to 7.5.
HR Delphini (Nova Delphini 1967) was a nova that appeared in 1967, reaching magnitude 3.5 at its peak.
Rho Aquilae is technically in Delphinus despite its name, a white A2Vn star 154 light-years away.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6891 is a planetary nebula of magnitude 10.5, located 7,200 light-years away. It has a blue-green color and a somewhat irregular shape.
NGC 6934 (Caldwell 47) is a globular cluster of magnitude 8.9, located 50,000 light-years away. It contains about 250,000 stars.
NGC 7006 is a distant globular cluster of magnitude 10.6, located 135,000 light-years away, making it one of the most remote globular clusters in the Milky Way's halo.
NGC 6905 (the Blue Flash Nebula) is a planetary nebula of magnitude 11.1, appearing as a small elliptical disk.
NGC 6928 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 13.9, part of a small group of galaxies.
The Delphinus Dwarf galaxy is a faint dwarf spheroidal galaxy discovered in 1999, a satellite of the Milky Way.

Dor.name: Dorado
Dor.description: Dorado is bordered by Caelum, Horologium, Reticulum, Hydrus, Mensa, Volans, and Pictor. It covers 179 square degrees, ranking 72nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Doradus (3.27m). The constellation contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

history: Dorado was created by Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the late 16th century. It first appeared on a 35-centimeter diameter celestial globe published by Petrus Plancius in 1598.
The constellation was created to represent the dolphinfish (Coryphaena hippurus), also known as mahi-mahi or dorado, a large tropical fish.
Unlike most constellations based on ancient Greek or Roman mythology, Dorado is one of the modern constellations created during the Age of Exploration.
Johann Bayer included Dorado in his 1603 star atlas Uranometria, cementing its place among the recognized constellations.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Dorado were not traditionally recognized as a constellation, as they are too far south to be visible from China.

stars_text: α Dor (3.27m) is the brightest star, a white A0IIIp giant 169 light-years away. It is a chemically peculiar star with abnormal abundances of certain elements.
β Dor (3.5m) is a yellow-white F5II bright giant or supergiant 1,040 light-years away. It is a Cepheid variable star ranging from magnitude 3.46 to 4.08 over 9.84 days.
γ Dor (4.2m) is a yellow-white F1V star 66 light-years away. It is the prototype of the Gamma Doradus variable stars, which pulsate due to internal gravity waves.
δ Dor (4.3m) is a white A7V main sequence star 145 light-years away.
ζ Dor (4.7m) is a yellow-white F7V star 38 light-years away.
S Dor is one of the most luminous stars known. It is a luminous blue variable in the Large Magellanic Cloud, about 169,000 light-years away, with a luminosity of about 1 million times the Sun.
R Dor is a red giant Mira variable in the Large Magellanic Cloud, ranging from magnitude 4.8 to 6.6 over 338 days.
HE 0437-5439 is a hypervelocity star traveling at 723 km/s, fast enough to escape the Milky Way's gravitational pull.
AB Doradus is a young quadruple star system 49 light-years away, about 50-150 million years old.
deep_sky_objects: The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is the most prominent deep-sky object in Dorado. At 160,000 light-years away, it is the third-closest galaxy to the Milky Way and the fourth-largest in the Local Group.
The LMC is a dwarf irregular galaxy spanning about 14,000 light-years in diameter, containing roughly 30 billion stars. It is visible to the naked eye as a faint cloud in the southern sky.

SN 1987A was a supernova that occurred in the LMC, visible to the naked eye. It was the closest observed supernova since Kepler's supernova in 1604 and provided unprecedented insights into stellar explosions.

The Tarantula Nebula (NGC 2070, 30 Doradus) is the most active star-forming region in the Local Group. Located in the LMC, it would cast shadows on Earth if placed at the distance of the Orion Nebula.
NGC 1566 (the Spanish Dancer Galaxy) is a spiral galaxy 38 million light-years away, magnitude 9.4. It is one of the brightest Seyfert galaxies and a beautiful face-on spiral.
NGC 1672 is a barred spiral galaxy 49 million light-years away, magnitude 10.3. Its bar structure drives gas into the nuclear regions, fueling star formation.
NGC 2080 (the Ghost Head Nebula) is an emission nebula in the LMC, featuring two bright regions resembling eyes.
NGC 1851 is a globular cluster magnitude 7.3, located 39,000 light-years away. It contains two distinct stellar populations.
NGC 1755 is an open cluster in the LMC, about 120 million years old.
The LMC X-1 is a high-mass X-ray binary containing a stellar-mass black hole, one of the first stellar black holes to be discovered.

Dra.name: Draco
Dra.description: Draco is bordered by Boötes, Hercules, Lyra, Cygnus, Cepheus, Ursa Minor, Camelopardalis and Ursa Major. It covers 1,083 square degrees, ranking 8th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Eltanin (γ Dra) (2.24m).

greek: Draco is one of the 48 constellations listed in Ptolemy's Almagest (2nd century), adopted from the list by Eudoxus of Cnidus (4th century BC). In ancient Greek it was called Ophis, meaning 'serpent'.

Gaius Julius Hyginus in De Astronomica reports that it was one of the Gigantes, who battled the Olympian gods for ten years in the Gigantomachy. The goddess Athena killed the dragon and tossed it into the sky upon his defeat.
As Athena threw the dragon, it became twisted on itself and froze at the cold north celestial pole before it could right itself. Aelius Aristides names him Aster or Asterius ('star' or 'starry').
Athens' Great Panathenaea festival celebrated Athena's victory over the dragon. The festival coincided with the culmination of the constellation's head as seen from the Athenian Acropolis.

The Catasterismi attributed to Eratosthenes identify Draco as Ladon, the dragon who guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides. When Heracles was tasked with stealing the golden apples during his twelve labors, he killed Ladon.
Hera transformed Ladon into a constellation. In the sky, Hercules is depicted with one foot on the head of Draco. Sometimes, Draco is represented as the monstrous son of Gaia, Typhon.
arab: Traditional Arabic astronomy does not depict a dragon in modern-day Draco, which is called the Mother Camels. Instead, two hyenas, represented by Eta Draconis and Zeta Draconis are seen attacking a baby camel (a dim star near Beta Draconis).

The baby camel is protected by four female camels, represented by Beta Draconis, Gamma Draconis, Nu Draconis, and Xi Draconis. The nomads who own the camels are camped nearby, represented by a cooking tripod composed of Upsilon, Tau, and Sigma Draconis.

Arabic astronomers also knew of the Greek interpretation of the constellation, referring to it in Arabic as At-Tinnin (التنين, 'the dragon'). This is the source of the formal name of Gamma Draconis, Eltanin, from raʾs al-tinnīn ('the head of the dragon').

stars_text: α Dra (Thuban, 3.7m) was the northern pole star from 3942 BC until 1793 BC. The Egyptian Pyramids were designed with an entrance passage geometrically aligned so that Thuban would be visible at night. Due to precession, it will again be the pole star around AD 21000. It is a blue-white giant 309 light-years from Earth. The name Thuban means 'head of the serpent'.
γ Dra (Eltanin, 2.2m) is the brightest star in Draco, an orange giant 148 light-years from Earth. The aberration of starlight was discovered in 1728 when James Bradley observed Gamma Draconis.
β Dra (Rastaban, 2.8m) is a yellow giant 362 light-years from Earth. Its name shares a meaning with Thuban, 'head of the serpent'.
η Dra (Athebyne) is a double star with a yellow-hued primary of magnitude 2.8 and a white-hued secondary of magnitude 8.2, separated by 4.8 arcseconds.
μ Dra (Alrakis) is a binary star with two white components of magnitude 5.6 and 5.7. The two components orbit each other every 670 years. The system is 88 light-years from Earth.
ν Dra is a similar binary star with two white components, 100 light-years from Earth. Both components are of magnitude 4.9 and can be distinguished in a small amateur telescope or binoculars.
ο Dra is a double star divisible in small telescopes. The primary is an orange giant of magnitude 4.6, 322 light-years from Earth. The secondary is of magnitude 7.8.

ψ Dra (Dziban) is a binary star divisible in binoculars and small amateur telescopes, 72 light-years from Earth. The primary is a yellow-white star of magnitude 4.6 and the secondary is a yellow star of magnitude 5.8.

R Dra is a red Mira-type variable star with a period of about 8 months. Its average minimum magnitude is approximately 12.4, and its average maximum magnitude is approximately 7.6. It was discovered to be a variable star by Hans Geelmuyden in 1876.
Kepler-10 is a star in Draco that has been confirmed to be orbited by Kepler-10b, an exoplanet.
deep_sky_objects: The Cat's Eye Nebula (NGC 6543) is a planetary nebula approximately 3,000 light-years away that was discovered by William Herschel in 1786. It is 9th magnitude and was named for its appearance in the Hubble Space Telescope.

NGC 6543 has a very complex shape due to gravitational interactions between the components of the multiple star at its center, the progenitor of the nebula approximately 1,000 years ago. It is located 9.6 arcminutes away from the north ecliptic pole.
IC 4677 is a nebula that appears as a bar 1.8 arcminutes to the west of the Cat's Eye Nebula. In long-term exposures, IC 4677 appears as a portion of a ring surrounding the planetary nebula.
NGC 5866 is a lenticular galaxy (sometimes considered to be Messier Object 102) that bears its name to a small group that also includes the spiral galaxies NGC 5879 and NGC 5907.

The Draco Dwarf Galaxy is one of the least luminous galaxies with an absolute magnitude of −8.6 and a diameter of only about 3,500 light years. It was discovered by Albert G. Wilson of Lowell Observatory in 1954.

Abell 2218 is a massive galaxy cluster located at a distance of 3 billion light-years (redshift 0.171). It acts as a gravitational lens for even more distant background galaxies, allowing astronomers to study those galaxies as well as the cluster itself.

Arp 188, also called the 'Tadpole Galaxy', features a 'tail' of stars 280,000 light-years long at a distance of 420 million light-years (redshift 0.0314). The tail of stars drawn off the galaxy appears blue because the gravitational interaction disturbed clouds of gas and sparked star formation.

Q1634+706 is a quasar that holds the distinction of being the most distant object usually visible in an amateur telescope. At magnitude 14.4, it appears star-like, though it is at a distance of 12.9 billion light-years.
The Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall, possibly the largest known structure in the universe, covers a part of the southern region of Draco.
meteor_showers_detail: The October Draconids, also called Giacobinids, is a meteor shower associated with the periodic comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner. The shower peaks on 8 October.
The Draconids experienced storms in 1933 and 1946, when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) was up to 10,000 meteors per hour. Further outbursts were observed in 1985, 1998, and 2011.
During the 2011 outburst, ZHR reached 400 meteors/hour, however it was largely unnoticed visually due to interference by the bright Moon.

The February Eta Draconids is a meteor shower that was discovered on February 4, 2011. Observers noted six meteors with a common radiant in a short period. Its parent is a previously unknown long-period comet.

Equ.name: Equuleus
Equ.description: Equuleus is bordered by Aquarius, Delphinus and Pegasus. It covers 72 square degrees, ranking 87th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Kitalpha (α Equ) (3.92m). It is the second smallest constellation in the night sky.

greek: In Greek mythology, one myth associates Equuleus with the foal Celeris (meaning 'swiftness' or 'speed'), who was the offspring or brother of the winged horse Pegasus. Celeris was given to Castor by Mercury.
Other myths say that Equuleus is the horse struck from Poseidon's trident, during the contest between him and Athena when deciding which would be the superior.
Because this section of stars rises before Pegasus, it is often called Equus Primus, or the First Horse. Equuleus is also linked to the story of Philyra and Saturn.
Created by Hipparchus and included by Ptolemy, it abuts Pegasus; unlike the larger horse, it is depicted as a horse's head alone.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars that correspond to Equuleus are located within the Black Tortoise of the North (北方玄武, Běi Fāng Xuán Wǔ).

stars_text: α Equ (Kitalpha, 3.9m) is the brightest star in Equuleus, a yellow star 186 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name means 'the section of the horse'.

γ Equ is an α2 CVn variable star, ranging between magnitudes 4.58 and 4.77 over a period of around 12.5 minutes. It is a white star 115 light-years from Earth, and has an optical companion of magnitude 6.1, 6 Equulei, which is divisible in binoculars.
6 Equ is an astrometric binary system itself, with an apparent magnitude of 6.07.
R Equ is a Mira variable that ranges between magnitudes 8.0 and 15.7 over nearly 261 days. It has a spectral type of M3e-M4e and has an average B-V colour index of +1.41.

ε Equ (1 Equulei) is a triple star 197 light-years away. The system has a primary of magnitude 5.4 that is itself a binary star; its components are of magnitude 6.0 and 6.3 and have a period of 101 years. The secondary is of magnitude 7.4 and is visible in small telescopes.

δ Equ is a binary star with an orbital period of 5.7 years, which at one time was the shortest known orbital period for an optical binary. The two components of the system are never more than 0.35 arcseconds apart.
deep_sky_objects: Due to its small size and its distance from the plane of the Milky Way, Equuleus is rather devoid of deep sky objects such as star clusters and nebulae.
Some very faint galaxies in the New General Catalogue between magnitudes 13 and 15 include NGC 7015, NGC 7040, and NGC 7046.
NGC 7045 is a triple star that was mistaken as a nebula by its discoverer, John Herschel.
Other faint galaxies in the Index Catalogue include IC 1360, IC 1361, IC 1364, IC 1367, IC 1375, and IC 5083. IC 1365 is a group of galaxies.
The magnitudes of these objects vary from 14.5 to 15.5, making them hard to see in even the largest of amateur telescopes.

Eri.name: Eridanus
Eri.description: Eridanus is bordered by Cetus, Fornax, Phoenix, Hydrus, Tucana, Horologium, Caelum, Lepus, Orion and Taurus. It covers 1,138 square degrees, ranking 6th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Achernar (α Eri) (0.46m).

babylonian: According to one theory, the Greek constellation takes its name from the Babylonian constellation known as the Star of Eridu (MUL.NUN.KI). Eridu was an ancient city in the extreme south of Babylonia.
Situated in the marshy regions, Eridu was held sacred to the god Enki-Ea who ruled the cosmic domain of the Abyss—a mythical conception of the fresh-water reservoir below the Earth's surface.
greek: Eridanus is connected to the myth of Phaethon, who took over the reins of his father Helios' sky chariot (i.e., the Sun), but did not have the strength to control it and so veered wildly in different directions, scorching both Earth and heaven.

Zeus intervened by striking Phaethon dead with a thunderbolt and casting him to Earth. The constellation was supposed to be the path Phaethon drove along; in later times, it was considered a path of souls.

Since Eridanos was also a Greek name for the Po (Latin Padus), in which the burning body of Phaethon is said by Ovid to have extinguished, the mythic geography of the celestial and earthly Eridanus is complex.
history: Eridanus was first conflated with the Nile River in Egypt, the constellation was also identified with the Po River in Italy. The stars of the modern constellation Fornax were formerly a part of Eridanus.

Eridanus is depicted in ancient sky charts as a flowing river, starting from Orion and flowing in a meandering fashion past Cetus and Fornax and into the southern hemispheric stars. Johann Bayer's Uranometria depicts the river constellation as a flowing river.
indian: The stars that correspond to Eridanus are also depicted as a river in Indian astronomy starting close to the head of Orion just below Auriga. Eridanus is called Srotaswini in Sanskrit, srótas meaning the course of a river or stream.
Specifically, it is depicted as the Ganges on the head of Dakshinamoorthy or Nataraja, a Hindu incarnation of Shiva. Dakshinamoorthy himself is represented by the constellation Orion.
chinese: The stars that correspond to Eridanus cannot be fully seen from China. In Chinese astronomy, the northern part is located within the White Tiger of the West (西方白虎, Xī Fāng Bái Hǔ).
The unseen southern part was classified among the Southern Asterisms (近南極星區, Jìnnánjíxīngqū) by Xu Guangqi, based on knowledge of western star charts.

stars_text: α Eri (Achernar, 0.5m) is the brightest star in Eridanus at its southern end, a blue-white hued main sequence star 144 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name means 'the river's end'.

Achernar is a very peculiar star because it is one of the flattest stars known. Observations indicate that its radius is about 50% larger at the equator than at the poles. This distortion occurs because the star is spinning extremely rapidly.
β Eri (Cursa, 2.8m) is a blue-white star 89 light-years from Earth. Its place to the south of Orion's foot gives it its name, which means 'the footstool'.

θ Eri (Acamar) is a binary star with blue-white components, distinguishable in small amateur telescopes and 161 light-years from Earth. The primary is of magnitude 3.2 and the secondary is of magnitude 4.3.
32 Eri is a binary star 290 light-years from Earth. The primary is a yellow-hued star of magnitude 4.8 and the secondary is a blue-green star of magnitude 6.1, visible in small amateur telescopes.
39 Eri is a binary star divisible in small amateur telescopes, 206 light-years from Earth. The primary is an orange-hued giant star of magnitude 4.9 and the secondary is of magnitude 8.

40 Eri is a triple star system consisting of an orange main-sequence star, a white dwarf, and a red dwarf. The system is 16 light-years from Earth. The white secondary of magnitude 9.5 is the most easily visible white dwarf. The red dwarf, of magnitude 11, orbits the white dwarf every 250 years.
p Eri is a binary star with two orange components, 27 light-years from Earth. The magnitude 5.8 primary and 5.9 secondary have an orbital period of 500 years.

ε Eri (Ran, 3.7m) is a star with one extrasolar planet similar to Jupiter. It is an orange-hued main-sequence star 10.5 light-years from Earth. Its one planet, with an approximate mass of one Jupiter mass, has a period of 7 years.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 1535 is a small blue-gray planetary nebula visible in small amateur telescopes, with a disk visible in large amateur instruments. It is 2000 light-years away and of the 9th magnitude.

A portion of the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex can be found in the far northeastern section of Eridanus. IC 2118 is a faint reflection nebula believed to be an ancient supernova remnant or gas cloud illuminated by nearby supergiant star Rigel in Orion.
NGC 1232, NGC 1234, NGC 1291 and NGC 1300 are galaxies in Eridanus. NGC 1300 is a grand design barred spiral galaxy.

NGC 1300 is a face-on barred spiral galaxy located 61 (plus or minus 8) million light-years away. The center of the bar shows an unusual structure: within the overall spiral structure, a grand design spiral that is 3,300 light-years in diameter exists. Its spiral arms are tightly wound.

The Eridanus Supervoid is a large supervoid (an area of the universe devoid of galaxies) discovered as of 2007. At a diameter of about one billion light years it is the second largest known void, superseded only by the Giant Void in Canes Venatici.

The Eridanus Supervoid was discovered by linking a 'cold spot' in the cosmic microwave background to an absence of radio galaxies in data of the United States National Radio Astronomy Observatory's Very Large Array Sky Survey.
meteor_showers_detail: The Nu Eridanids, a recently discovered meteor shower, radiate from the constellation between August 30 and September 12 every year. The shower's parent body is an unidentified Oort cloud object.
Another meteor shower in Eridanus is the Omicron Eridanids, which peak between November 1 and 10.

For.name: Fornax
For.description: Fornax is bordered by Cetus, Sculptor, Phoenix and Eridanus. It covers 398 square degrees, ranking 41st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Dalim (α For) (3.80m). The whole constellation is visible to observers south of latitude 50° N.

history: The French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille first described the constellation in French as le Fourneau Chymique (the Chemical Furnace) with an alembic and receiver in his early catalogue, before abbreviating it to le Fourneau on his planisphere in 1752.

He observed and catalogued almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope. He devised fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe.
All but one honoured instruments that symbolised the Age of Enlightenment. Lacaille Latinised the name to Fornax Chimiae on his 1763 chart.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars that correspond to Fornax are within the White Tiger of the West (西方白虎, Xī Fāng Bái Hǔ).

stars_text: α For (Dalim, 3.91m) was originally designated 12 Eridani by John Flamsteed before being named by Lacaille as the brightest star in the new constellation. It is a binary star that can be resolved by small amateur telescopes, 46.4 light-years from Earth.

The primary is a yellow-white subgiant 1.21 times as massive as the Sun that has begun to cool and expand after exhausting its core hydrogen, having swollen to 1.9 times the Sun's radius. The secondary star of magnitude 6.5 is 0.78 times as massive as the Sun.
The secondary has been identified as a blue straggler, and has either accumulated material from, or merged with, a third star in the past. It is a strong source of X-rays.

β For is a yellow-hued giant star of spectral type G8IIIb of magnitude 4.5 that has cooled and swelled to 11 times the Sun's diameter, 178 light-years from Earth. It is a red clump giant, which means it has undergone helium flash and is currently generating energy through the fusion of helium at its core.

ν For is 370 light-years distant from Earth. It is a blue giant star of spectral type B9.5IIIspSi that is 3.65 times as massive and around 245 times as luminous as the Sun, with 3.2 times its diameter.

ν For varies in luminosity over a period of 1.89 days—the same as its rotational period. This is because of differences in abundances of metals in its atmosphere; it belongs to a class of star known as an Alpha2 Canum Venaticorum variable.

ε For is a binary star system located 104.4 light-years distant from Earth. Its component stars orbit each other every 37 years. The primary star is around 12 billion years old and has cooled and expanded to 2.53 times the diameter of the Sun.

ω For is a binary star system composed of a blue main-sequence star of spectral type B9.5V and magnitude 4.96, and a white main sequence star of spectral type A7V and magnitude 7.88. The system is 470 light-years distant from Earth.
κ For is a triple star system composed of a yellow giant and a pair of red dwarfs.
R For is a long-period variable and carbon star.

LP 944-20 is a brown dwarf of spectral type M9 that has around 7% the mass of the Sun. Approximately 21 light-years distant from Earth, it is a faint object with an apparent magnitude of 18.69. Observations showed that its atmosphere contains much lithium and that it has dusty clouds.
λ2 For is a star about 1.2 times as massive as the Sun with a planet about as massive as Neptune, discovered by doppler spectroscopy in 2009. The planet has an orbit of around 17.24 days.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 1049 is a globular cluster 500,000 light-years from Earth. It is in the Fornax Dwarf Galaxy.

NGC 1360 is a planetary nebula in Fornax with a magnitude of approximately 9.0, 1,280 light-years from Earth. Its central star is of magnitude 11.4, an unusually bright specimen. It is five times the size of the famed Ring Nebula in Lyra at 6.5 arcminutes. Unlike the Ring Nebula, NGC 1360 is clearly elliptical.
The Fornax Dwarf galaxy is a dwarf galaxy that is part of the Local Group of galaxies. It is not visible in amateur telescopes, despite its relatively small distance of 500,000 light-years.

NGC 1097 is a barred spiral galaxy in Fornax, about 45 million light-years from Earth. At magnitude 9, it is visible in medium amateur telescopes. It is notable as a Seyfert galaxy with strong spectral emissions indicating ionized gases and a central supermassive black hole.

The Fornax Cluster is a cluster of galaxies lying at a distance of 19 megaparsecs (62 million light-years). It is the second richest galaxy cluster within 100 million light-years, after the considerably larger Virgo Cluster.

The Fornax Cluster covers an area of sky about 6° across or about 28 sq degrees. It lies primarily in the constellation Fornax, with its southern boundaries partially crossing into the constellation of Eridanus.

NGC 1365 is a barred spiral galaxy located at a distance of 56 million light-years from Earth. Like NGC 1097, it is also a Seyfert galaxy. Its bar is a center of star formation and shows extensions of the spiral arms' dust lanes.

The bright nucleus indicates the presence of an active galactic nucleus – a galaxy with a supermassive black hole at the center, accreting matter from the bar. It is a 10th magnitude galaxy associated with the Fornax Cluster.

NGC 1316 (Fornax A) is a radio galaxy with extensive radio lobes. One of the closer active galaxies to Earth at a distance of 62 million light-years, it appears in the optical spectrum as a large elliptical galaxy with dust lanes near its core.

These dust lanes have caused astronomers to discern that NGC 1316 recently merged with a small spiral galaxy. Because it has a high rate of type Ia supernovae, NGC 1316 has been used to determine the size of the universe.

NGC 1399 is a large elliptical galaxy, the central galaxy in the Fornax Cluster. The galaxy is 66 million light-years away from Earth. With a diameter of 130,000 light-years, it is one of the largest galaxies in the Fornax Cluster and slightly larger than Milky Way. William Herschel discovered this galaxy on October 22, 1835.

The Hubble Ultra Deep Field is located within Fornax. A team from University of Queensland described 40 unknown 'dwarf' galaxies in this constellation; ultra compact dwarfs are much smaller than previously known dwarf galaxies, about 120 light-years across.

GRB 190114C was a notable gamma ray burst explosion from a galaxy 4.5 billion light years away near the Fornax constellation, initially detected in January 2019. According to astronomers, it was 'the brightest light ever seen from Earth... biggest explosion in the Universe since the Big Bang'.

Gem.name: Gemini
Gem.description: Gemini lies between Taurus to the west and Cancer to the east, with Auriga and Lynx to the north. It covers 514 square degrees, ranking 30th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Pollux (β Gem) (1.15m).

babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, the stars Castor and Pollux were known as the Great Twins. The Twins were regarded as minor gods called Meshlamtaea and Lugalirra, meaning 'The One who has arisen from the Underworld' and the 'Mighty King.'
Both names can be understood as titles of Nergal, the major Babylonian god of plague and pestilence, who was king of the Underworld.
greek: In Greek mythology, Gemini was associated with the myth of Castor and Pollux, the twin children of Leda and Argonauts. Pollux was the son of Zeus, who seduced Leda, while Castor was the son of Tyndareus, king of Sparta and Leda's husband.
When Castor died, because he was mortal, Pollux begged his father Zeus to give Castor immortality. Zeus did so by uniting them together in the heavens.
Castor and Pollux were mythologically associated with St. Elmo's fire in their role as the protectors of sailors.
history: Gemini is prominent in the winter skies of the Northern Hemisphere and is visible the entire night in December-January. The easiest way to locate the constellation is to find its two brightest stars Castor and Pollux eastward from Taurus's Hyades cluster and Orion's Belt.

In classical antiquity, Cancer was the location of the Sun on the northern solstice. During the first century AD, axial precession shifted it into Gemini. In 1990, the location of the Sun at the northern solstice moved from Gemini into Taurus.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars that correspond to Gemini are located in two areas: the White Tiger of the West (西方白虎) and the Vermillion Bird of the South (南方朱雀).
In some cultures, the twin in Gemini refers to 'the unborn twin' and represents a spiritual or dual self that exists within.

stars_text: β Gem (Pollux, 1.15m) is the brightest star in Gemini, an orange-hued giant star 34 light-years from Earth. Pollux has an extrasolar planet revolving around it.

α Gem (Castor, 1.6m) is a remarkable sextuple star system 52 light-years from Earth. Two spectroscopic binaries are visible at magnitudes 1.9 and 3.0 with a period of 470 years. A wide-set red dwarf is also part of the system, an Algol-type eclipsing binary with a period of 19.5 hours.
γ Gem (Alhena, 1.9m) is a blue-white hued star 105 light-years from Earth.

δ Gem (Wasat, 3.5m) is a long-period binary star 59 light-years from Earth. The primary is a white star of magnitude 3.5, and the secondary is an orange dwarf of magnitude 8.2. The period is over 1000 years.
ε Gem (Mebsuta, 3.1m) is a yellow supergiant 900 light-years from Earth with an optical companion of magnitude 9.6 visible in binoculars.

ζ Gem (Mekbuda) is a Cepheid variable star with a period of 10.2 days, ranging from magnitude 3.6 to 4.2. It is a yellow supergiant 1,200 light-years away with a radius 60 times solar, making it approximately 220,000 times the size of the Sun.
η Gem (Propus) is a binary star 380 light-years away with a period of 500 years. The primary is a semi-regular red giant ranging from magnitude 3.1 to 3.9 over a 233-day period.
μ Gem (Tejat) is a red giant 230 light-years from Earth, about a hundred times larger than the Sun.
U Gem is a dwarf nova type cataclysmic variable discovered by J. R. Hind in 1855.
deep_sky_objects: M35 (NGC 2168) is a large, elongated open cluster of magnitude 5, discovered in 1745 by Swiss astronomer Philippe Loys de Chéseaux. It has an area of approximately 0.2 square degrees, the same size as the full moon.
M35 is visible to the unaided eye under dark skies and easily seen in binoculars. The 200 stars of M35 are arranged in chains that curve throughout the cluster. It is 2,800 light-years from Earth.
NGC 2158 is another open cluster in Gemini, visible in large amateur telescopes and very rich. It is more than 12,000 light-years from Earth.

NGC 2392, the Eskimo Nebula, is a planetary nebula with an overall magnitude of 9.2, located 4,000 light-years from Earth. In a small amateur telescope, its 10th magnitude central star is visible, along with its blue-green elliptical disk. It is said to resemble the head of a person wearing a parka.
The Medusa Nebula is a planetary nebula some 1,500 light-years distant.
Geminga is a neutron star approximately 550 light-years from Earth.
meteor_showers_detail: The Geminids is a bright meteor shower that peaks on December 13-14. It has a maximum rate of approximately 100 meteors per hour, making it one of the richest meteor showers.

The Epsilon Geminids peak between October 18 and October 29 and have only been recently confirmed. They overlap with the Orionids, which makes the Epsilon Geminids difficult to detect visually. Epsilon Geminid meteors have a higher velocity than Orionids.

Gru.name: Grus
Gru.description: Grus is bordered by Piscis Austrinus to the north, Sculptor to the northeast, Phoenix to the east, Tucana to the south, Indus to the southwest, and Microscopium to the west. It covers 366 square degrees, ranking 45th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alnair (α Gru) (1.73m).

history: The stars that form Grus were originally considered part of the neighboring constellation Piscis Austrinus (the southern fish), with Gamma Gruis seen as part of the fish's tail.

The stars were first defined as a separate constellation by astronomer Petrus Plancius, who created twelve new constellations based on observations of the southern sky by Dutch explorers Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman during the first Dutch trading expedition to the East Indies.

Grus first appeared on a 35-centimeter-diameter celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius. Its first depiction in a celestial atlas was in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603.
De Houtman included it in his southern star catalogue under the Dutch name Den Reygher, 'The Heron,' but Bayer followed Plancius and Hondius in using Grus.

An alternative name for the constellation, Phoenicopterus (Latin 'flamingo'), was used briefly during the early 17th century, seen in the 1605 work Cosmographiae Generalis by Paul Merula and a c. 1625 globe by Dutch globe maker Pieter van den Keere.
Grus and the nearby constellations Phoenix, Tucana and Pavo are collectively called the 'Southern Birds.'
chinese: The stars that correspond to Grus were generally too far south to be seen from China. In Chinese astronomy, Gamma and Lambda Gruis may have been included in the tub-shaped asterism Bàijiù, along with stars from Piscis Austrinus.
aboriginal: In Central Australia, the Arrernte and Luritja people living on a mission in Hermannsburg viewed the sky as divided between them, east of the Milky Way representing Arrernte camps and west denoting Luritja camps.
Alpha and Beta Gruis, along with Fomalhaut, Alpha Pavonis and the stars of Musca, were all claimed by the Arrernte.

stars_text: α Gru (Alnair, 1.7m) is the brightest star, a blue-white star of spectral type B6V located 101 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name, Alnair, means 'the bright one' and refers to its status as the brightest star in Grus. Alnair is around 380 times as luminous and has over 3 times the diameter of the Sun.

β Gru (Tiaki, 2.0-2.3m) is a red giant of spectral type M5III located 170 light-years from Earth. It is a variable star that has a diameter of 0.8 astronomical units. If placed in the Solar System, it would extend to the orbit of Venus.

γ Gru (Al Dhanab, 3.0m) is a blue-white subgiant of spectral type B8III located 211 light-years from Earth. It marks the crane's eye. It has finished fusing its core hydrogen and has begun cooling and expanding, transforming into a red giant.

δ Gru is an optical double whose components—Delta1 and Delta2—are separated by 45 arcseconds. Delta1 is a yellow giant (G7III, magnitude 4.0) 309 light-years away. Delta2 is a red giant (M4.5III) and semiregular variable that ranges between magnitudes 3.99 and 4.2, located 325 light-years from Earth.

μ Gru, composed of Mu1 and Mu2, is an optical double. Both stars are yellow giants of spectral type G8III about 2.5 times as massive as the Sun. Mu1 is magnitude 4.8 (275 light-years away), while Mu2 is magnitude 5.11 (265 light-years away).

π Gru is an optical double with a variable component. Pi1 is a semi-regular red giant of spectral type S5, ranging from magnitude 5.31 to 7.01 over a 191-day period, located 532 light-years from Earth. It is one of the brightest S-class stars visible to Earth viewers.

Gliese 832 is a red dwarf of spectral type M1.5V and apparent magnitude 8.66 located only 16.1 light-years distant, making it one of the nearest stars to the Solar System. A Jupiter-like planet orbits the red dwarf over a period of 9.4 years.

S5-HVS1 is a hypervelocity star traveling 1,755 km/s (3,930,000 mph), faster than any other star detected so far. It is about 29,000 light-years from Earth and may have been propelled out of the Milky Way after interacting with Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy.
deep_sky_objects: IC 5148, nicknamed the spare-tyre nebula, is a planetary nebula located around 1 degree west of Lambda Gruis. Around 3,000 light-years distant, it is expanding at 50 kilometers per second, one of the fastest rates of expansion of all planetary nebulae.

The Grus Quartet is a group of four interacting galaxies northeast of Theta Gruis: NGC 7552, NGC 7590, NGC 7599, and NGC 7582. The latter three occupy an area of sky only 10 arcminutes across and are sometimes referred to as the 'Grus Triplet.'
NGC 7552 and 7582 are exhibiting high starburst activity, thought to have arisen because of tidal forces from interacting. All four are part of a larger loose group called the IC 1459 Grus Group.

IC 1459 is a peculiar E3 giant elliptical galaxy located on the border of Grus with Piscis Austrinus. It has a fast counterrotating stellar core, and shells and ripples in its outer region. The galaxy has an apparent magnitude of 11.9 and is around 80 million light-years distant.

NGC 7424 is a barred spiral galaxy with an apparent magnitude of 10.4, located around 4 degrees west of the Grus Triplet. Approximately 37.5 million light-years distant, it is about 100,000 light-years in diameter and is thought to resemble the Milky Way.
Two ultraluminous X-ray sources and one supernova have been observed in NGC 7424. SN 2001ig was discovered in 2001 and classified as a Type IIb supernova.

NGC 7213 is a face-on type 1 Seyfert galaxy located approximately 71.7 million light-years from Earth. Appearing undisturbed in visible light, it shows signs of having undergone a collision when viewed at longer wavelengths, with disturbed patterns of ionized hydrogen including a filament of gas around 64,000 light-years long.
NGC 7410 is a spiral galaxy discovered by British astronomer John Herschel in October 1834. The galaxy has a visual magnitude of 11.7 and is approximately 122 million light-years distant from Earth.

Her.name: Hercules
Her.description: Hercules is bordered by Draco, Boötes, Corona Borealis, Serpens Caput, Ophiuchus, Aquila, Sagitta, Vulpecula, and Lyra. Covering 1,225 square degrees, it ranks 5th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Kornephoros (β Her) (2.78m).

babylonian: According to Gavin White, the Greek constellation of Hercules may be a distorted version of the Babylonian constellation known as the 'Standing Gods' (MUL.DINGIR.GUB.BA.MESH).

This figure was, like the similarly named 'Sitting Gods,' depicted as a man with a serpent's body instead of legs. The serpent element is now represented on the Greek star map by the figure of Draco that Hercules crushes beneath his feet.

The original name of Hercules—the 'Kneeler'—may be a conflation of the two Babylonian constellations of the Sitting and Standing Gods. Alternatively, it is possible that a large part of Hercules comprised another Babylonian constellation, the Sitting Dog (MUL.UR.GI).
greek: The earliest Greek references to the constellation do not refer to it as Hercules. Aratus described it as a 'Phantom form, like to a man that strives at a task,' calling him simply 'On His Knees.'

Eratosthenes (3rd century BCE) described it as Hercules, placed above Draco (representing the dragon of the Hesperides) and preparing to fight it, holding his lion's skin in his left hand and a club in his right.

Panyassis' Heracleia (5th century BCE) reportedly said Jupiter was impressed by Hercules' fight with the dragon and made it a constellation, with Hercules kneeling on his right knee, trying to crush Draco's head with his left foot while striking with his right hand.

Other ancient sources associated the constellation with various figures: Ceteus son of Lycaon, Theseus lifting the stone at Troezen, Thamyris blinded by the Muses, Orpheus killed by the women of Thracia, Ixion bound for trying to attack Juno, or Prometheus bound on Mount Caucasus.
history: In mid-northern latitudes, Hercules is best observed from mid-spring until early autumn, culminating at midnight on June 13.
The traditional visualization imagines Alpha Herculis (Rasalgethi, 'head of the kneeling one') as Hercules's head. His left leg is stepping on Draco's head, the dragon whom Hercules has vanquished.
A common form found in modern star charts uses the quadrangle formed by Pi, Eta, Zeta and Epsilon Herculis (known as the 'Keystone' asterism) as the lower half of Hercules's torso.
The solar apex—the direction of the Sun's motion in its orbit around the center of the Milky Way—is located within Hercules, between the constellation's left elbow and Vega in neighboring Lyra.
phoenician: Phoenician tradition is said to have associated this constellation with their sun god, who slew a dragon (Draco).
sumerian: The constellation is also sometimes associated with Gilgamesh, a Sumerian mythological hero.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars that correspond to Hercules are located in two areas: the Purple Forbidden enclosure (紫微垣) and the Heavenly Market enclosure (天市垣).
arab: Arab translators of Ptolemy named it in Arabic: الرقيس (al-raqis), meaning 'the player.' Hence its Swahili name Rakisi.

stars_text: β Her (Kornephoros, 2.8m) is the brightest star in Hercules, a yellow giant 148 light-years from Earth. Kornephoros means 'club-bearer.'

α Her (Rasalgethi, 3-4m) is a triple star system 359 light-years from Earth, partly resolvable in small amateur telescopes. Its common name means 'the kneeler's head.' The primary is an irregular variable bright giant with a diameter of roughly 400 solar diameters. The secondary is a blue-green hued spectroscopic binary of magnitude 5.6 that orbits the primary every 3,600 years.
γ Her (Almach, 3.8m) is a white giant 195 light-years from Earth, a double star divisible in small amateur telescopes with a widely separated 10th magnitude optical companion.
δ Her (3.1m) is a blue-white star 78 light-years from Earth, a double star divisible in small amateur telescopes with a magnitude 8.2 optical companion.

ζ Her (2.9m) is a binary star 35 light-years from Earth that is becoming divisible in medium-aperture amateur telescopes as the components widen to their peak in 2025. The system has a period of 34.5 years. The primary is a yellow-tinged star and the secondary is an orange star of magnitude 5.7.
μ Her is 27.4 light-years from Earth, notable for its proximity to the solar apex.
30 Her (g Herculis) is a semiregular red giant with a period of 3 months, ranging from magnitude 4.3 to 6.3. It is 361 light-years from Earth.
68 Her (u Herculis) is a Beta Lyrae-type eclipsing binary star 865 light-years from Earth with a period of 2 days, ranging from magnitude 4.7 to 5.4.
deep_sky_objects: M13, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, is the brightest globular cluster in the northern hemisphere. It lies between the stars Eta Her and Zeta Her and is visible to both the naked eye and binoculars as a magnitude 6 object.

M13 contains more than 300,000 stars and is 25,200 light-years from Earth. It has an apparent diameter of over 0.25 degrees (half the size of the full moon) and a physical diameter of more than 100 light-years. Individual stars in M13 are resolvable in a small amateur telescope.

M92 is a globular cluster of magnitude 6.4, 26,000 light-years from Earth. It is a Shapley class IV cluster, quite concentrated at the center with a very clear nucleus. The oldest globular cluster known at 14 billion years, its stars are resolvable in a medium-aperture amateur telescope.

NGC 6229 is a dimmer globular cluster with a magnitude of 9.4, the third-brightest globular in the constellation. It is 100,000 light-years from Earth and is a Shapley class IV cluster, fairly rich in the center and quite concentrated at the nucleus.
NGC 6210 is a planetary nebula of the 9th magnitude, 4,000 light-years from Earth, visible as a blue-green elliptical disk in amateur telescopes larger than 75 mm in aperture.
The Hercules Cluster (Abell 2151) is a cluster of galaxies in Hercules.

Hercules A is the brightest radio source in the constellation, an elliptical galaxy located 2.1 billion light-years away with a supermassive black hole (2.5 billion solar masses) that has radio jets extending for one-and-a-half million light-years.
The quasar 3C 345 is another bright radio source in Hercules with a jet that appears to move faster than the speed of light.
The Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, the largest structure in the universe, is located in Hercules.

AT2018cow is a large astronomical explosion detected on 16 June 2018 that generated significant interest among astronomers worldwide and may be considered a supernova tentatively named Supernova 2018cow.
meteor_showers_detail: The Tau Herculids meteor shower radiates from Hercules and is associated with the periodic comet 73P/Schwassmann-Wachmann.

Hor.name: Horologium
Hor.description: Horologium is bordered by Eridanus, Hydrus, Reticulum, Dorado, and Caelum. It covers 249 square degrees, ranking 58th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Hor (3.85m). The whole constellation is visible to observers south of 23°N.

history: French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first described the constellation as l'Horloge à pendule & à secondes (Clock with pendulum and seconds hand) in 1756, after observing and cataloguing almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.

Lacaille devised fourteen new constellations in previously uncharted regions of the southern celestial hemisphere, which were not visible from Europe. All but one honored scientific instruments, symbolizing the Age of Enlightenment.

The constellation name was Latinized to Horologium in a catalogue and updated chart published posthumously in 1763. The Latin term is ultimately derived from the Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον, for an instrument for telling the hour.

stars_text: α Hor (3.9m) is the brightest star in the constellation, located 115 light-years from Earth. It is an orange giant of spectral type K2III that has swollen to around 11 times the diameter of the Sun. German astronomer Johann Elert Bode depicted it as the pendulum of the clock, while Lacaille made it one of the weights.

δ Hor (4.93m) is the second-brightest star and forms a wide optical double with Alpha. Delta itself is a true binary system composed of a white main sequence star of spectral type A5V and its fainter companion of magnitude 7.29, located 179 light-years from Earth.
β Hor (5.0m) is a white giant 63 times as luminous as the Sun with an effective temperature of 8,303 K, located 312 light-years from Earth. It has been little-studied.
λ Hor is an aging yellow-white giant star of spectral type F2III that spins around at 140 km/second, and is hence mildly flattened at its poles. It is 161 light-years from Earth.

ν Hor (5.24m) is a white main sequence star of spectral type A2V located 169 light-years from Earth that is around 1.9 times as massive as the Sun. It has a debris disk with two components: an inner disk orbiting at 96 AU and an outer disk lying 410 AU from the star.

R Hor is a red giant Mira variable with one of the widest ranges in brightness known of stars in the night sky visible to the unaided eye. It has a minimum magnitude of 14.3 and a maximum magnitude of 4.7, with a period of approximately 13 months, around 1,000 light-years from Earth.
TW Hor is a semiregular variable red giant star that is classified as a carbon star, and is 1,370 light-years from Earth.

ι Hor is a yellow-white dwarf star 1.23 times as massive and 1.16 times as wide as the Sun with a spectral type of F8V, 57 light-years from Earth. Its chemical profile, movement and age indicate it formed within the Hyades cluster but has drifted around 130 light-years away from the other members. It has a planet at least 2.5 times as massive as Jupiter orbiting it every 307 days.
HD 27631 is a Sun-like star located 164 light-years from Earth which was found to have a planet at least 1.45 times as massive as Jupiter that takes 2,208 days (six years) to complete an orbit.

WASP-120 is a yellow-white main-sequence star around 1.4 times as massive as the Sun with a spectral type of F5V that is estimated to be 2.6 billion years old. It has a massive planet around 4.85 times the mass of Jupiter that completes its orbit every 3.6 days.

Gliese 1061 (13.06m) is a red dwarf of spectral type M5.5V that has 12% of the mass and 15% of the diameter of the Sun. Located 12 light-years away from Earth, it is the 20th-closest single star or stellar system to the Sun. In August 2019, it was announced that it had three planets, one of which lay in its habitable zone.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 1261 is a globular cluster of magnitude 8, located 53,000 light-years from Earth. It lies 4.7 degrees north-northeast of Mu Horologii.
Arp-Madore 1 is the most remote known globular cluster in the Milky Way at a distance of 123.3 kiloparsecs (402,000 light-years) from Earth.

NGC 1512 is a barred spiral galaxy 2.1 degrees west-southwest of Alpha Horologii with an apparent magnitude of 10.2. About five arcmin (13.8 kpc) away is the dwarf lenticular galaxy NGC 1510. The two are in the process of a merger which has been going on for 400 million years.

The Horologium-Reticulum Supercluster is a galaxy supercluster, second in mass only to the Shapley Supercluster in the local universe (anything within 200 mpc of Earth). It contains over 20 Abell galaxy clusters and covers more than 100 deg2 of the sky.

Hya.name: Hydra
Hya.description: Hydra is the largest of the 88 modern constellations, covering 1,303 square degrees. Despite its size, it contains only one moderately bright star, Alphard (α Hya, 1.98m). It borders fourteen constellations and stretches across the southern sky.

babylonian: The Greek constellation of Hydra is an adaptation of a Babylonian constellation. The MUL.APIN includes a 'serpent' constellation (MUL.DINGIR.MUŠ) that loosely corresponds to Hydra. It is one of two Babylonian 'serpent' constellations, a mythological hybrid of serpent, lion and bird.
greek: The shape of Hydra resembles a twisting snake, and features as such in some Greek myths. One myth associates it with a water snake that a crow served Apollo in a cup when it was sent to fetch water. Apollo saw through the fraud and angrily cast the crow, cup and snake into the sky.

Hydra is also associated with the monster Hydra, with its many heads, killed by Hercules, represented in another constellation. According to legend, if one of the Hydra's heads was cut off, two more would grow in its place. However, Hercules' nephew, Iolaus, seared the necks with a torch to prevent them from growing back and thus enabled Hercules to overcome the Hydra.
arab: The head of Hydra was collectively known as 'Min al Az'al,' meaning 'belonging to the uninhabited spot' in Arabic.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars that correspond to Hydra are located within the Vermilion Bird and the Azure Dragon.

stars_text: α Hya (Alphard, 2.0m) is the brightest star in the constellation, an orange giant of magnitude 2.0, 177 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name means 'the solitary one.'
β Hya is a blue-white star of magnitude 4.3, 365 light-years from Earth.
γ Hya (Naga) is a yellow giant of magnitude 3.0, 132 light-years from Earth.

ε Hya (Ashlesha) is Hydra's one bright binary star, which is difficult to split in amateur telescopes. It has a period of 1000 years and is 135 light-years from Earth. The primary is a yellow star of magnitude 3.4 and the secondary is a blue star of magnitude 6.7. The name Ashlesha corresponds to the Āshleshā Nakshatra, the lunar zodiacal constellation in Indian astronomy.

27 Hya is a triple star with two components visible in binoculars and three visible in small amateur telescopes. The primary is a white star of magnitude 4.8, 244 light-years from Earth. The secondary, a binary star, appears in binoculars at magnitude 7.0 but is composed of a magnitude 7 and a magnitude 11 star, 202 light-years from Earth.
54 Hya is a binary star 99 light-years from Earth, easily divisible in small amateur telescopes. The primary is a yellow star of magnitude 5.3 and the secondary is a purple star of magnitude 7.4.
σ Hya (Minchir, 4.54m) has a name from the Arabic for snake's nose. It is rather dim but marks the head of the snake.
R Hya is a Mira variable star 2000 light-years from Earth; it is one of the brightest Mira variables at its maximum of magnitude 3.5. It has a minimum magnitude of 10 and a period of 390 days.
V Hya is an unusually vivid red variable star 20,000 light-years from Earth. It varies in magnitude from a minimum of 9.0 to a maximum of 6.6.
U Hya is a semi-regular variable star with a deep red color, 528 light-years from Earth. It has a minimum magnitude of 6.6 and a maximum magnitude of 4.2, with a period of 115 days.

GJ 357 is an M-type main sequence star located only 31 light-years from the Solar System. This star has three confirmed exoplanets in its orbit, one of which, GJ 357 d, is considered to be a 'Super-Earth' within the circumstellar habitable zone.
WISE 0855-0714 is a brown dwarf, the closest (sub)stellar object of the constellation.
deep_sky_objects: M83 (NGC 5236), the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy, is an 8th magnitude face-on spiral galaxy. It is easily observed in skies south of 40°N latitude. It has been host to six supernovae. Large amateur telescopes above 12 inches aperture reveal its spiral arms, bar, and small, bright nucleus. A smaller sister to the Milky Way, it is a grand design spiral galaxy 40,000 light-years across.
M68 (NGC 4590) is a globular cluster visible in binoculars and resolvable in medium amateur telescopes. It is 31,000 light-years from Earth and of the 8th magnitude.

M48 (NGC 2548) is an open cluster that is visible to the naked eye under dark skies. Its shape has been described as 'triangular'; this 80-star cluster is unusually large, more than half a degree in diameter, larger than the diameter of the full Moon.

NGC 3242 is a planetary nebula of magnitude 7.5, 1400 light-years from Earth. Discovered in 1785 by William Herschel, it has earned the nickname 'Ghost of Jupiter' because of its striking resemblance to the giant planet. Its blue-green disk is visible in small telescopes and its halo is visible in larger instruments.

NGC 5694 is a globular cluster of magnitude 10.2, 105,000 light-years from Earth. Also called 'Tombaugh's Globular Cluster', it is a Shapley class VII cluster. Though it was discovered as a non-stellar object in 1784 by William Herschel, its status as a globular cluster was not ascertained until 1932, when Clyde Tombaugh looked at photographic plates taken near Pi Hydrae on 12 May 1931.

NGC 3314, usually delineated as NGC 3314a and NGC 3314b, is a pair of galaxies that appear superimposed, despite the fact that they are not related or interacting. The foreground galaxy, NGC 3314a, is at a distance of 140 million light-years, and is a face-on spiral galaxy. The background galaxy, NGC 3314b, is an oblique spiral galaxy.

ESO 510-G13 is a warped spiral galaxy located 150 million light-years from Earth. Though most galactic disks are flat because of their rate of rotation, their conformation can be changed. Astronomers speculate that this is due to interactions with other galaxies.
NGC 5068 may be a member of the M83 group, but its identity is disputed. It has a low surface brightness and has a diameter of 4.5 arcminutes.
NGC 4993 is an elliptical galaxy which was the source of events GW170817, GRB 170817A and SSS17a from the merger of two neutron stars.
meteor_showers_detail: The Sigma Hydrids peak on December 6 and are a very active shower. The parent body of the Sigma Hybrids is believed to be Comet Nishimura (C/2023 P1), which was discovered in 2023 by the Japanese astronomical photographer Hideo Nishimura.
The Alpha Hydrids are a minor shower that peaks between January 1 and 7.

Hyi.name: Hydrus
Hyi.description: Hydrus is bordered by eight constellations including Mensa, Eridanus, Horologium, Reticulum, Phoenix, Tucana, and Octans. It covers 243 square degrees, ranking 61st in size. Its brightest star is β Hyi (2.82m). The constellation remains below the horizon at latitudes north of 30°N.

history: Hydrus was one of the twelve constellations established by astronomer Petrus Plancius from the observations of the southern sky by the Dutch explorers Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman, who had sailed on the first Dutch trading expedition, known as the Eerste Schipvaart, to the East Indies.

It first appeared on a 35-cm (14 in) diameter celestial globe published in late 1597 (or early 1598) in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius. The first depiction of this constellation in a celestial atlas was in the German cartographer Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603.

De Houtman included it in his southern star catalogue the same year under the Dutch name De Waterslang, 'The Water Snake', it representing a type of snake encountered on the expedition rather than a mythical creature.

The French explorer and astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille called it l'Hydre Mâle on the 1756 version of his planisphere of the southern skies, distinguishing it from the feminine Hydra. The French name was retained by Jean Fortin in 1776 for his Atlas Céleste, while Lacaille Latinized the name to Hydrus for his revised Coelum Australe Stelliferum in 1763.
Herman Melville mentions it and Argo Navis in Moby Dick 'beneath effulgent Antarctic Skies', highlighting his knowledge of the southern constellations from whaling voyages.

stars_text: β Hyi (2.8m) is the brightest star in Hydrus, a yellow star lying 24 light-years from Earth. It has about 104% of the mass of the Sun and 181% of the Sun's radius, with more than three times the Sun's luminosity. The spectrum matches a stellar classification of G2 IV, a subgiant star.
