Thought to be between 6.4 and 7.1 billion years old, this star bears some resemblance to what the Sun may look like in the far distant future. It is also the closest bright star to the south celestial pole.

α Hyi (2.9m) is located at the northern edge of the constellation and just southwest of Achernar. It is a white sub-giant star situated 72 light-years from Earth. Of spectral type F0IV, it is beginning to cool and enlarge as it uses up its supply of hydrogen. It is twice as massive and 3.3 times as wide as the Sun and 26 times more luminous. A line drawn between Alpha Hydri and Beta Centauri is bisected by the south celestial pole.

γ Hyi is a red giant of spectral type M2III located 214 light-years from Earth in the southeastern corner of the constellation. It is a semi-regular variable star, pulsating between magnitudes 3.26 and 3.33. It is around 1.5 to 2 times as massive as the Sun, and has expanded to about 60 times the Sun's diameter, shining with about 655 times the luminosity of the Sun.

VW Hyi is a dwarf nova of the SU Ursae Majoris type, located 3 degrees northeast of Gamma. It is a close binary system that consists of a white dwarf and another star, the former drawing off matter from the latter into a bright accretion disk. One of the brightest dwarf novae in the sky, it has a baseline magnitude of 14.4 and can brighten to magnitude 8.4 during peak activity.

BL Hyi is another close binary system composed of a low-mass star and a strongly magnetic white dwarf. Known as a polar or AM Herculis variable, these produce polarized optical and infrared emissions and intense soft and hard X-ray emissions to the frequency of the white dwarf's rotation period, in this case 113.6 minutes.

π Hyi, composed of π1 Hyi and π2 Hyi, is an optical double star divisible in binoculars. Around 476 light-years distant, π1 is a red giant of spectral type M1III that varies between magnitudes 5.52 and 5.58. π2 is an orange giant of spectral type K2III and shining with a magnitude of 5.7, around 488 light-years from Earth.

η Hyi, composed of η1 and η2, is an optical double. η1 is a blue-white main sequence star of spectral type B9V located just over 700 light-years away. η2 (4.7m) is a yellow giant star of spectral type G8.5III around 218 light-years distant, which has evolved off the main sequence and is expanding and cooling. A planet, η2 Hydri b, greater than 6.5 times the mass of Jupiter was discovered in 2005, orbiting around η2 every 711 days at a distance of 1.93 AU.

HD 10180 is a Sun-like star which has seven planets, plus possibly an additional two for a total of nine, as of 2012 more than any other system to date, including the Solar System. Lying around 127 light-years from Earth, it has an apparent magnitude of 7.33.

GJ 3021 is a solar twin, a star very like the Sun, around 57 light-years distant with a spectral type G8V and magnitude of 6.7. It has a Jovian planet companion (GJ 3021 b) orbiting about 0.5 AU from its star, with a minimum mass 3.37 times that of Jupiter and a period of around 133 days. The system is complex as the faint star GJ 3021B orbits at a distance of 68 AU; it is a red dwarf of spectral type M4V.

HD 20003 (8.37m) is a yellow main sequence star of spectral type G8V a little cooler and smaller than the Sun around 143 light-years away. It has two planets that are around 12 and 13.5 times as massive as the Earth with periods of just under 12 and 34 days respectively.
deep_sky_objects: IC 1717 was a deep-sky object discovered by the Danish astronomer John Louis Emil Dreyer in the late 19th century. The object at the coordinate Dreyer observed is no longer there, and is now a mystery. It was very likely to have been a faint comet.

PGC 6240, known as the White Rose Galaxy, is a giant spiral galaxy surrounded by shells resembling rose petals, located around 345 million light years from the Solar System. Unusually, it has cohorts of globular clusters of three distinct ages suggesting bouts of post-starburst formation following a merger with another galaxy.
NGC 1511 is a spiral galaxy which lies edge on to observers on Earth and is readily viewed in amateur telescopes.

NGC 1466 is a globular cluster and an outlying component of the Large Magellanic Cloud. It contains many RR Lyrae-type variable stars. It has a magnitude of 11.59 and is thought to be over 12 billion years old. Two stars, HD 24188 of magnitude 6.3 and HD 24115 of magnitude 9.0, lie nearby in its foreground.

NGC 602 is composed of an emission nebula and a young, bright open cluster of stars that is an outlying component on the eastern edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy to the Milky Way.

Ind.name: Indus
Ind.description: Indus is bordered by Microscopium, Sagittarius, Telescopium, Pavo, Octans, Tucana, and Grus. It covers 294 square degrees, ranking 49th in size. Its brightest star is α Ind (3.11m). Indus lacks stars among the sky's brightest 100 in apparent magnitude.

history: The constellation was created by Petrus Plancius who made a fairly large celestial globe from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. The first depiction of this constellation in a celestial atlas followed in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603.
Plancius portrayed the figure as a nude male with three arrows in one hand and one in the other, as a native, lacking quiver and bow.
It is among the twelve constellations introduced by Keyser and de Houtman, which first appeared on a celestial globe in 1598.

stars_text: α Ind (3.1m) is the brightest star in the constellation, an orange giant 101 light-years away.
β Ind (3.7m) is an orange giant 600 light-years distant.
δ Ind (4.4m) is a white star 185 light-years from Earth.
The three stars Alpha, Beta, and Delta form a near-perfect right-angled triangle, such that Beta marks the right angle and is in the south-east.

ε Ind (4.7m) is one of the closest stars to Earth, approximately 11.8 light years away. It is an orange dwarf, meaning that the yellow dwarf Sun is slightly hotter and larger. The system has been discovered to contain a pair of binary brown dwarfs, and has long been a prime candidate in SETI studies. This star has the third-highest proper motion of all visible to the unaided eye, ranking behind Groombridge 1830 and 61 Cygni, and the ninth-highest overall. This will move the star into Tucana around 2640.

θ Ind is a binary star divisible in small amateur telescopes, 97 light-years from Earth. Its primary is a white star of magnitude 4.5 and its secondary is a white star of magnitude 7.0. It figures close to the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle of Alpha, Beta and Delta, the three brightest stars of Indus.
T Ind is the only bright variable star in Indus. It is a semi-regular, deeply colored red giant with a period of 11 months, 1900 light-years away. Its minimum magnitude is 7 and its maximum is 5.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 7038 is a galaxy in Indus.
NGC 7049 is a galaxy in Indus.
NGC 7090 is a galaxy in Indus.
IC 5152 is a dwarf irregular galaxy lying at a distance of about 1.7 million parsec (5.5 million light years), at the edge of the Local Group, although it is not a certain member.

ASASSN-15lh (SN 2015L) is a superluminous supernova detected by All Sky Automated Survey for SuperNovae (ASAS-SN) in 2015. Based on study by Subo Dong and team from the Kavli Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics (KIAA) at Peking University, it was approximately doubly luminous to any supernova detected, and at peak was almost 50 times more intrinsically luminous than the Milky Way. Its distance is approximately 3.82 gigalight-years, denoting an age approximately half that of the universe.

Lac.name: Lacerta
Lac.description: Lacerta is bordered by Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, Cygnus and Pegasus. It covers 201 square degrees, ranking 68th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Lac (Stellio) (3.76m).

history: Centred on a region of the sky without bright stars, Lacerta was not regarded as a constellation by ancient Western astronomers. Johannes Hevelius created it in 1687, initially naming it 'Stellio' after a lizard with star-like dorsal spots found along the Mediterranean coast.

Augustin Royer attempted to name this region 'Sceptrum et Manus Iustitiae' (the Hand of Justice and Sceptre) to honor Louis XIV in 1670. Johann Elert Bode created 'Frederici Honores' (Frederick's Glory) to honor Frederick the Great in 1787. Both names fell into disuse while Lacerta survived.
chinese: Although not included in ancient star charts of Europe and the Near East, the stars of Lacerta, along with some in the eastern portion of Cygnus, were combined by early Chinese astronomers into their 'Flying serpent'.
native_american: The Chumash people of California call this part of the sky 'Lizard' and include it in multiple stories.

stars_text: α Lac (Stellio, 3.8m) is a blue-white main-sequence star of spectral type A1 V, located 102 light-years from Earth. It is an optical double star that marks the lizard's brightest point.
β Lac (4.4m) is far dimmer than Alpha, a yellow giant located 170 light-years from Earth.
Roe 47 is a multiple star system consisting of five components with magnitudes ranging from 5.8 to 10.1.

EV Lac is a rapidly spinning magnitude 10 red dwarf with a strong magnetic field. It is a flare star that can emit powerful flares potentially visible to the naked eye, thousands of times more energetic than any from Earth's Sun.
HD 215441 is known as Babcock's Magnetic Star, notable for its strong magnetic field.
deep_sky_objects: Lacerta is typical of Milky Way constellations: it contains no bright galaxies or globular clusters, but instead features open clusters and double stars.
NGC 7243 is an open cluster 2,500 light-years from Earth, visible in small amateur telescopes. It has a few dozen scattered stars, the brightest of which are 8th magnitude.
IC 5217 is a faint planetary nebula found in this constellation.

BL Lacertae is the prototype of the BL Lacertae objects, which appear to be dim variable stars but are actually the variable nuclei of elliptical galaxies. They are similar to quasars and are a subtype of blazar.
BL Lacertae varies irregularly between magnitudes 14 and 17 over a few days. It lent its name to a whole type of celestial objects.
exoplanets: ADS 16402 is a binary star system in Lacerta around which a Jupiter-sized planet orbits. The planet HAT-P-1 exhibits an unexpectedly low density, about the same as cork.

Leo.name: Leo
Leo.description: Leo is bordered by Ursa Major, Leo Minor, Lynx, Cancer, Hydra, Sextans, Crater, Virgo and Coma Berenices. It covers 947 square degrees, ranking 12th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Regulus (α Leo) (1.35m).

ancient: Leo was one of the earliest recognized constellations, with archaeological evidence that the Mesopotamians had a similar constellation as early as 4000 BCE.
The Persians called Leo Ser or Shir; the Turks, Artan; the Syrians, Aryo; the Jews, Arye; the Indians, Simha—all meaning 'lion'.
Some mythologists believe that in Sumeria, Leo represented the monster Humbaba, who was killed by Gilgamesh.
babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, the constellation was called UR.GU.LA, the 'Great Lion'. The bright star Regulus was known as 'the star that stands at the Lion's breast'.
Regulus had distinctly regal associations, as it was known as the King Star.
greek: In Greek mythology, Leo was identified as the Nemean Lion which was killed by Heracles (Hercules to the Romans) during the first of his twelve labours.

The Nemean Lion would take women as hostages to its lair in a cave, luring warriors from nearby towns to save the damsel in distress, to their misfortune. The Lion was impervious to any weaponry; clubs, swords, and spears were useless against it.

Realizing he must defeat the Lion with his bare hands, Hercules slipped into the Lion's cave and engaged it at close quarters. When the Lion pounced, Hercules caught it in midair, grasping the Lion's forelegs and hind legs, and bent it backwards, breaking its back and freeing the trapped maidens.
Zeus commemorated this labor by placing the Lion in the sky.
roman: The Roman poet Ovid called it Herculeus Leo and Violentus Leo. Bacchi Sidus (star of Bacchus) was another of its titles, the god Bacchus always being identified with this animal.
Manilius called it Jovis et Junonis Sidus (Star of Jupiter and Juno).

stars_text: α Leo (Regulus, 1.34m) is a blue-white main-sequence star 77.5 light-years from Earth. It is a double star divisible in binoculars, with a secondary of magnitude 7.7. Its traditional name means 'the little king'.
β Leo (Denebola, 2.23m) is at the opposite end of the constellation from Regulus. It is a blue-white star 36 light-years from Earth. The name Denebola means 'the lion's tail'.

γ Leo (Algieba, 2.61m) is a binary star with a third optical component. The primary is a gold-yellow giant and the secondary is similar at magnitude 3.6. They have a period of 600 years and are 126 light-years from Earth. The unrelated tertiary, 40 Leonis, is magnitude 4.8. Algieba means 'the forehead'.
δ Leo (Zosma, 2.58m) is a blue-white star 58 light-years from Earth.

μ Leo (Rasalas, 3.88m) is a red star 124 light-years from Earth. Rasalas is also known as Alshemali, both names abbreviations of 'Al Ras al Asad al Shamaliyy', meaning 'The Lion's Head Toward the South'.
θ Leo (Chertan, 3.324m) is a white star about 165 light-years from Earth. The name Chertan derives from the Arabic al-kharātān 'two small ribs', originally referring to Delta Leonis and Theta Leonis.
Six of Leo's stars form an asterism called 'The Sickle,' which resembles a backwards question mark: Epsilon, Mu, Zeta, Gamma, Eta, and Alpha Leonis.

R Leo is a Mira variable red giant with a minimum magnitude of 10 and normal maximum of 6, periodically brightening to magnitude 4.4. Located 330 light-years from Earth, it has a period of 310 days and a diameter of 450 solar diameters.
Wolf 359 (CN Leonis) is one of the nearest stars to Earth at 7.8 light-years away. It is a red dwarf of magnitude 13.5 and a flare star that periodically brightens by one magnitude or less.
CW Leo (IRC +10216) is the brightest star in the night sky at the infrared N-band (10 μm wavelength).

SDSS J102915+172927 (Caffau's star) is a population II star in the galactic halo seen in Leo. It is about 13 billion years old, making it one of the oldest stars in the Galaxy. It has the lowest metallicity of any known star.
deep_sky_objects: Leo contains many bright galaxies, including Messier 65, Messier 66, Messier 95, Messier 96, Messier 105, and NGC 3628. The first two are part of the Leo Triplet.

M66 is a spiral galaxy that is part of the Leo Triplet, whose other two members are M65 and NGC 3628. It is 37 million light-years away and has a somewhat distorted shape due to gravitational interactions with the other members, which are pulling stars away from M66.
Both M65 and M66 are visible in large binoculars or small telescopes, but their concentrated nuclei and elongation are only visible in large amateur instruments.

M95 and M96 are both spiral galaxies 20 million light-years from Earth. Though visible as fuzzy objects in small telescopes, their structure is only visible in larger instruments. M95 is a barred spiral galaxy.
M105 is about a degree away from the M95/M96 pair. It is an elliptical galaxy of 9th magnitude, also about 20 million light-years from Earth.

NGC 2903 is a barred spiral galaxy discovered by William Herschel in 1784. It is very similar in size and shape to the Milky Way and is located 25 million light-years from Earth. Its core has many 'hotspots' near regions of star formation.
The Leo Ring, a cloud of hydrogen and helium gas, is found in the orbit of two galaxies within this constellation.
Leo is home to some of the largest structures in the observable universe, including the Clowes–Campusano LQG, U1.11, U1.54, and the Huge-LQG. The latter is the second largest structure known.
meteor_showers_detail: The Leonids occur in November, peaking on November 14–15, with a radiant close to Gamma Leonis. Its parent body is Comet Tempel-Tuttle, which causes significant outbursts every 35 years.
The normal peak rate is approximately 10 meteors per hour.
The January Leonids are a minor shower that peaks between January 1 and 7.
exoplanets: Gliese 436, a faint star in Leo about 33 light-years away from the Sun, is orbited by a transiting Neptune-mass extrasolar planet.

LMi.name: Leo Minor
LMi.pronunciation: /ˌliːoʊ ˈmaɪnər/ LEE-oh MY-nər, genitive /liːˌoʊnɪs mɪˈnɔːrɪs/ lee-OH-niss min-OR-iss
LMi.description: Leo Minor is bordered by Ursa Major, Lynx, Cancer and Leo. It covers 232 square degrees, ranking 64th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Praecipua (3.83m).

history: The classical astronomers Aratus and Ptolemy had noted the region of Leo Minor to be undefined and not containing any distinctive patterns. Ptolemy classified the stars in this area as amorphōtoi (not belonging to a constellation outline) within the constellation Leo.

Johannes Hevelius first depicted Leo Minor in 1687 when he outlined ten new constellations in his star atlas Firmamentum Sobiescianum, and included 18 of its objects in the accompanying Catalogus Stellarum Fixarum.
Hevelius chose the name Leo Minor or Leo Junior as a depiction that would align with its beastly neighbours the Lion and the Great Bear.
In 1845, English astronomer Francis Baily revised the catalogue of Hevelius's new constellations, assigning Greek letter Bayer designations to stars brighter than magnitude 4.5.

Richard A. Proctor gave the constellation the name Leaena 'the Lioness' in 1870, explaining that he sought to shorten constellation names to make them more manageable on celestial charts. This name did not catch on.
arab: German astronomer Christian Ludwig Ideler posited that the stars of Leo Minor had been termed Al Thibā' wa-Aulāduhā 'Gazelle with her Young' on a 13th-century Arabic celestial globe, recovered by Cardinal Stefano Borgia.
Arabist Friedrich Wilhelm Lach describes a different view, noting that they had been seen as Al Haud 'the Pond', which the Gazelle jumps into.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the stars Beta, 30, 37 and 46 Leonis Minoris made up Neiping, a 'Court of Judge or Mediator', or Shi 'Court Eunuch'.
These stars were also combined with stars of the neighbouring Leo to make up a large celestial dragon or State Chariot.
A line of four stars was known as Shaowei; it represented four Imperial advisors and may have been located in Leo Minor, Leo or adjacent regions.

stars_text: 46 LMi (Praecipua, 3.8m) is the brightest star in Leo Minor, an orange giant of spectral class K0III. Situated 95 light-years from Earth, it has around 32 times the luminosity and is 8.5 times the size of the Sun. Its colour is evident when seen through binoculars.

The name Praecipua appears to have been originally applied to 37 Leonis Minoris in the 1814 Palermo Catalogue, but later connected with 46 Leonis Minoris through an error perpetuated by subsequent astronomers.
37 LMi (4.69m) is a distant yellow supergiant of spectral type G2.5IIa and absolute magnitude of −1.84, around 578 light-years distant.

β LMi (4.4m) is a binary star system. The primary is a giant star of spectral class G9III with around double the mass, 7.8 times the radius and 36 times the luminosity of the Sun. The secondary is a yellow-white main sequence star of spectral type F8. The two orbit around a common centre of gravity every 38.62 years, lying 154 light-years away.

Leo Minor is unusual in that it does not have a star designated Alpha. Francis Baily allocated a Greek letter to only one star, Beta. It is unclear whether he intended to give 46 Leonis Minoris a Bayer designation, as he died before revising his proofs.

21 LMi (4.5m) is a rapidly rotating white main-sequence star of spectral type A7V, about 98 light-years away. It spins on its axis in less than 12 hours and is very likely flattened in shape. It is a Delta Scuti variable.
10 and 11 LMi (SU and SV Leonis Minoris) are yellow giants of spectral type G8III with average magnitudes 4.54 and 5.34 respectively. Both are RS Canum Venaticorum variables.
R and S Leonis Minoris are long-period Mira variables, while U Leonis Minoris is a semiregular variable. All three are red giants of spectral types M6.5e-M9.0e, M5e and M6 respectively.

G 117-B15A (RY Leonis Minoris) is a pulsating white dwarf of apparent magnitude 15.5. With a period of approximately 215 seconds and losing a second every 8.9 million years, this 400-million-year-old star has been proposed as the most stable celestial clock.

SX Leonis Minoris is a dwarf nova of the SU Ursae Majoris type identified in 1994. It consists of a white dwarf and a donor star, which orbit each other every 97 minutes. The dwarf star erupts every 34 to 64 days, reaching magnitude 13.4.
deep_sky_objects: Leo Minor contains many galaxies viewable in amateur telescopes. Patrick Moore described the constellation as having 'dubious claims to a separate identity' due to its faint stars.

NGC 3432 is located 3 degrees southeast of 38 Leonis Minoris, seen nearly edge-on. It is of apparent magnitude 11.7 and measures 6.8 by 1.4 arcminutes. Located 42 million light-years away, it is moving away from the Solar System at 616 km per second.
NGC 3003 is a barred spiral galaxy with an apparent magnitude of 12.3 and an angular size of 5.8 arcminutes, seen almost edge-on.
NGC 3344, 25 million light-years distant, is face-on towards Earth. Measuring 7.1 by 6.5 arcminutes in size, it has an apparent magnitude of 10.45.
NGC 3504 is a starburst barred spiral galaxy of apparent magnitude 11.67, measuring 2.1 by 2.7 arcminutes. It hosted supernovae in 1998 and 2001.
NGC 3486 is a spiral galaxy almost face-on towards Earth. It is of magnitude 11.05 and measures 7.1 by 5.2 arcminutes.
Arp 107 is a pair of galaxies in the process of merging, located 450 million light-years away.
NGC 3395 and NGC 3396 are a spiral and irregular barred spiral galaxy, respectively, that are interacting, located 1.33 degrees southwest of 46 Leonis Minoris.

Hanny's Voorwerp was discovered in Leo Minor in 2007 by Dutch school teacher Hanny van Arkel while participating in the Galaxy Zoo project. Lying near the 650-million-light-year-distant spiral galaxy IC 2497, it is around the same size as the Milky Way.
The voorwerp is thought to be the visual light echo of a quasar now gone inactive, possibly as recently as 200,000 years ago.
meteor_showers_detail: Discovered by Dick McCloskey and Annette Posen of the Harvard Meteor Program in 1959, the Leonis Minorid meteor shower peaks between October 18 and 29.
The shower's parent body is the long period comet C/1739 K1 (Zanotti). It is a minor shower, and can only be seen from the Northern Hemisphere.
exoplanets: HD 87883 is an orange dwarf of magnitude 7.57 and spectral type K0V, 18 parsecs distant from Earth. It is orbited by a planet around 1.78 times the mass of Jupiter every 7.9 years.
HD 82886 (Illyrian) is a yellow dwarf of spectral type G0 and visual magnitude 7.63. A planet 1.3 times the mass of Jupiter orbiting every 705 days was discovered in 2011.

Lep.name: Lepus
Lep.description: Lepus is bordered by Orion, Monoceros, Canis Major, Columba, Caelum and Eridanus. It covers 290 square degrees, ranking 51st among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Lep (Arneb) (2.58m).

greek: Lepus is most often represented as a hare being hunted by Orion, whose hunting dogs (Canis Major and Canis Minor) pursue it.
The constellation is also associated with the Moon rabbit.
arab: Four stars of this constellation (α, β, γ, δ Lep) form a quadrilateral and are known as 'Arsh al-Jawzā', 'the Throne of Jawzā' or Kursiyy al-Jawzā' al-Mu'akhkhar, 'the Hindmost Chair of Jawzā' in Arabic.
These same four stars are also called al-Nihāl, 'the Camels Quenching Their Thirst' in Arabic.

stars_text: α Lep (Arneb, 2.6m) is the brightest star of Lepus, a white supergiant located 1,300 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name, Arneb (أرنب 'arnab), means 'hare' in Arabic.
β Lep (Nihal, 2.8m) is a yellow giant 159 light-years from Earth. Its traditional name Nihal is Arabic for 'quenching their thirst'.
γ Lep (3.6m) is a double star divisible in binoculars. The primary is a yellow star 29 light-years from Earth. The secondary is an orange star of magnitude 6.2.
δ Lep (3.8m) is a yellow giant 112 light-years from Earth.
ε Lep (3.2m) is an orange giant 227 light-years from Earth.
κ Lep is a double star divisible in medium aperture amateur telescopes, 560 light-years from Earth. The primary is a blue-white star of magnitude 4.4 and the secondary is magnitude 7.4.

R Lep is a Mira variable star also called 'Hind's Crimson Star' for its striking red color and because it was named for John Russell Hind. It varies from a minimum of magnitude 9.8 to a maximum of 7.3, with a period of 420 days.
R Leporis is at a distance of 1,500 light-years. The color intensifies as the star brightens. It can be as dim as magnitude 12 and as bright as magnitude 5.5.
T Lep is also a Mira variable observed in detail by ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer.
RX Lep is a semi-regular red giant with a period of 2 months. It has a minimum magnitude of 7.4 and a maximum magnitude of 5.0.
deep_sky_objects: M79 is the only Messier object in Lepus. It is a globular cluster of magnitude 8.0, 42,000 light-years from Earth, discovered in 1780 by Pierre Méchain.
M79 is one of the few globular clusters visible in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere's winter. It is a Shapley class V cluster, which means it has an intermediate concentration towards its center.
M79 is often described as having a 'starfish' shape when viewed through telescopes.

babylonian: In Babylonian astronomy, Libra was known as MUL Zibanu (the "scales" or "balance"), or alternatively as the Claws of the Scorpion. The scales were held sacred to the sun god Shamash, who was also the patron of truth and justice.
greek: In ancient Greece, this area was not seen as a separate constellation but as the Scorpion's Claws. The name was used repeatedly by Aratus and became widespread in Hellenistic times.

In Arabic, zubānā means "scorpion's claws," and this resemblance of words may be why the Scorpion's claws transformed into the Scales. The constellation's two brightest stars, Zubenelgenubi and Zubeneschamali, mean "southern claw" and "northern claw" respectively.

It has been suggested that the scales are an allusion to the autumnal equinox, when the sun entered this part of the ecliptic and days and nights were equal. Libra's status as the equinox location earned it the name "First Point of Libra," though this ceased to be accurate in 730 BC due to precession.
roman: Libra only became a separate constellation in ancient Rome, when it began to represent the scales held by Astraea, the goddess of justice, who is associated with Virgo in Greek mythology. Ptolemy included it in his 48 asterisms, cataloguing 17 stars.
egyptian: In ancient Egypt, the three brightest stars of Libra (α, β, and σ Librae) formed a constellation that was viewed as a boat.

stars_text: Alpha Librae (Zubenelgenubi, "southern claw") is a multiple star system divisible into two stars with binoculars. The primary is a blue-white star of magnitude 2.7, while the secondary is a white F3V star of magnitude 5.2, located 74.9 light-years from Earth.

Beta Librae (Zubeneschamali, "northern claw") is the brightest star in Libra, a green-tinged star of magnitude 2.6 located 160-185 light-years from Earth. It forms the "northern claw" counterpart to Zubenelgenubi.

Gamma Librae (Zubenelakrab, "the scorpion's claw") completes the suite of names referring to Libra's archaic status as the scorpion's claws. It is an orange giant of magnitude 3.9, located 152 light-years from Earth.
Sigma Librae (Brachium) was formerly known as Gamma Scorpii despite being well inside Libra's boundaries. It was not redesignated as Sigma Librae until 1851 by Benjamin A. Gould.
Delta Librae is an Algol-type eclipsing variable star 304 light-years from Earth. It has a period of 2 days 8 hours, varying between magnitude 4.9 and 5.9.

Iota Librae is a complex multiple star system 377 light-years away, with both optical and true binary components. The primary is a blue-white star of magnitude 4.5 that is itself an indivisible binary with a 23-year period.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 5897 is Libra's brightest deep-sky object, a loose globular cluster 50,000 light-years from Earth. It is fairly large and has an integrated magnitude of 9.
IC 1059 is a galaxy located within the constellation boundaries of Libra.
meteor_showers_detail: The May Librids is a meteor shower that radiates from Libra during the month of May.

greek: In ancient times, Lupus was considered an asterism within Centaurus and was thought to represent an arbitrary animal, killed or about to be killed by Centaurus. An alternative visualization by Eratosthenes saw this constellation as a wineskin held by Centaurus.
The constellation was not separated from Centaurus until Hipparchus of Bithynia named it Therion (Medieval Latin: Fera, meaning "beast") in the 2nd century BC.
babylonian: The Greek constellation is probably based on the Babylonian figure known as the Mad Dog (UR.IDIM). This was a strange hybrid creature combining the head and torso of a man with the legs and tail of a lion.
The cuneiform sign 'UR' refers to a large carnivore, including lions, wolves, and dogs. It is often found in association with the sun god and the Bison-man, supposedly related to the Greek Centaurus.
arab: In Arab folk astronomy, Lupus together with Centaurus were collectively called al-Shamareekh, meaning the dense branches of the date palm's fruit.

Later, in Islamic Medieval astronomy, it was named al-Sab', a term used for any predatory wild beast (same as the Greek therion). In some manuscripts it was drawn as a lion, in others as a wolf, both conforming to the Sab' name.
history: In Europe, no particular animal was associated with Lupus until the Latin translation of Ptolemy's work identified it with the wolf, giving the constellation its modern name.

stars_text: Alpha Lupi has the proper name Uridim since September 2024, derived from the Babylonian constellation UR.IDIM (Uridimmu in Akkadian). It is an aging blue giant of spectral type B1.5 III located 460 light-years from Earth.

Alpha Lupi is a Beta Cephei variable, pulsating in brightness by 0.03 magnitude every 7 hours and 6 minutes. Most of Lupus's brightest stars are massive members of the nearest OB association, Scorpius-Centaurus.

Lacaille gave 29 stars Bayer designations in 1756, including the Latin letters a through h and labelling three stars as a and two stars each as Kappa, Nu, Xi, Tau, Phi, and Psi. Overall, there are 127 stars within Lupus's borders brighter than magnitude 6.5.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 5824 and NGC 5986 are globular clusters located toward the north of the constellation, with the dark nebula B 228 nearby.
NGC 5822 and NGC 5749 are two open clusters to the south, along with globular cluster NGC 5927 on the eastern border with Norma.

IC 4406, the Wolf-Rayet planetary nebula also called the Retina Nebula, lies on the western border. It is a cylindrical nebula at 5,000 light-years distance with dust lanes throughout its center, containing some of the hottest stars in existence.
NGC 5882 is a planetary nebula located toward the center of the constellation.

ESO 274-1 is a spiral galaxy seen edge-on, requiring a telescope with at least 12 inches of aperture. It is 9 arcminutes by 0.7 arcminutes with a small, elliptical nucleus and can only be seen under very dark skies.
The historic supernova SN 1006 appeared on April 30 to May 1, 1006, in the constellation of Lupus, as described by various historical sources.

history: Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius formed the constellation in 1687 from 19 faint stars between Ursa Major and Auriga that had earlier been part of the obsolete constellation Jordanus Fluvius.

Hevelius named it Lynx because of its faintness, challenging future stargazers by declaring that only the lynx-eyed (those with good sight) would be able to recognize it. He also used the name Tigris (Tiger) in his catalog but kept only Lynx in his atlas.

English astronomer John Flamsteed adopted the constellation in his catalog (published in 1712) and his subsequent atlas. Amateur astronomer Richard Hinckley Allen noted that the chief stars in Lynx "might well have been utilized by the modern constructor of Ursa Major to complete the quartette of feet."

stars_text: Alpha Lyncis is the brightest star with magnitude 3.14, an orange giant of spectral type K7III located 203 light-years away. Around twice the Sun's mass, it has evolved off the main sequence and swollen to 55 times the Sun's radius, emitting roughly 673 times its luminosity.

Alsciaukat (31 Lyncis), from the Arabic for "thorn," is the only star in Lynx with a proper name. Located 380 light-years away, it's an evolved giant 59 to 75 times the Sun's diameter and 740 times as luminous, varying in brightness by 0.05 magnitude over 25-30 days.

38 Lyncis is the second brightest star at magnitude 3.8. A moderate telescope reveals two components: a brighter blue-white star of magnitude 3.9 and a fainter lilac or blue-white star of magnitude 6.1.

15 Lyncis is a double system visible through telescopes, separating into two yellowish stars of magnitudes 4.7 and 5.8 that are 0.9 arcseconds apart. The pair orbit each other every 262 years and are 178 light-years distant.

10 Ursae Majoris is the third-brightest star in Lynx, though it was originally part of Ursa Major. A telescope reveals a yellow-white F4V star of magnitude 4.11 and a Sun-like G5V star of magnitude 6.18, which orbit each other every 21.78 years at a distance of 52.4 light-years.

Y Lyncis is a popular target for amateur astronomers, a semiregular variable ranging from magnitude 6.2 to 8.9. This red supergiant has a diameter around 580 times the Sun's, with a shorter 110-day pulsation period and a longer 1,400-day period possibly from rotation.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 2419, the "Intergalactic Wanderer," is Lynx's most notable deep-sky object. At 275,000-300,000 light-years from Earth, it's one of the most distant known globular clusters in our galaxy, likely in a highly elliptical orbit around the Milky Way.

NGC 2537, the Bear's Paw Galaxy, is a blue compact dwarf galaxy 17-30 million light-years away, located about 3 degrees north-northwest of 31 Lyncis. Nearby is IC 2233, a very flat spiral galaxy 26-40 million light-years away with low star formation rates.
The NGC 2841 group includes the loose triplet NGC 2541, NGC 2500, and NGC 2552 within Lynx. Using Cepheids as standard candles, the distance has been estimated at around 40 million light-years.

NGC 2770 is a spiral galaxy 88 million light-years away that hosted three Type Ib supernovae (SN 1999eh, SN 2007uy, and SN 2008D). SN 2008D was the first supernova detected by its early X-ray emissions rather than optical light.

APM 08279+5255 is a very distant quasar discovered in 1998, magnified by gravitational lensing. It appears to be a giant elliptical galaxy with a supermassive black hole 23 billion times the Sun's mass and has a redshift of 3.911.
The Lynx Supercluster, at redshift 1.26-1.27, was the most distant supercluster known when discovered in 1999. It comprises two main clusters (Lynx E and Lynx W) and several smaller clumps.

The Lynx Arc, 12 billion light-years away (redshift 3.357), contains a million extremely hot young blue stars with temperatures of 80,000-100,000 K, twice as hot as similar Milky Way stars. Visible only through gravitational lensing, it represents the early universe's "furious firestorms of star birth."
meteor_showers_detail: The September Lyncids are a minor meteor shower appearing around September 6. They were historically more prominent, described by Chinese observers in 1037 and 1063, and Korean astronomers in 1560.
The Alpha Lyncids were discovered in 1971 by Malcolm Currie and appear between December 10 and January 3.

greek: Lyra represents the lyre of Orpheus, whose music was so great that even rocks could be charmed. Joining Jason and the Argonauts, his music quelled the voices of the dangerous Sirens who sang tempting songs.

Orpheus married the nymph Eurydice, who died from a snake bite while fleeing an attack by Aristaeus. To reclaim her, Orpheus entered the Underworld, where his lyre charmed Hades into allowing her return on condition that Orpheus never look back until outside.

Near the very end, Orpheus faltered and looked back, causing Eurydice to be left in the Underworld forever. He spent the rest of his life wandering aimlessly, strumming his lyre and rejecting all marriage offers from women.

According to Eratosthenes, Orpheus failed to make a necessary sacrifice to Dionysus due to his regard for Apollo as supreme deity. Dionysus then sent his followers to rip Orpheus apart. Ovid tells a different story: women, in retribution for Orpheus's rejection of marriage, threw stones and spears until he was killed.
Both myths state that Zeus placed Orpheus's lyre in the sky, and the Muses buried his bones. After death, the goddess Athena honored Andromeda by placing her constellation in the sky.
roman: The Roman book De astronomia, attributed to Hyginus, records another myth that Lyra belonged to Theseus, "for he was skilful in all the arts and seems to have learned the lyre as well." The proximity to Hercules and Corona Borealis suggests these three constellations were invented as a group.
arab: The area corresponding to Lyra was seen by the Arabs as a vulture or an eagle diving with folded wings. The Persian Hafiz called it the Lyre of Zurah.
celtic: In Wales, Lyra is known as King Arthur's Harp (Talyn Arthur), and King David's harp. It has also been called the Manger of the Infant Saviour, Praesepe Salvatoris.
aboriginal: In Australian Aboriginal astronomy, the Boorong people in Victoria know Lyra as the Malleefowl constellation.
incan: Lyra was known as Urcuchillay by the Incas and was worshipped as an animal deity.

stars_text: Vega (Alpha Lyrae, magnitude -0.02 to 0.07) is the brightest star in Lyra and the fifth-brightest in the sky. Only 7.7 parsecs (25 light-years) distant, it's a Delta Scuti variable and was the pole star in 12,000 BCE, destined to become the pole star again around 14,000 CE.

Vega has been called "arguably the next most important star in the sky after the Sun." It was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed and to have its spectrum recorded, showing absorption lines for the first time. It's surrounded by a circumstellar debris disk similar to the Kuiper Belt.
Vega forms one corner of the famous Summer Triangle asterism with Altair and Deneb. It also forms a smaller triangle with Epsilon and Zeta Lyrae.

Epsilon Lyrae is a famous wide binary that can be separated by the naked eye under excellent conditions. Both components are themselves close binaries visible through telescopes, consisting of A- and F-type stars, with a fifth faint star recently discovered, making it a five-star system.

Beta Lyrae (Sheliak) is a binary composed of a blue bright giant and an early B-type star so close that the giant overflows its Roche lobe, transferring material to the secondary. The system shows eclipses, dropping nearly a full magnitude every 13 days, though its period is increasing by 19 seconds per year.
Gamma Lyrae (Sulafat) is a blue giant and the second-brightest star in the constellation, located around 190 parsecs distant and described as a "superficially normal" star.

RR Lyrae is the prototype of the RR Lyrae variables, pulsating population II stars used as standard candles to calculate distances to globular clusters. It varies between magnitudes 7 and 8 while exhibiting the Blazhko effect.

Delta Lyrae is an optical double with two stars lying along the same line of sight. Delta2 Lyrae is a red bright giant that varies semiregularly by 0.2 magnitudes with a 79-day period, while Delta1 Lyrae is a spectroscopic binary.
deep_sky_objects: M57, the Ring Nebula (NGC 6720), is one of the best known planetary nebulae, discovered in 1779 by Antoine Darquier. At 2,550 light-years distant, it is 6,000-8,000 years old and approximately one light-year in diameter.

The Ring Nebula's outer part appears red from ionized hydrogen, the middle region green from doubly ionized oxygen, and the hottest region blue from helium emission. The central white dwarf has a temperature of 120,000 kelvins.

Abell 46 is another planetary nebula whose central star, V477 Lyrae, is an eclipsing post-common-envelope binary consisting of a white dwarf and an oversized secondary component. The nebula has relatively low surface brightness compared to the central star.
NGC 6791 is a star cluster containing three age groups: 4 billion year-old white dwarfs, 6 billion year-old white dwarfs, and 8 billion year-old normal stars.

NGC 6745 is an irregular spiral galaxy 208 million light-years away that collided with a smaller galaxy several million years ago, creating a region filled with young, hot, blue stars. It's unknown whether the collision was a glancing blow or prelude to a full merger.

GRB 050525A was a remarkable long-duration gamma-ray burst that flared in 2005. The afterglow re-brightened 33 minutes after the original burst, only the third found to exhibit such an effect, with a light curve consistent with a supernova or hypernova (SN 2005nc).
meteor_showers_detail: The Lyrids meteor shower is one of the oldest known meteor showers, radiating from Lyra each April. It has been observed for over 2,600 years and typically produces 10-20 meteors per hour at its peak.
The June Lyrids is a minor meteor shower that appears in June, while the Alpha Lyrids occur in a different part of the year, providing multiple meteor viewing opportunities from this constellation.

Men.name: Mensa
Men.description: Mensa is bordered by Dorado, Hydrus, Octans, Chamaeleon, and Volans. It covers 153.5 square degrees, ranking 75th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Men (5.09m), making it the only constellation with no star brighter than magnitude 5.0.

history: Originally named 'Montagne de la Table' or 'Mons Mensae', Mensa was created by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille out of dim Southern Hemisphere stars in honor of Table Mountain, a South African mountain overlooking Cape Town near his observatory.

Lacaille recalled that the Magellanic Clouds were sometimes known as Cape clouds, and that Table Mountain was often covered in clouds when a southeasterly stormy wind blew. Hence he made a 'table' in the sky under the clouds.

Lacaille had observed and catalogued 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope. He devised 14 new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe.
Mensa was the only constellation that did not honor an instrument symbolic of the Age of Enlightenment. Sir John Herschel proposed shrinking the name to one word in 1844.

Although the stars of Mensa do not feature in any ancient mythology, Table Mountain has a rich mythology. Called 'Tafelberg' in Dutch and German, it has two neighboring mountains called 'Devil's Peak' and 'Lion's Head'.
Explorer Bartolomeu Dias saw the mountain as a mythical anvil for storms in the Cape of Good Hope, notorious for its storms.

stars_text: α Men (Hoerikwaggo, 5.09m) is a solar-type star (class G7V) 33.32 light-years from Earth. It came to within 11 light-years from Earth around 250,000 years ago and would have been considerably brighter—nearly second magnitude. It has a red dwarf companion star at about 30 AU separation.

γ Men (5.19m) is the second-brightest star in the constellation. Located 104.9 light-years from Earth, it is an aging 10.6 billion year-old orange giant of spectral type K2III about 1.04 times as massive as the Sun and 5 times its radius.

β Men (5.31m) is a yellow giant of spectral type G8III located 660 light-years from Earth. It is around 3.6 times as massive and 513 times as luminous as the Sun. It is 270 million years old and lies in front of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
ζ and η Men have infrared excesses suggesting they have circumstellar disks of dust. Zeta is a white giant around 394 light-years away, while Eta is an orange giant lying 650 light-years distant.

π Men (5.7m) is a solar-type (G1) star 59.62 light-years distant with a planetary system. In 2001, a substellar companion was discovered with a mass between 10.27 to 29.9 Jupiter masses—possibly a brown dwarf. A second super-Earth was announced in 2018, the first exoplanet detected by TESS submitted for publication.

HD 38283 (Bubup, 6.7m) is a Sun-like star of spectral type F9.5V located 124.3 light-years distant. In 2011, a gas giant with an Earth-like orbital period of 363 days and minimum mass one-third that of Jupiter was discovered.

HD 39194 (8.08m) is an orange dwarf located 86.21 light-years distant. Three planets in close orbit were discovered by HARPS in 2011, taking 5.6, 14, and 34 days to orbit with minimum masses 3.72, 5.94, and 5.14 times Earth's mass.

TZ Men is an eclipsing binary that varies between magnitude 6.2 and 6.9 every 8.57 days. It is composed of two white main-sequence stars in close orbit—one of spectral type A0V with twice the Sun's radius and 2.5 times its mass, the other A8V with 1.4 times the Sun's radius and 1.5 times its mass.

YY Men (8.05m) is an orange giant of spectral type K1III around 2.2 times as massive as the Sun with 12.7 times its diameter and 70 times its luminosity. It is a rapidly rotating FK Comae Berenices variable star that emits strong X-rays, thought to have formed from the merger of two stars in a contact binary system.

AH Men is a cataclysmic variable star system composed of a white dwarf and red dwarf that orbit each other every 2 hours 57 minutes. The white dwarf strips material off the red dwarf, creating an accretion disc that periodically ignites.
WISE 0535-7500 is a binary system composed of two sub-brown dwarfs of spectral class cooler than Y1 located 47 light-years away. They are 8 to 20 times Jupiter's mass and less than one AU apart.
deep_sky_objects: The Large Magellanic Cloud lies partially within Mensa's boundaries, although most of it lies in neighboring Dorado. It is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way located 163,000 light-years distant.
W Men is an unusual yellow-white supergiant within the LMC that belongs to a rare class known as R Coronae Borealis variables.
HD 268835 is a blue hypergiant in the LMC girded by a vast circumstellar disk of dust.
R71 is a luminous blue variable star in the LMC that brightened in 2012 to over a million times as luminous as the Sun.
NGC 1987 is a globular cluster in the LMC estimated to be around 600 million years old with a significant number of red aging stars.
NGC 1848 is a 27 million year old open cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

PKS 0637-752 is a distant quasar with redshift z = 0.651. It was chosen as the first target of Chandra X-Ray Observatory in 1999. The resulting images revealed a gas jet approximately 330,000 light-years long visible at radio, optical, and X-ray wavelengths.
meteor_showers_detail: Mensa has no known meteor showers.

Mic.name: Microscopium
Mic.description: Microscopium is bordered by Capricornus, Piscis Austrinus, Grus, Indus, Sagittarius, and touches Telescopium to the southwest. It covers 210 square degrees, ranking 66th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is γ Mic (4.67m). Given that its brightest stars are fifth magnitude, the constellation is invisible in light-polluted skies.

history: Microscopium lies in a region where Ptolemy had listed six 'unformed' stars behind the tail of Piscis Austrinus. Al-Sufi did not include these stars in his revision of the Almagest, presumably because he could not identify them.

Microscopium was introduced in 1751-52 by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille with the French name 'le Microscope', after he had observed and catalogued 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.

Lacaille devised fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honored instruments that symbolized the Age of Enlightenment.
Commemorating the compound microscope, the Microscope's name had been Latinized by Lacaille to Microscopium by 1763.

stars_text: γ Mic (4.68m) depicts the eyepiece of the microscope and is the brightest star in the constellation. Having spent much of its 620-million-year lifespan as a blue-white main sequence star, it has swollen and cooled to become a yellow giant of spectral type G6III with a diameter ten times that of the Sun, located 223 light-years from Earth.

Gamma likely passed within 1.14 to 3.45 light-years of the Sun some 3.9 million years ago. At around 2.5 times the mass of the Sun, it is possibly massive enough and close enough to have disturbed the Oort cloud.

α Mic (4.90m) is an aging yellow giant star of spectral type G7III located 400 light-years away. It has swollen to 17.5 times the Sun's diameter. It has a 10th magnitude companion visible in 7.5 cm telescopes, though this is a coincidental closeness rather than a true binary system.
ε Mic (4.7m) lies 166 light-years away and is a white star of spectral type A1V.

θ1 and θ2 Mic make up a wide double whose components are splittable to the naked eye. Both are white A-class magnetic spectrum variable stars with strong metallic lines, similar to Cor Caroli. They mark the constellation's specimen slide.
AX Mic (Lacaille 8760, 6.68m) is a red dwarf which lies only 12.9 light-years from the Solar System. It is the brightest red dwarf in the sky.

BO Mic (Speedy Mic) is a rapidly rotating star with 80% the Sun's diameter and a rotation period of 9 hours 7 minutes. An active star, it has prominent stellar flares that average 100 times stronger than the Sun's, emitting energy mainly in X-ray and ultraviolet bands. It lies 218 light-years away.

AT Mic is a binary star system, both members of which are flare star red dwarfs. The system may form a very wide triple system with AU Mic, a young star with a planetary system in the making with a debris disk. The three stars are candidate members of the Beta Pictoris moving group.

R and S Mic are Mira variables that are challenging for novice amateur astronomers. U and RY Mic are more difficult still. The Astronomical Society of Southern Africa in 2003 reported that observations of these four Mira variables were very urgently needed as data on their light curves was incomplete.
T Mic is a semiregular variable red giant that ranges between magnitudes 7.7 and 9.6 over 344 days.

DD Mic (11m) is a symbiotic star system composed of an orange giant of spectral type K2III and white dwarf in close orbit. The smaller star ionizes the stellar wind of the larger star. Its low metallicity combined with high galactic latitude indicates the system originated in the galactic halo of the Milky Way.

HD 205739 is a yellow-white main sequence star of spectral type F7V around 1.22 times as massive and 2.3 times as luminous as the Sun. It has a Jupiter-sized planet with an orbital period of 280 days discovered by the radial velocity method.
WASP-7 (9.54m) is a star of spectral type F5V about 1.28 times as massive as the Sun. Its hot Jupiter planet WASP-7b was discovered by transit method and orbits the star every 4.95 days.

HD 202628 is a sunlike star of spectral type G2V with a debris disk ranging from 158 to 220 AU distant. Its inner edge is sharply defined, indicating a probable planet orbiting between 86 and 158 AU from the star.
deep_sky_objects: Describing Microscopium as 'totally unremarkable', astronomer Patrick Moore concluded there was nothing of interest for amateur observers.
NGC 6925 is a barred spiral galaxy of apparent magnitude 11.3 which is lens-shaped, as it lies almost edge-on to observers on Earth, 3.7 degrees west-northwest of Alpha Microscopii.
SN 2011ei, a Type II Supernova in NGC 6925, was discovered by Stu Parker in New Zealand in July 2011.
NGC 6923 lies nearby NGC 6925 and is a magnitude fainter still.
The Microscopium Void is a roughly rectangular region of relatively empty space, bounded by incomplete sheets of galaxies from other voids.

The Microscopium Supercluster is an overdensity of galaxy clusters first noticed in the early 1990s. The component Abell clusters 3695 and 3696 are likely to be gravitationally bound, while the relations of Abell clusters 3693 and 3705 in the same field are unclear.
meteor_showers_detail: The Microscopiids are a minor meteor shower that appear from June to mid-July.

Mon.name: Monoceros
Mon.description: Monoceros is bordered by Canis Major, Canis Minor, Gemini, Hydra, Lepus, Orion, and Puppis. It covers 482 square degrees, ranking 35th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is β Mon (3.76m). Part of the galactic plane goes through Monoceros, concealing background galaxies with interstellar dust.

history: In Western astronomy, Monoceros is a relatively modern constellation, not one of Ptolemy's 48 in the Almagest. Its first certain appearance was on a globe created by cartographer Petrus Plancius in 1612 or 1613.
It was later charted by German astronomer Jakob Bartsch as Unicornu on his star chart of 1624.

German astronomers Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers and Ludwig Ideler indicate that the constellation may be older, quoting an astrological work from 1564 that mentioned 'the second horse between the Twins and the Crab has many stars, but not very bright'.
These references may ultimately be due to 13th century Scotsman Michael Scot, but refer to a horse and not a unicorn, and its position does not quite match.
Joseph Scaliger is reported to have found Monoceros on an ancient Persian sphere.
Astronomer Camille Flammarion believed that a former constellation, Neper (the 'Auger'), occupied the part of that sky now deemed Monoceros and Microscopium, but this is disputed.
chinese: Chinese asterisms Sze Fuh (the Four Great Canals), Kwan Kew, and Wae Choo (the Outer Kitchen) all lay within the boundaries of Monoceros.

stars_text: α Mon (3.93m) and γ Mon (3.98m) are the constellation's only stars visible to the naked eye in fourth magnitude, making Monoceros difficult to see.

β Mon (3.76m) is the brightest star—a triple star system where the three stars form a fixed triangle. The visual magnitudes are 4.7, 5.2, and 6.1. William Herschel discovered it in 1781 and called it 'one of the most beautiful sights in the heavens.'
ε Mon is a fixed binary with visual magnitudes of 4.5 and 6.5.
S Mon (15 Mon, 4.2-4.6m) is a bluish white variable star located at the center of NGC 2264. The variation in its magnitude is slight. It has a companion star of visual magnitude 8.

V838 Mon, a variable red supergiant star, had an outburst starting on January 6, 2002. In February, its brightness increased by a factor of 10,000 in one day. After the outburst, Hubble Space Telescope observed a light echo that illuminated the dust surrounding the star.
Plaskett's Star is a massive binary system whose combined mass is estimated to be almost 100 solar masses per 2008 calculations.

Scholz's Star is a binary system with a red dwarf primary and brown dwarf secondary. The system performed a close flyby of the Solar System approximately 70,000 years ago, traveling within 120,000 AU of the Sun within the Oort cloud.
A0620-00 is one of the nearest known black holes to the Solar System, at roughly 3,300 light-years (1,000 parsecs) distant. The black hole is estimated to be 6.6 solar masses.

CoRoT-7b and CoRoT-7c are two Super-Earth exoplanets in one planetary system. CoRoT-7b was detected by the CoRoT satellite and CoRoT-7c by HARPS. Until Kepler-10b in January 2011, CoRoT-7b was the smallest exoplanet to have its diameter measured, at 1.58 times Earth's (volume 3.95 times Earth's). Both planets were discovered in 2009.
deep_sky_objects: Messier 50 is an open cluster in Monoceros.

The Rosette Nebula (NGC 2237, 2238, 2239, and 2246) is a diffuse nebula with an overall magnitude of 6.0 located 4,900 light-years from Earth. Over 100 light-years in diameter, it has an associated star cluster and possesses many Bok globules in its dark areas. It was independently discovered in the 1880s by Lewis Swift and Edward Emerson Barnard.

The Christmas Tree Cluster (NGC 2264) is an open cluster named for its resemblance to a Christmas tree. Fairly bright at magnitude 3.9, it is 2,400 light-years from Earth. Variable star S Monocerotis represents the tree's trunk, while variable star V429 Monocerotis represents its top.

The Cone Nebula (NGC 2264), associated with the Christmas Tree Cluster, is a very dim nebula containing a dark conic structure. It appears clearly in photographs but is very elusive in a telescope. The nebula contains several Herbig-Haro objects, which are small irregularly variable nebulae associated with protostars.

NGC 2254 is an open cluster with magnitude 9.7, 7,100 light-years from Earth. It is a Shapley class f and Trumpler class I 2 p cluster, meaning it appears to be a fairly rich cluster overall, though it has fewer than 50 stars. It appears distinct from the background star field and is very concentrated at its center.

Hubble's Variable Nebula (NGC 2261) is a nebula with magnitude 10, 2,500 light-years from Earth. It is named for Edwin Hubble and was discovered in 1783 by Herschel. It is illuminated by R Monocerotis, a young variable star embedded in the nebula. The star's unique interaction makes it both an emission nebula and a reflection nebula. One hypothesis is that they represent a very early stage planetary system.
IC 447 is a reflection nebula in Monoceros.
meteor_showers_detail: The December Monocerids and Alpha Monocerids are meteor showers radiating from Monoceros.

Mus.name: Musca

source.discoverer: Petrus Plancius (from Keyser and de Houtman observations)

Mus.description: Musca is bordered by Crux, Carina, Chamaeleon, Apus, Circinus, and Centaurus. It covers 138 square degrees, ranking 77th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Mus (2.69m). It is the only official constellation depicting an insect.

history: Musca was one of the 12 constellations established by Petrus Plancius from observations of the southern sky by Dutch explorers Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman, who had sailed on the first Dutch trading expedition (Eerste Schipvaart) to the East Indies.

De Houtman included it in his southern star catalogue in 1598 under the Dutch name 'De Vlieghe' (The Fly). They assigned four stars to the constellation, with Beta marking the head, Gamma the body, and Alpha and Delta the left and right wings.
It first appeared on a 35-cm-diameter celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius, though was unnamed.

The first depiction in a celestial atlas was in German cartographer Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603, though Bayer termed it 'Apis' (the Bee), a name by which it was known for the next two centuries.
A 1603 celestial globe by Willem Blaeu depicts it as providing nourishment for the nearby constellation Chamaeleon—its tongue trying to catch the insect.
Nicolas Louis de Lacaille called it 'la Mouche' on the 1756 version of his planisphere of the southern skies. Jean Fortin retained the French name in 1776 for his Atlas Céleste.

Lacaille renamed it to Musca Australis (the Southern Fly) for his revised Coelum Australe Stelliferum in 1763—Australis since it counterparted the now-discarded constellation of Musca Borealis in Aries. Today, the name is simply Musca.
aboriginal_australian: The Wardaman people of the Northern Territory perceived the main stars of Musca as a ceremonial boomerang, part of the Central Arena—a sacred area surrounding Crux depicting the lightning creation beings and where they teach Wardaman customs.
Alpha and Beta also signified a ceremonial headband, while Gamma and Delta represented two armbands.

The Arrernte and Luritja peoples living on a mission in Hermannsburg viewed the sky as divided between them, east of the Milky Way representing Arrernte camps and west denoting Luritja camps. The stars of Musca, along with Fomalhaut, Alpha Pavonis, and Alpha and Beta Gruis, were all claimed by the Arrernte.
south_american: The Kalapalo people of Mato Grosso state in Brazil called Alpha and Beta Muscae (along with Beta and Kappa Crucis) Kutsu anangagï ('Ornate Hawk-Eagle's double flutes').

stars_text: α Mus (2.7m) is the brightest star in the constellation, lying south-southeast of Acrux in neighboring Crux. Located around 310 light-years away, it is a blue-white star of spectral type B2IV-V around 4,520 times as luminous and 8 times as massive as the Sun. It is a Beta Cephei variable with about 4.7 times the Sun's diameter, pulsating every 2.2 hours and varying by 1% in brightness.
γ Mus (3.84-3.86m) marks the fly's tail—a blue-white star of spectral type B5V that varies over a period of 2.7 days. It is a slowly pulsating B star around five times as massive as the Sun.

β Mus is a binary star system around 341 light-years distant composed of two blue-white main-sequence stars of spectral types B2V and B3V that orbit each other every 194 years. They are eight and six times as massive as the Sun and have about 3.5 times its diameter.
ζ2 Mus is a white main sequence star of spectral type A5V around 330 light-years distant. It is part of a triple star system with faint companions at 0.5 and 32.4 arc seconds distance.
η Mus is a multiple star system, the two main components forming an eclipsing binary with combined spectral type B8V and magnitude 4.77 that dips by 0.05 magnitude every 2.39 days.

Alpha, Beta, Gamma, HD 103079, Zeta2, and likely Eta are all members of the Lower Centaurus Crux subgroup of the Scorpius-Centaurus association, a group of predominantly hot blue-white stars that share a common origin and proper motion across the galaxy.
δ Mus (3.62m) marks the fly's left wing. It is an orange giant of spectral type K2III located around 91 light-years away.

ε Mus (3.99-4.31m) marks the right wing. It is a red giant of spectral type M5III and semiregular variable that ranges over approximately 40 days. It has expanded to 130 times the Sun's diameter and 1,800 to 2,300 times its luminosity. It was originally a star 1.5 to 2 times as massive as the Sun.
μ Mus (4.71-4.76m) is an orange giant of spectral type K4III that has been classified as a slow, irregular variable.
λ Mus is the third-brightest star in the constellation—a white main-sequence star of spectral type A7V around 128 light-years distant.
R Mus (5.93-6.73m) is a classical Cepheid variable ranging over 7.5 days. It is a yellow-white supergiant ranging between spectral types F7Ib and G2Ib, located around 2,037 light-years away.

S Mus (5.89-6.49m) is likewise a classical Cepheid, a yellow-white supergiant ranging between spectral types F6Ib and G0Ib over 9.66 days. A luminous star around 5.9 times as massive as the Sun, it is a binary star with a blue-white main-sequence star companion likely B3V to B5V with just over 5 solar masses—one of the hottest and brightest companions of a Cepheid known. The two orbit each other every 505 days.

θ Mus is a triple star system thought to be around 7,500 light-years distant. It consists of a spectroscopic binary composed of a Wolf-Rayet star (WC5 or 6) and an O-type main-sequence star (O6 or O7) that orbit each other every 19 days, and a blue supergiant (O9.5/B0Iab) set about 46 milliarcseconds apart. All three are highly luminous; combined, they are likely over a million times as luminous as the Sun.

TU Mus is a binary star system located around 15,500 light-years away made up of two hot, luminous, blue main-sequence stars of spectral types O7.5V and O9.5V with masses 23 and 15 times that of the Sun. The stars are so close they are in contact (overcontact binary) and are classed as a Beta Lyrae variable. The system ranges from magnitude 8.17 to 8.75 over around 1.4 days.

GQ Mus (Nova Muscae 1983) is a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and small star about 10% as massive as the Sun orbiting every 1.4 hours. The white dwarf accumulates material via its accretion disc. In 1983 it erupted, reaching magnitude 7.2. Discovered on 18 January 1983, it was the first nova from which X-rays were detected.

GRS 1124-683 (Nova Muscae 1991) is a binary object consisting of an orange main-sequence star (GU Muscae) of spectral type K3V-K4V and a black hole of around six solar masses. During the 1991 outburst, radiation was produced through positron annihilation.
GR Mus is an X-ray source composed of a neutron star of between 1.2 and 1.8 times the Sun's mass and a low-mass star likely around the Sun's mass in close orbit.

SY Mus is a symbiotic star system composed of a red giant and white dwarf. Although the larger star is transferring mass to the smaller, no periodic eruption occurs nor does an accretion disc form. The system varies in magnitude from 10.2 to 12.7 over 624.5 days.
V415 Mus is a nova that had an outburst on 8 June 2022 with apparent magnitude +8.7.
HD 111232 is a yellow main-sequence star around 78% as massive as the Sun, around 95 light-years distant. It has a planet around 6.8 times Jupiter's mass with an orbital period around 1,143 days.

HD 112410 is a yellow giant of spectral type G8III located around 439 light-years distant. With around 1.54 times the Sun's mass, it is cooling and expanding along the red-giant branch. It has a substellar companion calculated to have a mass 9.2 times that of Jupiter with an orbital period of 124.6 days at a distance around 0.57 AU.

HD 100546 is a young, blue-white Herbig Ae/Be star of spectral type B9V that has yet to settle on the main sequence—the closest of these stars to Earth around 320 light-years distant. It is surrounded by a circumstellar debris disk from 0.2 to 4 AU and again from 13 AU out to a few hundred AU, with evidence for a protoplanet forming at around 47 AU. A gap exists between 4 and 13 AU appearing to contain a large planet around 20 times Jupiter's mass, although further examination suggests it might be a brown dwarf or more than one planet.

LP 145-141 is a white dwarf located 15 light-years distant—the fourth-closest to the Solar System. It is considered a good candidate to look for Jupiter-like planets, on account of its proximity and mass.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 5189 is an unusual planetary nebula located on the border with Circinus, estimated to be around 1,750 light-years away. Its complex structure is due to multiple ejections of material from the aging central star, which are distorted by the presence of a likely binary companion.
The Engraved Hourglass Nebula (MyCn 18) is a magnitude-12.9 planetary nebula located 2.4 degrees east of Eta Muscae, lying about 8,000 light-years distant.
IC 4191 is a compact bluish planetary nebula of magnitude 10.6 near Mu, thought to lie around 10,750 light-years away.
NGC 4071 is a large, diffuse planetary nebula of magnitude 12.7 with a magnitude 12 central star west of Epsilon Muscae, thought to lie around 4,000 light-years away.
The Coalsack Nebula is a dark nebula located mainly in neighboring Crux that intrudes into Musca.
NGC 4463 is an open cluster located on the constellation's southwestern border. Around five light-years across, it is located around 3,400 light-years away.
NGC 4833 is a comparatively old globular cluster near Delta Muscae, catalogued by Lacaille in 1755. It is 21,200 light-years distant and somewhat obscured by dust clouds near the galactic plane.

NGC 4372 is a globular cluster near Gamma Muscae that is fainter than NGC 4833 and likewise partially obscured by dust, but spans more arc minutes. It is 18,900 light-years from Earth and 23,000 light-years from the Milky Way's center. Its extremely low metallicity indicates it is very old—one of the oldest clusters in the Milky Way.
The Dark Doodad Nebula extends south from NGC 4372, resembling a dark L-shaped river through a bright field of stars.
BHR 71 is another dark nebula in the constellation.
meteor_showers_detail: Musca has no known meteor showers.

Nor.name: Norma
Nor.description: Norma is bordered by Scorpius, Lupus, Circinus, Triangulum Australe and Ara. It covers 165 square degrees, ranking 74th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is γ² Nor (4.01m).

history: Norma was introduced in 1751-52 by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille with the French name l'Équerre et la Règle (the Square and Rule). He observed and catalogued 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.
Lacaille devised 14 new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honoured instruments that symbolised the Age of Enlightenment.
Lacaille portrayed Norma, Circinus and Triangulum Australe as a set square and ruler, a compass, and a surveyor's level in a set of draughtsman instruments in his 1756 map of the southern stars.
The constellation's name had been shortened and Latinised by Lacaille to Norma by 1763.

stars_text: Lacaille charted ten stars with Bayer designations Alpha through Mu in 1756. However, Alpha and Beta Normae were transferred to Scorpius and renamed N Scorpii and H Scorpii by Benjamin Apthorp Gould.

γ² Nor (4.0m) is Norma's brightest star, a yellow giant G8III located 129 light-years away. It is 2-2.5 times as massive as the Sun, has swollen to 10 solar diameters and shines with 45 solar luminosities.
γ¹ Nor is a yellow-white supergiant located around 1,500 light-years away. The two gamma stars form an optical double, not a true binary system.

ε Nor is a spectroscopic binary with two blue-white B3V main sequence stars of nearly equal mass orbiting every 3.26 days. A third B9V star is separated by 22 arcseconds. The system is 530 light-years distant.
η Nor is a yellow giant G8III with magnitude 4.65, shining with 66 solar luminosities.

ι¹ Nor is a multiple star system. The AB pair (mag 5.2 and 5.76) orbit every 26.9 years and are 2.77 and 2.71 solar masses. They lie 128 light-years away. A third component is a G8V yellow main sequence star of magnitude 8.02.

μ Nor is a remote blue supergiant O9.7Iab, one of the most luminous stars known, partially obscured by distance and dust. It could have between 250,000 and one million solar luminosities and up to 60 solar masses, though more likely around 500,000 solar luminosities and 40 solar masses.

S Nor is a Cepheid variable ranging from magnitude 6.12 to 6.77 with a period of 9.75 days. It is a yellow-white supergiant F8-G0Ib that is 6.3 solar masses, located at the centre of open cluster NGC 6087. It has a 2.4 solar mass B9.5V companion.
R Nor is a Mira variable ranging from magnitude 6.5 to 13.9 with an average period of 507.5 days. T Nor is another Mira variable ranging from magnitude 6.2 to 13.6 with a period of 244 days.
IM Nor is one of only ten recurrent novae known in the Milky Way. It erupted in 1920 and 2002, reaching magnitude 8.5 from a baseline of 18.3.

A binary system composed of two wolf-rayet stars, colloquially called Apep, has been identified as a possible progenitor of a long gamma-ray burst. Located around 8,000 light-years distant, it would be the first such system in the Milky Way.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6087 is the brightest open cluster in Norma with magnitude 5.4. It lies in the southeastern corner between Alpha Centauri and Zeta Arae. Around 100 million years old, it is about 3,300 light-years away and 14 light-years in diameter. Its brightest member is the Cepheid variable S Normae.

NGC 6067 has an integrated magnitude of 5.6 though it is indistinct in a rich star field. It is around 102 million years old and contains 891 solar masses. Two Cepheid variables (QZ Nor and V340 Nor) are cluster members.
Fainter open clusters include NGC 6134 (magnitude 7.2, 4,000 light-years away), NGC 6167 (magnitude 6.7), NGC 6115 near γ Nor, NGC 6031 and NGC 5999.

Shapley 1 (PK 329+02.1), the Fine-Ring Nebula, is a planetary nebula located around 4,900 light-years distant. Ring-shaped in appearance, it is thought to be cylindrical and oriented directly at Earth. Around 8,700 years old, it has integrated magnitude 13.6 and lies five degrees west-northwest of γ¹ Nor.
Mz 1 is a bipolar planetary nebula with an hourglass shape tilted at an angle, some 3,500 light-years distant.
Mz 3, the Ant Nebula, has a complex appearance with at least four outflow jets and two large lobes visible.

Abell 3627 (the Norma Cluster) is approximately 200 million light-years from Earth with a redshift of 0.016. It is one of the most massive galaxy clusters known, at ten times the average cluster mass. Abell 3627 is theorized to be the Great Attractor, a massive object pulling the Local Group, Virgo Supercluster, and Hydra-Centaurus Supercluster towards its location at 600-1000 km/s.
The Norma Arm is a minor galactic arm named after Norma for lying in its background.
meteor_showers_detail: The Gamma Normids (GNO) meteor shower is relatively weak, typically active from March 7 to 23, peaking on March 15. Its radiant is near γ² Nor.

Oct.name: Octans
Oct.description: Octans is bordered by Tucana, Indus, Pavo, Apus, Chamaeleon, Mensa and Hydrus. It covers 291 square degrees, ranking 50th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is ν Oct (3.73m).

history: Octans was one of 14 constellations created by French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille during his expedition to the Cape of Good Hope. It was originally named l'Octans de Reflexion (the reflecting octant) in 1752.

Lacaille observed and catalogued almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope. He devised fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honoured instruments that symbolised the Age of Enlightenment.
The constellation was published posthumously in 1763 in Lacaille's catalogue of the southern sky, the Coelum Australe Stelliferum.
In Europe, it became more widely known as Octans Hadleianus, in honor of English mathematician John Hadley, who invented the octant in 1730.
There is no real mythology related to Octans, due to its faintness, relative recentness, and extreme southerly latitude.

stars_text: Lacaille gave 22 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Upsilon in 1756, but omitted Omicron and Xi, and labelled three stars as Gamma and two stars each as Mu and Pi.
In 1879, Benjamin Gould added Xi, Phi, Chi, Psi, and Omega, as they were bright enough and their closeness to the south celestial pole warranted their names.
Octans is a generally inconspicuous constellation with only one star brighter than magnitude 4.

ν Oct is unusually the brightest member despite having a very late Bayer designation. A spectral class K1 IV subgiant with apparent magnitude 3.73, it has a white dwarf companion and is orbited by one exoplanet.
β Oct is the second brightest star in the constellation.
σ Oct (Polaris Australis), the southern pole star, is a magnitude 5.4 star just over 1 degree away from the true south celestial pole. Its relative faintness means it is not practical for navigation.
BQ Oct is a fainter magnitude 6.82 star located much closer to the South Pole (at less than a degree) than Sigma.
In addition to having the current southern pole star of Earth, Octans also contains the southern pole star of the planet Saturn, which is the magnitude 4.3 δ Oct.

At least four star systems have planets. μ² Oct is a binary system with a planet orbiting the brighter component. ν Oct A also has a planet. HD 142022 is a binary with a sunlike star hosting a massive planet with an orbital period of 1,928 days. HD 212301 is a yellow-white main sequence star with a hot jupiter completing an orbit every 2.2 days.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 2573 (Polarissima Australis) is a faint barred spiral galaxy that is the closest NGC object to the south celestial pole.
NGC 7095 and NGC 7098 are two barred spiral galaxies that are 115 million and 95 million light-years distant from Earth respectively.
The sparse open cluster Collinder 411 is also located in the constellation.

Oph.name: Ophiuchus
Oph.meteor_showers: Ophiuchids, Northern May Ophiuchids, Southern May Ophiuchids, Theta Ophiuchids
Oph.description: Ophiuchus lies between Aquila, Serpens, Scorpius, Sagittarius, and Hercules, northwest of the center of the Milky Way. It covers 948 square degrees, ranking 11th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Rasalhague (α Oph) (2.08m).

babylonian: There is no evidence of the constellation preceding the classical era. In Babylonian astronomy, a 'Sitting Gods' constellation seems to have been located in the general area of Ophiuchus.

Gavin White proposes that Ophiuchus may be remotely descended from this Babylonian constellation, representing Nirah, a serpent-god sometimes depicted with his upper half human but with serpents for legs.
greek: To the ancient Greeks, the constellation represented the god Apollo struggling with a huge snake that guarded the Oracle of Delphi.

Later myths identified Ophiuchus with Laocoön, the Trojan priest of Poseidon. He warned his fellow Trojans about the Trojan Horse and was later slain by a pair of sea serpents sent by the gods to punish him.
According to Roman era mythography, the figure represents the healer Asclepius, who learned the secrets of keeping death at bay after observing one serpent bringing another healing herbs.
To prevent the entire human race from becoming immortal under Asclepius' care, Jupiter killed him with a bolt of lightning, but later placed his image in the heavens to honor his good works.
history: The earliest mention of the constellation is in Aratus, informed by the lost catalogue of Eudoxus of Cnidus (4th century BC).
Aratus describes Ophiuchus as trampling on Scorpius with his feet. This is depicted in Renaissance to Early Modern star charts, beginning with Albrecht Dürer in 1515.
In some depictions (such as Johannes Kepler's De Stella Nova, 1606), Scorpius also seems to threaten to sting Serpentarius in the foot.
This arrangement has been taken as symbolic in later literature and placed in relation to the words spoken by God to the serpent in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3:15).
arab: In medieval Islamic astronomy (Azophi's Uranometry, 10th century), the constellation was known as Al-Ḥawwā', 'the snake-charmer'.

stars_text: α Oph (Rasalhague, 2.07m) is the brightest star, meaning 'head of the serpent charmer'. It is composed of an A-type bluish-white giant star and a K-type main sequence star. The primary is a rapid rotator with an inclined axis of rotation.
η Oph (Sabik, 2.43m) is a binary system. Its name means 'the preceding one'.
β Oph (Cebalrai, 'dog of the shepherd') is an evolved red giant star that is slightly more massive than the Sun.
λ Oph (Marfik, 'the elbow') is a binary star system with the primary being more massive and luminous than the Sun.

RS Oph is a recurrent nova whose brightness increases at irregular intervals by hundreds of times in just a few days. It is thought to be at the brink of becoming a Type Ia supernova. It erupts around every 15 years and usually has magnitude around 5.0 during eruptions, most recently in 2021.
