Barnard's Star, one of the nearest stars to the Solar System (only Alpha Centauri and Proxima Centauri are closer), lies in Ophiuchus. It is located to the left of β and just north of the V-shaped group of stars in an area once occupied by the obsolete constellation Taurus Poniatovii.

Barnard's Star has historically been subject to multiple claims of planets that were later disproven, until a confirmation of four planets in 2025. In 1998, an intense flare was observed. The star has been a target of plans for interstellar travel such as Project Daedalus.

The supernova of 1604 was first observed on October 9, 1604, near θ Oph. Johannes Kepler studied it extensively and it became known as Kepler's Supernova. He published his findings in De stella nova in pede Serpentarii (On the New Star in Ophiuchus's Foot).
It was a Type Ia supernova and the most recent Milky Way supernova visible to the unaided eye. Galileo used its brief appearance to counter the Aristotelian dogma that the heavens are changeless.

GJ 1214, a star in Ophiuchus, undergoes repeated cyclical dimming with a period of about 1.5 days consistent with a transiting planet. The planet's low density (about 40% that of Earth) suggests it might have a substantial component of hydrogen or steam. At just 42 light-years away, it is a feasible target for further observations.
deep_sky_objects: Ophiuchus contains several star clusters: IC 4665, NGC 6633, M9, M10, M12, M14, M19, M62, and M107, as well as the nebula IC 4603-4604.
M9 is a globular cluster which may have an extra-galactic origin.
M10 is a fairly close globular cluster, only 20,000 light-years from Earth. It has magnitude 6.6 and is a Shapley class VII cluster with 'intermediate' concentration.
M12 is a globular cluster around 5 kiloparsecs from the Solar System.
M14 is another globular cluster which is somewhat farther away.
M19 is oblate-shaped with multiple different types of variable stars.
M62 is a globular cluster rich in variable stars such as RR Lyrae variables and has two generations of stars with different element abundances.
M107 is also rich in variable stars.

NGC 6240 is an unusual galaxy merger remnant and starburst galaxy. At 400 million light-years distant, this 'butterfly-shaped' galaxy has two supermassive black holes 3,000 light-years apart. Astronomers estimate the black holes will merge in another billion years.
NGC 6240 has an unusually high rate of star formation due to heat generated by the orbiting black holes and the aftermath of the collision. Both nuclei are active galactic nuclei.

The Mamajek 2 cluster is a new nearby star cluster discovered in 2006 associated with the 4th magnitude star μ Oph. It appears to be a poor cluster remnant analogous to the Ursa Major Moving Group, but 7 times more distant (approximately 170 parsecs away).

Barnard 68 is a large dark nebula located 410 light-years from Earth. Despite its 0.4 light-year diameter, it only has twice the mass of the Sun, making it very diffuse and cold with a temperature of about 16 kelvins.
Barnard 68 will eventually collapse, inciting star formation. One unusual feature is its vibrations with a period of 250,000 years, possibly caused by a supernova shock wave.
The Ophiuchus Superbubble, discovered in 2005 using the Green Bank Telescope, is so large that it extends beyond the plane of the galaxy.
Voyager 1, the furthest man-made object from Earth, is traveling in the direction of Ophiuchus.
In November 2022, the nearest stellar black hole orbited by a G-type main-sequence star was identified as Gaia BH1 at around 1,560 light-years from the Sun.
meteor_showers_detail: Several meteor showers radiate from Ophiuchus: the Ophiuchids, Northern May Ophiuchids, Southern May Ophiuchids, and Theta Ophiuchids.

Ori.name: Orion
Ori.description: Orion is bordered by Taurus, Eridanus, Lepus, Monoceros and Gemini. It covers 594 square degrees, ranking 26th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Rigel (β Ori) (0.12m).

greek: In Greek mythology, Orion was a gigantic, supernaturally strong hunter, born to Euryale, a Gorgon, and Poseidon (Neptune), god of the sea.

One myth recounts Gaia's rage at Orion, who dared to say that he would kill every animal on Earth. The angry goddess tried to dispatch Orion with a scorpion. This is given as the reason that the constellations of Scorpius and Orion are never in the sky at the same time.
However, Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, revived Orion with an antidote. This is said to be the reason that the constellation of Ophiuchus stands midway between the Scorpion and the Hunter in the sky.
The constellation is mentioned in Horace's Odes, Homer's Odyssey and Iliad, and Virgil's Aeneid.
babylonian: The Babylonian star catalogues of the Late Bronze Age name Orion MULSIPA.ZI.AN.NA, 'The Heavenly Shepherd' or 'True Shepherd of Anu' – Anu being the chief god of the heavenly realms.
The Babylonian constellation is sacred to Papshukal and Ninshubur, both minor gods fulfilling the role of 'messenger to the gods'.

Papshukal is closely associated with the figure of a walking bird on Babylonian boundary stones. On the star map the figure of the Rooster is located below and behind the True Shepherd – both constellations represent the herald of the gods in bird and human forms.
egyptian: In ancient Egypt, the stars of Orion were regarded as a god, called Sah. Because Orion rises before Sirius, the star whose heliacal rising was the basis for the Solar Egyptian calendar, Sah was closely linked with Sopdet, the goddess who personified Sirius.
The god Sopdu is said to be the son of Sah and Sopdet. Sah is syncretized with Osiris, while Sopdet is syncretized with Osiris' mythological wife, Isis.
In the Pyramid Texts, from the 24th and 23rd centuries BC, Sah is one of many gods whose form the dead pharaoh is said to take in the afterlife.
history: The distinctive pattern of Orion is recognized in numerous cultures around the world, and many myths are associated with it. Orion is used as a symbol in the modern world.
The Armenians identified their legendary patriarch and founder Hayk with Orion. Hayk is also the name of the Orion constellation in the Armenian translation of the Bible.

The Bible mentions Orion three times, naming it 'Kesil' (literally – fool): Job 9:9 ('He is the maker of the Bear and Orion'), Job 38:31 ('Can you loosen Orion's belt?'), and Amos 5:8 ('He who made the Pleiades and Orion').
In ancient Aram, the constellation was known as Nephēlā', the Nephilim are said to be Orion's descendants.
arab: In medieval Muslim astronomy, Orion was known as al-jabbar, 'the giant'. Orion's sixth brightest star, Saiph, is named from the Arabic saif al-jabbar, meaning 'sword of the giant'.
chinese: In China, Orion was one of the 28 lunar mansions Sieu (Xiù). It is known as Shen (參), literally meaning 'three', for the stars of Orion's Belt.

The Chinese character 參 (pinyin shēn) originally meant the constellation Orion. Its Shang dynasty version, over three millennia old, contains at the top a representation of the three stars of Orion's Belt atop a man's head.
indian: The Rigveda refers to the constellation as Mriga (the Deer).
Nataraja, 'the cosmic dancer', is often interpreted as the representation of Orion. Rudra, the Rigvedic form of Shiva, is the presiding deity of Ardra nakshatra (Betelgeuse) of Hindu astrology.
The Jain Symbol carved in the Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves, India in 1st century BCE has a striking resemblance with Orion.
polynesian: The seven primary stars of Orion make up the Polynesian constellation Heiheionakeiki which represents a child's string figure similar to a cat's cradle.
Several precolonial Filipinos referred to the belt region as 'balatik' (ballista) as it resembles a trap that fires arrows by itself, usually used for catching pigs from the bush.

In Māori tradition, the star Rigel (known as Puanga or Puaka) is closely connected with the celebration of Matariki. The rising of Matariki (the Pleiades) and Rigel before sunrise in midwinter marks the start of the Māori year.

The Malay people refer to Orion as Buruj Belantik (literally 'The hunter constellation'). When near the western horizon, it is often used to indicate the direction of the qibla, the Islamic direction of prayer for the people of the Malay Archipelago.

stars_text: α Ori (Betelgeuse, variable ~0.5m) is a massive M-type red supergiant star nearing the end of its life. It is the second-brightest star in Orion and a semiregular variable star. It serves as the hunter's right shoulder. Generally the 11th-brightest star in the night sky, it has varied between 10th and 23rd-brightest by the end of 2019.

The end of Betelgeuse's life is expected to result in a supernova explosion that will be highly visible from Earth, possibly outshining the Moon and being visible during the day. This is most likely to occur within the next 100,000 years.

β Ori (Rigel, 0.12m) is a B-type blue supergiant that is the seventh-brightest star in the night sky. Similar to Betelgeuse, Rigel is fusing heavy elements in its core and will pass its supergiant stage soon, possibly ending in a supernova explosion. It serves as the hunter's left foot.

γ Ori (Bellatrix, 1.64m) is the 27th-brightest star in the night sky. It is a B-type blue giant, though too small to explode in a supernova. Bellatrix's luminosity is derived from its high temperature rather than a large radius. It marks Orion's left shoulder. Its name means 'the female warrior', and is sometimes known as the 'Amazon Star'. It is the closest major star in Orion at only 244.6 light-years.

δ Ori (Mintaka, 2.23m) is the faintest of the three stars in Orion's Belt despite its designation. Its name means 'the belt'. It is a multiple star system composed of a large B-type blue giant and a more massive O-type main sequence star. The Mintaka system constitutes an eclipsing binary variable star. It is the westernmost and northernmost of the Belt stars.

ε Ori (Alnilam, 1.69m) is named for the Arabic phrase meaning 'string of pearls'. It is the middle and brightest of the three stars of Orion's Belt. Alnilam is a B-type blue supergiant; despite being nearly twice as far from the Sun as the other Belt stars, its luminosity makes it nearly equal in magnitude. It is losing mass quickly, a consequence of its size. It is the farthest major star in Orion, at 1,344 light-years.

ζ Ori (Alnitak, 1.77m) means 'the girdle' and is the easternmost star in Orion's Belt. It is a triple star system, with the primary star being a hot blue supergiant and the brightest O-type star in the night sky.
κ Ori (Saiph, 2.06m) serves as Orion's right foot. It is of a similar distance and size to Rigel, but appears much fainter. Its name means 'the sword of the giant'.
λ Ori (Meissa, 3.33m) forms Orion's head and is a multiple star with a combined apparent magnitude of 3.33. Its name means 'the shining one'.

Orion's Belt consists of three bright stars: Alnitak (ζ Ori) is around 800 light-years away, 100,000 times more luminous than the Sun. Alnilam (ε Ori) is approximately 2,000 light-years away, 375,000 times more luminous than the Sun in ultraviolet. Mintaka (δ Ori) is 915 light-years away and 90,000 times more luminous; it is a double star with the two orbiting every 5.73 days.
deep_sky_objects: The Orion Nebula (M42) hangs from Orion's Belt as part of his sword. This spectacular object can be clearly identified with the naked eye as something other than a star. Using binoculars, its clouds of nascent stars, luminous gas, and dust can be observed.

The Trapezium cluster in M42 has many newborn stars, including several brown dwarfs, all at an approximate distance of 1,500 light-years. Named for the four bright stars that form a trapezoid, it is largely illuminated by the brightest stars, which are only a few hundred thousand years old.
Chandra X-ray Observatory observations show both the extreme temperatures of the main stars – up to 60,000 kelvins – and the star forming regions still extant in the surrounding nebula.
M43 (Messier 43 nebula) is located in Orion's Sword along with the Orion Nebula.

M78 (NGC 2068) is a nebula with an overall magnitude of 8.0, significantly dimmer than the Great Orion Nebula that lies to its south. However, it is at approximately the same distance, at 1,600 light-years from Earth. It can easily be mistaken for a comet in the eyepiece of a telescope. M78 is associated with the variable star V351 Orionis.

NGC 1999 is another fairly bright nebula close to the Great Orion Nebula. It has an integrated magnitude of 10.5 and is 1,500 light-years from Earth. The variable star V380 Orionis is embedded in NGC 1999.
IC 434, the Horsehead Nebula, is located near Alnitak (ζ Ori). It contains a dark dust cloud whose shape gives the nebula its name.
NGC 2174 is an emission nebula located 6,400 light-years from Earth.

The Flame Nebula (NGC 2024) can be revealed with a larger telescope, along with fainter and tighter multiple stars and nebulae. Barnard's Loop can be seen on very dark nights or using long-exposure photography.

All of these nebulae are part of the larger Orion molecular cloud complex, which is located approximately 1,500 light-years away and is hundreds of light-years across. Due to its proximity, it is one of the most intense regions of stellar formation visible from Earth.
The Orion molecular cloud complex forms the eastern part of an even larger structure, the Orion-Eridanus Superbubble, which is visible in X-rays and in hydrogen emissions.
meteor_showers_detail: Around October 20 each year, the Orionid meteor shower (Orionids) reaches its peak. Coming from the border with the constellation Gemini, as many as 20 meteors per hour can be seen.
The shower's parent body is Halley's Comet.

Pav.name: Pavo
Pav.description: Pavo is bordered by Octans, Apus, Ara, Telescopium and Indus. It covers 378 square degrees, ranking 44th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Peacock (α Pav) (1.91m). As one of the deep southern constellations, it remains below the horizon north of the 30th parallel.

history: Pavo was one of twelve constellations established by Petrus Plancius from observations of the southern sky by Dutch explorers Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman during the first Dutch trading expedition (Eerste Schipvaart) to the East Indies.
It first appeared on a 35 cm celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius. The first depiction in a celestial atlas was in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603.

De Houtman included it in his southern star catalogue the same year under the Dutch name 'De Pauww' (The Peacock). Pavo and the nearby constellations Phoenix, Grus, and Tucana are collectively called the 'Southern Birds.'
greek: According to Mark Chartrand, Plancius may not have been the first to designate these stars as a peacock. In Greek myth, the stars that are now the Peacock were Argos, builder of the ship Argo. He was changed by the goddess Juno into a peacock and placed in the sky along with his ship.
The peacock symbolized the starry firmament for the Greeks, and the goddess Hera was believed to drive through the heavens in a chariot drawn by peacocks.

In a different myth, Zeus changed Io, a princess of Argos, into a heifer to deceive Hera. Hera saw through the scheme and arranged for Argus Panoptes, a creature with one hundred eyes, to guard Io. Zeus sent Hermes to save Io; Hermes used music to lull Argus to sleep, then slew him.

Hera adorned the tail of a peacock—her favorite bird—with Argus's eyes in his honor. As recounted in Ovid's Metamorphoses: 'Argus lay dead; so many eyes, so bright quenched, and all hundred shrouded in one night. Saturnia retrieved those eyes to set in place among the feathers of her bird and filled his tail with starry jewels.'

It is uncertain whether the Dutch astronomers had the Greek mythos in mind. The 'peacock' in the new constellation likely referred to the green peacock encountered in the East Indies, rather than the blue peacock known to the ancient Greeks.
Another possible inspiration for the name may be from Reynier Pauw, the major financial supporter of the Dutch missions. 'Pauw' means pavo/peacock in Dutch.
aboriginal: Part of the constellation is referred to as 'the Saucepan,' particularly in Australia. The rather faint stars form a rough quadrangle southward of the main Peacock stars, with another pair extending eastward to form a handle. It is used as a navigational tool to find the southern celestial pole.
The Wardaman people of the Northern Territory saw the stars of Pavo and the neighbouring constellation Ara as flying foxes.
The Adnyamathanha people of the Flinders Ranges in South Australia call the Saucepan Mirarrityi, and it is used to represent their men's stories in their flag.

stars_text: α Pav (Peacock, 1.91m) is the brightest star in Pavo, near the constellation's northern border with Telescopium. Its proper name—Peacock—is an English translation of the constellation's name, assigned by the British HM Nautical Almanac Office in the late 1930s when the Royal Air Force insisted all bright stars must have names.

Peacock is a spectroscopic binary system of spectral type B2IV, located around 180 light-years from Earth. One estimate places the distance between the pair of stars as 0.21 astronomical units (AU)—half the distance between Mercury and the Sun. The two stars orbit each other in a mere 11 days and 18 hours.

β Pav (3.43m) is the second-brightest star in the constellation. A white giant of spectral class A7III, it is an aging star that has used up the hydrogen fuel at its core and has expanded and cooled after moving off the main sequence. It lies 135 light-years away.
δ Pav (3.56m) is a nearby Sun-like but more evolved star, lying just 19.9 light-years from Earth. This yellow subgiant of spectral type G8IV lies a few degrees west of Beta.
γ Pav (4.22m) is a solar-type star 30 light-years from Earth with stellar class F9V, located at the constellation's eastern border with Indus.

λ Pav is a bright irregular variable ranging between magnitudes 3.4 and 4.4—variation observable with the unaided eye. Classed as a Gamma Cassiopeiae variable or shell star, it is of spectral type B2II-IIIe and lies around 1,430 light-years distant.
κ Pav is a W Virginis variable—a subclass of Type II Cepheid. It ranges from magnitude 3.91 to 4.78 over 9 days and is a yellow-white supergiant pulsating between spectral classes F5I-II and G5I-II.
η Pav (3.6m) is a luminous orange giant of spectral type K2II some 350 light-years distant, located in the west of the constellation depicting the peacock's tail.
ξ Pav (4.38m) is a multiple star system visible in small telescopes as a brighter orange star and fainter white companion. Located around 470 light-years from Earth.

AR Pav is a faint but well-studied eclipsing binary composed of a red giant and smaller hotter star some 18,000 light-years from Earth. It has some features of a cataclysmic variable, with the smaller component most likely having an accretion disc. Visual magnitude ranges from 7.4 to 13.6 over 605 days.

HD 186302 is an 8th magnitude star that became the second star identified as a solar sibling in November 2018. This one is particularly sun-like, with the same spectrum (G2), virtually the same mass, and a twin spectrum revealing identical metallicity.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6752 is the fourth-brightest globular cluster in the sky, after Omega Centauri, 47 Tucanae and Messier 22. An estimated 100 light-years across, it is thought to contain 100,000 stars. Barely visible behind the cluster is Bedin I, a dwarf spheroidal galaxy.

NGC 6744 lies three degrees south of NGC 6752. This spiral galaxy is around 30 million light-years away from Earth and resembles the Milky Way, but is twice its diameter. A type 1c supernova (SN2005at) was discovered in the galaxy in 2005, peaking at magnitude 16.8.
IC 4662 is a dwarf galaxy of magnitude 11.62 that lies 10 arcminutes northeast of Eta Pavonis. Located only 8 million light-years away, it has several regions of high star formation.
IC 4965 is a 14th-magnitude galaxy that lies 1.7 degrees west of Alpha Pavonis. It is a central member of the Shapley Supercluster.

NGC 6810 and NGC 6872/IC 4970 are distant galaxies lying 87 and 212 million light-years away from Earth respectively. NGC 6810 shows galactic wind, while NGC 6872/IC 4970 is an interacting galaxy pair.
meteor_showers_detail: Pavo is the radiant of two annual meteor showers: the Delta Pavonids and August Pavonids.

The Delta Pavonids appear from 21 March to 8 April and generally peak around 5-6 April. They are thought to be associated with comet Grigg-Mellish. The shower was discovered by Michael Buhagiar from Perth, Australia, who observed meteors on six occasions between 1969 and 1980.
The August Pavonids peak around 31 August and are thought to be associated with the Halley-type Comet Levy (P/1991 L3).

Peg.name: Pegasus
Peg.description: Pegasus is bordered by Andromeda, Lacerta, Cygnus, Vulpecula, Delphinus, Equuleus, Aquarius and Pisces. It covers 1,121 square degrees, ranking 7th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Enif (ε Peg) (2.38m). The whole constellation is visible to observers north of 53°S.

babylonian: The Babylonian constellation IKU (field) had four stars of which three were later part of the Greek constellation Hippos (Pegasus).
greek: Pegasus, in Greek mythology, was a winged horse with magical powers. One myth regarding his powers says that his hooves dug out a spring, Hippocrene, which blessed those who drank its water with the ability to write poetry.
Pegasus was born when Perseus cut off the head of Medusa, who was impregnated by the god Poseidon. He was born with Chrysaor from Medusa's blood.
Eventually, Pegasus became the horse for Bellerophon, who was asked to kill the Chimera and succeeded with the help of Athena and Pegasus.

Despite this success, after the death of his children, Bellerophon asked Pegasus to take him to Mount Olympus. Though Pegasus agreed, he plummeted back to Earth after Zeus either threw a thunderbolt at him or sent a gadfly to make Pegasus buck him off.
persian: Persia recognized the constellation. Pegasus was depicted by al-Sufi in the tenth century as a complete horse facing east. This was unlike most other uranographers, who had depicted Pegasus as half of a horse, rising out of the ocean.

In al-Sufi's depiction, Pegasus's head is made up of the stars of Lacerta the lizard. Its right foreleg is represented by β Peg and its left foreleg by η Peg, μ Peg, and λ Peg; its hind legs are marked by 9 Peg. The back is represented by π Peg and μ Cyg, and the belly by ι Peg and κ Peg.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the modern constellation of Pegasus lies in The Black Tortoise of the north (北方玄武), where the stars were classified in several separate asterisms.
Epsilon and Theta Pegasi are joined with Alpha Aquarii to form Wei (危) 'rooftop,' with Theta forming the roof apex.
hindu: In Hindu astronomy, Pegasus is contained within the 25th nakshatra lunar mansion Purva Bhadrapada. More specifically, it represented a bedstead that was a resting place for the Moon.
guyana: For the Warrau and Arawak peoples in Guyana, the stars in the Great Square, corresponding to parts of Pegasus and Andromeda, represented a barbecue taken up to the sky by the seven hunters of the myth of Siritjo.

stars_text: ε Peg (Enif, 2.38m) is the brightest star in Pegasus, marking the horse's muzzle. An orange supergiant of spectral type K21b around 12 times as massive as the Sun, it lies around 690 light-years from Earth. It is an irregular variable, its apparent magnitude varying between 2.37 and 2.45.

AG Peg is an unusual star near Enif that brightened to magnitude 6.0 around 1885 before dimming to magnitude 9. Composed of a red giant and white dwarf (estimated at 2.5 and 0.6 solar masses respectively), its outburst taking over 150 years has been described as the slowest nova ever recorded.

α Peg (Markab, 2.48m), β Peg (Scheat), and γ Peg (Algenib), together with α And (Alpheratz) form the Great Square of Pegasus. Alpheratz was also known as both Delta Pegasi and Alpha Andromedae before being placed in Andromeda in 1922.

β Peg (Scheat, 2.31-2.74m) is the second brightest star, a red giant of spectral type M2.5II-IIIe located around 196 light-years away. It has expanded until it is some 95 times as large, with a total luminosity 1,500 times that of the Sun. Scheat is a semi-regular variable that varies over a period of 43.3 days.

γ Peg (Algenib, 2.82-2.86m) and α Peg (Markab, 2.48m) are blue-white stars of spectral types B2IV and B9III located 391 and 133 light-years distant respectively. They are enlarging and cooling to eventually become red giants. Algenib is a Beta Cephei variable that varies every 3 hours 38 minutes, and also exhibits slow pulsations every 1.47 days.

ζ Peg (Homam, 3.4m) lies seven degrees southwest of Markab. It is a blue-white main sequence star of spectral type B8V located around 209 light-years distant. It is a slowly pulsating B star that varies slightly in luminosity with a period of 22.952 hours, completing 1.04566 cycles per day.

η Peg (Matar, 2.94m) is the fifth-brightest star in the constellation, a multiple star system. The primary is a yellow giant (G2) and a yellow-white main sequence star (A5V) that are 3.2 and 2.0 times as massive as the Sun. The two revolve around each other every 2.24 years. A binary system of two G-type stars lies farther afield, taking 170,000 years to orbit if gravitationally bound.

51 Peg was the first Sun-like star discovered to have an exoplanet companion. 51 Pegasi b (unofficially named Bellerophon, officially Dimidium) is a hot Jupiter close to its star, completing an orbit every four days.
HD 209458 b provided the first evidence of atmospheric water vapor beyond the Solar System through spectroscopic analysis.
HR 8799 hosts extrasolar planets that are the first to be directly imaged.

IK Peg is a close binary comprising an A-type main-sequence star and white dwarf in very close orbit—the latter a candidate for a future type Ia supernova as its main star expands and transfers material to the smaller star.
deep_sky_objects: M15 (NGC 7078) is a globular cluster of magnitude 6.4, 34,000 light-years from Earth. It is a Shapley class IV cluster, fairly rich and concentrated towards its center. M15 was discovered in 1746 by Jean-Dominique Maraldi.
Pease 1 is a planetary nebula located within M15 and was the first planetary nebula known to exist within a globular cluster. It has an apparent magnitude of 15.5.

NGC 7331 is a spiral galaxy located 38 million light-years distant with a redshift of 0.0027. It was discovered by William Herschel in 1784 and was later one of the first nebulous objects described as 'spiral' by William Parsons.

NGC 7742 is a Type 2 Seyfert galaxy located 77 million light-years away with a redshift of 0.00555. It is an active galaxy with a supermassive black hole at its core. Its characteristic emission lines are produced by gas moving at high speeds around the central black hole.

Einstein's Cross is a quasar that has been lensed by a foreground galaxy. The elliptical galaxy is 400 million light-years away with a redshift of 0.0394, but the quasar is 8 billion light-years away. The lensed quasar resembles a cross because the gravitational force of the foreground galaxy creates four images.

Stephan's Quintet is a cluster of five galaxies at a distance of 300 million light-years and a redshift of 0.0215. First discovered by Édouard Stephan in 1877, the Quintet is unique for its interacting galaxies. Two galaxies in the middle have clearly begun to collide, sparking massive bursts of star formation and drawing off long 'tails' of stars.
Astronomers have predicted that all five galaxies in Stephan's Quintet may eventually merge into one large elliptical galaxy.
meteor_showers_detail: The July Pegasids radiate from Pegasus. Details about timing and parent body are not extensively documented in the available data.

Per.name: Perseus
Per.description: Perseus is bordered by Aries, Taurus, Auriga, Camelopardalis, Cassiopeia, Andromeda and Triangulum. It covers 615 square degrees, ranking 24th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Mirfak (α Per) (1.79m). It appears prominently in the northern sky during the Northern Hemisphere's spring.

greek: In Greek mythology, Perseus was the son of Danaë, who was sent by King Polydectes to bring the head of Medusa the Gorgon—whose visage caused all who gazed upon her to turn to stone.
Perseus slew Medusa in her sleep, and Pegasus and Chrysaor appeared from her body. Perseus continued to the realm of Cepheus whose daughter Andromeda was to be sacrificed to Cetus the sea monster.
Perseus rescued Andromeda from the monster by killing it with his sword. He turned Polydectes and his followers to stone with Medusa's head and appointed Dictys the fisherman king.
Perseus and Andromeda married and had six children. In the sky, Perseus lies near the constellations Andromeda, Cepheus, Cassiopeia (Andromeda's mother), Cetus, and Pegasus.
babylonian: In Neo-Assyrian Babylonia (911–605 BC), the constellation of Perseus was known as the Old Man constellation (SU.GI), then associated with East in the MUL.APIN, an astronomical text from the 7th century.
chinese: Four Chinese constellations are contained in the area of the sky identified with Perseus in the West.

Tiānchuán (天船), the Celestial Boat, was the third paranatellon of the third house of the White Tiger of the West, representing the boats that Chinese people were reminded to build in case of a catastrophic flood season. It incorporated Mu, Delta, Psi, Alpha, Gamma and Eta Persei.

Jīshuǐ (積水), the Swollen Waters, was the fourth paranatellon representing the potential of unusually high floods during late August and early September at the beginning of the flood season. Lambda and possibly Mu Persei lay within it.

Dàlíng (大陵), the Great Trench, was the fifth paranatellon representing the trenches where criminals executed en masse in August were interred. It was formed by Kappa, Omega, Rho, 24, 17 and 15 Persei.
The pile of corpses prior to their interment was represented by Jīshī (積屍, Pi Persei), the sixth paranatellon of the house.
The Double Cluster, h and Chi Persei, had special significance in Chinese astronomy.
polynesian: In Polynesia, Perseus was not commonly recognized as a separate constellation. The only people that named it were those of the Society Islands, who called it Faa-iti, meaning 'Little Valley.'

Algol may have been named Matohi by the Māori people, but the evidence for this identification is disputed. Matohi ('Split') occasionally came into conflict with Tangaroa-whakapau over which should appear in the sky, the outcome affecting the tides.

stars_text: β Per (Algol, 2.3-3.5m) is the best-known star in Perseus. From the Arabic رأس الغول Ra's al-Ghul meaning 'The Demon's Head,' it represents the head of the Gorgon Medusa in Greek mythology. It was called Horus in Egyptian mythology and Rosh ha Satan ('Satan's Head') in Hebrew.

Algol is located 92.8 light-years from Earth and varies in apparent magnitude from 2.3 to 3.5 over a period of 2.867 days. The star system is the prototype of Algol variables, eclipsing binary stars, though it is actually a triple star system.

The brightest component is a blue-white main-sequence star of spectral type B8V, 3.5 times as massive and 180 times as luminous as the Sun. The secondary is an orange subgiant star of type K0IV that has begun cooling and expanding to 3.5 times the radius of the Sun, with 4.5 times the luminosity and 80% of its mass.

These two are separated by only 0.05 astronomical units—five percent of the distance between Earth and Sun. The main dip in brightness arises when the larger fainter companion passes in front of the hotter brighter primary. The tertiary component is a main sequence star of type A7, located on average 2.69 AU from the other two stars.

α Per (Mirfak or Algenib, 1.79m) is the brightest star of Perseus with historical name meaning 'elbow' in Arabic. A supergiant of spectral type F5Ib located around 590 light-years away, Mirfak has 5,000 times the luminosity and 42 times the diameter of the Sun.

Mirfak is the brightest member of the Alpha Persei Cluster (Melotte 20, Collinder 39), an open cluster containing many luminous stars including Delta (3.0m), Psi (4.3m), 48 Persei (4.0m), and the 2.9 magnitude Beta Cephei variable Epsilon Persei.

ζ Per (2.86m) is the third-brightest star in the constellation. Around 750 light-years from Earth, it is a blue-white supergiant 26–27 times the radius of the Sun and 47,000 times its luminosity. It is the brightest star (as seen from Earth) of the Perseus OB2 Association or Zeta Persei Association.

ξ Per (Menkhib) is a blue giant of spectral type O7III, one of the hottest bright stars in the sky with a surface temperature of 37,500 K. It is one of the more massive stars, being between 26 and 32 solar masses, and is 330,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

ρ Per (Gorgonea Tertia, 3.3-4.0m) varies in brightness like Algol, but is a pulsating rather than eclipsing star. It is a red giant that has expanded for the second time to have a radius around 150 times that of the Sun. Its helium has been fused into heavier elements and its core is composed of carbon and oxygen. It is a semiregular variable of the Mu Cephei type with periods of 50, 120 and 250 days.

GK Per (Nova Persei 1901) is a bright nova discovered on 21 February 1901 by Scottish amateur astronomer Thomas David Anderson, appearing halfway between Algol and Delta Persei. It peaked at magnitude 0.2—almost as bright as Capella and Vega—then faded to magnitude 13 around 30 years later.

V718 Per is a star in the young open cluster IC 348 that appears to be periodically eclipsed by a giant planet every 4.7 years. This has been inferred to be an object with a maximum mass of 6 times that of Jupiter and an orbital radius of 3.3 AU.
deep_sky_objects: The galactic plane of the Milky Way passes through Perseus, but is mostly obscured by molecular clouds. The Perseus Arm is a spiral arm of the Milky Way that stretches across the sky from Cassiopeia through Perseus and Auriga to Gemini and Monoceros. This segment is towards the rim of the galaxy.

The Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884), sometimes known as h and Chi (χ) Persei, are two open clusters within the Perseus Arm. They are easily visible through binoculars and small telescopes. Both lie more than 7,000 light-years from Earth and are several hundred light-years apart.

Both clusters are approximately magnitude 4 and 0.5 degrees in diameter. They are Trumpler class I 3 r clusters, though NGC 869 is a Shapley class f and NGC 884 is a Shapley class e cluster. The constituent stars number over 100 in each cluster and range widely in brightness.

M34 is an open cluster that appears at magnitude 5.5, approximately 1,500 light-years from Earth. It contains about 100 stars scattered over a field of view larger than that of the full moon. M34 can be resolved with good eyesight but is best viewed using a telescope at low magnifications.

IC 348 is a young open cluster still contained within the nebula from which its stars formed. Located about 1,027 light-years from Earth, it is about 2 million years old and contains many stars with circumstellar disks. Many brown dwarfs have been discovered in this cluster; since brown dwarfs cool as they age, it is easier to find them in younger clusters.
M76, the Little Dumbbell Nebula, is a planetary nebula that appears two arc-minutes by one arc-minute across with an apparent brightness of magnitude 10.1.

NGC 1499 (California Nebula) is an emission nebula discovered in 1884–85 by American astronomer Edward E. Barnard. It is very difficult to observe visually because its low surface brightness makes it appear dimmer than most other emission nebulae.
NGC 1333 is a reflection nebula and a star-forming region.

NGC 1023 is a barred spiral galaxy of magnitude 10.35, around 30 million light-years from Earth. It is the principal member of the NGC 1023 group of galaxies and is possibly interacting with another galaxy.

NGC 1260 is either a lenticular or tightly wound spiral galaxy about 250 million light-years from Earth. It was the host galaxy of supernova SN 2006gy, one of the brightest ever recorded. It is a member of the Perseus Cluster (Abell 426), a massive galaxy cluster located 250 million light-years from Earth.

NGC 1275, a component of the Perseus Cluster, is a Seyfert galaxy containing an active nucleus that produces jets of material, surrounding the galaxy with massive bubbles. These bubbles create sound waves that travel through the Perseus Cluster, sounding a B flat 57 octaves below middle C.

NGC 1275 is a cD galaxy that has undergone many galactic mergers throughout its existence, as evidenced by the 'high velocity system'—the remnants of a smaller galaxy—surrounding it. Its active nucleus is a strong source of radio waves.
meteor_showers_detail: The Perseids are a prominent annual meteor shower that appear to radiate from Perseus from mid-July, peaking in activity between 9 and 14 August each year. Associated with Comet Swift–Tuttle, they have been observed for about 2,000 years.
The September Epsilon Perseids, discovered in 2012, are a meteor shower with an unknown parent body in the Oort cloud.

Phe.name: Phoenix
Phe.description: Phoenix is bordered by Sculptor, Grus, Tucana, Hydrus, Eridanus and Fornax. It covers 469 square degrees, ranking 37th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Ankaa (α Phe) (2.40m).

history: Phoenix was the largest of the 12 constellations established by Petrus Plancius from the observations of Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. It first appeared on a 35-cm diameter celestial globe published in 1597 (or 1598) in Amsterdam.

The first depiction of this constellation in a celestial atlas was in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603. De Houtman included it in his southern star catalog the same year under the Dutch name Den voghel Fenicx, "The Bird Phoenix", symbolising the phoenix of classical mythology.
The name Ankaa is derived from the Arabic al-'anqā', meaning 'the phoenix', and was coined sometime after 1800 in relation to the constellation.
arab: Unlike other modern constellations, Phoenix has actual precedent in ancient astronomy. The Arabs saw this formation as representing young ostriches, Al Ri'āl, or as a griffin or eagle.
The same group of stars was sometimes imagined by the Arabs as a boat, Al Zaurak, on the nearby river Eridanus.
chinese: The Chinese incorporated Phoenix's brightest star, Ankaa (Alpha Phoenicis), and stars from the adjacent constellation Sculptor to depict Bakui, a net for catching birds.

Phoenix and the neighbouring constellation of Grus together were seen by Julius Schiller as portraying Aaron the High Priest. These two constellations, along with nearby Pavo and Tucana, are called the Southern Birds.

stars_text: Ankaa (α Phe, 2.37m) is the brightest star in the constellation. It is an orange giant of spectral type K0.5IIIb, 77 light years distant from Earth and orbited by a secondary object about which little is known.

β Phe (3.31m) is the second brightest star and a binary system. The two components are both yellow giants of spectral type G8 with individual magnitudes of 4.0 and 4.1, and orbit each other every 168 years.

Zeta Phoenicis (Wurren) is an Algol-type eclipsing binary with magnitude fluctuating between 3.9 and 4.4 over 1.7 days. It consists of two blue-white B-type stars orbiting 0.05 AU from each other, with a third star around 600 AU away.
γ Phe (3.39-3.49m) is a red giant of spectral type M0IIIa lying 235 light years away. It is a variable star.

ψ Phe is a red giant of spectral type M4III that varies between magnitudes 4.3 and 4.5 over a period of around 30 days. Lying 340 light years away, it has around 85 times the diameter, but only 85% of the mass, of the Sun.

SX Phoenicis is a variable star which ranges from magnitude 7.1 to 7.5 over a period of just 79 minutes. Its spectral type varies between A2 and F4. It gives its name to a group of stars known as SX Phoenicis variables.

ν Phe (4.96m) is a yellow-white main sequence star of spectral type F9V lying 49 light years distant. It is around 1.2 times as massive as the Sun and likely surrounded by a disk of dust. It is the closest star in the constellation visible with the unaided eye.

HE0107-5240 is possibly one of the oldest stars yet discovered. It has around 1/200,000 the metallicity that the Sun has and hence must have formed very early in the history of the universe. With a visual magnitude of 15.17, it is 36,000 light years distant.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 625 is a dwarf irregular galaxy of magnitude 11.0 lying 12.7 million light years distant. Only 24,000 light years in diameter, it is an outlying member of the Sculptor Group. NGC 625 is thought to have been involved in a collision and is experiencing a burst of active star formation.

Robert's Quartet (NGC 87, 88, 89 and 92) is a group of four galaxies located around 160 million light-years away which are in the process of colliding and merging. They are within a circle of radius 1.6 arcmin, corresponding to about 75,000 light-years.

HLX-1 is an intermediate-mass black hole located in the galaxy ESO 243-49—the first one of its kind identified. It is hypothesized to be a remnant of a dwarf galaxy that was absorbed in a collision with ESO 243-49.

The Phoenix Cluster is a gigantic galaxy cluster around 7.3 million light years wide and 5.7 billion light years away, making it one of the most massive galaxy clusters. The central galaxy is producing an estimated 740 new stars a year.

El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915) is even larger, located around 7.2 billion light years away. It is composed of two subclusters in the process of colliding, resulting in the spewing out of hot gas visible in X-rays and infrared images.
meteor_showers_detail: The Phoenicids, also known as the December Phoenicids, were first observed on 3 December 1887. The shower was particularly intense in December 1956, and is thought related to the breakup of the short-period comet 289P/Blanpain.
The shower peaks around 4–5 December, though is not seen every year.
A very minor meteor shower peaks around July 14 with around one meteor an hour, though meteors can be seen anytime from July 3 to 18. This shower is referred to as the July Phoenicids.

Pic.name: Pictor
Pic.description: Pictor is bordered by Columba, Puppis, Carina, Caelum, Dorado and Volans. It covers 247 square degrees, ranking 59th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Pic (3.30m).

history: The French astronomer Abbé Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first described Pictor as le Chevalet et la Palette (the easel and palette) in 1756, after observing and cataloguing 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.
He devised 14 new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honored instruments that symbolised the Age of Enlightenment.
He labelled the constellation Equuleus Pictorius on his 1763 chart, the word "Equuleus" meaning small horse, or easel—perhaps from an old custom among artists of carrying a canvas on a donkey.
The German astronomer Johann Bode called it Pluteum Pictoris. The name was shortened to its current form in 1845 by the English astronomer Francis Baily on the suggestion of Sir John Herschel.

stars_text: α Pic (3.3m) is the brightest star in the constellation, an astrometric binary 97 light-years from Earth. The primary is an A-type star of spectral type A8VnkA6, a rapidly spinning star with a projected rotational velocity of 206 km/s and a shell of circumstellar gas.

β Pic (3.86m) is a white main sequence star of spectral type A6V located around 63.4 light-years distant. It is a member of the Beta Pictoris moving group—a group of 17 star systems around 12 million years old moving through space together.

In 1984 Beta Pictoris was the first star discovered to have a debris disk. Since then, two exoplanets with masses over ten times Jupiter have been discovered orbiting between 2.7 and 8 AU from the star.
Beta Pictoris b was discovered using direct imagery with the Very Large Telescope in late 2009, while Beta Pictoris c was discovered via doppler spectroscopy in August 2009.
γ Pic (4.5m) is an orange giant of spectral type K1III that has swollen to 11 times the diameter of the Sun. It lies 186 light-years distant from Earth.

δ Pic is an eclipsing binary of the Beta Lyrae type located 1,298 light-years from Earth. Composed of two blue stars of spectral types B3III and O9V, the system has a period of 1.67 days, and dips from magnitude 4.65 to 4.9. The stars are oval-shaped as they are gravitationally distorted by each other.

Kapteyn's Star is a nearby red dwarf at 12.78 light-years with magnitude 8.8. It has the largest proper motion of any star in the sky after Barnard's Star. Moving around the Milky Way in the opposite direction to most other stars, it may have originated in a dwarf galaxy that was merged into the Milky Way, with the main remnant being the Omega Centauri globular cluster.

HD 40307 is an orange main sequence star of spectral type K2.5V and magnitude 7.17 located about 42 light-years away. It hosts six super-Earth planets, one of which, HD 40307 g, lies in the circumstellar habitable zone and is not tidally locked.

RR Pictoris is a cataclysmic variable that flared up as a nova, reaching magnitude 1.2 on 9 June 1925. It is a close binary system composed of a white dwarf and secondary star that orbit each other every 3.48 hours. The system is estimated to lie around 1,300 light-years distant from Earth.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 1705 is an irregular dwarf galaxy 17 million light-years from Earth. It is one of the most active star forming galaxies in the nearby universe, despite the fact that its rate of star formation peaked around 30 million years ago.

Pictor A, around 485 million light-years away, is a double-lobed radio galaxy and a powerful source of radio waves in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere. From a supermassive black hole at its centre, a relativistic jet shoots out to an X-ray hot spot 800,000 light years away.
SPT-CL J0546-5345 is a massive galaxy cluster located around 7 billion light-years away with a mass equivalent to approximately 800 trillion suns.

GRB 060729 was a gamma-ray burst first observed on 29 July 2006. It is likely the signal of a type Ic supernova—the core collapse of a massive star. It was notable for its extraordinarily long X-ray afterglow, detectable 642 days (nearly two years) after the original event.

Psc.name: Pisces
Psc.description: Pisces is bordered by Triangulum, Andromeda, Pegasus, Aquarius, Cetus and Aries. It covers 889 square degrees, ranking 14th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alpherg (η Psc) (3.62m).

babylonian: Pisces originates from some composition of the Babylonian constellations Šinunutu4 "the great swallow" in current western Pisces, and Anunitum the "Lady of the Heaven", at the place of the northern fish.
In first-millennium BC texts known as the Astronomical Diaries, part of the constellation was also called DU.NU.NU (Rikis-nu.mi, "the fish cord or ribbon").
greek: Pisces is associated with the Greek legend that Aphrodite and her son Eros either shape-shifted into forms of fishes to escape, or were rescued by two fishes.
In the Greek version according to Hyginus, Aphrodite and Eros while visiting Syria fled from the monster Typhon by leaping into the Euphrates River and transforming into fishes.
The Roman variant of the story has Venus and Cupid (counterparts for Aphrodite and Eros) carried away from this danger on the backs of two fishes.

According to another origin tale, an egg rolled into the Euphrates, and some fishes nudged this to shore. Doves sat on the egg until Aphrodite (thereafter called the Syrian Goddess) hatched out of it. The fishes were then rewarded by being placed in the skies as a constellation.
history: Pisces was one of Ptolemy's 48 original constellations in his 2nd-century Almagest.

In 1690, the astronomer Johannes Hevelius in his Firmamentum Sobiescianum regarded the constellation Pisces as being composed of four subdivisions: Piscis Boreus (the North Fish), Linum Boreum (the North Cord), Linum Austrinum (the South Cord), and Piscis Austrinus (the South Fish).
The March equinox is currently situated in Pisces, directly south of ω Psc, and because of precession, it is gradually drifting westward toward Aquarius.

stars_text: Although Pisces is a large constellation, there are only two stars brighter than magnitude 4. It is the second dimmest of the zodiac constellations.
Alrescha (α Psc, 3.62m) means "the cord" and is a variable binary star 309.8 light-years away of spectral class A2.
Alpherg (η Psc, 3.62m) means "emptying" and is a yellow giant of spectral type G7 IIIa located 349 light-years away. It is a Gamma Cassiopeiae variable with a weak magnetic field.
γ Psc (3.70m) is a yellow giant of spectral type G8 III located 138 light-years away. The star hosts an exoplanet which was discovered in 2021.
ω Psc (4.03m) is an F-type star 106 light-years away that is either a subgiant or on the main sequence.
ε Psc (4.27m) is an orange giant of spectral type K0III located 190 light-years away. It has a candidate exoplanet.
Fumalsamakah (β Psc, 4.48m) means "mouth of the fish" and is a B6Ve class star 492 light-years away.
Revati (ζ Psc, 5.21m) means "rich" and is a quintuple star system of spectral type A7IV located 148 light-years away.

Van Maanen's Star is the closest-known solitary white dwarf to us. Located about 2° south of δ Psc with a high proper motion of 2.978″ annually. Its mass is about 67% of the Sun's, yet it has only 1% of the Sun's radius. The outer atmosphere has a temperature of approximately 6,110 K and is thought to be around 3 billion years old.
Due to the dimness of these stars, the constellation is essentially invisible in or near any major city due to light pollution.
deep_sky_objects: M74 is a loosely wound (type Sc) spiral galaxy found at a distance of 30 million light years. It has many clusters of young stars and associated nebulae, showing extensive regions of star formation. It was discovered by Pierre Méchain in 1780. It is the brightest member of the M74 Group.

A type II-P supernova was discovered in the outer regions of M74 by Robert Evans in June 2003; the star that underwent the supernova was later identified as a red supergiant with a mass of 8 solar masses.
NGC 488 is an isolated face-on prototypical spiral galaxy. Two supernovae have been observed in the galaxy.
NGC 520 is a pair of colliding galaxies located 105 million light-years away.

CL0024+17 is a massive galaxy cluster that lenses the galaxy behind it, creating arc-shaped images of the background galaxy. The cluster is at a distance of 3.6 billion light-years from Earth, while the background galaxy is at a distance of 5.7 billion light-years.

3C 31 is an active galaxy and radio source in Pisces 237 million light-years from Earth. Its jets, caused by the supermassive black hole at its center, extend several million light-years in opposing directions, making them some of the largest objects in the universe.
meteor_showers_detail: The Piscids is a meteor shower associated with Pisces.

PsA.name: Piscis Austrinus
PsA.description: Piscis Austrinus is bordered by Capricornus, Microscopium, Grus, Sculptor and Aquarius. It covers 245 square degrees, ranking 60th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Fomalhaut (α PsA) (1.17m).

history: Piscis Austrinus was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy, and it remains one of the 88 modern constellations.
In Greek mythology, this constellation is known as the Great Fish and it is portrayed as swallowing the water poured out by Aquarius, the water-bearer constellation.

The two fish of the constellation Pisces are said to be the offspring of the Great Fish. In Egyptian mythology, this fish saved the life of the Egyptian goddess Isis, so she placed this fish and its descendants into the heavens as constellations of stars.
babylonian: The constellation is also called the Southern Fish in contrast to the larger and dimmer Pisces (the Fish or Fishes). It was known to the ancient Sumerians as the "fish" and to the ancient Babylonians as the "great fish".
In Babylonian astronomy, Piscis Austrinus was part of the constellation Ea, representing the Babylonian god of wisdom. It was depicted as a man with the tail of a fish.
arab: Arab astronomers knew the constellation as Al Hut al Janubi ("the Southern Fish") or Al Hut ("the Fish").

stars_text: Fomalhaut (α PsA, 1.17m) is the brightest star in the constellation and the 18th brightest star in the night sky. Its name comes from the Arabic fum al-ħūt, meaning "mouth of the fish." It is a white A-type main sequence star located 25 light-years from Earth.

Fomalhaut is surrounded by a debris disk discovered by the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) in 1983. The disk is produced by collisions among icy bodies like those in the Solar System's Kuiper Belt.

In 2008, observations by the Hubble Space Telescope revealed what appeared to be a planet, Fomalhaut b, orbiting within the debris disk. However, later observations suggest this may have been a temporary dust cloud from a collision rather than a planet.

The Fomalhaut system includes two companion stars: Fomalhaut B (TW Piscis Austrini), an orange K-type star located 0.28 parsecs from Fomalhaut, and Fomalhaut C (LP 876-10), a red dwarf star located 0.32 parsecs away.
β PsA (4.29m) is a white A-type main sequence star approximately 148 light-years away.
γ PsA (4.46m) is an orange giant of spectral type K1III located about 220 light-years away.
δ PsA (4.20m) is a blue-white B-type subgiant approximately 170 light-years from Earth.
ε PsA (4.18m) is a blue-white B-type main sequence star roughly 400 light-years distant.

Lacaille 9352 is one of the brightest red dwarf stars as seen from Earth with magnitude 7.34. It is the 11th nearest star system to the Sun at just 10.74 light-years away. Despite its proximity, it is too faint to be seen without a telescope.
deep_sky_objects: The constellation contains relatively few deep-sky objects visible to amateur astronomers due to its location away from the Milky Way.
NGC 7172 is a Seyfert galaxy located approximately 110 million light-years away. It has an active galactic nucleus powered by a supermassive black hole.
NGC 7314 is a barred spiral galaxy of apparent magnitude 11.6 located about 55 million light-years away. It has a bright compact nucleus and is classified as a Seyfert galaxy.
NGC 7184 is a barred spiral galaxy approximately 114 million light-years away with a visual magnitude of 11.7.
Several other faint galaxies are scattered throughout the constellation, but most require large telescopes to observe.

Pup.name: Puppis
Pup.description: Puppis is bordered by Monoceros, Pyxis, Vela, Carina, Pictor, Columba, Canis Major and Hydra. It covers 673 square degrees, ranking 20th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Naos (ζ Pup) (2.25m).

egyptian: The constellation of Argo Navis is recorded in Greek texts, derived from ancient Egypt around 1000 BC. According to Plutarch, its equivalent in Egyptian astronomy was the Boat of Osiris.
greek: Puppis was originally part of Argo Navis, the legendary ship of Jason and the Argonauts. As Argo Navis was roughly 28% larger than the next largest constellation Hydra, it was sub-divided into three sections in 1752 by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille.
history: Lacaille referred to Puppis as Argus in puppi (the stern of the ship). Despite the division, Lacaille kept a single set of Bayer designations for the whole constellation. Therefore, Carina has the alpha, beta, and epsilon, Vela has gamma and delta, Puppis has zeta, and so on.

In 1844, John Herschel proposed complete dividing of Argo Navis in accordance with Lacaille's divisions. However, the constellation continued to be used into the 20th century, and officially received a three-letter designation alongside its divisions in 1922.
Puppis, along with Carina and Vela, was included in the list of modern IAU constellations in 1930.

planetary_systems: On July 1, 2003, a planet was found orbiting the star HD 70642. This planetary system is much like Jupiter with a wide, circular orbit and a long-period.

On May 17, 2006, HD 69830 was discovered to have three Neptune-mass planets, the first multi-planetary system without any Jupiter-like or Saturn-like planets. The star also hosts an asteroid belt at the region between middle planet to outer planet.

On June 21, 2007, the first extrasolar planet found in the open cluster NGC 2423, was discovered around the red giant star NGC 2423-3. The planet is at least 10.6 times the mass of Jupiter and orbits at 2.1 AU distance.

On September 22, 2008, two Jupiter-like planets were discovered around HD 60532. HD 60532 b has a minimum mass of 1.03 MJ and orbits at 0.759 AU. HD 60532 c has a minimum mass of 2.46 MJ and orbits at 1.58 AU.
In 2023, astronomers detected two ice giant type exoplanets (both with a mass of tens of earths) having a collision event around the 300 million year old star designated as 2MASS J08152329-3859234.
deep_sky_objects: As the Milky Way runs through Puppis, there are many open clusters in the constellation. M46 and M47 are two open clusters in the same binocular field. M47 can be seen with the naked eye under dark skies, and its brightest stars are 6th magnitude.

Messier 93 (M93) is another open cluster somewhat to the south. NGC 2451 is a very bright open cluster containing the star c Puppis, and the near NGC 2477 is a good target for small telescopes. The star Pi Puppis is the main component of a bright group of stars known as Collinder 135.

M46 is a circular open cluster with an overall magnitude of 6.1 at a distance of approximately 5400 light-years from Earth. The planetary nebula NGC 2438 is superimposed; it is approximately 2900 light-years from Earth.

M46 is classified as a Shapley class f and a Trumpler class III 2 m cluster. This means that it is a rich cluster that appears distinct from the star field, despite not being at its center. The cluster's stars, numbering between 50 and 100, have a moderate range in brightness.

Pyx.name: Pyxis
Pyx.description: Pyxis is bordered by Hydra, Puppis, Vela and Antlia. It covers 221 square degrees, ranking 65th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Pyx (3.68m). This faint constellation has no stars brighter than magnitude 3.0.

chinese: In ancient Chinese astronomy, Alpha, Beta, and Gamma Pyxidis formed part of Tianmiao, a celestial temple honouring the ancestors of the emperor, along with stars from neighbouring Antlia.
greek: The Ancient Greeks identified the four main stars of Pyxis as the mast of the mythological Jason's ship, Argo Navis.
history: The French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first described the constellation in French as la Boussole (the Marine Compass) in 1752, after he had observed and catalogued almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.

He devised fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honoured instruments that symbolised the Age of Enlightenment. Lacaille Latinised the name to Pixis Nautica on his 1763 chart.

German astronomer Johann Bode defined the constellation Lochium Funis, the Log and Line—a nautical device once used for measuring speed and distance travelled at sea—around Pyxis in his 1801 star atlas, but the depiction did not survive.

In 1844 John Herschel attempted to resurrect the classical configuration of Argo Navis by renaming it Malus the Mast, a suggestion followed by Francis Baily, but Benjamin Gould restored Lacaille's nomenclature.

stars_text: α Pyx (3.68m) is the brightest star in the constellation. Located 880 light-years distant from Earth, it is a blue-white giant star of spectral type B1.5III that is around 22,000 times as luminous as the Sun and has 9.4 times its diameter. Its light is dimmed by 30% due to interstellar dust.

β Pyx (3.97m) is a yellow bright giant or supergiant of spectral type G7Ib-II that is around 435 times as luminous as the Sun, lying 420 light-years distant away from Earth. It has a companion star of magnitude 12.5 separated by 9 arcseconds.
γ Pyx (4.02m) lies 207 light-years distant. It is an orange giant of spectral type K3III that has cooled and swollen to 3.7 times the diameter of the Sun after exhausting its core hydrogen.

T Pyxidis is a binary star system composed of a white dwarf with around 0.8 times the Sun's mass and a red dwarf that orbit each other every 1.8 hours. A recurrent nova, it has brightened to the 7th magnitude in the years 1890, 1902, 1920, 1944, 1966 and 2011 from a baseline of around 14th magnitude.

TY Pyxidis is an eclipsing binary star whose apparent magnitude ranges from 6.85 to 7.5 over 3.2 days. The system is classified as a RS Canum Venaticorum variable, a binary system with prominent starspot activity, and lies 184 light-years away.

The closest star to Earth in the constellation is Gliese 318, a white dwarf of spectral class DA5 and magnitude 11.85. Its distance has been calculated to be 26 light-years distant from Earth. It has around 45% of the Sun's mass, yet only 0.15% of its luminosity.
planetary_systems: Pyxis is home to three stars with confirmed planetary systems—all discovered by Doppler spectroscopy. A hot Jupiter, HD 73256 b, that orbits HD 73256 every 2.55 days, was discovered using the CORALIE spectrograph in 2003.

HD 73267 b was discovered with the High Accuracy Radial Velocity Planet Searcher (HARPS) in 2008. It orbits HD 73267 every 1260 days, a 7 billion-year-old star of spectral type G5V that is around 89% as massive as the Sun.

Gliese 317, a red dwarf of spectral type M2.5V that has around 42% the Sun's mass, is orbited by two gas giant planets. Around 50 light-years distant from Earth, it is a good candidate for future searches for more terrestrial rocky planets.
deep_sky_objects: Pyxis lies in the plane of the Milky Way, although part of the eastern edge is dark, with material obscuring our galaxy arm there. NGC 2818 is a planetary nebula that lies within a dim open cluster of magnitude 8.2.

K 1-2 is a planetary nebula whose central star is a spectroscopic binary composed of two stars in close orbit with jets emanating from the system. The surface temperature of one component has been estimated at as high as 85,000 K.
NGC 2627 is an open cluster of magnitude 8.4 that is visible in binoculars.

Discovered in 1995, the Pyxis globular cluster is a 13.3 billion year-old globular cluster situated around 130,000 light-years distant from Earth. Located in the galactic halo, it was noted to lie on the same plane as the Large Magellanic Cloud.
NGC 2613 is a spiral galaxy of magnitude 10.5 which appears spindle-shaped as it is almost edge-on to observers on Earth.

Henize 2-10 is a dwarf galaxy which lies 30 million light-years away. It has a black hole of around a million solar masses at its centre. Known as a starburst galaxy due to very high rates of star formation, it has a bluish colour due to the huge numbers of young stars within it.

Ret.name: Reticulum
Ret.description: Reticulum is bordered by Horologium, Dorado and Hydrus. It covers 114 square degrees, ranking 82nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Rhombus (α Ret) (3.33m). This faint southern constellation has no stars brighter than magnitude 3.0.

history: A constellation in this area was introduced by Isaac Habrecht II in his celestial globe in 1621, who named it Rhombus. It was replaced with a somewhat different constellation by the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in the eighteenth century.

During his stay at the Cape of Good Hope, Lacaille named the constellation le Réticule Rhomboide to commemorate the reticle in his telescope eyepiece. The name was later Latinized to Reticulum in his star catalogue Coelum Australe Stelliferum.

In 1810, the stars of Reticulum were used by William Croswell to produce the constellation Marmor Sculptile, which represented the bust of Christopher Columbus, but this did not catch on among astronomers.

The constellation Reticulum became officially recognized during the First General Assembly of the International Astronomical Union in 1922. The boundary for this and other constellations was drawn up by Belgian astronomer Eugène Delporte along arcs of right ascension and declination for epoch 1875.

stars_text: α Ret (Rhombus, 3.33m) is the brightest star in the constellation. The proper name Rhombus was officially approved on September 19, 2024.
β Ret is the second brightest star at an unspecified magnitude. Only two of the stars in this constellation are brighter than visual magnitude 5: Alpha and Beta Reticuli.
R Reticuli is a reddish Mira variable star. This variable was discovered by C. Ragoonatha Chary at the Madras Observatory in India.

ε Ret is a binary star system consisting of a spectral class K2IV star being orbited by a white dwarf. Based on parallax measurements, this system is located about 50 light years from the Sun. In 2000, a planetary companion was announced, orbiting the star ε Reticuli A.

ζ Ret (Zeta Reticuli) is a wide binary star system, with both members being similar to the Sun. It is located at a distance of about 39 light years. This system gained some notoriety in ufology when the alleged alien abductees Betty and Barney Hill named it as the home of their abductors.
deep_sky_objects: In 2005, a type Ia supernova was discovered in the spiral galaxy NGC 1559, located in the constellation.
The dwarf galaxy Reticulum II is enriched in r-process heavy elements.
The Horologium-Reticulum Supercluster is a galaxy supercluster that ranges from 700 million to 1.2 billion light-years from Earth.

Sct.name: Scutum
Sct.symbolism: the Shield of John III Sobieski
Sct.description: Scutum is bordered by Aquila, Sagittarius, Serpens Cauda. It covers 109.0 square degrees, ranking 84th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Sct (3.85m).

history: Scutum was named in 1684 by Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius. He originally called it Scutum Sobiescianum (Shield of Sobieski) to commemorate the victory of Christian forces led by Polish King John III Sobieski in the Battle of Vienna in 1683.
Five bright stars of Scutum (α, β, δ, ε, and η Sct) were previously known as stars in Aquila, numbered 1, 6, 2, 3, and 9 Aquilae respectively.
The constellation was adopted by the IAU in 1922 as one of the 88 modern constellations. Its boundaries are defined by a quadrilateral.
In Chinese astronomy, these stars were incorporated into Tien Pien, the Heavenly Casque (or Helmet), also associated with battle armor.

stars_text: α Sct (Alpha Scuti, 3.85m) is the brightest star, a K-type giant.
β Sct (Beta Scuti, 4.22m) is the second brightest, a binary system. The primary has a spectral type similar to the Sun but is 1,270 times brighter.
δ Sct (Delta Scuti, 4.72m) is a bluish white giant approaching the Solar System. Within 1.3 million years it will come within 10 light-years of Earth and become much brighter than Sirius.
UY Scuti is one of the largest known stars with a radius over 900 times that of the Sun.
RSGC1-F01 is another red supergiant with a radius over 1,450 solar radii.
Scutum contains several clusters of supergiant stars including RSGC1, Stephenson 2, and RSGC3.
deep_sky_objects: M11 (the Wild Duck Cluster) is the most prominent open cluster in Scutum. Named by William Henry Smyth in 1844 for its resemblance to a flock of ducks in flight.
M11 lies 6,200 light-years from Earth and is 20 light-years in diameter. It contains approximately 3,000 stars, making it a particularly rich cluster.
The cluster is around 220 million years old with an estimated mass between 3,700 and 11,000 solar masses.
M26 (NGC 6694) is another open cluster in the constellation.
NGC 6712 is a globular cluster found in the eastern part of the constellation.
IC 1295 is a planetary nebula located only 24 arcminutes from NGC 6712.
space_exploration: The space probe Pioneer 11 is moving in the direction of Scutum. It will not reach the nearest star in this constellation for over a million years, by which time its batteries will be long dead.

Ser.name: Serpens
Ser.description: Serpens is unique as the only constellation split into two disconnected regions: Serpens Caput (the head) and Serpens Cauda (the tail), separated by Ophiuchus. It covers 637 square degrees total, ranking 23rd in size. Its brightest star is Unukalhai (α Ser) (2.63m).

greek: In Greek mythology, Serpens represents a snake held by the healer Asclepius (Ophiuchus). Asclepius once killed a snake, but it was resurrected after a second snake placed a revival herb on it.
As snakes shed their skin yearly, they symbolized rebirth in ancient Greek society. Legend says Asclepius would revive dead humans using the same technique.
Serpens was sometimes depicted coiling around Ophiuchus, but more often shown passing behind his body or between his legs.
history: When Eugène Delporte established modern constellation boundaries in the 1920s, he split Serpens into two areas separated by Ophiuchus. These became Serpens Caput (head) and Serpens Cauda (tail).
Johann Bayer depicted Serpens separately from Ophiuchus, giving Serpens stars their own Bayer designations.
Serpens is the only one of the 88 modern constellations split into two disconnected regions in the sky.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, most Serpens stars formed part of Tianshi, a wall surrounding a marketplace in Ophiuchus and Hercules.
Two tail stars represented part of Shilou, the tower with the market office.
Another tail star represented Liesi (jewel shops).
Mu Serpentis marked Tianru, the crown prince's wet nurse, or sometimes rain.
babylonian: Two serpent constellations existed in Babylonian astronomy: Mušḫuššu and Bašmu.
Mušḫuššu was depicted as a hybrid of dragon, lion, and bird, loosely corresponding to Hydra.
Bašmu was a horned serpent roughly corresponding to the Serpens of Ptolemy.

stars_text: α Ser (Unukalhai, 2.63m) marks the heart of the serpent. This red giant (K2III) lies 73 light-years away and is easily visible even in light-polluted areas. A faint companion orbits the red giant.
β Ser (Zhou, 3.67m), γ Ser, and ι Ser form a distinctive triangle marking the snake's head. Kappa Serpentis (Gudja) lies midway between Gamma and Iota.
β Ser is a white main-sequence star about 490 light-years distant, possibly with a 10th-magnitude physical companion.
γ Ser is an F-type subgiant only 36 light-years away (magnitude 3.84), showing solar-like oscillations.
δ Ser is a multiple star system about 210 light-years away. It consists of four stars with a total magnitude of 3.79. The primary is a Delta Scuti variable white subgiant.
ε Ser and μ Ser are both third-magnitude A-type main-sequence stars forming the snake's body below the heart. Epsilon is an Am star, while Mu is a binary.
λ Ser is a Sun-like star (magnitude 4.42) only 39 light-years away with an orbiting exoplanet.
η Ser (Eta Serpentis) is the brightest star in the tail, a K-class red giant showing solar-like oscillations over 2.16 hours.
θ Ser and ξ Ser also mark the tail asterism. Xi is a triple star system 105 parsecs away, while Theta is a multiple system with two A-type stars.
PSR B1534+11 is a pulsar-neutron star binary system used to test Einstein's general relativity, validating predictions to within 0.2%.
deep_sky_objects: M5 (Messier 5) is a globular cluster about 8° southwest of α Ser. Located 25,000 light-years away, it's barely visible to the naked eye under good conditions.
M5 contains many RR Lyrae variables and two millisecond pulsars. It recedes from us at over 50 km/s.
Palomar 5 is a globular cluster south of M5. Tidal effects from the Milky Way are pulling stars away, forming a tidal tail over 30,000 light-years long. The cluster is over 11 billion years old.
The Eagle Nebula (M16) and its star cluster lie about 5,700 light-years away in Serpens Cauda. It measures 70 by 50 light-years.
M16 contains the famous Pillars of Creation, three dust clouds photographed by Hubble. Stars forming there average 45,000 K and produce radiation that will eventually destroy the pillars.
The Serpens Cloud is a massive star-forming molecular cloud in southern Serpens Cauda. Only 2 million years old and 1,300 light-years distant, it contains many protostars.
Serpens South is a protocluster discovered by Spitzer in the southern portion of the cloud, with ongoing star formation.
Hoag's Object, 600 million light-years away, is a rare ring galaxy. The outer ring contains young blue stars while the core has older yellow stars.
Arp 220 is an ultraluminous infrared galaxy 250 million light-years away. Two large spiral galaxies are colliding, with nuclei orbiting 1,200 light-years apart, causing extensive star formation.

Seyfert's Sextet is a group of six galaxies, four gravitationally interacting. At 190 million light-years away, it's one of the densest galaxy groups known. The four will eventually merge into a large elliptical galaxy.
meteor_showers_detail: Two daytime meteor showers radiate from Serpens: the Omega Serpentids and Sigma Serpentids.
Both showers peak between December 18 and December 25 and are normally observed using radio techniques.

Sex.name: Sextans
Sex.description: Sextans is bordered by Leo, Hydra, Crater. It covers 314.0 square degrees, ranking 47th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Sex (4.49m). It sits near the celestial equator.

history: Sextans was introduced by Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius in 1687, originally under the name Sextans Uraniae.
The constellation was named in memory of the astronomical sextant Hevelius lost when his observatory was destroyed by fire on September 26, 1679.
Despite the catastrophe, Hevelius rebuilt enough equipment to observe the great comet of December 1680.
John Flamsteed labeled 41 stars for the constellation, but none were above magnitude 4.5.
Benjamin Apthorp Gould later lettered the five brightest stars using Greek letters Alpha through Epsilon in his Uranometria Argentina.

stars_text: α Sex (Alpha Sextantis, 4.49m) is the brightest and only star above fifth magnitude. It's an aging A0 III star located 280±20 light-years away.
At 385 million years old, Alpha Sextantis is exhausting hydrogen at its core and leaving the main sequence.
γ Sex (Gamma Sextantis, 5.05m) is a binary consisting of two A-type main-sequence stars (A1 V and A4 V). They orbit each other in 77.55 years in an eccentric orbit.
The Gamma Sextantis system is 280±10 light-years away. The stars are separated by 0.4 arcseconds, requiring a telescope with 30 cm aperture to resolve.
β Sex (Beta Sextantis, 5.07m) is a B6 V main-sequence star 364±10 light-years distant. It's been used as a standard in the MK spectral classification system.
Beta Sextantis may be an Alpha2 Canum Venaticorum variable with a 15.4-day period.
35 Sextantis is a triple star system with two evolved K-type giants of equal mass orbiting each other over 23,000 years. The system is about 700 light-years away.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 3115 is an edge-on lenticular galaxy, the only noteworthy deep-sky object visible in amateur telescopes.
Sextans B is a fairly bright dwarf irregular galaxy at magnitude 6.6, located 4.3 million light-years from Earth. It's part of the Local Group.
The constellation hosts the COSMOS project field studied by the Hubble Space Telescope.
CL J1001+0220 is the most distant known galaxy cluster (as of 2016) at redshift z=2.506, located 11.1 billion light-years from Earth.

In 2015, astronomers reported evidence for Population III stars in the Cosmos Redshift 7 galaxy (at z=6.60) in Sextans. Such stars likely existed in the very early universe and started producing heavy elements needed for planets and life.
meteor_showers_detail: The Sextantids meteor shower radiates from this constellation.

Tau.name: Taurus
Tau.description: Taurus is bordered by Auriga, Perseus, Aries, Cetus, Eridanus, Orion, Gemini. It covers 797.0 square degrees, ranking 17th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Aldebaran (α Tau) (0.85m). Taurus is crossed by the galactic equator, celestial equator, and ecliptic.

ancient: The identification of Taurus with a bull dates to the Chalcolithic era and perhaps the Upper Paleolithic. Cave paintings at Lascaux (c. 15,000 BC) may depict Taurus alongside the Pleiades.
Taurus marked the vernal equinox from about 4000 BC to 1700 BC in the Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age.
In Babylonian astronomy, the constellation was called GU4.AN.NA, 'The Bull of Heaven.'
babylonian: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the goddess Ishtar sends Taurus (the Bull of Heaven) to kill Gilgamesh for spurning her advances.
Enkidu tears off the bull's hind part and hurls it into the sky, where it becomes Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.
The Bull of Heaven was closely associated with Inanna, the Sumerian goddess of love, fertility, and warfare.
egyptian: The Heavenly Bull was depicted in the Dendera zodiac, an Egyptian ceiling bas-relief showing the celestial hemisphere.

To the Egyptians, Taurus was a sacred bull associated with spring renewal. When the spring equinox entered Taurus, the constellation became covered by the Sun, symbolizing sacrifice leading to land renewal.
To early Hebrews, Taurus was the first constellation in their zodiac, represented by the first letter Aleph.
greek: In Greek mythology, Taurus was identified with Zeus, who took the form of a magnificent white bull to abduct Europa, a Phoenician princess.
In illustrations, only the front portion of Taurus is depicted, sometimes explained as the bull being partly submerged while carrying Europa to sea.
A second myth portrays Taurus as Io, a mistress of Zeus whom he changed into a heifer to hide from his wife Hera.
Greek mythographer Acusilaus identified the bull with the Cretan Bull, one of the Twelve Labors of Heracles.
other_cultures: The Druids held a Tauric religious festival while the Sun passed through the constellation.
Among the Inuit, the constellation is called Sakiattiat. The Hyades is Nanurjuk, representing the polar bear spirit.
In Buddhism, legends hold that Gautama Buddha was born when the full moon was in Taurus. Buddha's birthday is celebrated with the Wesak Festival.
history: In 1919, stars in the Hyades were photographed during the total solar eclipse by Arthur Eddington's expedition, confirming Einstein's general theory of relativity by showing the bending of light around the Sun.

stars_text: α Tau (Aldebaran, 0.85m) is the brightest star, an orange K5 III giant. Its Arabic name means 'the follower' (of the Pleiades). It forms the bull's bloodshot eye and has 1.16 solar masses with a candidate exoplanet.
The Hyades form a V or K-shaped asterism creating the bull's face profile. This is the nearest distinct open cluster after the Ursa Major Moving Group, spanning about 5° of sky.
θ Tau (Theta Tauri) is a naked-eye double star in the Hyades with 5.6 arcminute separation. Theta2 Tauri's proper name is Chamukuy.
