The Pleiades (M45) lie in the northwestern quadrant. This famous open cluster has seven prominent stars (the 'Seven Sisters') visible to the naked eye.

The Pleiades contains an estimated 500-1,000 stars all about 100 million years old, ranging from large bright stars to brown dwarfs and white dwarfs. The cluster will dissipate in another 250 million years.
β Tau (El Nath, 1.65m) forms the bull's northern horn. This white B7 III giant's Arabic name means 'the butting.' It also bears the designation Gamma Aurigae as it shares the border with Auriga.
ζ Tau (Tianguan) forms the bull's southern horn. This eclipsing binary completes an orbit every 133 days. The two horns are separated by 8° in the sky.
λ Tau is an eclipsing binary with a B3 star orbited by an A4 star. Every 3.953 days the system dims by 1.1 magnitudes. The stars are separated by only 0.1 AU, causing tidal distortions.
T Tauri is the prototype of T Tauri variable stars. It varies erratically between magnitude 9 and 13 over weeks or months. This newly formed stellar object is emerging from its gas and dust envelope.
The reflection nebula NGC 1555 is illuminated by T Tauri and varies in luminosity accordingly.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 1514 (the Crystal Ball Nebula) is a planetary nebula of historical importance. Discovered by William Herschel in 1790, it showed a star surrounded by nebulous cloud.
Herschel's 1790 discovery challenged the assumption that nebulae were simply unresolved star groups. In 1864, William Huggins used its spectrum to prove nebulae are luminous gas, not stars.
M1 (the Crab Nebula) lies 1.15° northwest of ζ Tau. This supernova remnant resulted from a Type II supernova visible on Earth on July 4, 1054.
The 1054 supernova reached magnitude -4 and was visible during the day, mentioned in Chinese texts. North American peoples also recorded it in canyon paintings and pottery.
The Crab Nebula remnant was discovered by John Bevis in 1731. It currently shines at magnitude 8.4, requiring a telescope to observe.
The Taurus-Auriga complex (Taurus dark clouds) is a star-forming region spanning 98 light-years containing 35,000 solar masses of material.
At 490 light-years (150 parsecs), the Taurus-Auriga complex is one of the nearest active star-forming regions. It's larger but less massive than the Orion Nebula.
NGC 1746 is an asterism about 10° northeast of Aldebaran, spanning 45 arcminutes.
meteor_showers_detail: The Taurid meteor shower radiates from Taurus during November.
The Beta Taurid meteor shower occurs during June and July in daytime, normally observed using radio techniques.
The Northern Taurids and Southern Taurids are both active between October 18-29, with the Southern stream being stronger.
Between November 1-10, the two Taurid streams equalize in strength.
space_exploration: The space probe Pioneer 10 is moving toward Taurus, though it won't near any stars in the constellation for thousands of years, by which time its batteries will be dead.

Sge.name: Sagitta
Sge.description: Sagitta is bordered by Vulpecula, Hercules, Aquila, and Delphinus. It covers 79.9 square degrees, ranking 86th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is γ Sge (3.51m). Only Equuleus and Crux are smaller constellations.

greek: The ancient Greeks called Sagitta 'Oistos' meaning 'the arrow'. It was one of the 48 constellations described by Ptolemy in the 2nd century.
Sagitta was regarded as the weapon that Hercules used to kill the eagle (Aquila) of Jove that perpetually gnawed Prometheus' liver. The constellation is located beyond the north border of Aquila.

Richard Hinckley Allen proposed that the constellation could represent the arrow shot by Hercules towards the Stymphalian birds (his sixth labour). These birds had claws, beaks, and wings of iron and lived on human flesh in the marshes of Arcadia.
The arrow lies between the constellations Aquila the Eagle, Cygnus the Swan, and Lyra the Vulture, representing these mythical iron birds. Hence the constellation was also called 'Herculea'.
Greek scholar Eratosthenes claimed it as the arrow with which Apollo exterminated the Cyclopes.
arab: In Arabic, the constellation became 'al-sahm' meaning 'arrow', though this name became Sham and was transferred to Alpha Sagittae only.
The Greek name was also mistranslated as 'hó istos' (the loom) and thus in Arabic 'al-nawl'. It was also called 'al-'anaza' meaning pike or javelin.

stars_text: The four brightest stars make up an arrow-shaped asterism located due north of the bright star Altair. The constellation is visible to observers north of 69°S, with midnight culmination occurring on July 17.

γ Sge (3.47m) is the brightest star, a red giant of spectral type M0 III located 258 light-years away. Ptolemy saw it as marking the arrow's head, while Bayer saw γ, η, and θ as depicting the arrow's shaft. With 90% of the Sun's mass, it has a radius 54 times larger and is 575 times as bright.

δ Sge is the second-brightest star and a binary system. The primary is a red supergiant (M2 II) with 3.9 solar masses and 152 solar radii, while the secondary is a blue-white main sequence star (B9.5V) with 2.9 solar masses. The two orbit each other every ten years. According to Bayer, δ and ζ depicted the spike of the arrow.
ζ Sge is a triple star system approximately 326 light-years from Earth, with A-type primary and secondary stars.

α Sge (Sham, 4.38m) is a yellow bright giant star (G1 II) located 382 light-years away. In his Uranometria, Bayer depicted α, β, and ε as the fins of the arrow. Four times the Sun's mass, it has swollen to 21 solar radii and 340 solar luminosities.
β Sge (4.38m) is a G-type giant located 420 light-years away. Around 129 million years old, it is 4.33 solar masses and has expanded to roughly 27 solar radii.

ε Sge (5.77m) is a double star whose components can be seen in a small telescope. The main star is a 331-million-year-old yellow giant (G8 III) around 3.09 solar masses, located 580 light-years distant. The 8.35-magnitude visual companion 87.4 arcseconds away is an unrelated blue supergiant around 7,000 light-years distant.
η Sge (5.09m) is an orange giant (K2 III) located 155.9 light-years away. It has a 61.1% chance of being a member of the Hyades-Pleiades stream of stars that share a common motion through space.

θ Sge is a double star system with components 12 arcseconds apart visible in a small telescope. The brighter component (6.5m) is a yellow-white main sequence star (F3 V) located 146.1 light-years away. The fainter companion (8.8m) is a G5 V main sequence star. A 7.4-magnitude orange giant (K2 III) is also visible 91 arcseconds away, located 842 light-years distant.

R Sge is a rare RV Tauri variable star that ranges from magnitude 8.2 to 10.4. Located around 8,100 light-years away, it has a radius 61.2 times the Sun's and is 2,329 times as luminous, yet is less massive than the Sun. An aging star that has left the asymptotic giant branch, it is on its way to becoming a planetary nebula.

FG Sge is a 'born again' star located around 4,000 light-years away. It reignited helium fusion shortly before becoming a white dwarf and has expanded from a blue supergiant to a K-class supergiant in less than 100 years. It is surrounded by the planetary nebula Henize 1-5 (magnitude 23).

S Sge is a classical Cepheid variable that varies from magnitude 5.24 to 6.04 every 8.38 days. It pulsates between spectral types F6 Ib and G5 Ib, and is around 6-7 solar masses and 3,500 times as luminous as the Sun. It is located around 5,100 light-years away.

U Sge is an eclipsing binary that varies between magnitudes 6.6 and 9.2 over 3.4 days. The system consists of a blue-white star (B8 V) and a yellow subgiant (G4 III-IV). The cooler subgiant has filled its Roche lobe and is passing material to the hotter star, making it a semidetached binary. The system is 900 light-years distant.

V Sge is the prototype of the V Sagittae variables, cataclysmic variables that are also super soft X-ray sources. It is expected to become a luminous red nova around the year 2083 when the two stars merge, briefly becoming the most luminous star in the Milky Way and one of the brightest in Earth's sky.

WZ Sge is a cataclysmic variable composed of a white dwarf (85% solar mass) and a brown dwarf companion (L2, 8% solar mass). Normally fainter than magnitude 15, it flared up in 1913, 1946, and 1978 to be visible in binoculars.
HD 231701 is a yellow-white main sequence star with a Jupiter-like planet discovered in 2007. The planet has at least 1.13 Jupiter masses and orbits at 0.57 AU with a 141.6-day period.

15 Sge is a solar analog with 1.08 solar masses, 1.115 solar radii, and 1.338 solar luminosities (magnitude 5.80). It has an L4 brown dwarf companion 69 times Jupiter's mass orbiting every 73.3 years. The system is estimated to be 2.5 billion years old.
deep_sky_objects: The band of the Milky Way and the Great Rift within it pass through Sagitta, with α, β, and ε Sagittae marking the Rift's border.

Messier 71 is a very loose globular cluster located between β and γ Sagittae, mistaken for some time as a dense open cluster. At a distance of about 13,000 light-years, it was first discovered by Philippe Loys de Chéseaux in 1745 or 1746. The cluster has a mass of around 53,000 solar masses and a luminosity of approximately 19,000 solar luminosities.

NGC 6886 is a planetary nebula with a hot central post-AGB star that has 55% of the Sun's mass yet 2,700 times its luminosity and a surface temperature of 142,000 K. The nebula has been expanding for between 1,280 and 1,600 years. It was discovered by Ralph Copeland in 1884 and is around 15,000 light-years from Earth.

The Necklace Nebula was originally a close binary where one component swallowed the other as it expanded to become a giant star. The smaller star remained in orbit inside the larger, whose rotation speed increased greatly, flinging its outer layers into space. This formed a ring with bright knots of gas from clumps of stellar material. Discovered in 2005, it is around 2 light-years wide (0.35 arcminutes) and 15,000 light-years from Earth.

Sgr.name: Sagittarius
Sgr.description: Sagittarius is bordered by Aquila, Scutum, Serpens Cauda, Ophiuchus, Scorpius, Corona Australis, Telescopium, Indus, Microscopium, and Capricornus. It covers 867 square degrees, ranking 15th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is ε Sgr (Kaus Australis) (1.79m). The constellation contains 15 Messier objects.

babylonian: The Babylonians identified Sagittarius as the god Nergal, a centaur-like creature firing an arrow from a bow. It is generally depicted with wings, two heads (one panther head and one human head), and a scorpion's stinger raised above its more conventional horse's tail.

The Sumerian name Pabilsag is composed of two elements: Pabil, meaning 'elder paternal kinsman' and Sag, meaning 'chief, head'. The name may be translated as the 'Forefather' or 'Chief Ancestor'. The figure is reminiscent of modern depictions of Sagittarius.
greek: In Greek mythology, Sagittarius is usually identified as a centaur: half human, half horse. However, some confusion surrounds the identity of the archer due to the Greeks' adoption of the Sumerian constellation.

Some identify Sagittarius as the centaur Chiron, the son of Philyra and Cronus, who was said to have changed himself into a horse to escape his jealous wife, Rhea, and who served as tutor to Jason. As there are two centaurs in the sky, some identify Chiron with the other constellation, Centaurus.
An alternative tradition holds that Chiron devised the constellations Sagittarius and Centaurus to help guide the Argonauts in their quest for the Golden Fleece.

A competing mythological tradition, as espoused by Eratosthenes, identified the Archer not as a centaur but as the satyr Crotus, son of Pan, who Greeks credited with the invention of archery. According to myth, Crotus often went hunting on horseback and lived among the Muses, who requested that Zeus place him in the sky, where he is seen demonstrating archery.

The arrow of this constellation points towards the star Antares, the 'heart of the scorpion'. Sagittarius stands poised to attack should Scorpius ever attack the nearby Hercules, or to avenge Scorpius's slaying of Orion.
history: On the west side of the constellation, Ptolemy also described the asterism Terebellum consisting of four 4th magnitude stars, including the closest and fastest moving member, Omega Sagittarii.

stars_text: As seen from the northern hemisphere, the constellation's brighter stars form an easily recognizable asterism known as 'the Teapot'. The stars δ Sgr (Kaus Media), ε Sgr (Kaus Australis), ζ Sgr (Ascella), and φ Sgr form the body of the pot; λ Sgr (Kaus Borealis) is the point of the lid; γ² Sgr (Alnasl) is the tip of the spout; and σ Sgr (Nunki) and τ Sgr form the handle.
Under dark skies, the Large Sagittarius Star Cloud can be seen rising in a north-westerly arc above the spout, like a puff of steam rising from a boiling kettle.

The constellation is often depicted as having the rough appearance of a stick-figure archer drawing its bow, with the fainter stars providing the outline of the horse's body. Sagittarius famously points its arrow at the heart of Scorpius, represented by the reddish star Antares.
ε Sgr (Kaus Australis, 1.79m) is the brightest star despite not having the alpha designation. The name means 'southern part of the bow'. It is about seven times as bright as α Sgr.
α Sgr (Rukbat, 3.96m) means 'the archer's knee' but despite having the alpha designation, it is not the brightest star of the constellation. It is towards the bottom center of the constellation.

σ Sgr (Nunki, 2.08m) is the constellation's second-brightest star, a B2V star approximately 260 light-years away. 'Nunki' is a Babylonian name of uncertain origin, but thought to represent the sacred Babylonian city of Eridu on the Euphrates, which would make Nunki the oldest star name currently in use.
ζ Sgr (Ascella, 2.61m) is actually a double star whose two components have magnitudes 3.3 and 3.5. It has an A2 spectrum.
δ Sgr (Kaus Meridionalis, 2.71m) is a K2 spectrum star about 350 light-years from Earth.

λ Sgr (Kaus Borealis), ε Sgr (Kaus Australis), and δ Sgr (Kaus Media) refer to the northern, southern, and center portions of the bow, respectively. Following the direct line formed by δ and γ² Sgr leads nearly directly to Antares. γ² Sgr is Alnasl, the Arabic word for 'arrowhead'.
η Sgr is a double star with component magnitudes of 3.18 and 10.
π Sgr (Albaldah) is actually a triple system whose components have magnitudes 3.7, 3.8, and 6.0.

β Sgr is shared by two star systems: β¹ Sgr (magnitude 3.96) and β² Sgr (magnitude 7.4). The two stars are separated by 0.36° in the sky and are 378 light-years from Earth. Located at the forelegs of the centaur, they have the traditional name 'Arkab', meaning 'Achilles tendon'.
Nova Sagittarii 2015 No. 2 was discovered on March 15, 2015 by John Seach near the center of the constellation. It reached a peak magnitude of 4.3 before steadily fading.
deep_sky_objects: The Milky Way is at its densest near Sagittarius, as this is where the Galactic Center lies. As a result, Sagittarius contains many star clusters and nebulae.

The Large Sagittarius Star Cloud is the brightest visible region of the Milky Way. It is a portion of the central bulge of the galaxy seen around the thick dust of the Great Rift, and is the innermost galactic structure that can be observed in visible wavelengths. It has several embedded clusters and superimposed dark nebulae.

The Small Sagittarius Star Cloud (Messier 24) has an apparent magnitude of 2.5 and fills a space to a depth of 10,000 to 16,000 light-years. Embedded in M24 is NGC 6603, a small very dense star cluster. NGC 6567, a dim planetary nebula, and Barnard 92, a Bok globule, are also nearby.

The Lagoon Nebula (Messier 8) is an emission nebula located 5,000 light-years from Earth, measuring 140 by 60 light-years (1.5°). Though it appears grey in telescopes to the unaided eye, long-exposure photographs reveal its pink hue. It is fairly bright with an integrated magnitude of 3.0. The central area is also known as the Hourglass Nebula, shaped by matter propelled by Herschel 36.

The Lagoon Nebula was discovered independently by John Flamsteed in 1680, Guillaume Le Gentil in 1747, and Charles Messier in 1764. It features three dark nebulae listed in the Barnard Catalogue. The nebula was instrumental in the discovery of Bok globules when Bart Bok studied prints intensively in 1947. Approximately 17,000 Bok globules were discovered in the nebula nine years later as part of the Palomar Sky Survey.

The Omega Nebula (Messier 17) is a fairly bright nebula, sometimes called the Horseshoe Nebula or Swan Nebula. It has an integrated magnitude of 6.0 and is 4,890 light-years from Earth. Discovered in 1746 by Philippe Loys de Chéseaux, observers have differed greatly in how they view the nebula, hence its myriad of names. Most often viewed as a checkmark, it was seen as a swan by George F. Chambers in 1889, a loon by Roy Bishop, and as a curl of smoke by Camille Flammarion.

The Trifid Nebula (M20, NGC 6514) is an emission nebula that lies less than two degrees from the Lagoon Nebula. Discovered by Charles Messier, it is located between 2,000 and 9,000 light-years from Earth and has a diameter of approximately 50 light-years. The outside is a bluish reflection nebula; the interior is pink with two dark bands that divide it into three areas, or 'lobes'. Hydrogen in the nebula is ionized by a central triple star that formed in the intersection of the two dark bands. M20 is associated with a magnitude 6.3 cluster.
The Red Spider Nebula (NGC 6537) is a bipolar planetary nebula located at a distance of about 4,000 light-years from Earth.
NGC 6559 is a star-forming region located at a distance of about 5,000 light-years from Earth, showing both emission (red) and reflection (blue) regions.
NGC 6445 is a planetary nebula with an approximate magnitude of 11. A large nebula at over one arcminute in diameter, it appears very close to the globular cluster NGC 6440.

NGC 6638 is a dimmer globular at magnitude 9.2 and is more distant than M71 at 26,000 light-years. It is a Shapley class VI cluster with intermediate concentration at its core. It is approximately a degree away from the brighter globulars M22 and M28.

Sagittarius A is a complex radio source near the western boundary with Ophiuchus. Astronomers believe that one of its components, Sagittarius A*, is associated with a supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy, with a mass of 2.6 million solar masses. Although not visible to the naked eye, Sagittarius A* is located off the top of the spout of the Teapot asterism.
The Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy is located just outside the Milky Way.

Baade's Window is an area with very little obscuring dust that shows objects closer to the Milky Way's center than would normally be visible. NGC 6522 (magnitude 8.6) and NGC 6528 (magnitude 9.5) are both globular clusters visible through Baade's Window. Located 20,000 and 24,000 light-years from Earth, with Shapley classes of VI and V respectively, both are moderately concentrated at their cores. NGC 6528 is closer to the galactic core at an approximate distance of 2,000 light-years.

2MASS-GC02 (Hurt 2) is a globular cluster at a distance of about 16,000 light-years from Earth. It was discovered in 2000 by Joselino Vasquez and confirmed by a team of astronomers under the leadership of R. J. Hurt at 2MASS.

Sco.name: Scorpius
Sco.description: Scorpius is bordered by Sagittarius, Ophiuchus, Libra, Lupus, Norma, Ara, and Corona Australis. It covers 497 square degrees, ranking 33rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Antares (α Sco) (0.96m). The constellation contains 4 Messier objects.

greek: In Greek mythology, several myths associated with Scorpius attribute it to Orion. According to one version, Orion boasted to the goddess Artemis and her mother, Leto, that he would kill every animal on Earth. Artemis and Leto sent a giant scorpion to kill Orion.
Their battle caught the attention of Zeus, who raised both combatants to the sky to serve as a reminder for mortals to curb their excessive pride.
In another version of the myth, Artemis' twin brother, Apollo, was the one who sent the scorpion to kill Orion after the hunter earned the goddess' favor by admitting she was better than him.
After Zeus raised Orion and the scorpion to the sky, the former hunts every winter but flees every summer when the scorpion comes. In both versions, Artemis asked Zeus to raise Orion.
In a Greek myth without Orion, the celestial scorpion encountered Phaethon while he was driving his father Helios' Sun Chariot.
babylonian: The Babylonians called this constellation MUL.GIR.TAB - the 'Scorpion'. The signs can be literally read as 'the creature with a burning sting'.

In some old descriptions the constellation of Libra is treated as the Scorpion's claws. Libra was known as the Claws of the Scorpion in Babylonian (zibānītu, compare Arabic zubānā) and in Greek (χηλαι).
javanese: The Javanese people of Indonesia call this constellation Banyakangrem ('the brooded swan') or Kalapa Doyong ('leaning coconut tree') due to the shape similarity.
polynesian: In Hawaii, Scorpius is known as the demigod Maui's Fishhook or Ka Makau Nui o Māui (meaning the Big Fishhook of Māui). The name of the fishhook was Manaiakalani.
bugis: Scorpius was divided into two asterisms used by Bugis sailors for navigation. The northern part (α, β, γ or σ Lib, δ, ε, ζ, μ, σ and τ Scorpii) was called 'bintoéng lambarué', meaning 'skate stars'. The southern part (η, θ, ι, κ, λ and ν Scorpii) was called 'bintoéng balé mangngiwéng', meaning 'shark stars'.

stars_text: Scorpius contains many bright stars. The constellation's bright stars form a pattern like a longshoreman's hook. Most of them are massive members of the nearest OB association: Scorpius-Centaurus.
α Sco (Antares, 0.96m) is the brightest star, named 'rival of Mars' because of its distinct reddish hue. Antares represents the heart of the scorpion.
λ Sco (Shaula) and υ Sco (Lesath) mark the tip of the scorpion's curved tail. Both names mean 'sting'. Given their proximity to one another, they are sometimes referred to as the Cat's Eyes.
β¹ Sco (Graffias or Acrab) is a triple star system.

δ Sco (Dschubba, 'the forehead'), after being a stable 2.3 magnitude star, flared in July 2000 to 1.9 in a matter of weeks. It has since become a variable star fluctuating between 2.0 and 1.6. This means that at its brightest it is the second brightest star in Scorpius.
θ Sco (Sargas) has a name of Sumerian origin.
ν Sco (Jabbah), ξ Sco, π Sco (Fang), σ Sco (Alniyat), and τ Sco (Paikauhale) are other notable named stars in the constellation.
U Scorpii is the fastest known nova, with a period of about 10 years.

AH Scorpii is a red supergiant star and one of the largest known stars, being 1,400 times larger than the Sun. It is also a luminous star, 340,000 times brighter than the Sun, although it is too faint to be seen by the naked eye, with a brightness varying from 6.5 to 9.6.

The close pair of stars ω¹ Scorpii and ω² Scorpii are an optical double which can be resolved by the unaided eye. One is a yellow giant, while the other is a blue B-type star in the Scorpius-Centaurus Association.

The star once designated γ Sco (despite being well within the boundaries of Libra) is today known as σ Lib. The entire constellation of Libra was considered to be claws of Scorpius (Chelae Scorpionis) in Ancient Greek times. A set of scales held aloft by Astraea (represented by adjacent Virgo) was formed from these westernmost stars during later Greek times. The division into Libra was formalized during Ancient Greek or Roman times.
deep_sky_objects: Due to its location straddling the Milky Way, Scorpius contains many deep-sky objects such as the open clusters Messier 6 (the Butterfly Cluster) and Messier 7 (the Ptolemy Cluster), NGC 6231 (by ζ² Sco), and the globular clusters Messier 4 and Messier 80.

Messier 80 (NGC 6093) is a globular cluster of magnitude 7.3, located 33,000 light-years from Earth. It is a compact Shapley class II cluster, indicating that it is highly concentrated and dense at its nucleus. M80 was discovered in 1781 by Charles Messier. It was the site of a rare discovery in 1860 when Arthur von Auwers discovered the nova T Scorpii.
NGC 6302, also called the Bug Nebula, is a bipolar planetary nebula.
NGC 6334, also known as the Cat's Paw Nebula, is an emission nebula and star-forming region.

Scl.name: Sculptor
Scl.description: Sculptor is bordered by Cetus, Aquarius, Piscis Austrinus, Grus, Phoenix, and Fornax. It covers 475 square degrees, ranking 36th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Scl (4.30m). The whole constellation is visible to observers south of latitude 50°N.

history: The region to the south of Cetus and Aquarius had been named by Aratus in 270 BC as 'The Waters' - an area of scattered faint stars with two brighter stars standing out. Professor Bradley Schaefer has proposed that these stars were most likely Alpha and Delta Sculptoris.

The French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first described the constellation in French as 'l'Atelier du Sculpteur' (the sculptor's studio) in 1751-52. He depicted it as a three-legged table with a carved head on it, and an artist's mallet and two chisels on a block of marble alongside it.

Lacaille had observed and catalogued almost 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope, devising fourteen new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. He named all but one in honour of instruments that symbolized the Age of Enlightenment.

stars_text: Lacaille gave 19 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Tau in 1756, but omitted Omicron and Xi, and labelled two stars as Kappa and Lambda. Nu and Rho Sculptoris were dropped from star catalogues due to their faintness. In 1879, Benjamin Gould added Xi Sculptoris as he felt the star was bright enough to warrant a name.

No stars brighter than 3rd magnitude are located in Sculptor. This is explained by the fact that Sculptor contains the south galactic pole where stellar density is very low. Overall, there are 56 stars within the constellation's borders brighter than or equal to apparent magnitude 6.5.
α Scl (4.3m) is the brightest star, an SX Arietis-type variable star with a spectral type B7IIIp located 780 light-years distant from Earth.

η Scl is a red giant of spectral type M4III that varies between magnitudes 4.8 and 4.9, pulsating with multiple periods of 22.7, 23.5, 24.6, 47.3, 128.7, and 158.7 days. Estimated to be around 1,082 times as luminous as the Sun, it is 460 light-years distant from Earth.
R Scl is a red giant that has been found to be surrounded by spirals of matter likely ejected around 1,800 years ago. It is 1,440 light-years distant from Earth.

The Mira variable stars T, U, V, and X Sculptoris are very urgently needed for observation as data on their light curves is incomplete, according to the Astronomical Society of Southern Africa in 2003.
deep_sky_objects: The constellation contains the Sculptor Dwarf, a dwarf galaxy which is a member of the Local Group, as well as the Sculptor Group, the group of galaxies closest to the Local Group.
The Sculptor Galaxy (NGC 253) is a barred spiral galaxy and the largest member of the Sculptor Group. It lies near the border between Sculptor and Cetus.
NGC 55 is another prominent member of the Sculptor Group, an irregular galaxy.

The Cartwheel Galaxy is a unique galaxy in Sculptor at a distance of 500 million light-years. The result of a merger around 300 million years ago, the Cartwheel Galaxy has a core of older, yellow stars, and an outer ring of younger, blue stars with a diameter of 100,000 light-years.

The smaller galaxy in the collision is now incorporated into the core, after moving from a distance of 250,000 light-years. The shock waves from the collision sparked extensive star formation in the outer ring.

Tel.name: Telescopium
Tel.description: Telescopium is a small constellation bordered by Sagittarius and Corona Australis to the north, Ara to the west, Pavo to the south, and Indus to the east, cornering on Microscopium to the northeast. It covers 252 square degrees, ranking 57th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alpha Telescopii (3.49m).

history: Telescopium was introduced in 1751-52 by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille with the French name 'le Telescope', depicting an aerial telescope. He created it after observing and cataloguing 10,000 southern stars during a two-year stay at the Cape of Good Hope.

Lacaille devised 14 new constellations in uncharted regions of the Southern Celestial Hemisphere not visible from Europe. All but one honored instruments that symbolized the Age of Enlightenment. The telescope originally stretched 40 degrees northward between Sagittarius and Scorpius.

The constellation was called Tubus Astronomicus in the eighteenth century. During that time, three telescope constellations existed—Tubus Herschelii Major between Gemini and Auriga and Tubus Herschelii Minor between Taurus and Orion, both of which fell out of use by the nineteenth century.

Later astronomers Francis Baily and Benjamin Gould shrank Telescopium's boundaries. The reduced constellation lost several bright stars to neighbors: Beta became Eta Sagittarii, Gamma became G Scorpii, Theta reverted to d Ophiuchi, and Sigma was placed in Corona Australis.

stars_text: α Tel (3.5m) is the brightest star in the constellation. It's a blue-white subgiant of spectral type B3IV located around 250 light-years away. It radiates nearly 800 times the Sun's luminosity and is estimated to be 5.2 times as massive with 3.3 times the Sun's radius.

δ¹ Tel and δ² Tel are two blue-white stars sharing the designation Delta Telescopii. Delta¹ is spectral type B6IV with magnitude 4.9, while Delta² is B3III with magnitude 5.1. They form an optical double, estimated to be around 710 and 1,190 light-years away respectively.

Gliese 754 is a faint (magnitude 12.23) red dwarf of spectral type M4.5V, one of the nearest 100 stars to Earth at only 19.3 light-years distant. Its eccentric orbit around the Galaxy indicates it may have originated in the Milky Way's thick disk.

ζ Tel (4.1m) is the second-brightest star in the constellation, an orange subgiant of spectral type K1III-IV. Around 1.53 times as massive as the Sun, it shines with 512 times its luminosity from 127 light-years away. It has been described as yellow or reddish in appearance.

ε Tel is a binary system with an orange giant primary (K0III, magnitude 4.52) and a 13th magnitude companion 21 arcseconds away, visible with a 15 cm telescope on a dark night. The system is 417 light-years distant.

ξ Tel is an irregular variable star that ranges between magnitudes 4.89 and 4.94. Located 1,079 light-years away, it's a red giant of spectral type M2III with a diameter around 5.6 times the Sun's and luminosity around 2,973 times the Sun.
RX Tel is a red supergiant irregular variable that varies between magnitudes 6.45 and 7.47, just visible to the unaided eye under good conditions.

RS Tel is a rare R Coronae Borealis variable—an extremely hydrogen-deficient supergiant thought to arise from the merger of two white dwarfs. It dims from magnitude 9.6 to 16.5 when carbon dust is expelled. Fewer than 100 such variables have been discovered.

PV Tel is a class B-type extreme helium star that is the prototype of PV Telescopii variables. It was found in 1952 to have very low hydrogen. One theory suggests it resulted from a merger between a helium white dwarf and a carbon-oxygen white dwarf.

RR Tel (Nova Telescopii 1948) is a symbiotic nova system composed of an M5III pulsating red giant and a white dwarf. It brightened by 7 magnitudes between 1944-48, reaching magnitude 6.0 before slowly fading to magnitude 12.

η Tel is a young white main sequence star (A0V, magnitude 5.0) in the 12-million-year-old Beta Pictoris moving group. It has a debris disk and brown dwarf companion (M7V or M8V) between 20-50 Jupiter masses. It's gravitationally bound to HD 181327, which has its own debris disk.

HD 191760 is a yellow subgiant (G3IV/V) just over 4 billion years old, slightly more massive than the Sun. It has a brown dwarf companion around 38 Jupiter masses orbiting at 1.35 AU every 505 days—unusually close within the 'brown-dwarf desert'.
deep_sky_objects: The Telescopium group is a group of twelve galaxies spanning three degrees in the northeastern part of the constellation, lying around 120 million light-years away. The brightest member is elliptical galaxy NGC 6868, with spiral galaxy NGC 6861 to the west.
NGC 6868 and NGC 6861 are the brightest members of two respective subgroups within the galaxy group, and are heading toward a future merger.
NGC 6584 is a globular cluster near Theta Arae, 45,000 light-years from Earth. It's an Oosterhoff type I cluster containing at least 69 variable stars, most of which are RR Lyrae variables.
IC 4699 is a 13th magnitude planetary nebula located midway between Alpha and Epsilon Telescopii.
IC 4889 is an elliptical galaxy of magnitude 11.3, located 2 degrees north-northwest of 5.3-magnitude Nu Telescopii. A 40 cm telescope reveals its central region and halo.

NGC 6845 is an interacting system of four galaxies (two spiral and two lenticular) occupying about 4' × 2', estimated to be around 287 million light-years distant. SN 2008da, a type II supernova, was observed in spiral galaxy NGC 6845A in June 2008.
SN 1998bw was a luminous supernova observed in the spiral arm of galaxy ESO184-G82 in April 1998. It is highly likely to be the source of gamma-ray burst GRB 980425.

Tri.name: Triangulum
Tri.description: Triangulum is a small constellation bordered by Andromeda to the north and west, Pisces to the west and south, Aries to the south, and Perseus to the east. It covers 132 square degrees and 0.320% of the night sky, ranking 78th of the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Beta Trianguli (Alaybasan) (3.00m).

babylonian: In Babylonian star catalogues, Triangulum together with Gamma Andromedae formed the constellation known as MULAPIN 'The Plough'. It was notable as the first constellation on tablets containing canonical star lists compiled around 1000 BC.

The Plough was the first constellation of the 'Way of Enlil'—the northernmost quarter of the Sun's path, corresponding to the 45 days on either side of summer solstice. Its heliacal rising in February marked the time to begin spring ploughing in Mesopotamia.
greek: The Ancient Greeks called Triangulum Deltoton (Δελτωτόν), as the constellation resembled an upper-case Greek letter delta (Δ). It was transliterated by Roman writers, then later Latinised as Deltotum.
Eratosthenes linked it with the Nile Delta, while the Roman writer Hyginus associated it with the triangular island of Sicily, formerly known as Trinacria due to its shape.
It was also called Sicilia, because the Romans believed Ceres, patron goddess of Sicily, begged Jupiter to place the island in the heavens.
Greek astronomers such as Hipparchos and Ptolemy called it Trigonon (Τρίγωνον), and later it was Romanized as Trigonum. Other names referring to its shape include Tricuspis and Triquetrum.
history: 17th-century German celestial cartographer Johann Bayer called the constellation Triplicitas and Orbis terrarum tripertitus, for the three regions Europe, Asia, and Africa.
Triangulus Septentrionalis was a name used to distinguish it from Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle.

Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius excised three faint stars (ι, 10 and 12 Trianguli) to form the new constellation Triangulum Minus in his 1690 Firmamentum Sobiescianum, renaming the original as Triangulum Majus. The smaller constellation was not recognized by the IAU when constellations were established in the 1920s.
arab: Alpha and Beta Trianguli were called Al Mīzān, which is Arabic for 'The Scale Beam'.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, Gamma Andromedae and neighboring stars including Beta, Gamma and Delta Trianguli were called Teen Ta Tseang Keun (天大将军, 'Heaven's great general'), representing honor in astrology and a great general in mythology.

stars_text: β Tri (Alaybasan, 3.00m) is the brightest star, a white giant 127 light-years from Earth. It's actually a spectroscopic binary system with a white A5IV primary (3.5 solar masses) beginning to evolve off the main sequence and a yellow-white F-type companion (1.4 solar masses). They orbit every 31 days and are surrounded by a dust ring extending from 50 to 400 AU.

α Tri (Caput Trianguli, 3.41m) is the second-brightest star, a yellow-white subgiant with a close dimmer companion. Also known as Ras al Muthallath, it lies at the apex of the triangle about 7 degrees north-northwest of Alpha Arietis.

γ Tri (Apdu, 4.00m) is a white main sequence star of spectral type A1Vnn about 112 light-years away. It's around double the size and 33 times as luminous as the Sun, rotating rapidly. Like Beta, it's surrounded by a dusty debris disk with radius 80 times Earth's orbital distance.

δ Tri (Deltoton, 5.25m) lies near Gamma and forms an optical triple with it and 7 Trianguli. Delta is a spectroscopic binary of two yellow main sequence stars similar to the Sun, located 35 light-years away—the closest system in the constellation. The two stars orbit each other every 10 days at just 0.1 AU apart.
7 Tri (magnitude 5.25) is much farther away at around 280 light-years, forming an optical system with Gamma and Delta.

ι Tri (Triminus) is a double star whose components can be separated by medium-sized telescopes into strong yellow and pale blue stars. Both are themselves close binaries. The brighter is a spectroscopic binary of two yellow-white stars orbiting every 39.88 days, with the primary being a Gamma Doradus variable pulsating over 1.45 days.
X Tri is an eclipsing binary system that ranges between magnitudes 8.5 and 11.2 over a period of 0.97 days.

RW Tri is a cataclysmic variable system composed of a white dwarf primary and orange K7V main sequence star. The white dwarf draws matter from its companion, forming a prominent accretion disc. The system is around 1,076 light-years distant.
R Tri is a long period (Mira) variable that ranges from magnitude 6.2 to 11.7 over 267 days. It's a red giant of spectral type M3.5-8e, lying around 960 light-years away.

HD 12545 (XX Tri) is an orange giant (K0III) around 520 light-years distant with magnitude 8.42. A huge starspot larger than the Sun's diameter was detected on its surface in 1999 using Doppler imaging.
HD 9446 is a Sun-like star around 171 light-years distant with two planets of 0.7 and 1.8 Jupiter masses, with orbital periods of 30 and 193 days respectively.

HD 13189 is an orange giant (K2II) about 2-7 times as massive as the Sun with a planetary or brown dwarf companion between 8 and 20 Jupiter masses, taking 472 days to orbit. It's one of the largest stars discovered to have a planetary companion.
deep_sky_objects: The Triangulum Galaxy (M33) was discovered by Giovanni Battista Hodierna in the 17th century. A distant member of the Local Group, it's about 2.3 million light-years away. At magnitude 5.8, it's bright enough to be seen by the naked eye under dark skies.

M33 is a diffuse object that is challenging to see under light-polluted skies, even with a small telescope or binoculars. Low power is required to view it. It lies near the Pisces border, 3.5 degrees west-northwest of Alpha Trianguli and 7 degrees southwest of Beta Andromedae.

M33 is a spiral galaxy with a diameter of 46,000 light-years, smaller than both the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way. A distance of less than 300 kiloparsecs between it and Andromeda supports the hypothesis that it is a satellite of the larger galaxy.
NGC 604 is an H II region within M33 where star formation takes place.
NGC 925 is a magnitude 12 spiral galaxy spanning 10 arcminutes, the largest NGC galaxy in Triangulum.

NGC 672 is a magnitude 11.6 barred spiral galaxy spanning 5 arcminutes. It appears to be interacting with nearby IC 1727. The two are 88,000 light-years apart and lie around 18 million light-years away.
NGC 672, IC 1727, and four nearby dwarf irregular galaxies constitute the NGC 672 group. All six appear to have had a burst of star formation in the last ten million years.

The NGC 672 group is thought connected to the NGC 784 group, named for its principal barred spiral galaxy. Together with two isolated dwarf galaxies, these fourteen appear to be moving in a common direction and may be located on a dark matter filament.

3C 48 was the first quasar ever to be observed, although its true identity was not uncovered until after that of 3C 273 in 1963. It has magnitude 16.2 and is located about 5 degrees northwest of Alpha Trianguli.

TrA.name: Triangulum Australe
TrA.description: Triangulum Australe is a small constellation bordered by Norma to the north, Circinus to the west, Apus to the south and Ara to the east. It covers 110 square degrees, ranking 83rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Atria (α TrA) (1.91m). The constellation is located within the Milky Way and forms a roughly equilateral triangle that is easily identifiable.

history: Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci explored the New World at the beginning of the 16th century. He made a star catalogue for his patron King Manuel I of Portugal, which is now lost. Vespucci wrote descriptions of southern stars including a triangle which may be either Triangulum Australe or Apus.

The first depiction of the constellation was provided in 1589 by Flemish astronomer Petrus Plancius on a 32½-cm diameter celestial globe published in Amsterdam. It was called Triangulus Antarcticus and incorrectly portrayed south of Argo Navis.

Plancius's student Petrus Keyzer, along with Dutch explorer Frederick de Houtman, coined the name Den Zuyden Trianghel. Triangulum Australe was more accurately depicted in Johann Bayer's 1603 celestial atlas Uranometria, where it was given its current name.

Nicolas Louis de Lacaille portrayed Norma, Circinus and Triangulum Australe as a set square and ruler, a compass, and a surveyor's level respectively in a set of draughtsman's instruments in his 1756 map of the southern stars.
German Johann Bode also depicted it as a surveyor's level, giving it the alternate name Libella in his Uranographia.
German poet Philippus Caesius saw the three main stars as representing the Three Patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (with Atria as Abraham).
aboriginal: The Wardaman people of the Northern Territory in Australia perceived the stars of Triangulum Australe as the tail of the Rainbow Serpent, which stretched from near Crux across to Scorpius.
Overhead in October, the Rainbow Serpent 'gives Lightning a nudge' to bring on the wet season rains in November.

stars_text: α TrA (Atria, 1.91m) is the brightest star and the 42nd-brightest in the night sky. Readily identified by its orange hue, it's a bright giant of spectral type K2 IIb-IIIa located 424 light-years away. With absolute magnitude -3.68, it's 5,500 times more luminous than the Sun.
Atria has a diameter 130 times that of the Sun. If placed at the center of the Solar System, it would almost reach the orbit of Venus. The proper name Atria is a contraction of its Bayer designation.

β TrA (2.85m) is a double star with an F1V main-sequence primary lying only 40 light-years away with absolute magnitude 2.38. Its companion, almost 3 arcminutes away, is a 13th-magnitude star which may or may not be in orbit around Beta.
γ TrA (2.87m) is an A1V main sequence star located 180 light-years away, completing the triangle with Alpha and Beta.
δ TrA (3.8m) is the fourth-brightest star, a yellow giant of spectral type G2Ib-II lying 606 light-years away. It's located outside the triangle near Beta.

ε TrA is an optical double lying halfway between Beta and Gamma. The brighter component (ε TrA A, 4.11m) is an orange K1.5III subgiant. The optical companion (ε TrA B, 9.32m) is a white A9IV/V main sequence star.

ζ TrA (4.91m) appears as a single F9V star but is actually a spectroscopic binary with a near companion, probably a red dwarf. The pair orbit each other every 13 days at just 0.1 AU apart. It's a young star and member of the Ursa Major moving group.

ι TrA is a multiple star system appearing as yellow and white stars through a 7.5 cm telescope. The brighter star (F4IV) is a spectroscopic binary of two yellow-white stars orbiting every 39.88 days. The primary is a Gamma Doradus variable, pulsating over 1.45 days. The fainter star is an optical companion, not associated with the system.
κ TrA (5.11m) is a yellow bright giant of spectral type G5IIa located around 1,207 light-years distant.
η TrA (5.89m) is a Be star of spectral type B7IVe which is 661 light-years from Earth.
R TrA is a cepheid variable that ranges from magnitude 6.4 to 6.9 over 3.389 days. It's a yellow-white giant of spectral type F7Ib/II.
S TrA is a cepheid variable that ranges from magnitude 6.1 to 6.8 over 6.323 days. It's a yellow-white giant of spectral type F8II.
U TrA is a cepheid variable with brightness changing from 7.5 to 8.3 over 2.568 days. It's a yellow-white giant of spectral type F8Ib/II.
RT TrA is an unusual carbon cepheid of spectral type R. It shows strong absorption bands in molecular fragments of C₂, ·CH and ·CN, and varies between magnitudes 9.2 and 9.97 over 1.95 days.
X TrA is a variable carbon star with average magnitude 5.63, lying near Gamma. It has two periods of around 385 and 455 days, and is of spectral type C5, 5(Nb).

EK TrA is a dwarf nova of the SU Ursae Majoris type, first noticed in 1978. It consists of a white dwarf and donor star orbiting every 1.5 hours. The white dwarf periodically erupts, reaching magnitude 11.2 in superoutbursts, 12.1 in normal outbursts, and remaining at magnitude 16.7 when quiet.
NR TrA was a slow nova which peaked at magnitude 8.4 in April 2008, before fading to magnitude 12.4 by September of that year.
HD 147018 is a Sun-like star (G9V, magnitude 8.3) found to have two exoplanets, HD 147018 b and HD 147018 c, discovered in 2009.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 6025 is an open cluster with about 30 stars ranging from 7th to 9th magnitude. Located 3 degrees north and 1 east of Beta Trianguli Australis, it lies about 2,500 light-years away and is about 11 light-years in diameter. Its brightest star is MQ Trianguli Australis at magnitude 7.1.
NGC 5979 is a planetary nebula of magnitude 12.3 with a blue-green hue at higher magnifications.
Henize 2-138 is a smaller planetary nebula of magnitude 11.0.
NGC 5938 is a remote spiral galaxy around 300 million light-years away, located 5 degrees south of Epsilon Trianguli Australis.
ESO 69-6 is a pair of merging galaxies located about 600 million light-years away. Their contents have been dragged out in long tails by the interaction.
culture: Triangulum Australe appears on the flag of Brazil, symbolizing the three states of the South Region.
It also appears as the only constellation used for the flag of secessionist movement The South Is My Country.

Tuc.name: Tucana

source.discoverer: Petrus Plancius (from Keyser & de Houtman observations)

Tuc.description: Tucana is bordered by Hydrus, Grus, Phoenix, Indus, and Octans. It covers 295 square degrees, ranking 48th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is α Tuc (Lang-Exster) at magnitude 2.87.

history: Tucana is one of twelve constellations established by astronomer Petrus Plancius from observations of the southern sky by Dutch explorers Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman during the first Dutch trading expedition to the East Indies.

It first appeared on a 35-centimeter celestial globe published in 1598 in Amsterdam by Plancius with Jodocus Hondius. The first depiction in a celestial atlas was in Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603.

De Houtman called it "Den Indiaenschen Exster, op Indies Lang ghenaemt" (the Indian magpie, named Lang in the Indies), referring to a hornbill, a bird native to the East Indies. A 1603 celestial globe by Willem Blaeu depicts it with a casque.

It was interpreted on Chinese charts as Niǎohuì (bird's beak), and in England as Brasilian Pye. Johannes Kepler and Giovanni Battista Riccioli termed it Anser Americanus (American Goose), and Caesius called it Pica Indica.
Tucana and the nearby constellations Phoenix, Grus and Pavo are collectively called the Southern Birds.
characteristics: Irregular in shape, Tucana is bordered by Hydrus to the east, Grus and Phoenix to the north, Indus to the west and Octans to the south.

As one of the deep southern constellations, it remains below the horizon at latitudes north of the 30th parallel in the Northern Hemisphere, and is circumpolar at latitudes south of the 50th parallel in the Southern Hemisphere.

stars_text: α Tuc (Lang-Exster, 2.86m) is the brightest star, an orange subgiant of spectral type K3III located 199 light-years away. With a surface temperature of 4300 K, it is 424 times as luminous as the Sun and 37 times its diameter. It is a spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of 11.5 years.
γ Tuc (4.00m) is a yellow-white sequence star of spectral type F4V and marks the toucan's beak. Located around 75 light-years from Earth, it was described by Richard Hinckley Allen as bluish.

β Tuc is a sextuple star system with six components total. The two brightest, β1 and β2, have magnitudes of 4.4 and 4.5 and are separated by 27 arcseconds. β3 Tucanae is separated by 10 arcminutes and visible to the naked eye. Each star is itself a binary.
δ Tuc consists of a blue-white primary (B9.5V, mag 4.49) at 251 light-years, contrasting with a yellowish companion (mag 9.3).

κ Tuc is a quadruple system 68 light-years away with combined magnitude 4.25. The brighter component (κ Tuc A, mag 5.33, F6V) is yellowish, while κ Tuc B (mag 7.58, K1V) lies 5 arcseconds northwest. A fainter pair of orange stars (K2V and K3V) can be resolved with high magnification.

ζ Tuc (4.20m) is a yellow-white main sequence star (F9.5V) just 28 light-years away. Its composition and mass are very similar to the Sun, making it a target for investigating possible life-bearing planets. It has a debris disk orbiting at minimum radius of 2.3 AU.

Five star systems have planets, four discovered by HARPS in Chile. HD 4308 has a super-Earth with a 15-day orbit. HD 215497 has a hot super-Earth (3-day orbit) and a Saturn-sized planet (567-day orbit). HD 221287 has a super-Jovian planet. HD 7199 has a planet 30% the mass of Jupiter with a 615-day orbit.
deep_sky_objects: 47 Tucanae (NGC 104) is the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky after Omega Centauri. Only 14,700 light-years distant, it is thought to be around 12 billion years old. At magnitude 3.9, it is visible to the naked eye.

47 Tucanae is a Shapley class III cluster with a clearly defined nucleus. Mostly composed of old yellow stars, it possesses a contingent of blue stragglers—hot stars hypothesized to form from binary star mergers.

NGC 362 is another bright globular cluster (mag 6.4) located 27,700 light-years away. It is also a Shapley class III cluster. Unusually, its orbit takes it very close to the Milky Way's center—approximately 3,000 light-years.

The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy and one of the nearest neighbors to the Milky Way at 210,000 light-years. Though it probably formed as a disk, tidal forces from the Milky Way have distorted it.
NGC 346 is a star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud with magnitude 10.3. Within it lies the triple star system HD 5980, each member among the most luminous stars known.

The Tucana Dwarf galaxy, discovered in 1990, is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy (type dE5) located 2,800,000 light-years from the Solar System—the second most remote member of the Local Group after the Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy.
NGC 7408 is a barred spiral galaxy located 3 degrees northwest of Delta Tucanae. It was initially mistaken for a planetary nebula.
The Hubble Deep Field South was created in 1998 from a two-week observation program by the Hubble Space Telescope focused on part of Tucana. The field includes the quasar QSO J2233-606.

UMa.name: Ursa Major
UMa.pronunciation: /ˌɜːrsə ˈmeɪdʒər/  UR-sə MAY-jər, genitive /ˌɜːrsiː məˈdʒɔːrɪs/ UR-see mə-JOR-iss
UMa.meteor_showers: Alpha Ursae Majorids, Kappa Ursae Majorids, October Ursae Majorids
UMa.description: Ursa Major is bordered by Draco, Camelopardalis, Lynx, Leo Minor, Leo, Coma Berenices, Canes Venatici, and Boötes. It covers 1,280 square degrees, ranking 3rd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alioth (ε UMa) at magnitude 1.76.

history: Ursa Major has been reconstructed as an Indo-European constellation. It was one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd century AD astronomer Ptolemy in his Almagest, who called it Arktos Megale.
The constellation has been seen as a bear, usually female, by multiple connected civilizations. This may stem from a common oral tradition of Cosmic Hunt myths stretching back more than 13,000 years.
greek: In Greek mythology, Zeus lusts after a young woman named Callisto, a nymph of Artemis. Zeus's jealous wife Hera discovers that Callisto has a son named Arcas as the result of her rape by Zeus and transforms Callisto into a bear as punishment.

Callisto, while in bear form, later encounters her son Arcas. Arcas almost spears the bear, but to avert the tragedy Zeus whisks them both into the sky—Callisto as Ursa Major and Arcas as the constellation Boötes.

Ovid called Ursa Major the Parrhasian Bear, since Callisto came from Parrhasia in Arcadia. The Greek poet Aratus called the constellation Helike (turning or twisting), because it turns around the celestial pole.
The Odyssey notes that it is the sole constellation that never sinks below the horizon and never bathes in the Ocean's waves, so it is used as a celestial reference point for navigation.
arab: Pre-Islamic Arabs recognized the Big Dipper and Ursa Minor as counterparts. Both were imagined as funeral processions with the ladle as a funerary bier and its handle as a train of mourners.

The Big Dipper is known as banāt an-na'sh al-kubrā (the greater daughters of the bier), better translated as the greater funeral procession, whilst Ursa Minor is known as the lesser funeral procession.
According to legend, the body on the bier is Na'ash, a man murdered by Al-judayy (the North Star), and the funeral procession is in pursuit of him.

Three pairs of stars along the southern border represent three pairs of footprints of a leaping gazelle: the first leap (ν and ξ UMa, Alula Borealis and Australis), the second leap (λ and μ UMa, Tania Borealis and Australis), and the third leap (ι and κ UMa, Talitha and Alkaphrah).
hindu: In Hinduism, Ursa Major is known as Saptarshi (Seven Sages), with each star representing one of the seven Rishis: Bhrigu, Atri, Angiras, Vasishtha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
The earliest mention is found in the Rigveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE), one of the oldest known texts in human history. It mentions the Saptarishi in connection with celestial order and cosmic significance.
The Mahabharata (c. 400 BCE – 400 CE) discusses Saptarishi Mandal as a guiding star for navigation. The Puranas describe the Saptarishis as divine sages who hold cosmic wisdom.
The fact that the two front stars point to the pole star is explained as the boon given to the boy sage Dhruva by Lord Vishnu.
chinese: In China and Japan, the Big Dipper is called the North Dipper (北斗, Chinese: běidǒu, Japanese: hokuto). Each of the seven stars had a specific name from ancient China.

Dubhe is Pivot (樞), Merak is Beautiful jade (璇), Phecda is Pearl (璣), Megrez is Balance (權), Alioth is Measuring rod of jade (玉衡), Mizar is Opening of the Yang (開陽), and Alkaid is Sword (劍) or Flickering light (搖光).
In Shinto, the seven largest stars of Ursa Major belong to Ame-no-Minakanushi, the oldest and most powerful of all kami.
In South Korea, a widow with seven sons found comfort with a widower. Her seven sons placed stepping stones in a river for her to cross. When they died, they became the constellation.
native_american: The Iroquois interpreted Alioth, Mizar, and Alkaid as three hunters pursuing the Great Bear. The first hunter (Alioth) carries a bow and arrow, the second (Mizar) carries a large pot (Alcor) to cook the bear, and the third (Alkaid) hauls firewood.
The Lakota people call the constellation Wičhákhiyuhapi, or Great Bear. The Wampanoag people referred to Ursa Major as maske, meaning bear.
The Wasco-Wishram Native Americans interpreted the constellation as five wolves and two bears left in the sky by Coyote.
germanic: To Norse pagans, the Big Dipper was known as Óðins vagn, Woden's wagon. Woden is poetically referred to by Kennings such as vagna verr (guardian of the wagon) or vagna rúni (confidant of the wagon).
uralic: In Finnish, the asterism is sometimes called Otava, which means a salmon weir. Ancient Finns believed the bear (Ursus arctos) was lowered to earth in a golden basket off Ursa Major, and when a bear was killed, its head was positioned on a tree to allow the bear's spirit to return.
In Sámi languages, the Big Dipper minus Dubhe and Merak is identified as the bow of the great hunter Fávdna (the star Arcturus). In North Sámi, it is called Fávdnadávgi (Fávdna's Bow).

The constellation features prominently in the Sámi anthem: Far to the north, under the Bow, the Land of the Sámi slowly comes into view. According to legend, Fávdna stands ready to fire his Bow every night but hesitates because he might hit Boahji (the Rivet, Polaris), which would cause the sky to collapse.

stars_text: ε UMa (Alioth, 1.76m) is the brightest star of Ursa Major and the 33rd-brightest in the sky. Its name refers to a black horse. It is the brightest of the chemically peculiar Ap stars—magnetic stars whose chemical elements are either depleted or enhanced and appear to change as the star rotates.

α UMa (Dubhe, 1.79m, the bear) is the second-brightest star and the 35th-brightest in the sky. With Merak, Dubhe forms the pointer stars that help locate Polaris. By tracing a line from Merak through Dubhe for 5 units, one's eye lands on Polaris.
η UMa (Alkaid, 1.85m) is situated at the end of the tail. It and Dubhe are the only Big Dipper stars not part of the Ursa Major Moving Group.
β UMa (Merak, 2.37m, the loins of the bear) is the second pointer star. Most Big Dipper stars have proper motions heading toward a common point in Sagittarius and form the Ursa Major Moving Group.
γ UMa (Phecda, 2.44m, thigh) is the third star in the bowl of the Big Dipper.
δ UMa (Megrez, root of the tail) marks the intersection of the body and tail of the bear, or the ladle and handle of the dipper.

ζ UMa (Mizar, girdle) is the second star from the end of the handle and the constellation's fourth-brightest star. It forms a famous double star with its optical companion Alcor (80 UMa), termed the horse and rider by the Arabs.
W Ursae Majoris is the prototype of a class of contact binary variable stars, ranging between magnitudes 7.75 and 8.48.

47 Ursae Majoris is a Sun-like star with a three-planet system. 47 UMa b (discovered 1996) orbits every 1078 days and is 2.53 Jupiter masses. 47 UMa c (2001) orbits every 2391 days at 0.54 Jupiter masses. 47 UMa d (2010) has an uncertain period between 8907–19097 days at 1.64 Jupiter masses.
TYC 3429-697-1, located east of θ UMa and southwest of the Big Dipper, is recognized as the state star of Delaware and is informally known as the Delaware Diamond.
deep_sky_objects: M81 is a nearly face-on spiral galaxy 11.8 million light-years from Earth. Like most spirals, it has a core of old stars with arms filled with young stars and nebulae. Along with M82, it is part of the galaxy cluster closest to the Local Group.
M82 is a nearly edgewise galaxy interacting gravitationally with M81. It is the brightest infrared galaxy in the sky. SN 2014J, an apparent Type Ia supernova, was observed in M82 on January 21, 2014.

M97 (Owl Nebula) is a planetary nebula 1,630 light-years from Earth with magnitude approximately 10. It was discovered in 1781 by Pierre Méchain and can be found along the bottom of the bowl of the Big Dipper.

M101 (Pinwheel Galaxy) is a face-on spiral galaxy 25 million light-years from Earth, discovered by Pierre Méchain in 1781. Its spiral arms have regions with extensive star formation and strong ultraviolet emissions. At magnitude 7.5, it is visible in binoculars and telescopes.
M108 and M109 are spiral galaxies also found in this constellation.
NGC 2787 is a lenticular galaxy 24 million light-years away. Unlike most lenticular galaxies, it has a bar at its center and a halo of globular clusters indicating its age and relative stability.

NGC 3079 is a starburst spiral galaxy 52 million light-years away. It has a horseshoe-shaped structure at its center indicating a supermassive black hole. The structure is formed by superwinds from the black hole.

NGC 3310 is another starburst spiral galaxy 50 million light-years away. Its bright white color is caused by its higher than usual rate of star formation, which began 100 million years ago after a merger.

I Zwicky 18 is a young dwarf galaxy 45 million light-years away. The youngest-known galaxy in the visible universe, it is about 4 million years old—about one-thousandth the age of the Solar System. It is filled with star forming regions creating hot, young, blue stars at a very high rate.
The Hubble Deep Field is located to the northeast of δ Ursae Majoris.
meteor_showers_detail: The Alpha Ursae Majorids are a minor meteor shower that may be caused by comet C/1992 W1 (Ohshita).
The Kappa Ursae Majorids are a newly discovered meteor shower, peaking between November 1 and November 10.
The October Ursae Majorids were discovered in 2006 by Japanese researchers and may be caused by a long period comet. The shower peaks between October 12 and 19.

UMi.name: Ursa Minor
UMi.pronunciation: /ˌɜːrsə ˈmaɪnər/  UR-sə MY-nər, Genitive: /ˌɜːrsiː mɪˈnɔːrɪs/ UR-see min-OR-iss
UMi.description: Ursa Minor is bordered by Camelopardalis, Draco, and Cepheus. It covers 256 square degrees, ranking 56th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Polaris at magnitude 1.97.

babylonian: In Babylonian star catalogues, Ursa Minor was known as the Wagon of Heaven (MULMAR.GÍD.DA.AN.NA), also associated with the goddess Damkina. It is listed in the MUL.APIN catalogue, compiled around 1000 BC, among the Stars of Enlil—the northern sky.
greek: According to Diogenes Laërtius, Thales of Miletus measured the stars of the Wagon by which the Phoenicians sail. The constellation was named Phoinikē (Phoenician Bear) for its use by the Phoenicians in navigation.

The tradition of naming the northern constellations bears appears to be genuinely Greek. The original bear is Ursa Major, and Ursa Minor was admitted as the second or Phoenician Bear only later, due to Thales' suggestion as a navigation aid to the Greeks.

In classical antiquity, the celestial pole was closer to Beta Ursae Minoris than to Alpha Ursae Minoris, and the entire constellation indicated the northern direction. Since the medieval period, Alpha Ursae Minoris (Polaris) has served as the North Star.

Another ancient name is Cynosura (Greek Κυνοσούρα, dog's tail). The mythographic tradition of Catasterismi makes Cynosura the name of an Oread nymph described as a nurse of Zeus, honoured by the god with a place in the sky.

An alternative myth tells of two bears that saved Zeus from his murderous father Cronus by hiding him on Mount Ida. Later Zeus set them in the sky, but their tails grew long from being swung up into the sky by the god.
Because Ursa Minor consists of seven stars, the Latin word for north (septentrio) comes from septem (seven) and triones (oxen), from seven oxen driving a plough, which the seven stars also resemble.
chinese: In Chinese astronomy, the main stars of Ursa Minor are divided between two asterisms: Gòuchén (Curved Array, including α, δ, ε, ζ, η, θ, λ UMi) and Běijí (Northern Pole, including β and γ UMi).
inuit: In Inuit astronomy, the three brightest stars—Polaris, Kochab, and Pherkad—were known as Nuutuittut (never moving), though the term is more frequently used in the singular to refer to Polaris alone. The Pole Star is too high in the sky at far northern latitudes to be of use in navigation.

stars_text: α UMi (Polaris, 1.97–2.00m) marks the Little Bear's tail and is the brightest star in the constellation. Located around 432 light-years away, it is a yellow-white supergiant (F7Ib–F8Ib) with around 6 times the Sun's mass, 2,500 times its luminosity, and 45 times its radius.

Polaris is the brightest Cepheid variable star visible from Earth, varying between magnitudes 1.97 and 2.00 over a period of 3.97 days. It is a triple star system with two yellow-white main-sequence companions at 17 and 2,400 AU.

β UMi (Kochab, 2.08m) is slightly less bright than Polaris. Located around 131 light-years away, it is an orange giant (K4III) that has used up the hydrogen in its core and moved off the main sequence.

Kochab is 450 times more luminous than the Sun and has 42 times its diameter, with a surface temperature of approximately 4,130 K. It is estimated to be around 2.95 billion years old and has a planetary companion around 6.1 times as massive as Jupiter with a 522-day orbit.

γ UMi (Pherkad, 3.04–3.09m) is a white bright giant (A3II-III) with around 4.8 times the Sun's mass, 1,050 times its luminosity and 15 times its radius. It is 487 light-years distant. Pherkad and Kochab are termed the guardians of the pole star.
Pherkad is a Delta Scuti variable—short period (six hours at most) pulsating stars used as standard candles and as subjects to study asteroseismology.

δ UMi (Yildun, 4.35m) is a white main-sequence star (A1V) located just over 3.5 degrees from the north celestial pole. Located 172 light-years from Earth, it has around 2.8 times the diameter and 47 times the luminosity of the Sun.
ζ UMi (4.95m) is a white star (A3V) that is the dimmest of the seven stars of the Little Dipper. It is likely to have been a B3 main-sequence star and is now slightly variable.
η UMi (4.95m) is a yellow-white main-sequence star (F5V) located 97 light-years distant. It is double the Sun's diameter, 1.4 times as massive, and shines with 7.4 times its luminosity.

ε UMi (4.22m) is a triple star system. A yellow giant (G5III), the primary is an RS Canum Venaticorum variable star and a spectroscopic binary with a companion 0.36 AU distant. A third star—an orange main-sequence star (K0)—is 8100 AU distant.
RR Ursae Minoris is a red giant (M5III) and semiregular variable ranging from magnitude 4.44 to 4.85 over a period of 43.3 days. It is located south of Kochab and Pherkad towards Draco.

T Ursae Minoris underwent a dramatic change in status—from being a long-period (Mira) variable ranging from magnitude 7.8 to 15 over 310–315 days, to being a semiregular variable. The star is thought to have undergone a shell helium flash in 1979.

RW Ursae Minoris is a cataclysmic variable star system that flared up as a nova in 1956, reaching magnitude 6. In 2003, it was still two magnitudes brighter than its baseline, and dimming at a rate of 0.02 magnitude per year. It is located in the galactic halo at approximately 16,300 light-years.

WISE 1506+7027 is a brown dwarf of spectral type T6 that is a mere 11.1 light-years away from Earth. A faint object of magnitude 14, it was discovered by the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) in 2011.
deep_sky_objects: The Ursa Minor Dwarf is a dwarf spheroidal galaxy discovered by Albert George Wilson in the Palomar Sky Survey in 1955. Its centre is around 225,000 light-years distant from Earth.

In 1999, the Hubble Space Telescope confirmed that the galaxy had a single burst of star formation around 14 billion years ago that lasted around 2 billion years, and is probably as old as the Milky Way itself.
NGC 3172 (Polarissima Borealis) is a faint magnitude-14.9 galaxy that happens to be the closest NGC object to the north celestial pole. It was discovered by John Herschel in 1831.

NGC 6217 is a barred spiral galaxy located 67 million light-years away. It can be located with a 10 cm or larger telescope as an 11th-magnitude object about 2.5 degrees east-northeast of Zeta Ursae Minoris. It is a starburst galaxy undergoing a high rate of star formation.

NGC 6251 is an active supergiant elliptical radio galaxy more than 340 million light-years away. It has a Seyfert 2 active galactic nucleus and is one of the most extreme examples of a Seyfert galaxy.
NGC 6251 may be associated with gamma-ray source 3EG J1621+8203, which has high-energy gamma-ray emission. It is noted for its one-sided radio jet—one of the brightest known—discovered in 1977.
meteor_showers_detail: The Ursids are a prominent meteor shower that occurs in Ursa Minor, peaking between December 18 and 25. Its parent body is the comet 8P/Tuttle.

Vel.name: Vela
Vel.description: Vela is bordered by Antlia, Pyxis, Puppis, Carina, and Centaurus. It covers 500 square degrees, ranking 32nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Gamma Velorum (1.75m).

greek: Vela was originally part of Argo Navis, one of Ptolemy's 48 classical constellations from the 2nd century. Argo represented the ship used by Jason and the Argonauts on their quest for the Golden Fleece in Greek mythology.

Johann Bayer depicted the constellation on his Uranometria of 1603 and gave stars Bayer designations from Alpha to Omega. However, his chart was inaccurate as the constellation was not fully visible from the Northern Hemisphere.

In 1752, French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille subdivided Argo into three parts: Carina (the keel), Vela (the sails), and Puppis (the poop deck). Despite the division, Lacaille kept Argo's original Bayer designations.

Because of this unusual history, Carina has the Alpha, Beta and Epsilon stars originally assigned to Argo Navis, while Vela's brightest stars are Gamma and Delta, and Puppis has Zeta as its brightest star.
history: In early celestial maps, Vela was depicted as part of the ship Argo Navis, often shown with the flying fish constellation Volans nearby and being chased by the predatory fish Dorado.

stars_text: γ Vel (Gamma Velorum, 1.75m) is the brightest star and a complex multiple star system 1,116 light-years away. The primary Gamma2 is a spectroscopic binary with two very hot blue stars orbiting every 78.5 days.
The brighter component of Gamma2 is an O7.5 main-sequence star 280,000 times as luminous as the Sun, 30 times as massive, and 17 times the diameter with a surface temperature of 35,000 K.

The second component of Gamma2 is an extremely rare Wolf-Rayet star, the closest and brightest example in the sky. It has a surface temperature of 57,000 K and is 170,000 times as luminous as the Sun, radiating most energy in ultraviolet.
Gamma1 is a blue-white B2III star of magnitude 4.3, separated from Gamma2 by 41 arcseconds and easily separable in binoculars. The two pairs are at least 12,000 AU apart.

δ Vel (Delta Velorum or Alsephina, 1.95m) is a multiple star system about 80 light-years away and one of the brightest eclipsing binaries in the sky. Together with Kappa Velorum, Iota Carinae, and Epsilon Carinae, it forms the False Cross.
The False Cross is a diamond-shaped asterism sometimes mistaken for the Southern Cross, causing errors in astronavigation.

Delta A is an eclipsing binary of two A-type white stars orbiting every 45.2 days at 0.5 AU, with magnitude drops of 0.4 during eclipse. Delta B is a magnitude 5.1 yellow G-class star 26-72 AU away, taking 142 years to orbit.
κ Vel (Kappa Velorum or Markeb, 2.47m) is a blue-white B2IV-V spectroscopic binary. The two orbit each other every 116.65 days, but the companion's properties remain unclear.
λ Vel (Lambda Velorum or Suhail, 2.14-2.3m) is an orange K4Ib-II supergiant 545 light-years distant. It has 11,000 times the Sun's luminosity, 9-12 times its mass, and 207 times its diameter.

ο Vel (Omicron Velorum, 3.57-3.63m) is a blue-white B3III-IV subgiant 495 light-years away. A slowly pulsating B star, it varies over 2.8 days and is the brightest star in IC 2391, the Omicron Velorum Cluster.
Seven star systems have planets. HD 75289 is a G0V star with a hot Jupiter orbiting in 3.51 days at 0.0482 AU. WASP-19 has a hot Jupiter orbiting every 0.7 days.
HD 73526 is a G6V star with two Jupiter-mass planets orbiting in 187 and 377 days. HD 85390 is a K1.5V orange dwarf 111 light-years away with a planet 42 Earth masses orbiting every 788 days.
Luhman 16 is a binary brown dwarf system only 6.6 light-years away, the third-closest system to the Solar System. Its discovery was announced on March 11, 2013.
deep_sky_objects: NGC 3132, the 'Eight-Burst Nebula' or 'Southern Ring Nebula,' is a planetary nebula on the border with Antlia. NGC 2899 is an unusual red-hued planetary nebula. Vela contains 32 more planetary nebulae.
The Gum Nebula is a faint emission nebula believed to be the remains of a million-year-old supernova. Within it lies the smaller and younger Vela Supernova Remnant.

The Vela Supernova Remnant is the nebula of a supernova explosion believed to have been visible from Earth around 10,000 years ago. It contains the Vela Pulsar, the first pulsar to be identified optically.
NGC 2736, also known as the Pencil Nebula, lies nearby the Vela Pulsar.
HH-47 is a Herbig-Haro Object, a young star about 1,400 light-years away ejecting material at tremendous speed (up to a million kilometers per hour). This material glows as it hits surrounding gas.

NGC 2670 is an open cluster with magnitude 7.8 located 3,200 light-years away. Its stars are arranged suggesting a bow and arrow shape. It's a Trumpler class II 2 p cluster with less than 50 stars ranging moderately in brightness.
NGC 2547 is an open cluster 2 degrees south of Gamma Velorum containing around 50 stars of magnitudes 7 to 15.

NGC 3201 is a globular cluster discovered by James Dunlop on May 28, 1826. Its stellar population is inhomogeneous, varying with distance from the core. Redder, cooler stars tend to be located closer to the core.
RCW 36 is a star-forming region in Vela and one of the nearest sites of massive star formation. It has given rise to a cluster of several hundred young stars that power an HII region.
meteor_showers_detail: The Delta Velids, Gamma Velids, and Puppid-velids meteor showers radiate from Vela and neighboring constellations.

Vir.name: Virgo
Vir.description: Virgo is bordered by Boötes, Coma Berenices, Leo, Crater, Corvus, Hydra, Libra, and Serpens Caput. It covers 1,294 square degrees, ranking 2nd among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Spica (α Vir) (0.98m).

babylonian: In the Babylonian MUL.APIN (c. 10th century BC), part of this constellation was known as 'The Furrow,' representing the goddess Shala and her ear of grain. Spica retains this tradition, as it is Latin for 'ear of grain.'

The constellation of Virgo in Hipparchus corresponds to two Babylonian constellations: the 'Furrow' in the eastern sector and the 'Frond of Erua' in the western sector. The Frond of Erua was depicted as a goddess holding a palm-frond.
The constellation became associated with fertility as grain was one of the major products of the Mesopotamian furrow.
greek: Early Greek astronomy associated the Babylonian constellation with Demeter, their goddess of wheat, agriculture, and autumn. The Romans associated it with their goddess Ceres.
Alternatively, the constellation was sometimes identified as the virgin goddess Iustitia or Astraea, holding the scales of justice in her hand (now separated as the constellation Libra).

Another Greek myth identifies Virgo as Erigone, the daughter of Icarius of Athens. Icarius was favored by Dionysus and killed by his shepherds while intoxicated, after which Erigone hanged herself in grief.
In some versions, Dionysus placed the father and daughter in the stars as Boötes and Virgo respectively.
The constellation is also associated with the spring goddess Persephone, the daughter of Zeus and Demeter who married Hades and resided in the Underworld.
In the Poeticon Astronomicon by Hyginus (1st century BC), Parthenos is the daughter of Apollo and Chrysothemis, who died a maiden and was placed among the stars.
Virgo is also associated with Dike, the goddess of justice and daughter of Zeus, represented holding the scales of justice.
history: During the Middle Ages, Virgo was sometimes associated with the Blessed Virgin Mary.
hindu: In Hindu astrology, Virgo is known as Kanyā (कन्या), the sixth sign of the sidereal zodiac ruled by the planet Budha (बुद्ध; Mercury).
Classified as an earth sign with a dual (mutable) nature, Kanyā is traditionally associated with intellect, analytical ability, service, health, and disciplined work.
Classical texts such as the Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra describe natives of this sign as intelligent, detail-oriented, practical, modest, and skilled in communication.

stars_text: α Vir (Spica, 0.98m) is the brightest star in Virgo and the 15th-brightest star in the night sky. The constellation can be located by 'following the arc to Arcturus and speed on to Spica' from the Big Dipper.
Other bright stars include β Vir (Zavijava), γ Vir (Porrima), δ Vir (Auva), and ε Vir (Vindemiatrix).
Fainter named stars include ζ Vir (Heze), η Vir (Zaniah), ι Vir (Syrma), κ Vir (Kang), λ Vir (Khambalia), and φ Vir (Elgafar).
The 7 main stars of Virgo form 2 distinct patterns: Beta, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon, and Eta form an asterism called 'The Bowl of Virgo.' Together with Spica and Theta Virginis, they form a Y shape.
70 Vir has one of the first known extrasolar planetary systems with one confirmed planet 7.5 times Jupiter's mass.
χ Vir (Chi Virginis) has one of the most massive planets ever detected, with a mass of 11.1 times Jupiter.
61 Vir is a sun-like star with three known planets: one super-Earth and two Neptune-mass planets.
SS Vir is a variable star with a noticeable red color, varying from magnitude 9.6 to 6.0 over approximately one year.

There are 35 verified exoplanets orbiting 29 stars in Virgo, including PSR B1257+12 (three planets), 70 Virginis (one planet), Chi Virginis (one planet), 61 Virginis (three planets), NY Virginis (two planets), and 59 Virginis (one planet).
deep_sky_objects: Virgo contains the Virgo Cluster, a galaxy cluster located 5° to 12° west of ε Vir (Vindemiatrix), making this constellation especially rich in galaxies.

M49 (elliptical), M58 (spiral), M59 (elliptical), M60 (elliptical), M61 (spiral), M84 (lenticular), M86 (lenticular), M87 (elliptical), M89 (elliptical), and M90 (spiral) are all members of the Virgo Cluster.
M87 is the largest galaxy in the Virgo Cluster at 60 million light-years away. It's a major radio source with a jet of electrons flung out by its central supermassive black hole.

On April 10, 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope project released the first direct image of M87's central black hole. With a mass of at least 7.2 billion times the Sun, it's the most massive black hole in the Milky Way's immediate vicinity.
M84 is an elliptical radio galaxy 60 million light-years away. Gas clouds orbit its core at approximately 400 km/s, indicating a black hole with mass 300 million times that of the Sun.
