M104, the Sombrero Galaxy, is an edge-on spiral galaxy 28 million light-years away. It has a bulge of older stars larger than normal, surrounded by large bright globular clusters and a prominent dust lane of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
NGC 4438 is a peculiar galaxy with an active galactic nucleus 50 million light-years away. Its supermassive black hole ejects jets of matter, creating bubbles up to 78 light-years in diameter.
NGC 4261 has a black hole 20 light-years from its center with mass 1.2 billion solar masses. Located 45 million light-years away, it has an unusually dusty disk 300 light-years in diameter.
NGC 4639 is a face-on barred spiral galaxy 78 million light-years away. Its outer arms have many Cepheid variables used to calibrate type Ia supernovae as standard candles for distant galaxies.
Virgo is home to quasar 3C 273, the first quasar ever identified. With magnitude ~12.9, it's also the optically brightest quasar in the sky.
meteor_showers_detail: The Virginids and Mu Virginids meteor showers radiate from Virgo.

Vol.name: Volans
Vol.description: Volans is bordered by Carina, Pictor, Dorado, Mensa, and Chamaeleon. It covers 141 square degrees, ranking 76th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Beta² Volantis (3.62m).

history: Volans is one of the 12 constellations introduced by Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the late 16th century. It was first depicted on Petrus Plancius' globe in 1598.
Plancius called the constellation Vliegendenvis (flying fish). In 1603, Johann Bayer included it in his star atlas Uranometria under the name Piscis Volans, the flying fish.
John Herschel proposed shrinking the name to one word in 1844, noting that Lacaille himself had abbreviated his constellations thus on occasion. This was universally adopted.
Volans represents a type of tropical fish that can jump out of the water and glide through the air on wings.
In early celestial maps, the flying fish was often depicted as accompanying the ship Argo Navis and being chased by the predatory fish represented by the adjoining constellation Dorado.
On May 10, 2023, TOI-715 b, the first exoplanet in the conservative habitable zone about 1.55 times larger than Earth, was discovered in Volans by TESS.

stars_text: Lacaille gave 12 stars Bayer designations Alpha through Kappa in 1756 and labeled two stars as Gamma and Kappa.
γ Vol (Gamma Volantis) is a double star observable with a small telescope. Its two components have magnitudes 3.8 and 5.6.
ε Vol (Epsilon Volantis) is also a double star with magnitudes 4.4 and 7.3, visible with a small telescope.
The Astronomical Society of Southern Africa reported in 2003 that observations of variable stars R and S Volantis were urgently needed as data on their light curves was incomplete.
HD 76700 is a sun-like star about 195 light-years distant that has been found to have a planet.
deep_sky_objects: The Lindsay-Shapley ring (AM0644-741) is a ring galaxy 300 million light-years from Earth. Named for its discoverers, it was found near the Large Magellanic Cloud in 1960.

Like the Cartwheel Galaxy in Sculptor, the Lindsay-Shapley ring's unusual shape results from a collision many millions of years ago. The blue ring, 150,000 light-years in diameter, formed when a shock wave created a ring of hot blue stars.
The yellow core is an amalgamation of the progenitors' cores.
NGC 2442 is an intermediate-spiral galaxy 50 million light-years from Earth located in Volans.
Graham's Object, also called Das Rheingold or Nibelungen Ring, is a ring-shaped galaxy at R.A. 6h 41.4m / Decl. -74° 19' (2000.0) in Volans.
meteor_showers_detail: No meteor showers are associated with Volans.

Vul.name: Vulpecula
Vul.description: Vulpecula is bordered by Cygnus, Lyra, Hercules, Sagitta, Delphinus, and Pegasus. It covers 268 square degrees, ranking 55th among the 88 constellations in size. Its brightest star is Alpha Vulpeculae (Anser) (4.44m).

history: Vulpecula was created by Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius in the 17th century. It has no classical mythology associated with it.
The constellation represents a small fox. The brightest star, Alpha Vulpeculae, carries the traditional name Anser, which refers to the goose the little fox holds in its jaws.

stars_text: There are no stars brighter than 4th magnitude in Vulpecula. The brightest star is α Vul (Alpha Vulpeculae or Anser, 4.44m), a red giant approximately 291 light-years away.
Alpha Vulpeculae is an optical binary with separation of 413.7" that can be split using binoculars. The name Anser refers to the goose the little fox holds in its jaws.
23 Vul (23 Vulpeculae) is the second brightest star in the constellation.
In 1967, the first pulsar, PSR B1919+21, was discovered in Vulpecula by Jocelyn Bell, supervised by Antony Hewish, in Cambridge. They observed pulses repeating with a period of 1.3373 seconds.
The signal was identified as coming from a rapidly rotating neutron star. Terrestrial origin was ruled out because the object reappeared after a sidereal day instead of a solar day.
Fifteen years after the first pulsar discovery, the first millisecond pulsar, PSR B1937+21, was also discovered in Vulpecula, only a few degrees in the sky away from PSR B1919+21.

HD 189733 b is one of the closest extrasolar planets studied by the now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope. On July 11, 2007, a team led by Giovanna Tinetti found solid evidence for significant water vapor in the planet's atmosphere.
Although HD 189733b with atmospheric temperatures above 1,000°C is far from habitable, this finding increases the likelihood that water would be found on a more Earth-like planet in the future.
Soft gamma repeater SGR 1935+2154 is located in Vulpecula. In 2020 it emitted a fast radio burst, the first one observed in the Milky Way.
deep_sky_objects: M27, the Dumbbell Nebula, is a large, bright planetary nebula discovered by Charles Messier in 1764 as the very first object of its kind. It can be seen with good binoculars in a dark sky, appearing as a dimly glowing disk approximately 8 arcminutes in diameter.
The Dumbbell Nebula is approximately 9,800 years old. A telescope reveals its double-lobed shape, similar to an hourglass.

Brocchi's Cluster (Collinder 399) is an asterism formerly thought to be an open cluster. It's also called 'the Coathanger' because of its distinctive star pattern when viewed with binoculars or a low power telescope.

NGC 7052 is an elliptical galaxy 214 million light-years from Earth. It has a central dusty disk 3,700 light-years in diameter and a supermassive black hole with mass 300 million solar masses in its nucleus.

Astronomers surmise that NGC 7052's disk is the remnant of a smaller galaxy that merged with it. Jets emanate from the galaxy, and it has very strong radio emissions, classifying it as a radio galaxy.
The eastern part of Vulpecula is occupied by the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, a galaxy filament with a length of 3,000 megaparsecs, making it the largest known structure in the universe.

Vul OB1 is an OB-association of nearly 100 OB-stars and over 800 young stellar objects in the galactic plane at a distance of about 2,300 parsec. It contains emission-line nebulae Sh-86, Sh-87, and Sh-88.
Vul OB1 has a length of about 100 parsec and is sculpting many pillar-like structures in this region.
meteor_showers_detail: No meteor showers are associated with Vulpecula.
